Regulation Status: Afghanistan has no AI-specific legislation, decree, draft instrument or sectoral AI rule, and the Ministry of Communications and Information Technology has issued no AI governance measure. Pre-2021 general instruments such as the Cyber Crime Law (2017) contain no provisions written for AI systems. The state operates AI-enabled CCTV and facial-recognition surveillance in Kabul with no governing legal framework.
Policy Lever: No policy lever is applied to AI: there is no national AI strategy, published guidance, sandbox, funding program or body with an AI mandate. Government involvement with AI consists of procuring and operating AI-enabled surveillance technology.
Governance Type: Governance is centralized in the supreme leadership and the ministries, without a dedicated AI regulator, a coordination mechanism or any provincial rule-making role. Judicial and independent review of state technology use, including surveillance, is absent.
Actor Involvement: Policy-making on technology excludes industry and civil society, and domestic academic work on AI—such as the Afghanistan Academy of Sciences conference on legal challenges of AI use and articles from Jami University in Herat—has no institutional channel into decision-making. The administration does not participate in international AI governance processes or declarations.
Enforcement Level: Nothing is enforced because no AI rule, penalty, enforcement body or monitoring mechanism exists.

Regulation Status: The only binding AI-specific domestic instrument is Council of Ministers Decision No. 479, dated 24 July 2024, approving a methodology and technical standards for the use of artificial intelligence, which applies to public institutions. The draft Law 'On Artificial Intelligence' (106 articles, 9 chapters, 13 annexes) transposing Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 completed public consultation on 26 June 2026 and has not been enacted, while Parliament ratified the Council of Europe Framework Convention on Artificial Intelligence by Law No. 93, dated 18 September 2026, a treaty not yet in force internationally. Other AI uses fall under Law No. 124/2024 on Personal Data Protection and Law No. 25/2024 on Cybersecurity, neither of which contains AI-specific provisions.
Policy Lever: Policy is delivered through sub-legal acts and administrative deployment rather than statute: Decision No. 479/2024 sets standards for public bodies, and AKSHI operates an AI laboratory and systems including Diella, now also carried in the office of a Minister of State for Artificial Intelligence. Funding is project-based, no regulatory sandbox operates, and no body holds a statutory AI compliance mandate.
Governance Type: Oversight centres on AKSHI for government AI, with data protection, cybersecurity, financial and competition regulators applying their general remits and coordinating informally. Courts have begun to shape the field through the Constitutional Court's 8 October 2026 Diella decision and a civil claim over the image used for Diella, while no subnational tier plays a role.
Actor Involvement: Participation is channelled through the government's online public consultation portal, where civil society organisations including SCiDEV commented on the draft AI law and the draft National AI Strategy 2025-2030; no permanent multi-stakeholder forum exists for industry or universities. Internationally, Albania signed the Council of Europe Framework Convention on Artificial Intelligence on 15 June 2026, ratified it by Law No. 93, dated 18 September 2026, and aligns with the EU AI Act through accession Chapter 10.
Enforcement Level: Enforcement touching AI runs solely through data-protection and cybersecurity law, as no AI-specific penalties, supervisory authority or audit regime is in force.
Specific Laws: Council of Ministers Decision No. 479, dated 24 July 2024, on the methodology and technical standards for the use of artificial intelligence in the Republic of Albania (2024), Law No. 124/2024 on Personal Data Protection (2024), Law No. 25/2024 on Cybersecurity (2024), Law No. 93, dated 18 September 2026, on the ratification of the Council of Europe Framework Convention on Artificial Intelligence and Human Rights, Democracy and the Rule of Law (CETS No. 225, signed 15 June 2026), Law on Electronic Governance (amended), National Strategy for Digital Agenda 2022-2026, National Cybersecurity Strategy 2025-2030 (2025), Draft Law 'On Artificial Intelligence' in public consultation 29 May - 26 June 2026, Draft National Artificial Intelligence Strategy 2025-2030

Regulation Status: AI is governed by the non-binding National Artificial Intelligence Strategy (2024), whose regulatory-framework pillar has not been turned into legislation. Binding duties touching AI come from general instruments only: Law No. 25-11 amending Law No. 18-07 on personal data protection, Presidential Decree No. 25-320 establishing the national data governance system, and the cybersecurity decrees. Work in 2026 remained institutional, with five multisectoral follow-up meetings chaired by the Ministry of Higher Education and Scientific Research, the latest on 20 October 2026.
Policy Lever: Policy runs through the 2024 strategy, ministry-led coordination structures and state funding for AI skills, research infrastructure and startups. No published AI guidance, regulatory sandbox or AI procurement rule exists, and the bodies involved cannot impose obligations.
Governance Type: AI governance is concentrated in the executive, with the higher education ministry chairing implementation alongside the AI Council, the Scientific Council for Artificial Intelligence and the High Commission for Digitalisation. Coordination is formalized through an interministerial follow-up commission and five thematic commissions, while sub-national authorities and independent reviewers play no part.
Actor Involvement: Academia leads the domestic process through the Scientific Council for Artificial Intelligence and the Ministry of Higher Education and Scientific Research, industry input stays informal and civil society is absent. Internationally, Algeria moved beyond declarations such as the African Union Continental AI Strategy by signing the founding agreement of the World Artificial Intelligence Cooperation Organization on 16 July 2026.
Enforcement Level: Enforcement touching AI rests on general data protection and cybersecurity law, with no AI-specific penalty, decision, authority or audit programme.
Specific Laws: National Artificial Intelligence Strategy (2024), Law No. 25-11 amending Law No. 18-07 on Personal Data Protection (2025), Presidential Decree No. 25-320 establishing the National Data Governance System (2025), Presidential Decree No. 26-07 on Cybersecurity Units in Public Institutions (2026), Agreement on the Establishment of the World Artificial Intelligence Cooperation Organization (2026), African Union Continental AI Strategy (2024)

Regulation Status: Andorra has no dedicated AI statute; AI is reached through adapted general law, principally the Penal Code reform approved on 15 July 2026 criminalising AI-generated non-consensual sexual images and the Llei 29/2021 qualificada de protecció de dades personals as amended by Llei 12/2024. The Council of Europe Framework Convention on Artificial Intelligence (CETS 225), signed on 5 September 2024, is unratified and not yet in force, and the February 2024 Codi d'Ètica de la Intel·ligència Artificial is voluntary.
Policy Lever: Policy rests on the voluntary Code of Ethics for Artificial Intelligence, the Estratègia de Transformació Digital 2030 and funded business digitalisation grants, with the Penal Code provision on AI-generated sexual images as the sole binding AI lever. Institutional capacity sits with the data-protection regulator and an advisory unit inside Andorra Digital, neither holding an AI-specific legal mandate.
Governance Type: Governance is centralised in the national executive and the Agència Andorrana de Protecció de Dades, without sectoral AI regulators or a standing coordination mechanism. Parish comuns act only as deployers subject to national law, while independent scrutiny comes from APDA resolutions and advisory interventions and from ordinary courts.
Actor Involvement: Domestic AI policy-making is government-led, with no standing roles for industry, NGOs, unions or the Universitat d'Andorra, and firms engaged mainly as grant recipients and suppliers. External engagement is strong relative to domestic process: early signature of the Council of Europe Framework Convention on Artificial Intelligence, participation in its drafting committee, hosting of a Council of Europe AI conference, and alignment with UNESCO and OECD principles.
Enforcement Level: Enforcement touching AI is incidental to APDA data-protection supervision and ordinary criminal prosecution, with no AI audits, AI-specific decisions or dedicated AI authority.
Specific Laws: Llei 29/2021 de protecció de dades personals (LQPD) (2021), Llei 12/2024 (amendment to LQPD) (2024), Codi d'Ètica de la Intel·ligència Artificial d'Andorra (2024), Reforma del Codi penal criminalising AI-generated non-consensual sexual images (approved 15 July 2026), Estratègia de Transformació Digital 2030 (2024), Programa de Digitalització d'Empreses (2026), Council of Europe Framework Convention on Artificial Intelligence and Human Rights, Democracy and the Rule of Law CETS 225 (signed 2024, unratified)

Regulation Status: The only binding rules touching AI are the deepfake and artificial-dissemination provisions of Law No. 6/26 Against False Information on the Internet, in force since 4 August 2026, which bind platforms for one content type and carry no implementing regulation or designated AI authority. The horizontal MINTTICS Proposta de Lei sobre a Inteligência Artificial, consulted in September 2025 and approved by the Council of Ministers, obtained general approval in the National Assembly but has not been enacted, and the revised Personal Data Protection Law with its chapter on processing by artificial intelligence systems is still pending.
Policy Lever: Policy runs through the ICT Strategic Framework 2023-2027, the UNESCO Readiness Assessment Methodology exercise led by MINTTICS, and bills before the National Assembly, with the single binding element being the deepfake provisions of Law No. 6/26. Spending is channelled through Presidential Order No. 342/26 and the World Bank-financed Angola Digital Acceleration Project; no regulatory sandbox, AI procurement rule or body with a statutory AI mandate exists.
Governance Type: AI governance is concentrated in MINTTICS at central government level, with the Agency for Data Protection limited to data-protection supervision and the Banco Nacional de Angola at the stage of diagnosing AI use in banking. Provinces play no role, no standing interministerial mechanism links the parallel MINTTICS and data-protection reforms, and independent or judicial review of AI questions has not occurred.
Actor Involvement: Participation runs through time-limited public consultations on the AI bill and the data protection revision, supplemented by professional events such as the Fórum Nacional de Inteligência Artificial 2026. Internationally Angola engages via UNESCO, the African Union and the Inter-Parliamentary Union; domestically no industry, civil society or academic body holds a standing role.
Enforcement Level: Penalties reach AI-generated content through Law No. 6/26 and far larger fines sit in the unenacted AI bill, but no enforcement decision, dedicated AI authority or audit practice exists.
Specific Laws: Law No. 6/26 Against False Information on the Internet (2026), Proposta de Lei sobre a Inteligência Artificial / Draft Law on Artificial Intelligence (public consultation 2025, Council of Ministers approval 2025, general parliamentary approval 2026), Draft Personal Data Protection Law revising Law No. 22/11 with a chapter on processing by artificial intelligence systems (public consultation 2025), Presidential Order No. 342/26 authorising procurement of an artificial intelligence platform for the public sector (2026), ICT Strategic Framework 2023-2027 (Livro Branco das TIC), Personal Data Protection Law No. 22/11 (2011)

Regulation Status: No AI-specific legislation is in force and no AI bill has been tabled in Parliament, though the Prime Minister has confirmed that draft AI legislation exists and the ministry's AI focal point stated in September 2026 that policies and legislation are being crafted. Governance of AI-related harms rests on the Data Protection Act, 2013 and the Electronic Crimes Act, 2013, which contain no AI provisions; the UNESCO Artificial Intelligence Readiness Assessment Report (2025) identifies their modernisation, including impact assessments for high-risk applications, as an outstanding gap.
Policy Lever: Policy action consists of the completed UNESCO Readiness Assessment Methodology exercise, a ministerial AI focal point and participation in the Caribbean AI Task Force, with no national AI strategy adopted. Deployment efforts such as Project Optimus and the announced government data centre with AI capability proceed without a regulatory sandbox, AI procurement rules or a dedicated AI funding programme.
Governance Type: AI matters are concentrated in one ministry with a single focal point, supported by occasional workshops rather than a standing coordination mechanism. Telecommunications oversight through the Telecommunications Division and the regional ECTEL framework carries no AI mandate, and no judicial or independent review of AI has occurred.
Actor Involvement: Domestic participation runs through one-off UNESCO- and UWI-linked workshops and conferences involving ministries, industry, civil society and academia, with no standing consultative body. International engagement is the most developed channel, covering the Santiago Declaration on Ethical AI, UNESCO's Readiness Assessment Methodology, the Commonwealth AI Consortium and the Caribbean AI Task Force Final Report of July 2026.
Enforcement Level: Enforcement is absent because no AI obligations exist, no authority holds an AI remit, and monitoring is limited to the one-off 2025 readiness assessment.
Specific Laws: Data Protection Act, 2013 (No. 10 of 2013), Electronic Crimes Act, 2013, UNESCO Artificial Intelligence Readiness Assessment Report for Antigua and Barbuda (2025), Santiago Declaration on Ethical AI (2023), Caribbean AI Task Force Final Report (2026)

Regulation Status: Argentina has no enacted binding AI-specific legislation at national level; Personal Data Protection Law 25.326 (2000), consumer and sectoral rules carry the legal weight, supplemented by AI-specific administrative instruments addressed to the state apparatus, namely Disposición AAIP 2/2023 and SIGEN Resolución 197/2026. Several AI bills sit before Congress, including the responsible-AI framework bill with a majority committee dictamen, a bill creating a Registro Nacional de Sistemas de Inteligencia Artificial tabled in April 2026, deepfake bills, and the Executive's June 2026 bill on AI-operated companies. President Milei restated at the UN General Assembly on 23 September 2026 a commitment not to regulate AI preventively.
Policy Lever: Policy works through soft instruments and investment incentives: the Plan Nacional de Inteligencia Artificial (2019), Resolución 90/2021, AAIP Resolución 161/2023 and Disposición 2/2023, the SIGEN Guía de Controles Inteligencia Artificial (2026), the Mesa Estratégica de Inteligencia Artificial en la Justicia (2026), and the RIGI regime attracting AI data-centre investment. No body holds statutory compliance powers over AI systems.
Governance Type: Governance is fragmented, with a lead ministry plus sectoral bodies and no statutory inter-agency AI mechanism; the Ministerio Público Fiscal set its own AI programme through Resolución PGN 64/2026. Provinces and the City of Buenos Aires issue their own AI frameworks for public administration, and judicial review operates case by case.
Actor Involvement: Industry, academia and civil society feed in through congressional hearings and agency consultations rather than standing bodies, and the government's 2026 posture favours dialogue with technology investors. International engagement is limited to non-binding instruments and observer participation in Council of Europe AI standard-setting.
Enforcement Level: Enforcement touching AI runs solely through general data-protection and consumer powers, with no AI-specific obligations, sanctions or published audit results.
Specific Laws: Personal Data Protection Law 25.326 (2000), Plan Nacional de Inteligencia Artificial – ArgenIA (2019), Resolución 90/2021 – Programa de Inteligencia Artificial, AAIP Resolución 161/2023 – Programa de Transparencia y Protección de Datos Personales en el uso de la Inteligencia Artificial, Disposición AAIP 2/2023 – Recommendations for Reliable Artificial Intelligence, BCRA Comunicación A 7724 (2023), SIGEN Resolución 197/2026 – Guía de Controles Inteligencia Artificial, Ministerio de Justicia Resolución 469/2026 – Mesa Estratégica de Inteligencia Artificial en la Justicia, Resolución PGN 64/2026 – Programa de Inteligencia Artificial del Ministerio Público Fiscal, Régimen de Incentivo para Grandes Inversiones under Law 27.742 (2024) extended by Decreto 105/2026, Decreto 742/2026 of the Province of Buenos Aires – Marco Provincial para el Desarrollo, Uso y Gobernanza de la Inteligencia Artificial (subnational), Decreto 97/2026 of the City of Buenos Aires on AI in public management (subnational), Bill 3003-D-2024 on responsible AI (pending, majority committee dictamen), Executive bill reforming the Ley General de Sociedades to create AI-operated companies (2026, pending), bill creating a Registro Nacional de Sistemas de Inteligencia Artificial (2026, pending)

Regulation Status: Armenia has no AI-specific binding instrument; AI use falls under the Law on the Protection of Personal Data (No. 49-ZR) and the Law on Cybersecurity in force since 4 January 2026, neither of which contains an AI provision. The only legal texts naming AI are the 2026 amendment to the Law on the Structure and Activities of the Government, which created the Ministry of High-Tech Industry and Artificial Intelligence with an AI and cloud policy remit, and the Council of Europe Framework Convention on Artificial Intelligence and Human Rights, Democracy and the Rule of Law, signed on 27 January 2026 and not yet ratified. The ministry announced in October 2026, with UNDP, that strategic documents and a regulatory framework for AI are still to be prepared.
Policy Lever: Policy runs through funding and promotion rather than regulation: state support under Law No. HO-498-N, the Firebird and Eleveight AI compute facilities, the AI Virtual Institute, AI curriculum rollout in schools and a UNDP memorandum of 9 October 2026 on AI governance and literacy. The ministry's statutory AI mandate is one of policy development, with no compliance or enforcement powers and no sandbox or AI procurement rules.
Governance Type: AI governance is concentrated in one executive body, the Ministry of High-Tech Industry and Artificial Intelligence, with no dedicated AI regulator, no formal inter-agency coordination structure and no subnational layer. Independent checks are confined to occasional research and media commentary on AI infrastructure and the policy gap.
Actor Involvement: Policy-making is driven by the government with technology investors and infrastructure partners, while universities contribute research and civil society is consulted only occasionally. International channels are the strongest: the Council of Europe Framework Convention signature, EU4Digital and EU AI cooperation, UNDP partnership and bilateral cooperation with the United States.
Enforcement Level: Enforcement of AI obligations does not exist because no AI-specific duty or penalty has been enacted, leaving only general data protection and cybersecurity powers.
Specific Laws: Council of Europe Framework Convention on Artificial Intelligence and Human Rights, Democracy and the Rule of Law (STCE n°225) (signed 2026), Law on the Structure and Activities of the Government as amended to rename the Ministry of High-Tech Industry and Artificial Intelligence (2026), Law No. HO-498-N on State Support for the High-Tech Sector (2025), Law of the Republic of Armenia on Cybersecurity (in force 2026), Law No. 49-ZR on the Protection of Personal Data (2015), Digital Transformation Strategy (2021-2025)

Regulation Status: Australia has no AI Act: the National AI Plan of 2 December 2025 confirmed reliance on existing laws and sector regulators, and the Australian Standards for AI announced on 15 July 2026 and endorsed by National Cabinet in August 2026 remain at consultation stage through the September 2026 paper Getting it right: Building AI infrastructure that works for Australia, with bills expected in early 2027. Binding obligations in force are domain-specific: the eSafety Age-Restricted Material (Phase 2) Industry Codes impose age-assurance duties on generative AI and AI companion services from 9 March 2026, and the Digital Transformation Agency policy binds 94 non-corporate Commonwealth entities. The cross-sector automated decision-making transparency obligation in Australian Privacy Principle 1 commences 10 December 2026, and the Online Safety Amendment (Digital Duty of Care) Bill 2026, which extends safety duties to AI chatbots, passed the House of Representatives on 28 October 2026 and awaits the Senate.
Policy Lever: Policy runs on soft law plus funding: the Voluntary AI Safety Standard, Guidance for AI Adoption, the Expectations of data centres and AI infrastructure developers, a funded AI Safety Institute commissioning CSIRO research and joining international joint testing, and the Office of AI created in the Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet on 15 July 2026. Binding levers stay confined to the online safety codes, the mandatory public-sector AI policy and the automated decision-making obligation commencing in December 2026.
Governance Type: Oversight is dispersed across independent statutory regulators coordinated through the Digital Platform Regulators Forum and, since July 2026, the Office of AI in the Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet, with Commonwealth-state commitments settled at National Cabinet. States implement national settings, keep data centre planning powers and govern their own agency AI use, while courts, tribunals and the Ombudsman intervene case by case.
Actor Involvement: Government consults industry, creators, civil society and researchers through published processes including the Getting it right consultation paper, the Copyright and AI Reference Group and the parliamentary Joint Select Committee on Artificial Intelligence, which gave early advice to the Prime Minister on 12 October 2026, but no standing statutory advisory body exists. International engagement is extensive, covering the OECD, the Global Partnership on AI, the AI safety institute network and international standards work.
Enforcement Level: Enforcement rests with existing regulators using penalty-backed powers, with eSafety taking repeated published action against generative AI services under the Age-Restricted Material Codes and the OAIC having issued guidance on 30 September 2026 ahead of enforcing the automated decision-making obligation.
Specific Laws: Privacy Act 1988 as amended by the Privacy and Other Legislation Amendment Act 2024 (automated decision-making transparency obligation commencing 10 December 2026), Online Safety Act 2021 and the Age-Restricted Material (Phase 2) Industry Codes (2025, in force 9 March 2026), Online Safety Amendment (Digital Duty of Care) Bill 2026 (passed the House of Representatives 28 October 2026), Australian Consumer Law (Competition and Consumer Act 2010), Copyright Act 1968, National AI Plan (2025), Australian Standards for AI announcement (2026) and the consultation paper Getting it right: Building AI infrastructure that works for Australia (2026), Expectations of data centres and AI infrastructure developers (2026), Voluntary AI Safety Standard (2024), Guidance for AI Adoption (2025), Policy for the responsible use of AI in government version 2.0 (2025)

Regulation Status: Austria regulates AI through the directly applicable EU AI Act as amended by the Digital Omnibus on AI, Regulation (EU) 2026/1744, which was published on 24 July 2026, entered into force on 27 July 2026 and moved Annex III high-risk obligations to 2 December 2027 and Annex I embedded systems to 2 August 2028, while prohibitions, AI literacy, GPAI duties and Article 50 transparency apply today. Nationally, the amendment of the Allgemeines Verwaltungsverfahrensgesetz 1991 and the Verwaltungsstrafgesetz 1991, published as BGBl. I Nr. 86/2026 on 16 October 2026 and in force since 17 October 2026, authorises chatbot submissions, fully automated decisions and no-stop procedures in administrative proceedings. National execution lags: the planned Künstliche Intelligenz Durchführungsgesetz is still at concept stage, no notifying or market surveillance authority is designated, and no national AI regulatory sandbox operates despite the 2 August 2026 deadline.
Policy Lever: The binding layer is the EU AI Act supplemented by two national AI-specific statutes — the KI-Servicestelle provisions in the KommAustria-Gesetz and TKG 2021 and the 2026 AVG/VStG amendment — alongside RTR and Datenschutzbehörde guidance and funding and public-sector programmes including aws AI Adoption, Digital Überall Plus and the Public AI Initiative. Chancellor Stocker ended Artificial Intelligence Mission Austria 2030 in September 2026 and tasked State Secretary Pröll with a replacement strategy due in the first half of 2027; institutional capacity remains advisory, with the KI-Servicestelle and the KI-Beirat holding no compliance powers.
Governance Type: AI governance is federal, with the Bundeskanzleramt leading AI Act implementation, the RTR KI-Servicestelle serving as the information hub, and the Datenschutzbehörde and sectoral regulators acting within existing remits pending the planned Künstliche Intelligenz Durchführungsgesetz, which envisages a division of labour among existing authorities rather than a single AI agency. Coordination is organised through the AI Policy Forum, the KI-Beirat, the AI Stakeholder Forum and the Public AI Initiative that also links Länder and municipalities, while the Datenschutzbehörde and the administrative courts supply independent review of individual AI uses.
Actor Involvement: Structured input runs through the AI Stakeholder Forum, ministerial Begutachtung procedures and the standing expert KI-Beirat, so industry and civil society act as consultees while academic and legal experts hold permanent advisory seats. Internationally Austria works through the European AI Board, the OECD and the G7 Hiroshima AI Process.
Enforcement Level: AI Act penalties are legally defined but unenforceable in Austria because no market surveillance authority has been designated and no national penalties regime has been passed, leaving data protection law as the only route under which decisions on AI use have been issued.
Specific Laws: EU AI Act / Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (2024), Digital Omnibus on AI / Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 (2026), AVG and VStG amendment on digital administration and AI / BGBl. I Nr. 86/2026 (2026), KommAustria-Gesetz amendment establishing the KI-Servicestelle / BGBl. I Nr. 6/2024 (2024), TKG 2021 §194a (2024 amendment), Digital Austria Act 2.0 (2025), Public AI Initiative (2026), KI-Maßnahmenpaket (2025), Artificial Intelligence Mission Austria 2030 / AIM AT 2030 (2021, ended September 2026), KI-Umsetzungsplan 2024 (2024), Austrian Data Protection Act / DSG (2018, amended), GDPR / Regulation (EU) 2016/679 (2016)

Regulation Status: The binding layer consists of the 21 April 2026 amendments criminalising non-consensual AI-generated depictions of a person's image or voice and AI-generated sexual material, and requiring visible labelling of AI-generated photo, video and audio distributed through media or telecommunications networks, backed by administrative fines. These rules apply today but reach only synthetic content; the dedicated AI legal framework promised by 2027 under the Artificial Intelligence Strategy 2025-2028 remains undrafted, with MPs proposing a general AI law at the Milli Majlis autumn session on 30 September 2026.
Policy Lever: Azerbaijan governs AI mainly through presidential decrees, strategies and targeted statutory amendments, supplemented by a 2026 regulatory pilot-project framework for state-body digital solutions and funding commitments in the Action Plan for Accelerating Digital Development 2026-2028. No body holds AI inspection, approval or sanctioning powers.
Governance Type: AI governance is centralised in the presidency, with the Digital Development Council providing formal inter-ministerial coordination and the Ministry of Digital Development and Transport leading implementation. Independent oversight is absent and no tier of government below the national level has a role.
Actor Involvement: Policy formation is state-led, with industry and academic contributions channelled through government working groups and the Digital Development Council rather than open consultation, and domestic civil society absent from the process. Internationally Azerbaijan cooperates through Turkic States frameworks and bilateral partnerships while remaining outside the Council of Europe AI Convention.
Enforcement Level: Penalties exist for every AI obligation in force, but enforcement is handled by general criminal and administrative bodies and no AI-specific decision or audit has been published.
Specific Laws: Artificial Intelligence Strategy of the Republic of Azerbaijan for 2025-2028 (Presidential Decree No. 530, 2025), Criminal Code amendments introducing Articles 148-2 and 242-1 on illegal use of artificial intelligence (2026), amendments to the Law on Information, Informatization and Protection of Information introducing Article 13-2.7 on labelling of AI-generated content (2026), amendments to the Law on Media and the Code of Administrative Offences on AI-generated content (2026), Decree on Certain Measures to Improve Activities in the Fields of Digitalization, E-Government, Artificial Intelligence and Innovation establishing the Digital Development Council (2026), Action Plan for Accelerating Digital Development for 2026-2028 (2026), Rules for the Implementation of Regulatory Pilot Projects for Testing the Effectiveness of Digital Solutions Applied by State Bodies (2026), Digital Economy Development Strategy 2026-2029 (2025)

Regulation Status: AI obligations sit inside sectoral and general instruments: clause 2.8 of URCA's Code of Practice for Content Regulation (Revised 2024) requires licensed broadcasters to hold internal policies on AI and synthetic media, section 18 of the Electricity Act, 2024 gives URCA an unexercised power to make AI regulations for electricity, and the Data Protection Act, 2025 - passed in December 2025 but still listed as not in force - defines profiling to include artificial intelligence and limits solely automated decisions. The Speech from the Throne of May 2026 promised an Artificial Intelligence Governance Act with a national AI commission, and the Ministry of Innovation and National Development announced a National AI Committee in June 2026 to draft it; no bill has been tabled. Coverage is therefore narrow and content-specific rather than horizontal.
Policy Lever: Levers are thin: a single binding AI clause in URCA's broadcasting content code, an unused AI regulation-making power in the Electricity Act, 2024, announced AI literacy and skills funding from an IDB loan, and a National AI Committee tasked with drafting the first AI legislation. No national AI strategy, guidance suite, regulatory sandbox or AI procurement rule has been published.
Governance Type: Governance is sectorally fragmented: URCA regulates AI use by communications and broadcasting licensees and holds a dormant power over electricity, while the Data Protection Commissioner oversees automated processing and profiling. Coordination is informal and ministry-led pending the promised national AI commission, there is no subnational tier, and independent review has so far been limited to a professional-conduct referral.
Actor Involvement: Structured domestic input on AI has come through regulator and ministry processes - URCA's 2024 content code consultation with broadcast licensees and the 2025 consultation on the draft Data Protection Bill - with a private sector advisory forum covering business, technology, academia and civil society announced but not seated. Internationally the country engages through CARICOM, UNESCO and United Nations AI discussions and sought a place in a UN AI disaster-resilience programme.
Enforcement Level: Enforcement of the few AI provisions rests on URCA's general licensing powers, and no AI-related sanction, decision or audit has been published.
Specific Laws: Electricity Act (2024), URCA Code of Practice for Content Regulation (Revised 2024, ECS 78/2024), Data Protection Act (2025, passed December 2025, not yet in force), Data Protection (Privacy of Personal Information) Act (2003), Artificial Intelligence Governance Act (announced in the Speech from the Throne, May 2026, not yet tabled)

Regulation Status: Bahrain has no AI statute in force: the 38-article Artificial Intelligence Regulation Law endorsed by the Shura Council in April 2024 is still pending in the Council of Representatives after government objections, and separate 2026 bills to criminalise deepfakes (Shura Council February 2026, MPs' bill of October 2026 carrying five years' imprisonment and a BD50,000 fine) remain proposals. The operative AI-specific instrument is the Information & eGovernment Authority's General Policy for the Use of Artificial Intelligence Version 1.0 of 30 July 2025, which binds government entities only, alongside the Personal Data Protection Law No. 30 of 2018 and the Information Technology Crimes Law No. 60 of 2014, neither of which contains provisions written for AI. A National Artificial Intelligence Strategy remains in draft.
Policy Lever: Policy runs through administrative instruments and guidance — the General Policy for the Use of Artificial Intelligence, the GCC Guiding Manual on the Ethics of Artificial Intelligence Use and World Economic Forum-developed procurement guidelines — plus funded skills and talent programmes from Tamkeen, the iGA and Bahrain Polytechnic. The AI regulatory sandbox the government offered as an alternative to the draft AI law has not been created, and no body holds a legal AI compliance mandate.
Governance Type: AI governance is centralised in the Information & eGovernment Authority under the Ministerial Committee for Information Technology and Communication, with the Central Bank of Bahrain addressing AI risk inside its existing rulebook and the Personal Data Protection Authority applying the 2018 law. Governorates have no role and no court or independent body has influenced AI rules.
Actor Involvement: AI policy is produced by government bodies — the iGA, the Ministerial Committee for Information Technology and Communication and state-linked agencies — with academic and industry input channelled through training and readiness exercises rather than standing advisory roles. Domestic civil society has no documented part, while external engagement runs through the GCC and UNESCO.
Enforcement Level: Enforcement rests on general data protection and cybercrime powers, since the draft AI Regulation Law's penalties are not in force and no AI oversight unit has been established.
Specific Laws: Draft Artificial Intelligence Regulation Law (38 articles, Shura Council approved April 2024, pending in the Council of Representatives), General Policy for the Use of Artificial Intelligence Version 1.0 (2025), GCC Guiding Manual on the Ethics of Artificial Intelligence Use (adopted 2025), draft National Artificial Intelligence Strategy (in preparation 2026), draft amendment to the Information Technology Crimes Law criminalising deepfake content (2026), Personal Data Protection Law No. 30 of 2018, Information Technology Crimes Law No. 60 of 2014

Regulation Status: Bangladesh has no AI statute: the only binding AI rule is the AI-generated-content offence in Section 25 of the Cyber Protection Act 2026, enacted 10 April 2026 and amended 30 June 2026, with a further Cyber Protection (Amendment) Act draft published by the ICT Division in mid-September 2026 and still before a cabinet committee. The National AI Policy Bangladesh 2026-2030 (Draft V2.0, 9 February 2026) remains unadopted after its consultation closed on 8 February 2026, and the Law, Justice and Parliamentary Affairs Minister said on 2 September 2026 that a draft AI law will go to parliament after expert review. Personal Data Protection Act 2026 and the data governance framework touch AI only incidentally.
Policy Lever: Policy is driven by a drafting ministry rather than statutory levers: the ICT Division steers the draft National AI Policy and drafted the Cyber Protection (Amendment) Act, while enforcement powers sit with cyber security bodies under general law. Bangladesh Bank announced on 1 November 2026 that an AI-based cybersecurity policy for banks is still to be introduced, and the sandbox and funding instruments in the draft policy remain unimplemented.
Governance Type: AI governance is centralized in the ICT Division of the Ministry of Posts, Telecommunications and Information Technology, with the National AI Policy Steering Committee providing cross-ministry coordination and the Bangladesh Telecommunication Regulatory Commission and National Cyber Security Agency handling AI-generated content. There is no subnational tier and no independent body with a review role over AI rules.
Actor Involvement: Participation is consultative: industry, academia and civil society entered through the time-limited public consultations on the draft National AI Policy and the draft Cyber Protection (Amendment) Act, plus UNESCO-supported readiness and civil-service training work. International engagement runs through UNESCO and UNDP, with the Council of Europe Framework Convention on Artificial Intelligence named only as a draft-policy aspiration.
Enforcement Level: Enforcement touches AI only through criminal cyber content powers exercised by police cyber units, the National Cyber Security Agency and the Bangladesh Telecommunication Regulatory Commission, with no published decisions or audits under the AI-content provision.
Specific Laws: Cyber Protection Act (2026), Cyber Protection Ordinance (2025), Cyber Protection (Amendment) Act (draft, 2026), Personal Data Protection Act (2026), National Data Governance Ordinance (2025), National AI Policy Bangladesh 2026-2030 (Draft V2.0, 2026), National Strategy for Artificial Intelligence: Bangladesh (2020)

Regulation Status: Barbados governs AI through general law alone: the Data Protection Act, 2019-29 applies to automated processing, profiling and decisions based on automated processing, but contains nothing drafted for AI systems. No AI bill is before Parliament and no AI-specific binding rule covers any sector. Government action in 2026 consisted of ministerial statements, skills initiatives and deployment of public-sector AI tools rather than legislation.
Policy Lever: Policy action is limited to capacity-building and rhetoric: the National Digital Skills Empowerment Campaign, a deep tech fellowship and an announced assessment of AI's impact on the Barbadian workforce made in October 2026. No AI-specific binding instrument, national guidance document, regulatory sandbox or dedicated AI body exists.
Governance Type: Governance is centralised in a single ministry, with the Data Protection Commissioner the only regulator whose powers reach automated processing. Independent review exists on paper through the Data Protection Tribunal and the courts, and no subnational tier plays any part.
Actor Involvement: Engagement is led by government and directed outward: United Nations advocacy, hosting the UN Independent International Scientific Panel on Artificial Intelligence, and participation in CARICOM and Caribbean Telecommunications Union work including the Caribbean AI Task Force, whose Final Report was launched in July 2026. Domestic involvement of industry, unions and academia is event-based rather than structured.
Enforcement Level: Enforcement reaching AI rests solely on the general powers of the Data Protection Commissioner under the Data Protection Act, 2019-29, and no AI-related action or audit has been taken.
Specific Laws: Data Protection Act, 2019-29 (2019)

Regulation Status: Belarus has no enacted AI-specific legislation. A national law on AI technologies drafted by the United Institute of Informatics Problems of the National Academy of Sciences on the basis of the CIS Model Law on Artificial Intelligence Technologies remains at the preparatory stage, with no bill before the National Assembly. The only AI-specific binding text in preparation is the draft Law "On amending laws on personal data protection" published for public consultation on 13 July 2026, which adds an article on automated decision-making using AI and was submitted to the Council of Ministers on 4 September 2026.
Policy Lever: Belarus governs AI through state programs, technical standardization and tax incentives rather than binding rules, combining the State Programs "Digital Belarus" and "Belarus Intellectual" for 2026-2030 with High-Tech Park benefits under Decree No. 8. Standards work by Gosstandart is the most developed lever, while no institution holds legal AI compliance powers.
Governance Type: Governance is centralized and executive-led: the National Academy of Sciences drafts AI legislation and is earmarked as sectoral AI regulator, the Ministry of Communications and Informatization runs the Digital Belarus program and the national AI framework, and Gosstandart issues AI standards. Coordination occurs through temporary working groups and presidential and parliamentary advisory councils, with no subnational tier and no independent judicial or ombudsman oversight.
Actor Involvement: Policy-making is driven by state institutions, with the National Academy of Sciences as lead expert body and industry engaged through the High-Tech Park, standardization committees and public consultation on the personal data bill. Independent domestic civil society is excluded, and international engagement is confined to CIS, EAEU and Union State channels plus interstate standardization and UNDP technical cooperation.
Enforcement Level: With no AI-specific obligations, penalties or enforcement body in place, only general personal data and administrative law can be applied to AI-related conduct.
Specific Laws: State Program "Digital Belarus" for 2026-2030 (Council of Ministers Resolution No. 793 of 30 December 2025), State Program "Belarus Intellectual" for 2026-2030 (Council of Ministers Resolution No. 796 of 30 December 2025), Law of the Republic of Belarus No. 99-Z on Personal Data Protection (2021) and the draft Law "On amending laws on personal data protection" of 13 July 2026 on automated decisions taken with artificial intelligence, Decree No. 8 on the Development of the Digital Economy (2017), State Program of Innovative Development for 2026-2030 (Decree No. 448 of 22 December 2025), CIS Model Law on Artificial Intelligence Technologies (2025, drafted by the National Academy of Sciences of Belarus and adopted by the CIS Interparliamentary Assembly)

Regulation Status: Belgium's binding AI framework is the directly applicable EU AI Act as amended by the Digital Omnibus on AI (Regulation (EU) 2026/1744): prohibitions and AI-literacy duties since 2 February 2025, general-purpose AI and penalty provisions since 2 August 2025, Article 50 transparency since 2 August 2026, the non-consensual intimate-content prohibition from 2 December 2026, and Annex III high-risk duties only from 2 December 2027. No national AI statute exists; BIPT's lead role rests on the Government Declaration of 31 January 2025 and the 2025-2029 Federal Government Agreement, with an implementing bill announced but not tabled in the Chamber. The only Belgian binding AI text is the AI chapter of the Royal Decree of 20 July 2026 approving the real-estate agents' code of ethics, in force 1 October 2026, alongside a pending bill on AI-generated deepfakes in the Criminal Code.
Policy Lever: Policy runs through the EU AI Act plus one narrow Royal Decree AI chapter, soft-law guidance from BIPT, FPS Economy and the APD/GBA, and the federal AI strategy presented by Minister Vanessa Matz in September 2026. Funding flows through TRAIL, regional programmes and EuroHPC, but no sandbox operates and no authority yet holds statutory AI compliance powers.
Governance Type: Governance is dispersed across a politically designated lead regulator (BIPT), the APD/GBA, sectoral supervisors and twenty-one Article 77 rights bodies, coordinated by FPS Economy and the AI Steering Committee. Regions pursue independent AI strategies and funding, while judicial and independent review of AI remains occasional.
Actor Involvement: Industry and academia hold seats in the AI Steering Committee and the Data and AI Ethics Advisory Committee, with AI4Belgium channelling wider stakeholder input, while civil society takes part through consultation. Internationally Belgium acts through the EU AI Board, EuroHPC JU and OECD processes.
Enforcement Level: AI Act penalty ceilings apply in principle while Belgium lacks an enabling statute, a formally designated and resourced AI supervisor, and any published AI-specific enforcement decision.
Specific Laws: EU AI Act / Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (2024), Digital Omnibus on AI / Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 (2026), Royal Decree of 20 July 2026 approving the code of ethics of the Professional Institute of Real Estate Agents, including its artificial intelligence chapter (2026), Royal Decree establishing the AI Steering Committee (2024), Royal Decree establishing the Data and AI Ethics Advisory Committee (2023/2024), Federal Government Agreement 2025-2029 (2025), Government Declaration of 31 January 2025 designating BIPT (2025), National Convergence Plan for the Development of Artificial Intelligence (2019), Federal AI strategy presented September 2026 (2026), Flanders AI Policy Plan 2024-2028 (2024), GDPR / Regulation (EU) 2016/679 (2016)

Regulation Status: The only binding AI-specific instrument is Practice Direction No. 18 of 2025 (Ethical Use of Generative Artificial Intelligence in Court Proceedings), in force in the Senior Courts since 12 August 2025, which imposes disclosure, verification and human-oversight duties on judges, attorneys and court users. No AI statute or national AI strategy exists; the Data Protection Act 2021, Digital Government Act 2022 and Telecommunications Act (Cap. 229) carry no AI-specific provisions, and economy-wide AI activity remains in non-binding documents such as the Global Digital Services Investment Policy and Strategy (2025) and the National Digital Infrastructure Plan (2025).
Policy Lever: Belize uses one narrow binding instrument for the courts, judiciary guidance and training, and conferences such as the Ministry of E-Governance's "Cybersecurity in the Age of AI" (May 2026). No national AI principles document, dedicated funding programme, regulatory sandbox or AI procurement rule exists, and no body holds an AI-specific legal mandate.
Governance Type: Governance is fragmented across central-government bodies without a designated AI regulator or formal coordination structure, and local government plays no part. The independent judiciary, through the Rules Committee of the Senior Courts, is the only institution exercising rule-making authority over AI.
Actor Involvement: Domestic engagement is confined to sectoral workshops with industry bodies and informal academic contributions, with civil society absent from AI policy work. Belize's substantive activity is regional: the Caribbean Telecommunications Union and UNESCO Caribbean AI Policy Roadmap processes and its 2026 presidency of the SICA regional digital strategy group.
Enforcement Level: Enforcement exists only as judges applying Practice Direction No. 18 of 2025 inside court proceedings, with no recorded sanction, no AI enforcement authority and no routine monitoring.
Specific Laws: Practice Direction No. 18 of 2025 (Ethical Use of Generative Artificial Intelligence in Court Proceedings), Senior Courts Act (2022), Digital Government Act (2022), Data Protection Act (2021), Telecommunications Act (Cap. 229), National Digital Agenda 2022-2025, Global Digital Services Investment Policy and Strategy (2025), National Digital Infrastructure Plan (2025)

Regulation Status: Benin governs AI through the Stratégie Nationale d'Intelligence Artificielle et des Mégadonnées (SNIAM) 2023-2027, approved by the Council of Ministers on 18 January 2023, which sets four programmes but imposes no obligations. The only binding rules reaching AI are general ones: the Code du Numérique (Loi No. 2017-20 of 2018, amended by Loi No. 2020-35 of 2021), whose article 576 on unauthorised montages of a person's image or words is used against AI-manipulated content, and Loi No. 2009-09 on personal data. The Ministry of Digital Transformation and Innovation created in May 2026 and the Comité national du numérique established by décret n° 2026-579 of 2 September 2026 add institutions, not binding AI rules.
Policy Lever: Policy works through strategy, guidance, skills and ecosystem programmes rather than regulation: the Ministry of Digital Transformation and Innovation steers SNIAM implementation, the Agence des Systèmes d'Information et du Numérique executes state digital projects and publishes non-binding legal briefs on AI use in administration, and the Autorité de Protection des Données Personnelles enforces general data law. Funded activity covers training, research and the 2026 National AI Olympiads, with no sandbox or AI procurement rules.
Governance Type: AI governance is centralized in the Ministry of Digital Transformation and Innovation, with the Agence des Systèmes d'Information et du Numérique as operational arm and the Comité national du numérique created in September 2026 coordinating state digital policy from the Presidency. The APDP and the Centre national d'investigations numériques intervene only within general data-protection and cybercrime remits, and courts enter through criminal cases on manipulated images.
Actor Involvement: Domestic participation is consultative and project-based: industry, startups and universities fed into the SNIAM and into training and innovation programmes, while civil society involvement remains outside formal structures. Internationally Benin aligns with African Union and Smart Africa frameworks, ratified the Malabo Convention in 2024 and co-adopted the 2026 francophone African AI guidelines, without treaty-level AI commitments.
Enforcement Level: Enforcement touching AI runs entirely through general Code du numérique and data-protection powers, exercised in 2026 through CNIN warnings and arrests over AI-manipulated images, with no AI-specific sanctions, authority or published decisions.
Specific Laws: Stratégie Nationale d'Intelligence Artificielle et des Mégadonnées (SNIAM) 2023-2027, Code du Numérique (Loi No. 2017-20 of 2018, amended by Loi No. 2020-35 of 2021, article 576), Loi No. 2009-09 of 2009 on Protection of Personally Identifiable Information, Décret n° 2026-579 of 2 September 2026 creating the Comité national du numérique

Regulation Status: Bhutan governs AI entirely through soft instruments: the National AI Strategy (NAIS) 2025, the Ethical and Responsible AI Guidelines 2026 issued by the GovTech Agency, the Guideline for Generative Artificial Intelligence Usage in the Civil Service (2024), and the Bhutan AI Readiness Assessment (AIRA) Report 2024. No AI bill has reached Parliament despite the National Assembly's June 2025 motion calling for a regulatory framework, and Bhutan still has no standalone data protection statute, leaving only the minimal privacy provisions of the Information, Communications and Media Act of Bhutan 2018. AI-specific expectations bind no one and extend in practice only to the civil service.
Policy Lever: Policy works through soft guidance and capacity-building — NAIS 2025, the Ethical and Responsible AI Guidelines 2026, the civil-service generative AI guideline, and GovTech's AI Startup and AI Lab Programs. There is no binding AI rule, regulatory sandbox or AI procurement requirement, and GovTech holds no legal AI mandate.
Governance Type: AI policy is centralized in the GovTech Agency, with the GovTech Commission chaired by the Prime Minister giving broad digital oversight and the Gross National Happiness Commission supplying values framing. Local government plays no AI role and no independent or judicial review of AI decisions exists.
Actor Involvement: Participation is consultative and episodic: industry, universities, development partners and the Bhutan AI Society fed into AIRA 2024 and NAIS 2025, but none holds a standing formal role. International engagement runs through UNDP, UNESCO and the 50-in-5 campaign rather than treaty or standards bodies.
Enforcement Level: Bhutan has no AI enforcement machinery, penalties or audit regime, and monitoring rests on one-off readiness studies.
Specific Laws: Ethical and Responsible AI Guidelines 2026, National AI Strategy (NAIS) 2025, Guideline for Generative Artificial Intelligence Usage in the Civil Service (2024), Bhutan AI Readiness Assessment (AIRA) Report (2024), Digital Strategy: Intelligent Bhutan (2024), National Digital Identity Act of Bhutan (2023), Information, Communications and Media Act of Bhutan (2018)

Regulation Status: Bolivia has no enacted AI law. Proyecto de Ley 178/2024-2025, which would create an AI authority in AGETIC, prohibited practices and fines of up to ten minimum salaries, was approved by the Senate on 22 October 2025 and remains pending in the Chamber of Deputies, while deputies from Cochabamba announced a further AI bill in October 2026. In-force instruments, Agenda Digital 2030 (Decreto Supremo 5367) and Decreto Supremo 5519 restructuring AGETIC, govern digital government rather than AI systems, and regional commitments under the Santiago Declaration (2023) and Cartagena Declaration (2024) are non-binding.
Policy Lever: Policy runs through state projects and cooperation rather than rules: the BolivIA sovereign model launched in August 2026, the AGETIC-UNESCO agreement of 27 August 2026 to run the Readiness Assessment Methodology, and a Google Career Launchpad training agreement announced in September 2026. Agenda Digital 2030 remains the governing policy document, and no AI guidance, sandbox, funding line or legally mandated AI body exists.
Governance Type: Governance is concentrated in the central executive, with AGETIC consolidated as the digital-state agency by Decreto Supremo 5519 and the Ministry of Planning leading the BolivIA platform, coordinated only through the general ICT council CTIC-EPB. Subnational governments and independent review bodies play no part in AI matters.
Actor Involvement: Engagement is overwhelmingly external, through the regional AI declarations, the UNESCO readiness assessment and participation in regional ministerial meetings. Domestic industry and civil society have no structured route into AI policy, and academic involvement remains commentary rather than formal advice.
Enforcement Level: No AI obligation, penalty or enforcement authority is in force, and oversight consists of the single UNESCO readiness assessment started in August 2026.
Specific Laws: Proyecto de Ley 178/2024-2025, Promoción, Gestión y Uso de la Inteligencia Artificial (approved by the Senate 22 October 2025, pending in the Chamber of Deputies), Agenda Digital 2030 (Decreto Supremo 5367, 2025), Decreto Supremo 5519 (2026) transferring ADSIB functions to AGETIC, Santiago Declaration on Artificial Intelligence (2023), Cartagena Declaration on Artificial Intelligence (2024)

Regulation Status: No dedicated AI law or state-level AI strategy exists, and no AI bill is before the Parliamentary Assembly. The one binding AI-specific commitment is the Council of Europe Framework Convention on Artificial Intelligence and Human Rights, Democracy and the Rule of Law, ratified by Presidency decision of 3 September 2026 (Official Gazette of BiH – International Agreements 9/26) and in force since 28 September 2026, which requires implementing measures that have not been enacted. Domestically, AI is touched only by the automated decision-making provisions of the Law on Personal Data Protection (Official Gazette of BiH 12/25).
Policy Lever: Policy action rests on the ratified Framework Convention plus non-binding internal documents: the General Secretariat's recommendations for institutional use of AI tools and the Parliamentary Assembly's Roadmap for Artificial Intelligence (2026). Funding, procurement rules, sandboxes and a mandated AI institution are absent, and capacity building is carried by UNDP, OHCHR and OSCE support.
Governance Type: Authority over AI is dispersed by the constitutional structure, with no state-level lead body and entity governments holding the legislative powers that would carry AI rules. Coordination is ad hoc through donor-convened conferences, and no judicial or independent-review body has shaped AI rules.
Actor Involvement: Domestic engagement remains event-based, built around the conference convened by the Ministry of Human Rights and Refugees and the Ministry of Communications and Transport with UNDP, OHCHR and OSCE, which drew in academia, civil society and industry without creating standing roles. International exposure is the most developed strand, through ratification of the Council of Europe Framework Convention on Artificial Intelligence and EU candidate status.
Enforcement Level: Nothing AI-specific is enforced, with sanctions and supervision reaching AI only through data protection and criminal law and no AI case decided.
Specific Laws: Council of Europe Framework Convention on Artificial Intelligence and Human Rights, Democracy and the Rule of Law (CETS No. 225, signed 9 December 2025, ratified by Presidency decision of 3 September 2026, Official Gazette of BiH – International Agreements 9/26, in force 28 September 2026), Law on Personal Data Protection of Bosnia and Herzegovina (2025, Official Gazette of BiH 12/25), Roadmap for Artificial Intelligence of the Parliamentary Assembly of Bosnia and Herzegovina (2026), Development Strategy of the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina 2021-2027 (entity-level, mentions artificial intelligence)

Regulation Status: Botswana has no AI-specific legislation in force or before Parliament; the first National Artificial Intelligence Policy, informed by the UNESCO Readiness Assessment Methodology completed in 2024-2025 and validated in May 2025, remains at drafting stage through 2026. AI is reached only incidentally by general digital law: the Data Protection Act, 2024 (Act No. 18 of 2024, effective 14 January 2025) regulates solely automated decision-making and profiling and requires impact assessments for automated processing, while the Digital Services Act, 2025 and Cybersecurity Act, 2025 carry no AI provisions.
Policy Lever: Policy action consists of preparatory work: the draft National Artificial Intelligence Policy, the UNESCO Readiness Assessment Methodology exercise, and an AI strategy collaboration with Estonia. Funding flows to general digital transformation through SmartBots and the Digital Delta Data Centre rather than AI-specific programs, and there is no sandbox, AI procurement rule or AI authority.
Governance Type: AI-adjacent governance is centralised in the Ministry of Communications and Innovation and BOCRA, which hosts the Information and Data Protection Commission, alongside the Digital Services Authority and National Cyber Security Authority created in 2025 for adjacent fields. There is no dedicated AI body, standing coordination mechanism, subnational competence or judicial and independent review of AI matters.
Actor Involvement: AI policy-making is government-led from the Ministry of Communications and Innovation, with occasional industry exposure at summits and academic research feeding readiness analysis rather than formal advisory structures, and no documented domestic civil society participation. International engagement is the strongest channel, through the UNESCO readiness assessment, the Estonia partnership, Smart Africa Alliance membership, African Union digital frameworks and attendance at the 2026 AI Impact Summit.
Enforcement Level: No AI-specific obligation, sanction or enforcement authority exists, and oversight rests on general data protection and cybersecurity powers that have produced no recorded AI-related action.
Specific Laws: Data Protection Act, 2024 (Act No. 18 of 2024), Digital Services Act, 2025, Cybersecurity Act, 2025, draft National Artificial Intelligence Policy (2025-2026, not adopted), UNESCO Readiness Assessment Methodology country report for Botswana (2025)

Regulation Status: Brazil regulates AI through sector-specific binding instruments — Resolução TSE 23.755 of 2 March 2026 on synthetic content in electoral propaganda, Resolução CFM 2.454/2026 on AI in medicine, Portaria MGI 3.485 of 24 April 2026 on AI governance in the federal administration and Lei 15.123/2025 on AI-assisted violence against women — layered on general law (LGPD Law 13.709/2018, Marco Civil Law 12.965/2014, ECA Digital Law 15.211/2025 in force since 17 March 2026). The horizontal AI Legal Framework PL 2338/2023, approved by the Senate on 10 December 2024, remains before the Chamber of Deputies special committee awaiting the rapporteur's opinion, with the vote postponed past the October 2026 elections. Obligations therefore bind only in defined domains.
Policy Lever: Policy runs through indirect binding law (LGPD, ECA Digital), four narrow AI-specific binding norms in elections, medicine, federal administration and criminal law, and a funding and soft-law layer comprising PBIA 2024-2028, the ANPD AI regulatory sandbox in testing until December 2026 and Lei 15.504/2026 data-centre incentives. The ANPD publishes AI guidance and priority-theme plans and monitors platforms and AI tools, but its AI competence derives from data-protection law rather than a statutory AI mandate.
Governance Type: Governance is plural and only loosely coordinated: sectoral regulators and self-regulatory councils set their own AI rules while the ANPD acts as presumptive lead only under the pending PL 2338/2023. Courts, especially the electoral courts, actively define the applicable standards, and several states and municipalities have adopted their own AI laws and decrees.
Actor Involvement: Industry, civil society and academia engage through public hearings, regulator consultations and the ANPD sandbox rather than permanent co-governance bodies. Internationally Brazil is a leading actor, shaping G20, BRICS, UNESCO and UN AI governance processes.
Enforcement Level: Enforcement touching AI runs through LGPD sanctions of up to 2% of Brazilian turnover and ECA Digital fines of up to R$50 million applied by the ANPD, with the electoral courts producing the only published decisions applying AI-specific rules.
Specific Laws: Lei Geral de Proteção de Dados - LGPD (Law No. 13,709/2018), Marco Civil da Internet (Law No. 12,965/2014), Estatuto da Criança e do Adolescente Digital - ECA Digital (Law No. 15,211/2025, in force 17 March 2026), Lei No. 15,123/2025 (AI-enabled violence against women - Criminal Code amendment), Lei No. 15,352/2026 (ANPD converted into a regulatory agency), Lei No. 15,504/2026 (data centre tax incentives for AI investment), Resolução TSE No. 23,755/2026 amending Resolução TSE No. 23,610/2019 (AI and synthetic content in electoral propaganda), Resolução CFM No. 2,454/2026 (AI in medicine), Portaria MGI No. 3,485/2026 (AI governance policy in the federal public administration), Plano Brasileiro de Inteligência Artificial - PBIA 2024-2028, Estratégia Brasileira de Inteligência Artificial - EBIA (2021), PL 2338/2023 (AI Legal Framework - pending in the Chamber of Deputies), Goiás State Complementary Laws No. 205/2025 and No. 215/2026, Distrito Federal Decreto No. 48,901/2026, Ceará State Law No. 17,611/2021, Porto Alegre Municipal Law No. 14,644/2026

Regulation Status: Brunei governs AI through voluntary means: AITI's Guide on Artificial Intelligence Governance and Ethics for Brunei Darussalam, issued in 2025 and reissued as a second edition in 2026 after a November 2025 public consultation, imposes no legal obligation. The only binding law reaching AI is the general Personal Data Protection Order 2025, administered and enforced by AITI, whose substantive provisions commenced on 1 January 2026 and which contains no AI-specific provision.
Policy Lever: Policy runs on soft law and national strategy: the two editions of AITI's Guide on Artificial Intelligence Governance and Ethics, the cross-cutting Data and Artificial Intelligence Strategy within Digital Brunei 2030 (2026), and the regional ASEAN Guide on AI Governance and Ethics. The only binding lever touching AI is the general Personal Data Protection Order 2025, and state investment in AI compute and a national large language model operates without an AI regulatory sandbox or AI procurement rules.
Governance Type: Governance is centralised in AITI under the Ministry of Transport and Infocommunications, with cross-government coordination through the Digital Brunei Council that issued Digital Brunei 2030. Districts have no regulatory tier, and independent judicial or ombudsman review of AI governance is absent.
Actor Involvement: Government, industry and academia sit together on AITI's AI Governance and Ethics Working Group, and two public consultation papers in July 2024 and November 2025 drew comment from technology communities and the public. Civil society has no standing role, and international engagement runs through ASEAN instruments rather than treaties or standards bodies.
Enforcement Level: Brunei's AI guidance is voluntary and unenforced, with the only applicable penalties and the only active supervisory machinery coming from the general Personal Data Protection Order 2025 administered by AITI.
Specific Laws: Guide on Artificial Intelligence Governance and Ethics for Brunei Darussalam, Second Edition (2026), Guide on Artificial Intelligence Governance and Ethics for Brunei Darussalam (2025), Personal Data Protection Order (2025), Digital Brunei 2030: The Digital Brunei Transformation Plan (2026) including the Data and Artificial Intelligence Strategy, Digital Economy Masterplan 2025, ASEAN Guide on AI Governance and Ethics (2024)

Regulation Status: Binding AI rules in Bulgaria come from the directly applicable EU AI Act as amended by Regulation (EU) 2026/1744, under which prohibitions, AI-literacy, general-purpose AI and transparency duties apply while Annex III high-risk obligations run from 2 December 2027. No national supplementary law is in force: the Council of Ministers scheduled a Law introducing national measures implementing Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 as item 21 of its July-December 2026 legislative programme, and an opposition Act on the Use and Development of Artificial Intelligence (bill 52-654-01-151) was tabled on 24 September 2026. A Health Act amendment introducing AI-based risk screening of disability (TELK) decisions passed first reading on 14 October 2026.
Policy Lever: Policy rests on the directly applicable EU AI Act plus the 2020 Concept for the Development of Artificial Intelligence in Bulgaria until 2030, with the Ministry of Innovation and Digital Transformation holding the AI policy mandate under the Council of Ministers decree published in State Gazette issue 76 of 21 August 2026 and drafting the implementing law. Economic levers are research and infrastructure funding, including INSAIT and public-sector AI deployments such as the SIGMA public-procurement control system, rather than regulatory tools; the national AI regulatory sandbox required by 2 August 2027 does not exist.
Governance Type: Governance is ministry-led and only partly plural: the Ministry of Innovation and Digital Transformation, which absorbed the Ministry of Electronic Governance in 2026, coordinates policy, seven bodies designated in June 2025 cover fundamental rights, and financial supervisors hold market surveillance roles by operation of the AI Act. Coordination is informal, there is no subnational layer, and independent review of AI decisions has not been exercised.
Actor Involvement: Engagement is strongest at EU level through the European AI Board and AI Act coordination formats, supplemented by the Joint Statement on AI Opportunity Partnership approved on 7 October 2026. Domestic participation is consultative: industry associations and academic institutions feed into draft legislation and parliamentary committee hearings, while civil society input runs only through generic public consultations.
Enforcement Level: Enforcement is dormant: without a designated market surveillance authority, national penalty rules or any AI-specific decision, only directly applicable EU-level obligations and general-law action bite.
Specific Laws: EU AI Act / Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (2024), as amended by Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 (Digital Omnibus on AI, 2026), Concept for the Development of Artificial Intelligence in Bulgaria until 2030 (2020), Council of Ministers Decision No. 398 (2025), draft Act on the Use and Development of Artificial Intelligence (bill 52-654-01-151, 2026), draft Law introducing national measures implementing Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (item 21, Council of Ministers Legislative Programme July-December 2026), draft Strategy for Digital Transformation of the Republic of Bulgaria 2026-2030 (2026)

Regulation Status: Burkina Faso has no dedicated AI law and none before the Assemblée législative du peuple; AI is reached only through the general data regime recast on 3 August 2026 by Loi n°037-2026/ALP and Loi organique n°038-2026/ALP, both promulgated on 22 September 2026, which replaced Loi n°001-2021/AN and its Article 19 duty to disclose the criteria behind AI-based processing. The Feuille de route nationale sur l'intelligence artificielle 2026-2030, validated in June 2026 and presented on 23 October 2026 with a 30 billion FCFA envelope, is a strategy without binding force and has not yet been officially published. Deputies received an AI briefing on 15 July 2026 to prepare future digital legislation.
Policy Lever: Policy runs through strategy and capacity-building: the 2026-2030 AI roadmap with its 'Vertus' ethical framework, the 'IA pour tous' programme, awareness sessions for ministry chiefs of staff and Primature staff, and training of some thirty deputies in July 2026. Binding levers remain the general personal data and information-systems security laws, and SPIVTEN acts without compliance powers.
Governance Type: AI governance is concentrated in the Ministry of Digital Transition and its SPIVTEN secretariat under a centralized military transitional authority. The merger of the Conseil supérieur de la communication and the Commission de l'Informatique et des Libertés into ARCOD, whose president Wendingoudi Louis Modeste Ouédraogo was appointed in 2026, leaves one converged regulator alongside the ministry, with coordination handled through ad hoc workshops and no subnational tier.
Actor Involvement: Participation runs through ministry-convened workshops that brought in the private sector, universities, research centres, youth and civil society during preparation and validation of the national AI roadmap, with no permanent consultative body. Internationally, Burkina Faso signed up to the six-country West African AI guidelines launched alongside the Global Dialogue on AI in July 2026.
Enforcement Level: Nothing AI-specific is enforced: oversight rests with the general data protection regulator, now ARCOD, and no AI audit, investigation or sanction has been recorded.
Specific Laws: Feuille de route nationale sur l'intelligence artificielle 2026-2030 (2026), Loi n°037-2026/ALP portant protection des personnes physiques à l'égard du traitement des données à caractère personnel (2026), Loi organique n°038-2026/ALP portant création de l'Autorité de régulation de la communication et du traitement des données à caractère personnel (2026), Loi n°001-2021/AN portant protection des données à caractère personnel (2021, abrogée), Loi portant sécurité des systèmes d'information (2024), Stratégie nationale de développement de l'économie numérique SN@DEN 2018-2027 (2018), Lignes directrices pour une intelligence artificielle éthique, inclusive et responsable (2026)

Regulation Status: Burundi has no binding AI legislation. Its only AI-specific instrument is the Stratégie Nationale de l'Intelligence Artificielle 2026-2030, validated in Bujumbura on 21-22 April 2026 by the Ministry of Finance, Budget and Digital Economy with UNDP support, a six-pillar roadmap that promises regulatory and ethical frameworks later. General law reaches AI indirectly through Loi n°1/03 of 10 March 2026 on personal data protection and Loi n°1/10 of 16 March 2022 on cybercrime, neither of which regulates AI systems as such.
Policy Lever: Policy action consists of non-binding planning documents, the Stratégie Nationale de l'Intelligence Artificielle 2026-2030 and the Stratégie Nationale de Gouvernance des Données validated 7 November 2025, both supported by UNDP. Dedicated funding, a sandbox and AI procurement rules are absent, and no body holds a legal AI mandate.
Governance Type: AI governance is concentrated in one ministry, the Ministère des Finances, du Budget et de l'Économie numérique, working with UNDP, with coordination confined to ad hoc workshops. No subnational tier, court or independent oversight body plays any role in AI rules.
Actor Involvement: Involvement centres on the UNDP-supported strategy validation workshop of 21-22 April 2026, which drew ministries, private-sector actors and academics on a one-off basis. International engagement rests on African Union and UNESCO membership and the September 2026 KOAFEC ministerial in Seoul.
Enforcement Level: Enforcement of AI rules is impossible because no AI-specific obligation, supervisory authority or monitoring programme exists, leaving only general data protection and cybercrime penalties.
Specific Laws: Stratégie Nationale de l'Intelligence Artificielle 2026-2030 (validated April 2026), Stratégie Nationale de Gouvernance des Données (2025), Loi n°1/03 du 10 mars 2026 portant protection des données à caractère personnel, Loi n°1/10 du 16 mars 2022 portant prévention et répression de la cybercriminalité au Burundi

Regulation Status: Cambodia governs AI only through general instruments: Sub-Decree 110 (2017) on the ICT Licensing Regime and the Law on Anti-Technology Fraud, passed on 3 April 2026, which criminalises technology-enabled fraud and scam-compound operations without AI-specific provisions. The Draft National Artificial Intelligence Strategy 2025-2030, the Draft MPTC AI Development Promotion Strategy and the Draft Law on Personal Data Protection remain unadopted, and the strategy itself rules out a comprehensive AI law in favour of a step-by-step approach.
Policy Lever: Policy works through soft and promotional instruments: the UNESCO-supported AI Readiness Assessment, the MISTI/UN-ESCAP AI report, draft national and ministerial AI strategies, and government platforms such as ai.gov.kh, verify.gov.kh and TranslateKH. The one funded programme is the AFD-financed National AI and Data Science Research Centre; no regulatory sandbox, AI procurement rule or AI body with legal powers exists.
Governance Type: AI governance is centralised in MPTC, supported by MISTI, the National Council of Science, Technology and Innovation and the Cambodia Academy of Digital Technology, with coordination handled ad hoc through an inter-ministerial working group. Provincial authorities have no role and there is no independent or judicial oversight of AI.
Actor Involvement: Domestic participation is consultative and episodic, channelled through ministry workshops and public comment on the draft strategies, with academia the most engaged non-state actor via the Cambodia Academy of Digital Technology. International engagement is the strongest strand, running through ASEAN, UNESCO, UN-ESCAP and the 2026 Geneva global AI governance meeting.
Enforcement Level: No AI-specific obligation exists to enforce, so general ICT licensing and anti-technology-fraud powers are the only levers touching AI, and AI oversight is limited to one-off readiness studies.
Specific Laws: Draft National Artificial Intelligence Strategy 2025-2030 (2025, not yet adopted), Draft MPTC Artificial Intelligence Development Promotion Strategy (2026, not yet adopted), Draft Law on Personal Data Protection (2025, not yet enacted), Sub-Decree 110 on the ICT Licensing Regime (2017), Law on Anti-Technology Fraud (2026), Cambodia Digital Economy and Society Policy Framework 2021-2035 (2021), Cambodia Digital Government Policy 2022-2035 (2022), National Startup Development Strategy 2026-2030 (2026), Cambodia AI Readiness Assessment Report (2025)

Regulation Status: Cameroon has no binding AI-specific legislation and no AI bill before the National Assembly. The National Artificial Intelligence Strategy (SNIA), launched on 7 July 2025 by the Minister of Posts and Telecommunications at the second CONIA, is a non-binding roadmap to 2040 whose governance pillar proposes a Cameroonian AI Authority, a Presidential Council on AI and a future framework law. Law No. 2024/017 of 23 December 2024 on personal data protection became fully applicable after its eighteen-month compliance period ended on 23 June 2026, but it is a general-purpose instrument that regulates profiling and automated decisions without addressing AI as such.
Policy Lever: Policy rests on the non-binding SNIA roadmap and on general data protection and cybersecurity law, with no AI-specific binding instrument, no funded AI programme in disbursement, no AI procurement rules and no regulatory sandbox. A further national digital economy strategy incorporating AI development was reported as being finalised in October 2026, and institutional capacity remains limited to ministerial stewardship by MINPOSTEL.
Governance Type: Governance is centralised in the Ministry of Posts and Telecommunications, which prepared and launched the SNIA, while ANTIC and ART operate on cybersecurity and telecommunications without AI powers. Coordination is episodic through the CONIA consultations, and neither subnational authorities nor independent review bodies play a part.
Actor Involvement: Stakeholder input is channelled through the two editions of the Concertations Nationales sur l'Intelligence Artificielle (June 2024 and July 2025), which brought together public bodies, the private sector, civil society and researchers before the SNIA launch; no permanent advisory structure has followed. International engagement is continental and multilateral, anchored on the African Union Continental Artificial Intelligence Strategy.
