Enforcement Level: Enforcement capacity for AI is absent, with no AI obligations, no competent authority and no monitoring, while the general data protection regime applicable since 23 June 2026 still lacks an operating supervisory authority.
Specific Laws: National Artificial Intelligence Strategy - SNIA (2025), Law No. 2024/017 of 23 December 2024 on Personal Data Protection

Regulation Status: Canada has no binding federal AI statute: the Artificial Intelligence and Data Act died with Bill C-27 in January 2025, and the AI for All strategy released 4 June 2026 chose targeted, incremental bills over a standalone AI act. Binding AI-specific rules exist only inside government through the Treasury Board Directive on Automated Decision-Making and its Algorithmic Impact Assessment. Bill C-34, which would impose duties on social media and AI chatbot services, and Bill C-36, which adds automated-decision transparency rights to a new privacy statute, are both at second reading in the House of Commons.
Policy Lever: Federal levers are predominantly soft: a mandatory directive for government systems, a layered set of guidance and voluntary codes, and large funding envelopes under AI for All covering compute, the national AI institutes and the Canadian AI Safety Institute. Policy leadership sits with the Ministry of Artificial Intelligence and Digital Innovation, which sponsors Bills C-34 and C-36 and ran the AI transparency consultation that closed 23 September 2026, but no federal body holds AI compliance powers.
Governance Type: Authority is dispersed across a lead ministry with no regulatory powers, independent federal regulators applying general law to AI, and provinces writing their own AI-adjacent rules. Advisory structures were reshaped on 2 October 2026 when the Prime Minister's National Council on Artificial Intelligence was launched and the AI Strategy Task Force completed its mandate.
Actor Involvement: Policy development is industry- and academia-led through the Prime Minister's National Council on Artificial Intelligence and the national AI institutes, while domestic civil society organisations campaign against their exclusion from these bodies. Public input runs through open consultations such as the AI transparency survey that closed 23 September 2026.
Enforcement Level: AI-specific enforcement is confined to administrative compliance inside the federal public service, while regulators reach private-sector AI only through general privacy and consumer law, as in the OpenAI findings of 6 May 2026.
Specific Laws: Directive on Automated Decision-Making (2019, fourth version in force 24 June 2025), AI for All: Canada's National Artificial Intelligence Strategy (2026), Bill C-34 Safe Social Media Act enacting the Digital Safety Act and Digital Safety Commission of Canada Act (introduced 10 June 2026, second reading debate 21 October 2026), Bill C-36 Protecting Privacy and Consumer Data Act (introduced 15 June 2026, at second reading), AI Strategy for the Federal Public Service 2025-2027, Voluntary Code of Conduct on the Responsible Development and Management of Advanced Generative AI Systems (2023), OSFI Guideline E-23 Model Risk Management (2025, effective 1 May 2027), Council of Europe Framework Convention on Artificial Intelligence and Human Rights, Democracy and the Rule of Law (signed 11 February 2025), Quebec Act to modernize legislative provisions as regards the protection of personal information / Law 25 (2021), Ontario Strengthening Cyber Security and Building Trust in the Public Sector Act / Bill 194 (2024)

Regulation Status: Cabo Verde has no AI-specific legislation and none in the legislative process; AI is addressed through strategy, notably the Agenda Digital de Cabo Verde 2035 approved by Resolução n.º 72/2026 and the Estratégia Nacional de Dados, with a dedicated AI strategy for public administration launched for drafting in April 2026. General instruments — the personal data protection law as amended by Lei n.º 121/IX/2021, the cybercrime law and the electronic commerce law — reach AI uses without any AI-written provision. The Comissão Nacional de Proteção de Dados frames AI publicly as a data-governance question rather than applying dedicated rules.
Policy Lever: Policy action consists of strategy and capacity-building: the Agenda Digital de Cabo Verde 2035, the Estratégia Nacional de Dados, the AI strategy for public administration under development with World Bank support, and the announced Centro de Excelência Digital e de Inteligência Artificial. No binding AI instrument, published AI guidance, regulatory sandbox or AI procurement rule is in place.
Governance Type: Governance is centralised in the executive, with the Secretaria de Estado da Economia Digital and NOSi leading and no body holding an AI mandate. The independent data protection commission provides the only non-executive voice in the AI debate, and municipalities have no role.
Actor Involvement: Domestic participation is informal: industry engages through technology forums and academics contribute episodically, while civil society holds no consultative role. International engagement is the most developed channel, via the Smart Africa Alliance, African Union frameworks, the Lusophone data protection network and World Bank-supported data work.
Enforcement Level: Nothing AI-specific is enforced, and only general data protection and cybercrime penalties could reach AI uses.
Specific Laws: Agenda Digital de Cabo Verde 2035 (Resolução n.º 72/2026), Estratégia Nacional de Dados (2025), Estratégia de Inteligência Artificial para a Administração Pública (under development, 2026), Lei n.º 121/IX/2021 amending the Personal Data Protection Law (Lei n.º 41/VIII/2013), Estratégia Nacional para a Governação Digital de Cabo Verde

Regulation Status: The Central African Republic has no AI-specific legislation, no draft AI bill and no national AI strategy. The only binding texts reaching algorithmic activity are Loi n° 24-001 (2024) on personal data protection, whose supervisory authority is not publicly identified, and Loi n° 22.002 (2022) on electronic transactions. Conflict and limited state capacity keep AI rulemaking off the legislative agenda.
Policy Lever: Policy activity consists of announcements and donor projects rather than instruments: a planned AI centre of excellence with Dure Technologies, a Huawei-supported administration digitalisation programme, and the World Bank CARDIP digital project. The Agence Centrafricaine de Développement du Digital operates on digital transformation generally, with no AI guidance, funding line, sandbox or procurement rule in operation.
Governance Type: Governance of AI is not organised: a single ministry handles digital policy, with the Agence Centrafricaine de Développement du Digital executing projects and no lead AI authority, coordination body or independent review mechanism. Sub-national administrations have no role.
Actor Involvement: Engagement on AI runs through bilateral contacts with foreign technology firms and development partners rather than domestic consultation, including presidential meetings on data and AI investment at the 81st UN General Assembly. Industry, civil society and academia have no structured role, and international participation is passive membership of the African Union and United Nations.
Enforcement Level: Nothing specific to AI is enforced or monitored, and documented misuse of AI tools inside the country has produced no regulatory or judicial response.
Specific Laws: Loi n° 24-001 portant protection des données à caractère personnel (2024), Loi n° 23.008 portant création de l'Agence Centrafricaine de Développement du Digital (2023), Loi n° 22.002 régissant les transactions électroniques (2022)

Regulation Status: Chad has no dedicated AI statute; AI entered binding law through the reform of the Agence Nationale de Sécurité Informatique et de Certification Électronique (Ordonnance n°001/PR/2026 of 22 January 2026, ratified by Loi n°003/AN-SENAT/2026 of 18 March 2026 and promulgated by Décret n°148/PR/2026 of 23 March 2026), which updates key concepts and extends ANSICE's regulation, investigation and sanction powers to artificial intelligence systems, digital platforms and social networks. Loi n°007/PR/2015 on personal data protection and Loi n°009/PR/2015 on cybersecurity and cybercrime remain the general framework, and Décret n°2690/PR/PM/MTENDA/2025 of 21 October 2025 created a Direction générale de l'Intelligence Artificielle inside the Ministry of Telecommunications, Digital Economy and Digitalisation of the Administration without conferring regulatory powers. A national AI strategy for 2026-2030 entered pre-validation on 8 October 2026 and is not adopted.
Policy Lever: Chad's levers are an AI directorate in the digital economy ministry created in October 2025, ANSICE's statutory powers extended to AI systems in March 2026, and donor-funded preparation work including the United Nations Economic Commission for Africa-supported national AI strategy 2026-2030 now in pre-validation. No funding programme, regulatory sandbox, AI procurement rule or published AI guidance exists.
Governance Type: AI governance is executive and centralised in N'Djamena, shared between the Direction générale de l'Intelligence Artificielle of the Ministry of Telecommunications, Digital Economy and Digitalisation of the Administration and ANSICE, whose reformed statute brings AI systems into its supervisory scope. Coordination is ad hoc and internationally sponsored, and neither provinces nor courts play any part.
Actor Involvement: International organisations lead: UNESCO through the Readiness Assessment Methodology, the United Nations Economic Commission for Africa through the data governance maturity assessment scoring Chad 30.27 percent and the AI strategy work, and the United Nations Development Programme through the transformation and AI strategy procurement. Domestic industry, civil society and academia appear in validation workshops and forums without any standing role in policy-making.
Enforcement Level: Enforcement is nominal: ANSICE now holds statutory authority over AI systems but has issued no AI-related decision, and monitoring is limited to one-off readiness diagnostics.
Specific Laws: Loi n°003/AN-SENAT/2026 du 18 mars 2026 portant ratification de l'Ordonnance n°001/PR/2026 du 22 janvier 2026 portant réforme de l'Agence Nationale de Sécurité Informatique et de Certification Électronique, promulguée par Décret n°148/PR/2026 du 23 mars 2026 (2026), Décret n°2690/PR/PM/MTENDA/2025 portant réorganisation du Ministère des Télécommunications, de l'Économie numérique et de la Digitalisation de l'Administration, créant la Direction générale de l'Intelligence Artificielle (2025), Loi n°007/PR/2015 portant protection des données à caractère personnel (2015), Loi n°006/PR/2015 portant création de l'Agence Nationale de Sécurité Informatique et de Certification Électronique (2015), Loi n°009/PR/2015 sur la cybersécurité et la lutte contre la cybercriminalité (2015), Stratégie nationale de gouvernance des données validée le 7 octobre 2026 (2026), projet de Stratégie nationale d'intelligence artificielle 2026-2030 en prévalidation (2026), Stratégie nationale de développement du numérique 2020-2030

Regulation Status: No AI-specific statute binds in Chile: the government bill regulating AI systems (Boletín 16821-19, merged with 15869-19) was approved in general by the Senate Committee on Future Challenges on 26 October 2026 and dispatched to the Senate floor, with the Executive committed to filing a total substitutive indication before 4 December 2026 that replaces the EU-style risk tiers with an innovation-enabling framework. A separate bill sanctioning AI-generated deepfakes (Boletín 17795) passed the Chamber of Deputies in general on 23 July 2026. Binding rules reaching AI are general: Law 21.663 on cybersecurity, in force since 2025, and Law 21.719 on personal data protection, whose 1 December 2026 start the Senate voted on 28 October 2026 to postpone to 15 October 2027 through Boletín 18.623-07.
Policy Lever: Chile governs AI through soft law and funding: the National AI Policy and its updated action plan, the MinCiencia–Segpres instruction on AI in public services, SERNAC guidance, and state-backed research through CENIA and Latam-GPT. Enforceable instruments are confined to general cybersecurity and personal data protection law, and no body holds a statutory AI mandate.
Governance Type: A lead ministry, MinCiencia, sets AI policy and coordinates sectoral regulators through the National AI Policy action plan, with the proposed AI authority still contained in the pending bill. Courts intervene case by case and no subnational tier plays a role.
Actor Involvement: Industry, civil society and academia feed into AI policy through published consultations, Senate committee hearings and expert reports rather than standing formal seats. Internationally Chile is prominent, anchoring the regional agenda through the Santiago Declaration and taking part in OECD, UNESCO and United Nations AI governance work.
Enforcement Level: No AI-specific obligation is enforceable, so action is confined to general-law instruments such as ANCI's cybersecurity supervision of designated Operators of Vital Importance and occasional court rulings.
Specific Laws: AI Systems Regulation Bill (Boletín 16821-19, 2024, approved in general by the Senate Future Challenges Committee on 26 October 2026; Executive total substitutive indication committed for December 2026), Bill regulating AI-generated content and deepfakes (Boletín 17795, approved in general by the Chamber of Deputies, 2026), Law 21.719 on Protection of Personal Data (2024, effective 1 December 2026; postponement to 15 October 2027 approved by the Senate in first stage, Boletín 18.623-07, 2026), Law 21.806 amending Law 21.719 (2026), Law 21.663 on Cybersecurity Framework (2024, in force 2025), National AI Policy and Action Plan update (Decreto N° 12 of 2025), MinCiencia–Segpres Oficio N° 711/2023 on AI use in the State, Santiago Declaration on Ethical AI in Latin America and the Caribbean (2023)

Regulation Status: China regulates AI through a stack of dedicated binding administrative measures rather than a single statute: algorithmic recommendation, deep synthesis, generative AI services, AI-generated content labeling and, since 15 July 2026, anthropomorphic AI interaction services, reinforced by the amended Cybersecurity Law in force 1 January 2026. Filing, security assessment and labeling duties apply today across online services, finance, education and healthcare platforms, while non-public-facing generative systems stay outside the generative AI rules and comprehensive AI legislation is still only a planned project in the 2026 legislative work plans of the State Council and the NPC Standing Committee.
Policy Lever: Policy combines filing, pre-launch security assessment, mandatory labeling and data rules with a maintained suite of national standards and TC260 guidance, plus industrial levers such as the AI Plus Initiative, state AI funds and MIIT's AI ethics review pilot. CAC, MIIT, NDRC and SAMR exercise approval and compliance powers routinely.
Governance Type: Governance is centralized under the CAC, which coordinates national AI policy and issues rules jointly with sectoral ministries; local governments implement national rules and add promotion-oriented local legislation. Courts now adjudicate AI disputes under nationwide Supreme People's Court guidance, but no independent body reviews AI regulatory decisions.
Actor Involvement: Domestic participation is channelled through state-run consultations, TC260 technical committees and state-affiliated academic institutes, with independent civil society excluded. Internationally China is a leading actor, hosting the World Artificial Intelligence Cooperation Organization and pushing the Global AI Governance Initiative and Action Plan alongside ISO, ITU and UN work.
Enforcement Level: Enforcement is active and visible through registration gatekeeping, nationwide rectification campaigns and published sanctions against named non-compliant AI services, with most individual decisions reported in aggregate.
Specific Laws: Internet Information Service Algorithmic Recommendation Management Provisions (2022), Internet Information Service Deep Synthesis Management Provisions (2022), Interim Measures for the Management of Generative Artificial Intelligence Services (2023), Measures for Labeling Artificial Intelligence-Generated Synthetic Content and GB 45438-2025 (2025), Cybersecurity Law Amendment with artificial intelligence provisions (effective 1 January 2026), Interim Measures for the Administration of Artificial Intelligence Anthropomorphic Interaction Services (2026), Implementation Opinions on the Standardized Application and Innovative Development of Intelligent Agents (2026), Opinions of the Supreme People's Court on the Trial of Cases Involving Artificial Intelligence Disputes (2026), Opinions of the State Council on Deepening Implementation of the Artificial Intelligence Plus Initiative (2025), AI Safety Governance Framework 2.0 (2025), New Generation Artificial Intelligence Development Plan (2017)

Regulation Status: Colombia has no horizontal AI statute: the government bill PL 043-25/324-25-C died on 19 June 2026 and Proyecto de Ley 025 de 2026 Cámara, filed on 21 July 2026 with a first-debate report proposing an Autoridad Reguladora de Inteligencia Artificial, is still in committee alongside Proyecto de Ley 065 de 2026 Senado. Binding rules sit inside general law and administrative acts—the AI aggravation in Ley 2502 de 2025, upheld in Constitutional Court judgment C-212 de 2026, the algorithmic supervision and transparency duties for delivery platforms in Ley 2466 de 2025, SIC External Circular No. 2 of 2024, and Acuerdo PCSJA24-12243 for the judicial branch—while CONPES 4144 de 2025 remains a non-binding roadmap.
Policy Lever: Policy runs through spending and guidance: the CONPES 4144 de 2025 plan of COP 479,273 million, the ethical guide for public entities, MinTIC's 2026 MSPI AI security lineamientos and the CRC regulatory sandbox hosting the ConTIGO Digital AI experiment. Binding levers are confined to SIC External Circular No. 2 of 2024, the Ley 2502 de 2025 aggravation, the Ley 2466 de 2025 platform algorithm duties and Acuerdo PCSJA24-12243, and no body holds a statutory AI compliance mandate.
Governance Type: Governance is centred on MinCiencias and MinTIC, with the SIC as data-protection and consumer authority, the CRC through its sandbox, the Ministerio de Trabajo on platform algorithms and the Consejo Superior de la Judicatura for courts, coordinated via the DNP's CONPES 4144 follow-up. Subnational authorities deliver national programmes without regulating, and the Constitutional Court has repeatedly shaped AI limits.
Actor Involvement: AI policy is shaped through consultations, congressional hearings and the CRC sandbox rather than standing multistakeholder bodies, with industry, academia and civil society all heard occasionally. Internationally Colombia acts through the OECD, UNESCO, Latin American declarations and the SIC's cooperation with foreign data-protection authorities, and is not party to a binding AI treaty.
Enforcement Level: Enforcement touching AI runs through general data-protection, consumer, labour and criminal powers, with the Ley 2502 de 2025 aggravation the only AI-specific penalty applied and no AI audit or public monitoring regime.
Specific Laws: CONPES 4144 – Política Nacional de Inteligencia Artificial (2025), Ley 2502 de 2025 – Penal Code reform on identity impersonation using artificial intelligence (2025), Ley 2466 de 2025 – labour reform provisions on algorithmic management in digital delivery platforms (2025), Ley 1581 de 2012 – Data Protection Law (2012), SIC External Circular No. 2 of 2024 – AI Personal Data Processing Guidelines (2024), Acuerdo PCSJA24-12243 – guidelines on artificial intelligence use in the Judicial Branch (2024), Guía Ética para la Implementación, Desarrollo y Uso de Sistemas de Inteligencia Artificial en Entidades Públicas de Colombia (2025), Lineamientos de Seguridad y Privacidad de la Información para Sistemas de Inteligencia Artificial – MSPI update (2026), Proyecto de Ley 025 de 2026 Cámara – AI regulation bill (pending), Proyecto de Ley 065 de 2026 Senado – AI regulation bill (pending), Sentencia C-212 de 2026 and Sentencia T-323 de 2024 of the Constitutional Court

Regulation Status: Comoros has no AI-specific legislation, draft bill or binding rule, and no AI provision inside general law. The legal trust layer consists of Loi n°21-011/AU portant Code de l'Information et de la Communication (2021), Loi n°21-012/AU on cybersecurity and the fight against cybercrime (promulgated by Décret 22-003/PR, 18 January 2022) and the Law on the Protection of Personal Data of 29 June 2021, none of which mentions AI systems, while digital policy rests on the non-binding Stratégie Comores Numérique 2028. The African Union Convention on Cyber Security and Personal Data Protection, signed on 29 January 2018, remains unratified.
Policy Lever: Comoros operates no AI policy instrument, funding programme, sandbox or procurement rule, relying instead on general data protection, cybersecurity and communications laws that say nothing about AI. Institutional capacity is confined to the telecommunications regulator ANRTIC and the digital development agency ANADEN, neither with an AI remit.
Governance Type: AI governance structures are absent: digital matters sit with the ministry responsible for telecommunications, ANRTIC and ANADEN, with no coordinating body and no AI mandate anywhere. The autonomous islands play no role, and no independent or judicial oversight of AI exists.
Actor Involvement: No domestic industry, civil society or academic actors have been mobilised around AI governance, and no consultation has been held. International engagement is passive membership of the African Union and the United Nations, alongside the unratified African Union Convention on Cyber Security and Personal Data Protection signed on 29 January 2018.
Enforcement Level: Enforcement is non-existent because there are no AI obligations, no designated supervisory authority and no monitoring of AI systems, leaving only general cybercrime and data protection penalties on the books.
Specific Laws: Stratégie Nationale Comores Numérique 2028 (2019), Loi n°21-011/AU portant Code de l'Information et de la Communication (2021), Loi n°21-012/AU sur la cybersécurité et la lutte contre la cybercriminalité (2021, promulguée par Décret 22-003/PR de 2022), Loi portant protection des données à caractère personnel (2021), Décret 065/2009 établissant l'ANRTIC (2009)

Regulation Status: Congo has no binding rule addressed to AI systems or their outputs: Loi n° 14-2024 du 23 mai 2024 creating the Centre africain de recherche en intelligence artificielle (CARIA) is institutional, and the loi portant orientation et développement de la recherche scientifique adopted by the National Assembly on 8 April 2026 announces an AI ethical framework and a national ethics committee without creating obligations. Conduct in AI-related data processing is governed by Loi n° 29-2019 du 10 octobre 2019 portant protection des données à caractère personnel, whose supervisory commission was created by Loi n° 5-2025 du 29 mars 2025 and installed in January 2026. A national AI strategy drafted by a technical committee launched on 6 May 2026 with UNDP support remains unpublished.
Policy Lever: Policy runs through promotional levers: the statutory AI research centre CARIA created by Loi n° 14-2024, UNECA and UNDP-backed capacity building and strategy drafting, and youth AI training such as the FONEA programme launched in October 2026. No AI-specific binding instrument, published national AI guidance, regulatory sandbox or AI procurement rule exists.
Governance Type: AI governance is executive-led and centred on the Ministry of Posts, Telecommunications and the Digital Economy, supported by the ARPCE, CARIA and the Ministry of Scientific Research and Technological Innovation, with coordination through a temporary technical committee. Departments play no part, and courts and independent bodies have not reviewed AI matters.
Actor Involvement: Participation is concentrated in government, academia and international partners, with UNECA and UNDP financing the research centre and strategy work and industry drawn into ARPCE-convened consultations. Domestic civil society has taken part in workshops only, with no formal standing role.
Enforcement Level: No AI obligation is enforceable, no authority owns AI supervision, and no AI-related sanction or audit has been recorded.
Specific Laws: Loi n° 14-2024 du 23 mai 2024 portant création du centre africain de recherche en intelligence artificielle, Loi portant orientation et développement de la recherche scientifique (adopted by the National Assembly, 2026), Loi n° 29-2019 du 10 octobre 2019 portant protection des données à caractère personnel, Loi n° 5-2025 du 29 mars 2025 portant création de la commission nationale pour la protection des données à caractère personnel, Loi n° 11-2009 du 25 novembre 2009 creating the Agence de régulation des postes et des communications électroniques, Stratégie nationale de l'intelligence artificielle (under preparation since 2026), Vision Congo Digital 2025

Regulation Status: Costa Rica governs AI through the non-binding National Artificial Intelligence Strategy (ENIA) 2024-2027 and its August 2025 Action Plan, backed by two binding instruments that address AI inside broader rules: Chapter 7 of the National Digital Technologies Code (Executive Decree 44507-MICITT), mandatory for all public institutions, and Executive Decree 45961-MSP of 14 October 2026 on the Sistema Nacional de Video Protección Ciudadana, which permits AI analysis of surveillance footage, limits biometric recognition and bars decisions taken solely by automated means. Four AI bills, among them Expedientes 23771, 23919 and 24484, remain unapproved, with 23771 on the plenary agenda since 23 October 2024 and never called to a vote, while the voluntary INTE/ISO/IEC 42001:2026 standard and the general data-protection Law No. 8968 complete the framework.
Policy Lever: Policy runs mainly on soft-law levers — the ENIA and its Action Plan, the voluntary INTE/ISO/IEC 42001:2026 standard and technical guidelines in the National Digital Technologies Code — complemented by capacity-building partnerships with UNESCO, UNDP, Cisco and Google. MICITT acts without a legal AI mandate, no regulatory sandbox operates, and the National AI Centre of Excellence remains pending.
Governance Type: AI governance is centralized in MICITT, which issues the National Digital Technologies Code and leads the ENIA, while PRODHAB enforces Law No. 8968 and the Ministry of Public Security applies its own video-protection decree. Coordination happens through the ENIA Action Plan rather than a formal AI mechanism, sub-national bodies have no role, and external scrutiny has come from universities commenting on pending bills.
Actor Involvement: The ENIA was drafted through structured consultation with industry, civil society and academia with European Union support, and Costa Rica hosted a UN-backed National Dialogue on AI Ethics and Governance. International engagement runs through the OECD, UNESCO and UNDP and regional leadership in Central America, with no binding AI treaty signed.
Enforcement Level: Enforcement rests on PRODHAB's general data-protection powers, with no AI-specific sanctions, supervisory authority or routine auditing of AI systems.
Specific Laws: National Artificial Intelligence Strategy ENIA 2024-2027 (2024), ENIA Action Plan (2025), Executive Decree 44507-MICITT – National Digital Technologies Code, Chapter 7 on Artificial Intelligence (2024), Executive Decree 45961-MSP – Reglamento del Sistema Nacional de Video Protección Ciudadana (2026), INTE/ISO/IEC 42001:2026 (2026), Law No. 8968 – Protection in the Handling of Personal Data (2011), Bill 23771 – Ley de Regulación de la Inteligencia Artificial en Costa Rica (pending), Bill 23919 – Ley para la Promoción Responsable de la Inteligencia Artificial en Costa Rica (pending), Bill 24484 – Ley para la Implementación de Sistemas de Inteligencia Artificial (pending)

Regulation Status: Croatia's binding AI framework is the directly applicable EU AI Act, whose prohibitions, AI literacy duty, general-purpose AI rules and Article 50 transparency obligations apply, with Annex III high-risk duties deferred to 2 December 2027 and Annex I to 2 August 2028 by the Digital Omnibus on AI, Regulation (EU) 2026/1744, in force since 27 July 2026. The national Act on Implementation of Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 is still being drafted by a Ministry of Justice, Administration and Digital Transformation working group and was listed for third-quarter 2026 consultation without being published. Only the seven Article 77 fundamental-rights authorities, including the Personal Data Protection Agency and the Ombudswoman, have been designated; the market surveillance and notifying authorities have not.
Policy Lever: Croatia uses the EU AI Act as its only AI-specific binding lever, supplemented by Personal Data Protection Agency guidance on AI and data protection and on AI system development, and by digital-transition funding under the National Recovery and Resilience Plan, the Digital Croatia Strategy 2032 and EuroHPC projects. The National Plan for the Development of Artificial Intelligence to 2032 with its €932.1 million envelope and 33-measure Action Plan to 2028 entered a 30-day public consultation on 16 October 2026, and the national AI regulatory sandbox required by Article 57, whose deadline the Digital Omnibus moved to 2 August 2027, is not operating.
Governance Type: Governance is a lead-ministry model: the Ministry of Justice, Administration and Digital Transformation drafts the implementing act and the National Plan, seven designated authorities cover fundamental-rights oversight, and coordination happens in project-based working groups rather than a statutory mechanism. No subnational tier regulates AI, while the ombudsperson offices, the Personal Data Protection Agency and the courts provide periodic independent scrutiny.
Actor Involvement: Ministries, the Personal Data Protection Agency, ombudsperson offices, academia, industry and civil society took part in the 133-member working group behind the National Plan and in the group drafting the implementing act, but these roles are project-based rather than standing. Internationally Croatia acts through the European AI Board, the European Data Protection Board and EU digital policy coordination.
Enforcement Level: AI Act penalty ceilings apply in Croatia, but with no market surveillance authority designated, no national penalty rules adopted and no AI-specific decision issued, enforcement rests on general data-protection supervision.
Specific Laws: EU AI Act / Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (2024), Digital Omnibus on AI / Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 (2026), Draft Act on Implementation of Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (2026), National Plan for the Development of Artificial Intelligence to 2032 with Action Plan to 2028 (draft, 2026), Digital Croatia Strategy 2032, National Roadmap for Digital Decade Policy, Act on Implementation of the Digital Services Act (2025)

Regulation Status: AI is governed by the Estrategia para el Desarrollo y Uso de la Inteligencia Artificial, approved in May 2024 within the Política para la Transformación Digital y Agenda Digital Cubana, a Council of Ministers policy document without binding force. Legally enforceable duties touching AI arise only from general law, chiefly Ley 149 de Protección de Datos Personales and Decreto-Ley 35 de Telecomunicaciones. The Ley General de Ciencia, Tecnología e Innovación approved on 18 December 2025 frames science and innovation generally and creates no AI obligations.
Policy Lever: Policy is executed through the 2024 AI Strategy and its six axes (ethics, human capital, applications, public administration, innovation, communication), coordinated by the Ministerio de Comunicaciones, with the Consorcio de Inteligencia Artificial de Cuba as the main delivery vehicle since November 2025. Economic levers remain limited to institutional coordination and the mapping of some 37 provincial AI projects, without AI funding programmes, procurement rules or a sandbox.
Governance Type: AI governance is centralized in MINCOM under a Council of Ministers policy, with inter-ministerial tasks assigned in the digital transformation policy and operational coordination through the AI Consortium led by the Parque Científico Tecnológico de La Habana and the Academia de Ciencias de Cuba. There is neither a subnational tier with AI competence nor an independent reviewing institution.
Actor Involvement: Participation is structured but state-channelled: universities, research centres, state enterprises, ministries and the Unión de Informáticos de Cuba sit in the AI Consortium, while independent civil society is absent. Internationally Cuba engages at declaratory level through UNESCO, the Readiness Assessment Methodology country report and regional AI ethics summits rather than through binding treaties or standards bodies.
Enforcement Level: No AI-specific sanction, enforcement decision or audit programme exists, and oversight rests on general data-protection and telecommunications powers plus one-off strategy and readiness assessments.
Specific Laws: Política para la Transformación Digital, Agenda Digital Cubana y Estrategia para el Desarrollo y Uso de la Inteligencia Artificial (2024), Ley 149 de Protección de Datos Personales (2022, in force 2023), Resolución 58 de 2022 del Ministerio de Comunicaciones, Decreto Ley 35 de Telecomunicaciones (2021), Ley General de Ciencia, Tecnología e Innovación (2025)

Regulation Status: Cyprus is governed by the directly applicable EU AI Act, whose prohibitions, AI literacy duty, general-purpose AI rules and Article 50 transparency obligations bind now, while high-risk system obligations were postponed to December 2027 and August 2028 by the Digital Omnibus on AI. Nationally, Council of Ministers decisions of January 2025 designated competent authorities, and the Artificial Intelligence Law of 2026 — which would set supervision procedures, authority powers, penalties and an AI regulatory sandbox — completed public consultation on 16 September 2026 and has not been enacted.
Policy Lever: Policy works through the directly applicable AI Act plus EU-funded capacity building — the Pharos-CY AI Factory Antenna, an 'AI for Government' scheme and EuroHPC access. Domestic soft law is limited to the ai.cy portal and the National AI Strategy 2032, and the designated authorities have legal mandates but no national procedural rules, sandbox or exercised compliance powers.
Governance Type: Governance is compact and centralised around the Commissioner of Communications, with the Commissioner for Personal Data Protection supervising data matters and the Deputy Ministry of Research, Innovation and Digital Policy coordinating nationally and in the European AI Board. A National AI Authority and an Interministerial AI Council are proposed in the National AI Strategy 2032 but not established, and there is no sub-national layer.
Actor Involvement: Participation is consultative rather than institutionalised: the National AI Taskforce gives academic, industry and legal advice, and open e-consultations on the Artificial Intelligence Law of 2026 and the National AI Strategy 2032 drew employer-federation and disability-group comment. International engagement runs through EU structures, chiefly the European AI Board and EU-funded programmes.
Enforcement Level: Enforcement is latent: authorities are designated and EU penalty ceilings exist, while national penalties, inspection powers and monitoring await the unenacted Artificial Intelligence Law of 2026 and no action has been taken.
Specific Laws: EU AI Act / Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (2024), Digital Omnibus on AI / Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 (2026), Artificial Intelligence Law of 2026 (draft, public consultation closed 16 September 2026), Council of Ministers decisions designating AI Act competent authorities (January 2025), National AI Strategy of Cyprus 2032 (2026), Cyprus National AI Strategy (2020), GDPR / Regulation (EU) 2016/679 (2016), Processing of Personal Data (Protection of the Individual) Law 125(I)/2018

Regulation Status: AI is regulated chiefly by the directly applicable EU AI Act, whose prohibitions, AI literacy, general-purpose AI and Article 50 transparency duties bind providers and deployers in Czechia while Annex III high-risk obligations run from 2 December 2027 under the Digital Omnibus Regulation (EU) 2026/1744. The national adaptation Act on Artificial Intelligence, which would designate market surveillance authorities, create a sandbox and set administrative offences, reached the Legislative Council of the Government in August 2026 and remains unadopted. Narrow national AI statutes are in force: police biometric identification under Act No. 273/2008 Coll. and SAE Level 3 automated driving under Act No. 361/2000 Coll.
Policy Lever: The binding layer is the EU AI Act supplemented by narrow national statutes on police biometric identification and automated driving, while policy is steered through the National Artificial Intelligence Strategy 2030, the AI Implementation Plan approved by Government Resolution No. 394 of 28 May 2025 and CZK 207 million of implementation funding for 2026–2028. The Czech Telecommunication Office's AI supervision department began work on 1 September 2026, and the sandbox to be run by the Czech Standardisation Agency awaits enactment of the Act on Artificial Intelligence.
Governance Type: Governance centres on the Ministry of Industry and Trade as coordinator and the Czech Telecommunication Office as prospective lead market surveillance authority and single point of contact, with the Office for Personal Data Protection, Czech National Bank, Czech Standardisation Agency and conformity assessment bodies covering their sectors. The Committee for Artificial Intelligence under the Government Council for Information Society provides formal inter-ministerial coordination; there is no sub-national regulatory tier and independent scrutiny rests with the courts pending the Public Defender of Rights role in the draft Act.
Actor Involvement: Policy development runs through the Committee for Artificial Intelligence and the government commissioner for AI, seating ministries, regulators, industry bodies such as the Czech AI Association and the Confederation of Industry, and academic institutions, with civil society and employer unions commenting through the inter-ministerial procedure on the draft Act. Externally Czechia acts through the European AI Board, European standardisation bodies and OECD AI work.
Enforcement Level: Enforcement remains preparatory: EU penalty ceilings apply but national sanctioning and procedural rules are unadopted, the designated supervisor's new unit lacks statutory powers, and no AI-specific decision has been issued.
Specific Laws: EU AI Act – Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (2024), Digital Omnibus on AI – Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 (2026), National Artificial Intelligence Strategy of the Czech Republic 2030 (2024), AI Implementation Plan of the EU AI Act in the Czech Republic – Government Resolution No. 394 (2025), Czech Cybersecurity Act No. 265/2025 Coll. (2025), Amendment to Act on Police of the Czech Republic No. 273/2008 Coll. – biometric identification (2025), Amendment to Road Traffic Act No. 361/2000 Coll. – SAE Level 3 automated driving (2026), Draft Act on Artificial Intelligence and on amendments to related acts, file No. 503/26 (draft, 2026)

Regulation Status: Côte d'Ivoire governs AI through non-binding strategy: the Stratégie Nationale de l'Intelligence Artificielle (SNIA 2030) of 13 March 2025, the Stratégie Nationale de Gouvernance des Données (SNGD 2030) and the digital roadmap to 2035 presented on 1 June 2026. Binding obligations reach AI only through general law, chiefly Loi 2013-450 on personal data protection, and the October 2026 parliamentary session placed AI on the agenda for training deputies rather than for a bill.
Policy Lever: Levers are entirely promotional: the SNIA 2030 and SNGD 2030 strategies, the Pacte de l'Alliance nationale pour l'intelligence artificielle signed with CGECI and CCI-CI on 11 September 2026, a proposed 'Safe AI Côte d'Ivoire' label, and large announced funding including an AI university in the Plan National de Développement 2026-2030. No body holds a legal AI mandate.
Governance Type: AI governance is centralised in the Ministère de la Transition numérique et de l'Innovation technologique, which drafted and owns SNIA 2030, while ARTCI and the Agence Nationale de la Sécurité des Systèmes d'Information operate within their existing digital mandates. The planned national AI committee and Agence Nationale pour l'Intelligence Artificielle remain unestablished, and neither local authorities nor courts shape AI rules.
Actor Involvement: The SNIA 2030 was built through a broad consultation of administration, private sector, academia and civil society, and industry involvement was formalised through the September 2026 national AI alliance pact with CGECI and CCI-CI. Participation remains project-based rather than statutory, and international engagement runs through UNESCO, the African Union and Smart Africa.
Enforcement Level: Nothing AI-specific is enforceable, so supervision is confined to ARTCI's data protection powers and ANSSI's cybersecurity role, with no AI audit, case or sanction recorded.
Specific Laws: Stratégie Nationale de l'Intelligence Artificielle (SNIA 2030, 2025), Stratégie Nationale de Gouvernance des Données (SNGD 2030, 2025), Stratégie numérique à l'horizon 2035 (2026), Pacte de l'Alliance nationale pour l'intelligence artificielle (2026), Loi 2013-450 relative à la protection des données à caractère personnel (2013), Loi 2024-532 relative aux communications électroniques (2024), Loi 2017-803 sur l'orientation de la société de l'information (2017)

Regulation Status: The Democratic Republic of the Congo has no AI-specific legislation or bill; AI enters the statute book only through Ordonnance-loi n° 23/010 du 13 mars 2023 portant Code du numérique, which governs personal data, cybersecurity and digital services and lists artificial intelligence among the ethics matters a national digital body must watch. Policy direction rests on the Stratégie nationale de l'intelligence artificielle and the Politique sectorielle de l'économie numérique, presented and validated in Kinshasa on 4 August 2026 after a technical validation workshop held 23-27 July 2026, neither of which binds. UNESCO's Readiness Assessment Methodology report records the absence of a dedicated AI legal framework, coordination organ or national ethics commission.
Policy Lever: Policy action consists of strategy and announced spending: the Stratégie nationale de l'intelligence artificielle and Politique sectorielle de l'économie numérique of August 2026, the Plan national du numérique 2026-2030 with its roughly USD 1.5 billion envelope, and a planned national AI academy. Binding levers reach AI only through the Code du numérique and its 2026 ministerial orders on digital services, and no body holds a legal AI mandate.
Governance Type: Governance is centralised in the executive: the Ministry of Posts, Telecommunications and Digital Economy drives AI strategy, the Ministry of Scientific Research and the Agence de développement du numérique hold adjacent responsibilities, and ARPTC provisionally combines the roles of digital regulator, electronic-certification authority and data-protection authority. Coordination happens through ad hoc interinstitutional drafting and validation committees, provinces play no part, and no judicial or independent review of AI has occurred.
Actor Involvement: Engagement is project-based and donor-driven: UNESCO supported the RAM assessment and the drafting of the SNIA, and public bodies, technical and financial partners, private operators and sector experts attended the technical validation workshop of 23-27 July 2026 and the launch of 4 August 2026. Domestic industry, civil society and universities contribute through these one-off processes rather than standing bodies, and international involvement runs through UNESCO, bilateral digital cooperation talks with France and African Union membership.
Enforcement Level: No AI obligations exist to enforce, no authority holds an AI remit, and oversight has consisted of one UNESCO readiness assessment alongside general data-protection supervision by ARPTC.
Specific Laws: Ordonnance-loi n° 23/010 du 13 mars 2023 portant Code du numérique, Stratégie nationale de l'intelligence artificielle (2026), Politique sectorielle de l'économie numérique (2026), Plan national du numérique 2026-2030 (2026), Arrêtés ministériels n° 004 et n° 005 du 11 mars 2026 relatifs aux activités et services numériques, Loi n° 20/017 du 25 novembre 2020 relative aux télécommunications et aux technologies de l'information et de la communication

Regulation Status: Denmark applies the EU AI Act directly, supplemented nationally by Lov nr. 467 af 14. maj 2025 (Act on Supplementary Provisions to the Regulation on Artificial Intelligence), in force since 2 August 2025, which designates Digitaliseringsstyrelsen, Datatilsynet and Domstolsstyrelsen as market surveillance authorities for prohibited AI practices and sets fine powers. The broader AI-loven (bill L 111, introduced 18 February 2026, intended to enter into force on 2 August 2026 and to repeal Lov nr. 467) lapsed when the Folketing was dissolved for the 24 March 2026 election, so the full national market-surveillance framework is not yet enacted. Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 (Digital Omnibus on AI), in force since 27 July 2026, postponed Annex III high-risk obligations to 2 December 2027 and Annex I to 2 August 2028; a Copyright Act amendment protecting against realistic digitally generated imitations of personal characteristics was introduced in the Folketing in October 2026 and is still under consideration.
Policy Lever: Denmark relies on the directly applicable EU AI Act plus national supervisory and penalty powers in Lov nr. 467 af 14. maj 2025, a maintained body of regulator guidance on prohibited practices and the GDPR-AI interface, and an operating regulatory sandbox run jointly by Datatilsynet and Digitaliseringsstyrelsen. Funding flows through the Joint Government Digital Strategy 2026-2029 and the AI-Boost European Digital Innovation Hub, and the lead authority has already exercised inspection powers.
Governance Type: Supervision is concentrated in Digitaliseringsstyrelsen as lead market surveillance authority, notifying authority and single point of contact, with Datatilsynet and Domstolsstyrelsen holding carved-out shares of Article 5 oversight. Local government implements rather than regulates, and independent scrutiny runs through the courts and the Ombudsman rather than an administrative appeals body.
Actor Involvement: Industry, civil society organisations and researchers feed in through public hearings on the AI-loven, the Data Ethics Council and the AI regulatory sandbox, none of which confers a standing seat in AI rule-making. Denmark is highly active at EU level, negotiating the Digital Omnibus on AI during its Council Presidency and sitting on the EU AI Board.
Enforcement Level: Penalties exist for prohibited AI practices and the lead authority has run and published its first sectoral inspections, but no infringement decision or sanction under AI-specific law has been issued and the broader national enforcement statute remains unenacted.
Specific Laws: EU AI Act / Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (2024), Digital Omnibus on AI / Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 (2026), Act on Supplementary Provisions to the Regulation on Artificial Intelligence / Lov nr. 467 af 14. maj 2025 (2025), Bill L 111 on Supplementary Provisions to the Regulation on Artificial Intelligence (AI-loven) (2026, lapsed), Danish Data Protection Act (2018), Joint Government Digital Strategy 2026-2029 / Den fællesoffentlige digitaliseringsstrategi 2026-2029 (2025), Bill amending the Copyright Act on protection against digitally generated imitations of personal characteristics (2026, pending)

Regulation Status: Djibouti governs AI through general digital law: the Code du numérique (Loi n°019/AN/23/9ème L), whose 156-article personal data regime took effect on 30 June 2025, and Loi n°195/AN/25/9ème L creating the Autorité Nationale de Cybersécurité. The first Stratégie Nationale d'Intelligence Artificielle (SNIA) 2026-2030, presented at the national AI forum on 2-3 September 2026, is a non-binding roadmap, and the accompanying UNESCO readiness assessment places the country at an 'emerging' stage with regulation its weakest area.
Policy Lever: Policy action rests on the non-binding SNIA 2026-2030, UNESCO and ESCWA readiness diagnostics, training programmes including E-SKILLS, and a national AI prototyping competition. Instruments that bind AI developers are general-purpose, and no institution has a legal AI mandate.
Governance Type: AI governance is centralized in one ministry working with the General Secretariat of the Government, with ad hoc inter-ministerial participation around the strategy and the national forum. Regions play no part, and independent review of AI is absent, the Autorité Nationale de Cybersécurité holding a cybersecurity rather than AI remit.
Actor Involvement: Strategy preparation drew industry, academia, youth innovators and some civil society figures into UNESCO- and ESCWA-facilitated consultations and the first national AI forum, with no permanent consultative body. International engagement runs through UNESCO, ESCWA, the ITU, IGAD, Smart Africa and the African Union.
Enforcement Level: Nothing AI-specific is enforced, supervision rests with general digital and cybersecurity bodies, and monitoring consists of a single readiness study.
Specific Laws: Stratégie Nationale d'Intelligence Artificielle (SNIA) 2026-2030, Code du numérique (Loi n°019/AN/23/9ème L, 2023, personal data protection provisions in force 30 June 2025), Loi n°195/AN/25/9ème L portant création de l'Autorité Nationale de Cybersécurité (2025), Stratégie Nationale de Cybersécurité 2024-2030, Loi n°18/AN/23/9ème L portant ratification de la Convention de l'Union Africaine sur la Cybersécurité et la Protection des données à caractère personnel (2024)

Regulation Status: Dominica has no dedicated AI legislation, no binding AI rules and no national AI strategy; the September 2026 Cullen International review of the Caribbean lists only Cuba and the Dominican Republic as having adopted national AI strategies. The National Digital Transformation Strategy 2022-2026 sets digital-government and connectivity goals rather than AI obligations, and the absence of comprehensive data protection legislation leaves no general statute that a regulator could adapt to AI.
Policy Lever: Dominica deploys no AI-specific policy levers: binding rules, published guidance, a sandbox and AI procurement rules are all absent, and no body holds an AI mandate. Digital policy runs through the National Digital Transformation Strategy 2022-2026, delivered with United Nations Development Programme support, while the World Bank-funded Caribbean Digital Transformation Project financed an AI rooftop-mapping pilot.
Governance Type: AI governance in Dominica is undefined: no ministry, regulator or oversight body has been assigned responsibility for AI, and no coordination or subnational mechanism touches it. The only independent engagement is the Eastern Caribbean Supreme Court's work on a judicial AI-use policy, while policy development happens through the Caribbean Telecommunications Union and CARICOM rather than any domestic institution.
Actor Involvement: Dominica runs no domestic stakeholder process on AI, leaving industry, civil society and academia without structured input. Its involvement is collective and regional, through CARICOM's COTED-ICT endorsement of the UNESCO Caribbean Artificial Intelligence Policy Roadmap on 7 July 2026 and the Caribbean Telecommunications Union's Caribbean Artificial Intelligence Task Force, whose final report was launched at the first Caribbean AI Forum on 23-24 July 2026.
Enforcement Level: Dominica has no AI-specific obligations, penalties, supervisory authority or monitoring programme, so nothing is enforced.
Specific Laws: Dominica National Digital Transformation Strategy 2022-2026 (not AI-specific)

Regulation Status: The only binding AI rules are the Ley 74-25 Penal Code articles, in force since 3 August 2026, that punish fabricating or disseminating intimate or deceptive content with artificial intelligence by up to ten years' imprisonment. Governance otherwise rests on Decreto 498-23, which approved the Estrategia Nacional de Inteligencia Artificial (ENIA) with an action plan to 31 December 2030 and requires executive entities to coordinate AI projects with the Gabinete de Innovación y Desarrollo Digital. Two Senate AI bills were merged in the Comisión de Educación Superior, Ciencia y Tecnología in September 2026 and the merged text was still under committee analysis on 6 October 2026.
Policy Lever: Levers are executive and promotional: Decreto 498-23 and Decreto 338-23 assign AI coordination to OGTIC and the Gabinete de Innovación y Desarrollo Digital, the ENIA sets priorities to 2030, and investment flows through the NVIDIA-supported CEIA-RD and public-sector AI training. The National AI Ethics Code remains a draft awaiting presidential decree, and no AI regulatory sandbox or AI procurement rule is in operation.
Governance Type: AI governance is centralised in OGTIC under the Gabinete de Innovación y Desarrollo Digital, a formal interinstitutional coordination mechanism, with DIGEIG and the Ministerio de Administración Pública handling public-sector ethics and the Chamber of Deputies maintaining a permanent AI commission. Sub-national bodies have no regulatory role and judicial or independent review of AI has not occurred.
Actor Involvement: Participation is consultative and episodic: industry, academia and civil society fed into the ENIA, the draft National AI Ethics Code and Senate committee hearings without standing statutory roles. Internationally the country is highly active, hosting the June 2026 UNESCO-linked regional ministerial summit on AI ethics and engaging in the Santiago and Cartagena declarations, PARLATINO model-law work and the Red GEALC.
Enforcement Level: Enforcement is confined to potential criminal prosecution of AI-generated harmful content under Ley 74-25, with no AI regulator, administrative sanctions or published cases.
Specific Laws: Ley 74-25 Código Penal (2025, in force 3 August 2026, AI-generated content offences), Decreto 498-23 approving the Estrategia Nacional de Inteligencia Artificial – ENIA and its action plan (2023), Decreto 338-23 creating the Gabinete de Innovación y Desarrollo Digital (2023), Draft National Artificial Intelligence Ethics Code for the public administration (DIGEIG, 2026, awaiting approval by decree), Merged Senate bill on the ethical and safe use of artificial intelligence (in committee since September 2026), National Innovation Policy 2030 (2022), Ley 172-13 on Personal Data Protection (2013)

Regulation Status: Timor-Leste has no AI-specific legislation, and the UNESCO Readiness Assessment Methodology country report completed in 2025 with the Ministry of Transport and Communications confirms the absence of AI provisions in existing ICT and data-privacy law; the country also lacks a general personal data protection law and authority. Governance activity remains confined to the Timor Digital 2032 national digital strategy, which is being revised to incorporate AI, and to connectivity, national data centre and cybersecurity work presented at the Global AI and Digital Summit in Seoul in October 2026. Constitutional data-protection rights and general electronic-commerce rules apply without any provision drafted for AI systems.
Policy Lever: Policy action consists of soft commitments: endorsement of the UNESCO Recommendation on the Ethics of Artificial Intelligence, the 2025 UNESCO AI Readiness Assessment delivered with the Ministry of Transport and Communications, TIC Timor and Catalpa International, the planned revision of Timor Digital 2032, and a Government Dialogue on Artificial Intelligence held on 24 August 2026. No binding instrument, funded AI programme, sandbox or dedicated institution backs these commitments.
Governance Type: AI policy is concentrated in central government, principally the Ministry of Transport and Communications and TIC Timor, with the Presidency of the Council of Ministers convening the Government Dialogue on Artificial Intelligence with the Presidency of the Republic in August 2026. Coordination is event-driven rather than institutional, and neither municipalities nor independent review bodies play any part.
Actor Involvement: Domestic stakeholder involvement has been limited to the UNESCO-led readiness workshops of April and May 2025, which convened ministries, academia, civil society, development partners and Catalpa International on a one-off basis, and the single-session Government Dialogue of August 2026. International engagement is the more active channel, through the UNESCO Recommendation on the Ethics of Artificial Intelligence, attendance at the 2025 AI Action Summit, the Global AI and Digital Summit in Seoul in October 2026, and ASEAN membership with its non-binding AI governance instruments.
Enforcement Level: Nothing is enforced because no AI obligation, penalty or competent authority exists, leaving the 2025 UNESCO readiness assessment as the sole monitoring output.
Specific Laws: Timor Digital 2032 National Digital Strategy (2023-2032), UNESCO AI Readiness Assessment Methodology country report for Timor-Leste (2025)

Regulation Status: Ecuador regulates AI through binding subordinate rules of the Superintendencia de Protección de Datos Personales: the Norma General para la Garantía del Derecho de Protección de Datos Personales en el Uso de Sistemas de Inteligencia Artificial (Resolución SPDP-SPD-2026-0009-R, reformed by Resolución SPDP-SPD-2026-0037-R), which imposes risk management, impact assessment, transparency, audit and security duties on anyone using AI to process personal data, and the Norma General para el Tratamiento de Datos Biométricos, which restricts mass facial recognition. No statutory AI law exists: the Pleno archived the Proyecto de Ley Orgánica de Regulación y Promoción de la Inteligencia Artificial with 88 votes in September 2026, and twelve AI-related bills, led by the Proyecto de Ley Orgánica para el Desarrollo, Uso Ético y Gobernanza de la Inteligencia Artificial, remain before the Comisión de Educación. Coverage therefore cuts across sectors but is conditioned on personal-data processing.
Policy Lever: Policy runs through binding SPDP resolutions on AI and biometric data, a ministerial AI strategy adopted by Acuerdo Ministerial MINTEL-MINTEL-2025-0030, and the advisory Comité de Inteligencia Artificial created by Acuerdo MINTEL-MINTEL-2023-0019. Funding is decentralised across institutions, with no sandbox, AI procurement rules or published compliance guidance.
Governance Type: Governance is concentrated in the Superintendencia de Protección de Datos Personales, which both writes and enforces the binding AI rules, alongside the digital-transformation ministry that owns the national strategy, linked by the advisory Comité de Inteligencia Artificial. Municipal action is limited to Quito's development declaration, and judicial or independent review of AI rests on general constitutional standards.
Actor Involvement: Industry, academia and civil society feed into AI policy through the Comité de Inteligencia Artificial, SPDP consultations on draft resolutions and legislative hearings, none of which carries a standing decision role. International engagement runs through UNESCO, the ITU, the Global Privacy Assembly and bilateral cooperation with the United Arab Emirates.
Enforcement Level: Enforcement sits with the Superintendencia de Protección de Datos Personales, which has sanctioned general data-protection breaches but has issued no published decision or audit under the AI norm.
Specific Laws: Resolución SPDP-SPD-2026-0009-R, Norma General para la Garantía del Derecho de Protección de Datos Personales en el Uso de Sistemas de Inteligencia Artificial (2026), Resolución SPDP-SPD-2026-0037-R reforming that norm (2026), Resolución SPDP-SPD-2026-0039-R, Norma General para el Tratamiento de Datos Biométricos (2026), Resolución SPDP-SPD-2026-0007-R, Política para el Desarrollo y Uso de la Inteligencia Artificial en Procesos Administrativos de la SPDP (2026), Acuerdo Ministerial MINTEL-MINTEL-2025-0030, Estrategia para el Fomento del Desarrollo y Uso Ético y Responsable de la Inteligencia Artificial en el Ecuador 2025-2029 (2026), Acuerdo Ministerial MINTEL-MINTEL-2023-0019 creating the Comité de Inteligencia Artificial (2023), Ley Orgánica de Protección de Datos Personales (2021), Ley Orgánica para la Transformación Digital y Audiovisual (2023), Ley Orgánica para el Fortalecimiento de la Ciberseguridad (2026), Política Pública de Transformación Digital 2025-2030 (2025)

Regulation Status: Egypt governs AI through dedicated non-binding instruments: the Egyptian Charter for Responsible AI (2023), the National AI Strategy Second Edition (2025-2030) and the March 2026 suite comprising the Guide to Egypt's National AI Governance Framework (edition 2.0), the National Guidelines for Trustworthy and Responsible AI (edition 2.0) and the National Generative AI Guidelines, which set four risk tiers and a dual-check compliance logic without legal force. The Draft Artificial Intelligence Law is before Parliament and has not been enacted, so the only binding rules reaching AI are general or sectoral: Personal Data Protection Law No. 151/2020 with Executive Regulations issued by Decree No. 816 of 2025, whose compliance grace period ended on 1 November 2026, the Non-Banking Financial Technology Law No. 5 of 2022 with FRA Board Decrees Nos. 139, 140 and 141 of 2023, and Cybercrime Law No. 175 of 2018.
Policy Lever: Egypt's toolkit is soft law plus capacity building: the March 2026 governance framework and guidelines, the Applied Innovation Center, the Egyptian AI Institute and policymaker training with UNDP and GSMA. The Financial Regulatory Authority's InsurTech sandbox is operating and hosts AI insurance projects, while the national AI sandbox co-designed with UNDP under the July 2026 agreement has not launched.
Governance Type: Authority is centralised in MCIT and the National Council for Artificial Intelligence, Quantum Computing and Emerging Technologies, renamed by Cabinet in January 2026, with ECRAI operationalising the framework and ITIDA handling technical verification and validation. Sectoral regulators hold assigned roles that only the FRA has actively used, governorates have none, and independent review is limited to general court jurisdiction.
Actor Involvement: Policy development runs through MCIT and ECRAI with standing industry and academic representation on the NCAI, while domestic civil society is not formally included. International engagement spans the OECD, UNESCO, ITU, GSMA and the July 2026 UNDP agreement on responsible AI governance, without accession to a binding AI treaty.
Enforcement Level: Enforcement rests on general data protection, fintech and cybercrime law, since ECRAI's certification and audit functions under the March 2026 framework lack statutory backing and have produced no decisions.
Specific Laws: National AI Strategy First Edition (2021), Egyptian Charter for Responsible AI (2023), National AI Strategy Second Edition (2025-2030), Guide to Egypt's National AI Governance Framework edition 2.0 (2026), Egypt National Guidelines for Trustworthy and Responsible AI edition 2.0 (2026), Egypt's National Generative AI Guidelines (2026), Personal Data Protection Law No. 151/2020, Personal Data Protection Law Executive Regulations issued by Minister of Communications and Information Technology Decree No. 816 of 2025, Non-Banking Financial Technology Law No. 5 of 2022, Financial Regulatory Authority Board Decrees Nos. 139, 140 and 141 of 2023, Anti-Cyber and Information Technology Crimes Law No. 175 of 2018, Cloud First Policy (2024), Draft Artificial Intelligence Law (before Parliament, 2026)

Regulation Status: El Salvador governs AI through a dedicated statute, the Ley de Fomento a Inteligencia Artificial y Tecnologías (Decreto Legislativo 234 of 26 February 2025, in force 11 March 2025), reformed by Decreto 363 (2025), with operative secondary rules in ANIA Resolución 0001/2025 applicable since 2 September 2025. Those rules define 'consequential decisions', require registration in six domains spanning health, credit and insurance, biometrics, public powers, employment and education, and impose disclosure that a decision was AI-driven plus a route to contest it before a human reviewer. Obligations bind across those domains today, but there is no penalty regime and compliance rests on annual self-certification against ANIA-recognised standards and evidence requests.
Policy Lever: Policy runs through binding instruments concentrated in ANIA: Decreto 234 with its Decreto 363 reform, Resolución 0001/2025 setting registration and verification rules, the Ley de Tecnologías Robóticas (Decreto 340 of 3 July 2025) that ANIA also applies, and Decreto 674 of 23 September 2026 declaring national AI and robotics projects of public utility with direct contracting and fast-tracked permits and visas. Economic tools are concentrated in compute and data infrastructure, including NVIDIA B300 operation and the Nemotron Personas El Salvador dataset, while soft law remains thin and the statutory sandbox is a compliance pathway rather than a documented operating programme.
Governance Type: Authority is centralized in ANIA, a presidential agency given technical, budgetary and administrative autonomy by Decreto 363, with the Agencia de Ciberseguridad del Estado handling adjacent data protection and cybersecurity duties. There is no multi-regulator coordination mechanism and no subnational role, and independent scrutiny is limited to internal contestation rights and audit of AI procurement.
Actor Involvement: Policy-making is executive-led, with industry engaged through ANIA advisers, summits and vendor partnerships rather than published consultation, and domestic civil society and universities holding no formal role. International engagement is prominent: co-chairing the UN Global Dialogue on AI Governance, the UNESCO readiness assessment, and accession to the US-led Pax Silica initiative.
Enforcement Level: Supervision is designed to be supportive rather than punitive: ANIA verifies that registered entities hold controls, no AI-specific penalties are defined, and no enforcement decision has been published.
Specific Laws: Ley de Fomento a Inteligencia Artificial y Tecnologías, Decreto Legislativo No. 234 (2025), Reformas a la Ley de Fomento a Inteligencia Artificial y Tecnologías, Decreto Legislativo No. 363 (2025), Resolución No. 0001/2025 de la Agencia Nacional de Inteligencia Artificial (2025), Ley de Tecnologías Robóticas, Decreto Legislativo No. 340 (2025), Disposiciones Especiales para la Ejecución de los Proyectos Nacionales de Inteligencia Artificial, Robótica y Otras Tecnologías Similares, Decreto Legislativo No. 674 (2026), Ley para la Protección de Datos Personales (2024), Ley de Ciberseguridad (2024)

Regulation Status: No AI-specific law is in force and none has reached the legislature. The Ministry of Transport, Telecommunications and Artificial Intelligence Systems has produced terms of reference and a draft bill foreseeing a national AI authority, but no text has been published or tabled, and the only binding adjacent instrument, Ley 1/2016 de Protección de Datos de Carácter Personal, says nothing about AI.
Policy Lever: Policy consists of preparatory drafting inside the Ministry of Transport, Telecommunications and Artificial Intelligence Systems, together with capacity-building such as the UNESCO AI and robotics training programme launched in July 2026 and a new National Digital Economy Strategy being finalised with World Bank support. There is no AI guidance, funding programme, regulatory sandbox or AI procurement rule.
Governance Type: Governance is concentrated in a single central ministry and its Directorate General for Artificial Intelligence Systems, with no coordinating body, no provincial competence and no independent reviewer. The data protection supervisory body foreseen by Ley 1/2016 has never been constituted, so no institution outside the executive touches AI.
Actor Involvement: Participation is ministry-led and episodic: sector technicians attended closed drafting sessions, universities convened the II Foro Nacional de Inteligencia Artificial sponsored by Deep Learning Indaba, and companies met at AI Business Malabo 2026. Domestic civil society is absent, while international engagement runs through African Union and UNESCO frameworks and bilateral training cooperation with China and Russia.
Enforcement Level: Nothing AI-specific is enforceable, no body owns AI oversight, and the adjacent data protection regime has produced no decisions since 2016.
Specific Laws: Ley 1/2016 de Protección de Datos de Carácter Personal (2016), Agenda Digital para Guinea Ecuatorial (ADIGE) 2019-2025, Anteproyecto de Ley reguladora de la Inteligencia Artificial (draft, 2025)

Regulation Status: Eritrea has no AI-specific legislation, no draft AI bill and no AI provision inside general law. The legal anchors that could host AI rules are the Communications Proclamation No. 102/1998, administered by the Ministry of Transport and Communications, and the privacy guarantee of the 1997 Constitution, which has never entered into force; neither refers to artificial intelligence, and the country has no data protection statute or authority.
Policy Lever: Eritrea deploys no policy levers for AI: neither binding rules nor guidance, funding, sandboxes or procurement requirements, and no body holds an AI mandate. Government activity in the digital domain is confined to state control of telecommunications through EriTel under the Ministry of Transport and Communications, with ICT infrastructure described as underdeveloped in the African Development Bank's interim country strategy for 2025-2027.
Governance Type: Governance is fully centralized: a single ministry oversees communications, regional administrations have no regulatory competence, and no independent judicial or oversight institution reviews executive decisions. Nothing in that structure is directed at artificial intelligence.
Actor Involvement: Policy-making is closed to industry, civil society and academia, which are state-controlled or absent. International exposure is nominal and derives from membership rather than action: the African Union Continental Artificial Intelligence Strategy (2024) covers Eritrea without any national declaration, implementation plan or standards contribution.
Enforcement Level: There is no AI enforcement in Eritrea, with no obligations, penalties, designated authority or monitoring.

Regulation Status: Estonia has no standalone national AI statute and applies the directly effective EU AI Act, whose prohibitions, AI literacy duty, general-purpose AI rules and Article 50 transparency obligations bind today, while Annex III high-risk duties run from 2 December 2027 under Regulation (EU) 2026/1744. National implementation consists of the 2 November 2024 designation of fundamental-rights bodies published on kratid.ee, TTJA guidance and Ministry of Justice and Digital Affairs guidance on Article 50 issued 5 August 2026. The implementing act naming TTJA, fixing penalties and creating the AI regulatory sandbox through amendments to the General Part of the Economic Activities Code Act and the State Fees Act remains in preparation.
Policy Lever: Estonia relies on the EU AI Act as its single binding lever and layers domestic soft law on top: the AI and Data Action Plan (Kratt) 2024–2026, the Data and AI White Paper 2024–2030, kratid.ee explainers and ministry guidance on Article 50. Economic levers are substantial — Eesti.ai with €11 million in 2026, the AI Leap education programme and a state-run AI test environment open since February 2026 — but the statutory regulatory sandbox and penalty provisions still await adoption.
Governance Type: AI governance is centred on TTJA as lead market surveillance authority with the Data Protection Inspectorate, the Gender Equality and Equal Treatment Commissioner and the Information System Authority in sectoral roles, steered by the Ministry of Justice and Digital Affairs and the Ministry of Economic Affairs and Communications plus the Government Office's Eesti.ai team. There is no sub-national layer, and independent review of AI decisions has not produced case law.
Actor Involvement: Industry holds the most structured position through the Eesti.ai Advisory Board and AI Leap corporate partnerships, with academics advising on the same bodies and domestic civil society absent from formal structures. International engagement runs through the European AI Board, Council of Europe and OECD channels plus bilateral cooperation such as the 2025 Estonia–Ukraine digital memorandum.
Enforcement Level: The EU penalty framework applies directly and TTJA prepares supervision, but no enforcement action has been taken, national penalty provisions are unadopted and monitoring is limited to occasional studies and parliamentary scrutiny.
Specific Laws: EU AI Act / Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (2024), Digital Omnibus on AI / Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 (2026), AI and Data Action Plan (Kratt) 2024–2026 (2024), Data and AI White Paper 2024–2030 (2024), Draft Act amending the General Part of the Economic Activities Code Act and the State Fees Act establishing the AI regulatory sandbox (2025), Ministry of Justice and Digital Affairs guidance on Article 50 transparency obligations (2026), GDPR / Regulation (EU) 2016/679 (2016), Personal Data Protection Act (2018), AI Action Plan (Kratt) 2022–2023 (2022), National AI Strategy (Kratt 1.0) (2019)

Regulation Status: Ethiopia governs AI through the non-binding National Artificial Intelligence Policy adopted by the Council of Ministers in June 2024, alongside Artificial Intelligence Institute Establishment Council of Ministers Regulation No. 510/2022, which creates the Ethiopian Artificial Intelligence Institute and gives it licensing, evaluation and certification functions over AI products and imported AI systems. Binding duties on AI developers and deployers arise only from general law, chiefly the Personal Data Protection Proclamation No. 1321/2024, and the draft National Data Governance Proclamation referred to the House of Peoples' Representatives on 28 September 2026 regulates data for AI research and digital services rather than AI systems. No cross-sector AI statute has been tabled.
Policy Lever: Ethiopia uses institutional and promotional levers: the Ethiopian Artificial Intelligence Institute under Regulation No. 510/2022, the 2024 National Artificial Intelligence Policy, an AI Startup Center with incubation cohorts, an AI UniPod with UNDP and Addis Ababa University, and the general regulatory sandbox created by Startup Proclamation No. 1396/2025. No AI standards, codes or procurement rules have been issued, and the Institute's certification and licensing powers remain unexercised.
Governance Type: Governance is centralized on the Ethiopian Artificial Intelligence Institute, an autonomous federal body reporting to the Prime Minister's Office, with the Ethiopian Communications Authority enforcing data protection, the Ministry of Innovation and Technology providing policy oversight and INSA covering cybersecurity. Coordination is informal, regional states have no role, and independent or judicial scrutiny of AI governance is absent.
Actor Involvement: Participation by industry, academia and civil society came through the consultative process behind the National Artificial Intelligence Policy and through Institute programmes, but is episodic rather than institutionalized in standing bodies. Internationally Ethiopia is highly active, hosting continental AI governance dialogues in Addis Ababa, completing the UNESCO Readiness Assessment Methodology, endorsing the Paris AI Action Summit statement, cooperating with WHO on AI for health, and working within the African Union Continental AI Strategy and Smart Africa Alliance.
Enforcement Level: No AI-specific penalties, enforcement decisions or audits exist, and the general data-protection regime under Proclamation No. 1321/2024 has yet to produce published enforcement action.
Specific Laws: National Artificial Intelligence Policy (2024), Artificial Intelligence Institute Establishment Council of Ministers Regulation No. 510/2022, Personal Data Protection Proclamation No. 1321/2024, Startup Proclamation No. 1396/2025, Cybersecurity Policy (2024), Digital Ethiopia 2025 Strategy, draft National Data Governance Proclamation (2026)

Regulation Status: Fiji has no binding AI-specific legislation and no AI bill before Parliament; AI commitments sit in the Cabinet-approved National Digital Strategy 2025-2030, which targets a national AI framework by 2027, alongside a 2024 ministerial announcement of measures to protect users from AI threats. Harms involving AI fall back on the Online Safety Act 2018 and the Cybercrime Act 2021, which contain no AI-written provisions, and the Ministry of Education's AI policy for schools was still in consultation in September 2026.
Policy Lever: Fiji relies on non-binding levers: the National Digital Strategy 2025-2030, the Cabinet-endorsed National Privacy and Personal Data Protection Policy of October 2025, and a draft Ministry of Education AI policy. Practical work runs through donor- and partner-supported capacity programmes such as the AI Hub launched in 2024 rather than through funded government schemes, a sandbox, or a mandated institution.
Governance Type: AI policy is centralised in the Ministry of Communications, with the Ministries of Education and Trade pursuing sector initiatives and coordination handled informally. There is no subnational tier of AI rule-making and no judicial or independent-review involvement in AI governance.
Actor Involvement: Industry and academic actors feed into AI policy through National Digital Strategy consultations, the AI Hub and expert reporting, while domestic civil-society input is occasional rather than structured. Internationally Fiji acts through the Pacific Islands Forum, endorsing the region's first collective AI position in September 2026, alongside bilateral digital cooperation with Australia and India and UNESCO support.
Enforcement Level: With no AI-specific obligations in force and no designated authority, enforcement depends entirely on general online safety and cybercrime provisions that happen to capture AI-related conduct.
