Specific Laws: National Digital Strategy 2025-2030, Online Safety Act (2018), Cybercrime Act (2021), National Privacy and Personal Data Protection Policy (2025), Pacific Digital and Artificial Intelligence Technology Principles (2026)

Regulation Status: Finland is governed by the directly applicable EU AI Act, supplemented by the Act on the Supervision of Certain Artificial Intelligence Systems (1377/2025) and amendments to market surveillance, Financial Supervisory Authority and Energy Authority legislation in force since 1 January 2026. Prohibited practices, general-purpose AI duties and Article 50 transparency obligations apply today, with Traficom supervising transparency since 2 August 2026, while high-risk obligations were postponed to 2 December 2027 by Regulation (EU) 2026/1744. The second implementing bill, creating the AI regulatory sandbox, real-world testing rules and the register of high-risk AI in critical infrastructure, was submitted to Parliament as HE 270/2026 on 22 October 2026.
Policy Lever: Finland combines binding EU and national AI instruments with regulator guidance from Traficom, the Data Protection Ombudsman and Tukes, AI literacy work including the Ministry of Education and Culture Citizens' AI Competence Framework (2026), and innovation funding through Business Finland. Supervision rests on repurposed sectoral authorities with explicit legal AI mandates, and the statutory regulatory sandbox is still before Parliament.
Governance Type: Governance is highly decentralised: fifteen sectoral authorities supervise the AI Act under Traficom's statutory coordination and single-point-of-contact role, with the Ministry of Economic Affairs and Employment steering legislative preparation. There is no subnational regulatory layer, and independent scrutiny comes from legislative review bodies and general ombudsman and court oversight rather than AI case law.
Actor Involvement: Industry, civil society and academia engage through published consultations, ministry working groups and expert roundtables rather than standing institutional roles. Internationally Finland is active in EU AI Act governance, EU digital consortia such as ALT-EDIC, and OECD AI cooperation.
Enforcement Level: Full penalty powers and designated supervisors have existed since 1 January 2026, but enforcement so far consists of guidance, complaint handling and transparency monitoring with no published AI Act decisions.
Specific Laws: EU AI Regulation (2024/1689), Digital Omnibus on AI amending Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (Regulation (EU) 2026/1744), Act on the Supervision of Certain Artificial Intelligence Systems (1377/2025), Amendments to Market Surveillance of Products Act (2025), Government Proposal HE 270/2026 amending the Act on the Supervision of Certain Artificial Intelligence Systems (2026), Citizens' AI Competence Framework (2026), Finland's Digital Compass (2022), Artificial Intelligence 4.0 Programme (2020-2022), Finland AI Strategy (2017)

Regulation Status: France applies the EU AI Act directly, with prohibitions and AI literacy since 2 February 2025, GPAI obligations since 2 August 2025 and Article 50 transparency since 2 August 2026, while high-risk obligations were pushed to 2 December 2027 and 2 August 2028 by the Digital Omnibus Regulation (EU) 2026/1744. Domestic AI-specific rules bind for deepfakes (loi SREN of 21 May 2024), algorithmic video surveillance (loi of 19 May 2023, experiment extended to 1 March 2027) and patient information on medical AI. National designation of competent authorities and penalty rules is still carried by the DDADUE bill adopted by the Sénat on 18 February 2026 and stalled in the Assemblée nationale, so implementation remains incomplete.
Policy Lever: France combines directly applicable EU rules, domestic AI statutes and a maintained corpus of CNIL, ANSSI, HAS and DINUM guidance with France 2030 funding channelled through Bpifrance. Institutional capacity sits with CNIL's AI department, PEReN's technical expertise and INESIA's evaluation work, none of which yet exercises AI Act compliance powers.
Governance Type: AI oversight is spread across roughly fifteen sectoral regulators under a Ministry of the Economy-led scheme, with DGCCRF as single point of contact and CNIL designated reference authority only once the DDADUE bill passes. Sub-national bodies deploy but do not regulate AI, while courts, the Défenseur des droits and the independent CNIL act as external checks.
Actor Involvement: Consultation is real but discretionary: industry and civil society respond to CNIL and ministry consultations, while academia is embedded in INESIA and CNIL methodology work. Internationally France is among the most active states, hosting the AI Action Summit and participating in Council of Europe, OECD and European standardisation processes.
Enforcement Level: Enforcement touching AI is carried out under the GDPR by CNIL and under criminal law for deepfakes, with AI Act sanctioning powers not yet conferred on any authority by national statute.
Specific Laws: EU AI Act (Regulation 2024/1689, 2024), Digital Omnibus Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 amending the AI Act (2026), General Data Protection Regulation (Regulation 2016/679), Loi n° 2024-449 du 21 mai 2024 visant à sécuriser et réguler l'espace numérique (SREN), Loi n° 2023-380 du 19 mai 2023 relative aux Jeux Olympiques et Paralympiques de 2024 (algorithmic video surveillance, extended to 1 March 2027), Loi n° 78-17 Informatique et Libertés (1978, amended), Code de la santé publique Article L.4001-3 (2021), National AI Strategy under France 2030 (2021, updated 2025), National Strategy on Data and AI in Healthcare 2025-2028, INESIA Roadmap 2026-2027 (2026), Projet de loi DDADUE n° 118 (2025-2026) designating AI Act competent authorities, adopted by the Sénat 18 February 2026 and pending before the Assemblée nationale, Proposition de loi relative à l'instauration d'une présomption d'utilisation des contenus culturels par les fournisseurs d'intelligence artificielle (adopted by the Sénat 8 April 2026, pending as n° 2634), Proposition de loi n° 3149 visant à garantir le développement de systèmes d'intelligence artificielle éthique et sécurisé (tabled 15 September 2026)

Regulation Status: Gabon's binding AI rules sit in Ordonnance n°0011/PR/2026 du 26 février 2026 on the use of social networks via digital platforms, which defines AI systems, prohibits non-consensual and false-attribution deepfakes, requires labelling of AI-generated or heavily modified content, imposes 24-hour takedown of reported content, and lets the Haute Autorité de la Communication audit platform detection systems. Loi n°025/2023 du 12 juillet 2023 adds AI definitions and rules on automated decision-making and profiling to the personal data protection law. Coverage stays confined to online content and personal data, and platforms have twelve months from the April 2026 publication to come into conformity.
Policy Lever: Policy combines one binding ordinance on AI-generated content, an institutional build-out through the Direction Générale des Technologies Émergentes created by decree on 22 May 2026 and the Comité Technique National sur l'IA, and preparatory work: the UNESCO readiness assessment of 2024 and the national AI strategy drafting launched with UNDP on 28 September 2026, which produced 22 challenges and 36 recommendations but no adopted strategy. Economic levers remain generic innovation measures.
Governance Type: AI governance is centralised in the executive: the Ministry of Digital Economy and its Direction Générale des Technologies Émergentes set policy, the Haute Autorité de la Communication regulates AI-generated content under powers enlarged by Ordonnance n°0013/PR/2026, and the Comité Technique National sur l'IA coordinates. The rules were made by presidential ordinance, and the Constitutional Court dismissed as inadmissible the only challenge brought against a HAC platform measure.
Actor Involvement: Industry, academia and civil society were convened by the Ministry of Digital Economy and UNDP for the national AI strategy diagnostic in Libreville from 28 September to 2 October 2026 and sit on the Comité Technique National sur l'IA, but these are episodic consultations rather than standing roles. Gabon engages internationally through UNESCO, UNDP, UNECA, ITU and African Union frameworks without having ratified the Malabo Convention.
Enforcement Level: AI-related penalties exist on paper and the HAC has acted against platforms under general communication powers, including the suspension lifted on 24 October 2026, but no decision or audit has been issued under the AI provisions while operators remain inside the twelve-month compliance window.
Specific Laws: Ordonnance n°0011/PR/2026 du 26 février 2026 portant réglementation de l'usage des réseaux sociaux via les plateformes numériques en République Gabonaise (2026), Ordonnance n°0012/PR/2026 du 26 février 2026 modifiant le Code de la communication (2026), Ordonnance n°0013/PR/2026 du 26 février 2026 modifiant la loi n°014/2023 relative à la Haute Autorité de la Communication (2026), Loi n°025/2023 du 12 juillet 2023 portant modification de la loi n°001/2011 du 25 septembre 2011 relative à la protection des données à caractère personnel (2023), Loi n°027/2023 du 12 juillet 2023 portant réglementation de la cybersécurité et de la lutte contre la cybercriminalité (2023), Décret portant création, attributions et organisation de la Direction Générale des Technologies Émergentes (2026), Stratégie nationale d'intelligence artificielle (in preparation, 2026)

Regulation Status: The Gambia has no AI-specific legislation, strategy or binding instrument; the Digital Cooperation Organization's October 2025 country report and the Oxford Tech and Justice assessment of June 2026 both record the absence of any AI regulatory framework. The Personal Data Protection and Privacy Act 2025, assented on 7 November 2025, and the Information and Communications Act 2009 are general instruments that reach AI-related data processing and electronic services incidentally. The National Digital Economy Master Plan 2023-2033 refers to artificial intelligence as a capability to be developed but creates no obligations.
Policy Lever: Policy action on AI is limited to aspirational references in the National Digital Economy Master Plan 2023-2033 and a 2024 memorandum of understanding with Presight on digital transformation. Binding leverage comes only from general instruments, principally the Personal Data Protection and Privacy Act 2025, and no AI guidance, funding scheme, sandbox or dedicated unit exists.
Governance Type: Technology policy is set centrally by the Ministry of Communications and Digital Economy, with PURA regulating communications under the Information and Communications Act 2009 and GICTA handling government ICT, and none of these bodies has been given responsibility for AI. There is no coordination mechanism, no subnational tier and no record of judicial or independent review touching AI.
Actor Involvement: No structured domestic engagement with industry, civil society or academia on AI has taken place, because no AI policy process has been opened. International exposure runs through African Union membership and the Digital Cooperation Organization, whose October 2025 country report assessed The Gambia's AI readiness, rather than through national participation in AI governance forums.
Enforcement Level: Nothing AI-specific is enforced, and the only penalties capable of reaching AI use are the general data protection and communications sanctions, which have not been applied to AI.
Specific Laws: Personal Data Protection and Privacy Act (2025), Information and Communications Act (2009), National Digital Economy Master Plan 2023-2033

Regulation Status: Georgia has no cross-sector AI law and no adopted national AI strategy; the UNESCO Readiness Assessment Methodology country report and the June 2026 roadmap article place the country at a foundational stage of AI governance. The single binding AI-specific instrument is the National Bank of Georgia Regulation on Managing Risks for Data-based Statistical, Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning Models, applying to financial institutions, alongside the general Law on Personal Data Protection No. 3144/2023 covering profiling and automated decision-making. The Council of Europe Framework Convention on Artificial Intelligence (CETS No. 225), signed in September 2024, remains unratified.
Policy Lever: Policy runs through funding and donor-supported analysis rather than regulation: the 2026 State Budget earmarks money for AI development, GITA supports startups and AI education, and the EU/UNESCO/PMCG readiness assessment produced the evidence base for a first national AI strategy that has not been adopted. The only binding lever is the National Bank of Georgia model risk regulation, and institutional responsibility stays fragmented and thinly resourced.
Governance Type: AI-relevant competence is dispersed informally among innovation, digital governance, data protection and financial supervision bodies, with no lead authority and no formal coordination mechanism beyond a project steering committee. External scrutiny comes from the Public Defender's 2025 special report and analytical work by organisations such as IDFI, not from courts or sub-national authorities.
Actor Involvement: Participation is project-based: industry, civil society and academia were engaged through the EU-funded UNESCO/PMCG readiness assessment and its April 2026 Tbilisi forum, but no standing multistakeholder structure exists. Internationally Georgia is a Council of Europe AI Convention signatory, a UNESCO Recommendation adherent and a participant in Eastern Partnership digital cooperation.
Enforcement Level: Enforcement rests on general data protection powers and sectoral banking supervision, with no AI-specific penalties, published AI enforcement decisions or routine AI auditing.
Specific Laws: Law on Personal Data Protection No. 3144/2023 (in force March 2024), National Bank of Georgia Regulation on Managing Risks for Data-based Statistical, Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning Models (2022), Council of Europe Framework Convention on Artificial Intelligence CETS No. 225 (signed September 2024, not ratified), Digital Governance Strategy of Georgia 2024-2029, Public Defender of Georgia Special Report on Artificial Intelligence and Human Rights (2025)

Regulation Status: Germany applies the directly binding EU AI Act and executes it nationally through the Gesetz zur Marktüberwachung und Innovationsförderung von künstlicher Intelligenz (KI-MIG), in force since 29 July 2026, which designates the Bundesnetzagentur as central market surveillance, contact and complaints body, sets the national penalty framework and mandates at least one AI regulatory sandbox. Prohibitions, general-purpose AI duties and transparency obligations apply and national penalties became applicable on 2 August 2026, while Annex III high-risk obligations were postponed to 2 December 2027 by the Digital Omnibus on AI, Regulation (EU) 2026/1744. The regime is horizontal in design and operational in its institutions, but incomplete in application.
Policy Lever: Germany combines directly applicable EU binding law with a national execution statute, a dense standards and guidance layer (DIN Normungsroadmap KI, BSI, Datenschutzkonferenz, federal administration guidelines) and economic levers including Hightech Agenda Deutschland KI funding, AI compute investment and the statutory AI regulatory sandbox at the Bundesnetzagentur. The supervisory machinery is designated, staffed and equipped with an AI Service Desk, but compliance powers have not yet been exercised publicly.
Governance Type: Germany runs a hybrid model: one designated central authority, the Bundesnetzagentur, with a statutory coordination and competence centre and complaints office, sitting on top of retained sectoral regulators, the federal and Länder data protection authorities and an instruction-free market surveillance chamber for biometric applications. Courts actively shape AI-related duties, particularly on copyright and automated data analysis.
Actor Involvement: Industry associations and research institutes have repeated, institutionalised roles in German AI policy-making and in the Hightech Agenda roadmaps, while civil society is consulted through ordinary legislative and consultation channels without a permanent seat. Germany is a frontline actor in EU law-making, Council of Europe treaty work and international AI standardisation.
Enforcement Level: A comprehensive statutory penalty, supervision and complaints framework is in force and penalties became applicable on 2 August 2026, but no decisions, sanctions or audit results have been published.
Specific Laws: Gesetz zur Marktüberwachung und Innovationsförderung von künstlicher Intelligenz (KI-MIG, 2026), EU AI Act - Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (2024), Digital Omnibus on AI - Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 (2026), Hightech Agenda Deutschland and KI-Roadmap (2025/2026), Bundesdatenschutzgesetz (2018), Federal guidelines for AI use in public administration (2025), Normungsroadmap Künstliche Intelligenz (2023), Council of Europe Framework Convention on Artificial Intelligence (2024)

Regulation Status: Ghana governs AI through a policy roadmap, the National Artificial Intelligence Strategy 2025-2035 launched by President Mahama on 24 April 2026, while binding coverage rests on the general Data Protection Act, 2012 (Act 843) and Cybersecurity Act, 2020 (Act 1038). The Emerging Technologies Bill, 2025, which would create an Emerging Technologies Agency, is in stakeholder consultation, the Data Protection Bill, 2025 covering AI systems, automated decision-making and deepfakes is not enacted, and the Bank of Ghana announced on 10 October 2026 that an AI directive for the financial sector is under development. No AI-specific obligation is in force in any sector.
Policy Lever: Policy runs through non-binding levers: the National Artificial Intelligence Strategy 2025-2035, the Ghana Artificial Intelligence Practitioners' Guide (2025) developed with GIZ FAIR Forward, and the UNESCO-supported AI readiness assessment funded by the European Union. Funding pledges for an AI Computing Centre and a National AI Fund are announced rather than disbursed, and the only operating sandboxes, at the Bank of Ghana and under the Securities and Exchange Commission's Regulatory Sandbox Licensing Guidelines 2026, are fintech instruments rather than AI rules.
Governance Type: AI governance is centralised in the Ministry of Communication, Digital Technology and Innovations, with the Data Protection Commission, Cyber Security Authority, National Communications Authority and Bank of Ghana acting within existing sectoral mandates and KNUST's Responsible AI Lab providing technical leadership. Inter-agency work is ad hoc through consultations and validation workshops, subnational bodies have no role, and no judicial or independent review of AI has occurred.
Actor Involvement: The Ministry of Communication, Digital Technology and Innovations built the strategy and readiness assessment with KNUST's Responsible AI Lab, supported by UNESCO, the European Union, Smart Africa, GIZ FAIR Forward and The Future Society, and validated through separate academic, private-sector and civil-society sessions. Industry and civil society are consulted episodically, while academia holds the most continuous advisory position.
Enforcement Level: Enforcement touching AI consists of the Data Protection Commission's 2026 compliance drive, which moved from education to spot checks in health, education and finance and police referrals under Act 843, with no AI-specific penalties, authority or audits.
Specific Laws: Data Protection Act, 2012 (Act 843), Cybersecurity Act, 2020 (Act 1038), National Artificial Intelligence Strategy 2025-2035 (launched 2026), Ghana Artificial Intelligence Practitioners' Guide (2025), Emerging Technologies Bill, 2025 (proposed), Data Protection Bill, 2025 (proposed)

Regulation Status: Greece is bound by the directly applicable EU AI Act (Regulation (EU) 2024/1689) and has enacted Law 5321/2026 (Government Gazette A' 114 of 20 July 2026), which designates competent authorities, creates complaint and sanction procedures, a public-sector AI systems registry, an Artificial Intelligence Observatory and transparency duties for AI-generated content, and repeals the AI chapter of Law 4961/2022. Prohibited practices, general-purpose AI duties and AI literacy obligations apply today; the Annex III high-risk regime was deferred to 2 December 2027 and the Annex I regime to 2 August 2028 by the Digital Omnibus on AI (Regulation (EU) 2026/1744). The national framework is complete on institutions but incomplete on implementing decisions, harmonised standards and the regulatory sandbox.
Policy Lever: Greece combines the binding EU AI Act with national Law 5321/2026, a Special Secretariat for Artificial Intelligence and Data Governance within the Ministry of Digital Governance and Artificial Intelligence, literacy and transparency guidance, and funded compute programmes such as the Pharos AI Factory and the DAEDALUS supercomputer. The statutory AI regulatory sandbox and real-world testing regime exist in law but have not begun operating.
Governance Type: Governance is spread across the Ministry of Digital Governance and Artificial Intelligence with its Special Secretariat for Artificial Intelligence and Data Governance, the Hellenic Data Protection Authority as lead market surveillance authority and single point of contact, EETT as notifying authority and host of the Coordination and Expertise Centre, and sectoral market surveillance authorities. Independent bodies with fundamental-rights powers and judicial remedies supply external checks, and no subnational tier regulates AI.
Actor Involvement: Policy-making draws on the academic-led High-Level Advisory Committee, opengov.gr public consultations on the AI Act implementation bill, and AI Act consultation forums attended by industry and the digital-rights NGO Homo Digitalis. Internationally Greece acts through the EU AI Board, EuroHPC, the OECD and UNESCO-linked initiatives rather than through a nationally ratified AI treaty.
Enforcement Level: A complete national sanctions, complaints and supervision framework has existed only since Law 5321/2026 took effect in July 2026, and no AI-specific enforcement decision or monitoring report has been published.
Specific Laws: Law 5321/2026 on Measures Implementing Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (Artificial Intelligence Act) (2026), EU AI Act / Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (2024), Digital Omnibus on AI amending the AI Act, Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 (2026), Law 4961/2022 on Emerging Information and Communication Technologies and Digital Governance (2022, AI provisions repealed by Law 5321/2026), A Blueprint for Greece's AI Transformation (2024), Law 5188/2025 implementing the Data Governance Act (2025)

Regulation Status: Grenada has no AI-specific legislation, draft bill or regulatory proposal, and the September 2026 Caribbean regulatory review confirms that no Caribbean state covered, Grenada included, has adopted an AI-specific framework. The closest adjacent instrument, the Data Protection Act, No. 1 of 2023, remains not in force and contains no AI provision. Official AI activity consists of deploying AI tools in Parliament and government services rather than regulating them.
Policy Lever: Policy activity amounts to public-sector AI adoption — AI tools for parliamentarians and AI-enabled government services run through the Division of ICT — rather than governance instruments. The regional UNESCO Caribbean AI Policy Roadmap endorsed through CARICOM is the only AI policy text Grenada has signed on to, and no national strategy, guidance, sandbox or dedicated institution exists.
Governance Type: Governance is centralized in one ministry's ICT division with no statutory AI mandate, no coordination body and no independent oversight. External engagement runs through CARICOM, the OECS, the Caribbean Telecommunications Union and UNESCO rather than domestic institutions.
Actor Involvement: Domestic stakeholder engagement on AI is absent, with no consultations, working groups or advisory roles for industry, civil society or universities. International participation is the only active strand: endorsement of UNESCO's regional AI roadmap through CARICOM and statements on inclusive, responsible AI use in United Nations land and drought fora.
Enforcement Level: There is nothing to enforce, as Grenada has no AI obligations, penalties, competent authority or monitoring programme.
Specific Laws: Data Protection Act, No. 1 of 2023 (assented 9 May 2023, not yet in force), UNESCO Caribbean Artificial Intelligence Policy Roadmap (endorsed by CARICOM COTED-ICT, 2026)

Regulation Status: Guatemala has no AI-specific law in force. The only AI-specific binding proposal, Iniciativa 6657 on AI-generated falsified content, is pending in Congress alongside personal data protection bills (Iniciativas 6105 and 6572) and Iniciativa 6626 on digital-government interoperability, none reported out of committee. A government AI strategy drafted by the Secretaría Nacional de Ciencia y Tecnología is due to close at the end of 2026, with a multisectoral national strategy planned for 2027.
Policy Lever: Policy action is diagnostic and preparatory: the UNDP-supported AI Landscape Assessment, the UNESCO Readiness Assessment Methodology report delivered to the Superintendencia de Telecomunicaciones, the HumanIA forum convened by the Vice-Presidency and Senacyt, and SEGEPLAN's AI Community of Practice session of October 2026. No binding instrument, published national guidance, sandbox or funded AI programme is in place.
Governance Type: AI governance is embryonic and executive-centred, with Senacyt drafting the government strategy, the Comisión Presidencial de Gobierno Abierto y Electrónico registered as convenor of the Estrategia Nacional de Inteligencia Artificial, SEGEPLAN hosting an AI Community of Practice and the Superintendencia de Telecomunicaciones holding the UNESCO ethics diagnostic. Which institution will lead AI governance is postponed to the multisectoral process beginning in 2027.
Actor Involvement: Engagement is led by the executive together with international partners, principally UNDP and UNESCO, through assessments and the HumanIA dialogue forum, with the Superintendencia de Telecomunicaciones hosting regional AI dialogue in October 2026. Domestic industry, civil society and academic participation is consultative and occasional, with the broad multisectoral process scheduled for 2027.
Enforcement Level: Guatemala enforces nothing on AI, with no sanctions, competent authority or supervisory practice beyond two external diagnostic studies.
Specific Laws: Ley de Acceso a la Información Pública, Decreto 57-2008 (incidentally touches personal data); Iniciativa 6657, Ley de Protección Digital contra Contenidos Falsificados por Inteligencia Artificial (2025, pending); Iniciativa 6626, Ley de Interoperabilidad del Gobierno Digital (2025, pending); Iniciativa 6572, Ley de Protección de Datos Personales (2025, pending); Iniciativa 6105, Ley de Protección de Datos Personales (2022, pending); UNESCO Readiness Assessment Methodology report on AI ethics (2026); Estrategia Nacional de Inteligencia Artificial (in preparation)

Regulation Status: Guinea governs AI by strategy, not law: the Ministry in charge of digital economy validated the National Artificial Intelligence Roadmap 2026-2035 on 20 December 2025, built on the UNDP Artificial Intelligence Landscape Assessment of October 2025, and it creates no obligations. Binding digital instruments, including Loi L/2016/037/AN on cybersecurity and personal data protection and the 2021 decree on electronic transactions reinforced in May 2026, contain no AI-specific provision. Work begun on 19 June 2026 on a National Data Governance Strategy remains at stakeholder-consultation stage.
Policy Lever: Policy runs through a validated ten-year roadmap, donor-funded capacity work with the United Nations Development Programme, public-sector AI and cybersecurity training at the École nationale d'administration in October 2026, and the private AI Xcelerate programme. Institutional capacity is limited to a ministry portfolio and a presidential adviser without regulatory powers.
Governance Type: Authority is concentrated in the executive, combining the Ministry of Communication, Digital Economy and Innovation with a presidential adviser for new technologies and artificial intelligence, supported by the Cité des Sciences et de l'Innovation de Guinée. Coordination with other ministries is event-based, and neither subnational authorities nor independent review bodies take part.
Actor Involvement: Participation is consultative and event-driven: government, business, universities and civil society were convened for the AILA assessment, the roadmap validation and the June 2026 data governance workshop. Internationally Guinea partners with the United Nations Development Programme and Smart Africa and speaks at United Nations AI fora as an African Union member.
Enforcement Level: Nothing about AI is enforceable in Guinea, and monitoring extends only to the one-off national AI landscape diagnostic.
Specific Laws: National Artificial Intelligence Roadmap 2026-2035 (validated December 2025), Loi L/2016/037/AN relative à la cybersécurité et à la protection des données à caractère personnel (2016), Décret D/092/PRG/SGG/2021 portant sur les transactions électroniques (2021), Stratégie Nationale de Gouvernance des Données (drafting launched June 2026), Loi Plan 2026-2040 and Loi-Programme 2026-2030 for the Simandou 2040 programme (2026)

Regulation Status: Guinea-Bissau has no AI-specific legislation, draft bill or binding instrument. The governing digital-policy act remains Decreto n.º 10/2025, which approved the Estratégia Nacional para a Transformação Digital (ENTD.GW), launched on 29 January 2025 and centred on connectivity, public-sector digitalisation and cybersecurity, with artificial intelligence named only as an emerging technology. The Conselho Nacional de Transição, installed after the military takeover of 26 November 2025, approved a digital-integrity law against false and manipulated online content on 20 May 2026, which contains no provision written for AI systems.
Policy Lever: Guinea-Bissau deploys no AI policy levers, binding or non-binding. Digital policy effort is concentrated in the ENTD.GW strategy and in donor-supported connectivity and e-government work backed by UNDP and UNU-EGOV.
Governance Type: There is no institutional architecture for AI governance: no lead body, no sectoral AI mandates, no coordination mechanism and no independent review. Authority over digital policy rests with the Ministério dos Transportes, Telecomunicações e Economia Digital and, for telecommunications, with the Autoridade Reguladora Nacional (ARN), under a transitional administration whose legislative functions are exercised by the Conselho Nacional de Transição.
Actor Involvement: No domestic stakeholder group participates in AI policy, since no AI policy process exists. External involvement runs through development partners—UNDP and UNU-EGOV—supporting the ENTD.GW digital transformation strategy, without any AI-specific international commitment.
Enforcement Level: No AI enforcement framework, competent authority or monitoring activity exists, and only general criminal provisions on false online content could reach AI-generated material.
Specific Laws: Estratégia Nacional para a Transformação Digital (ENTD.GW), approved by Decreto n.º 10/2025; Lei n.º 5/2010, Lei de Base das Tecnologias de Informação e Comunicação (2010); Lei da Integridade Digital on the dissemination of false information on the internet, approved by the Conselho Nacional de Transição on 20 May 2026

Regulation Status: Guyana governs AI through general instruments only: the Data Protection Act 2023, the Electronic Communications and Transactions Act 2023, the Open Data Act 2024 and the Digital Identity Card Act brought into force on 31 March 2026, none of which addresses AI systems. Government effort is concentrated on deployment — Mount Sinai health diagnostics, AI-backed digitisation of the National Insurance Scheme, AI-enabled policing and surveillance, and the Cerebras 100MW data centre at Wales — while Minister Kwame McCoy told the Inter-Parliamentary Union Assembly in April 2026 that legislative frameworks still have to be built.
Policy Lever: Policy levers are limited to general legislation, state-led deployment and infrastructure deals, with no AI guidance, code of practice, regulatory sandbox or AI procurement rule issued. The Data Protection Office, headed by a Commissioner appointed in February 2026, is the only institution whose work touches AI-adjacent automated processing.
Governance Type: AI governance is centralised in the executive, driven by the President and the Minister within the Office of the Prime Minister. No dedicated regulator, coordination structure, subnational competence or independent-review channel shapes AI rules.
Actor Involvement: Domestic AI policy is made inside government, with industry present as technology supplier and civil society and academia limited to workshops and awareness sessions. International engagement is the most developed channel, through CARICOM and the Caribbean Telecommunications Union, the UNESCO Caribbean AI Policy Roadmap, the UN Global Dialogue on AI Governance and the Inter-Parliamentary Union.
Enforcement Level: Nothing AI-specific is enforced, and the newly established Data Protection Office has taken no AI-related action under the Data Protection Act 2023.
Specific Laws: Data Protection Act 2023 (No. 18 of 2023), Electronic Communications and Transactions Act 2023 (No. 12 of 2023), Open Data Act 2024, Digital Identity Card Act (in force 31 March 2026), UNESCO Caribbean AI Policy Roadmap endorsed by CARICOM COTED-ICT (2026)

Regulation Status: Haiti has no AI-specific law, decree or regulation, and no AI bill in any legislative process; the transitional executive has issued no AI decree and Parliament remains non-functional. The only texts reaching AI indirectly are the Arrêté fixant les règles relatives à la protection des données à caractère personnel of 15 May 2018 and the cyber-offence provisions of the Code Pénal (2020). A national roadmap for responsible AI adoption is being drafted outside government by Banj, the Internet Society Haiti Chapter, the École Supérieure d'Infotronique d'Haïti and the Association for Responsible AI under the Inter-American Development Bank-financed ProAI programme.
Policy Lever: Policy activity consists of donor-funded capacity-building rather than rule-making: the IDB-financed ProAI programme run by the incubator Banj, the ProAI network, and a central bank research fund cohort with AI as a priority theme. No guidance, standard, sandbox, procurement rule or AI-mandated public body exists.
Governance Type: There is no state AI governance architecture: no lead body, no interministerial coordination, no subnational competence and no judicial or independent oversight of AI. What coordination exists is private and donor-driven, through the four-party ProAI protocol and the ProAI network launched in August 2026.
Actor Involvement: AI policy discussion in Haiti is carried by a private incubator, a civil-society internet body, a university and an AI association under an IDB-financed programme, not by a government consultation process. Internationally, Haiti participates through ITU and WSIS events, UNESCO cooperation with CONATEL and IDB projects.
Enforcement Level: Nothing is enforced because nothing binding on AI exists, and the only oversight output is a single central bank study.
Specific Laws: Arrêté fixant les règles relatives à la protection des données à caractère personnel (2018), Code Pénal (2020) cyber-offence provisions, Programme de création d'opportunités numériques en Haïti par l'intelligence artificielle (ProAI, 2026) national AI roadmap in preparation

Regulation Status: Honduras has no AI-specific legislation in force and no comprehensive AI bill before the Congreso Nacional. The single legislative initiative touching AI is the June 2026 proposal to reform the Ley Contra el Acoso Escolar (Decreto 96-2014) so that AI-generated intimate montages and digital impersonation are punishable, a narrow and unadopted use-case measure. The Plan Nacional de Gobierno Digital 2023-2026 mentions AI as a challenge without imposing duties.
Policy Lever: Policy action remains soft and project-based: the Plan Nacional de Gobierno Digital 2023-2026, the UNESCO AI readiness assessment completed with SENACIT and DIGER in 2026, a CONATEL-ITU cybersecurity project citing AI risks, an IDB-backed AI tool for public management, and the October 2026 Google Gemini teacher-training programme. No funding scheme, regulatory sandbox, AI procurement rule or body with a legal AI mandate exists.
Governance Type: AI governance has no owner: DIGER handles digital government, CONATEL telecoms and SENACIT science, and cooperation occurs only through individual projects such as the UNESCO readiness assessment. Subnational government and independent review play no part.
Actor Involvement: Domestic stakeholders have no structured route into AI policy, with academic contributions confined to UNAH legal scholarship and industry presence limited to the Google training agreement. International engagement is the most developed strand, through the UNESCO readiness assessment, the SICA regional digital strategy and the Santiago Declaration.
Enforcement Level: Nothing is enforced because no AI obligation, penalty or supervisory authority exists, and the only oversight activity is the one-off 2026 UNESCO readiness diagnostic.
Specific Laws: Plan Nacional de Gobierno Digital 2023-2026, Política Nacional de la República Digital 2022-2025, proposed reform to the Ley Contra el Acoso Escolar (Decreto 96-2014) penalising AI-generated content and digital impersonation (bill, 2026), UNESCO AI Readiness Assessment Methodology report for Honduras (2026)

Regulation Status: AI regulation rests on the directly applicable EU AI Act (Regulation 2024/1689), implemented nationally by Act LXXV of 2025 and Government Decree 344/2025 (X.31.), in force since 1 December 2025, which designate the notifying and market surveillance authorities, set fines in forint and create the Hungarian Artificial Intelligence Council. Prohibitions, general-purpose AI rules and Article 50 transparency duties apply, while Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 (Digital Omnibus on AI, in force 27 July 2026) moved Annex III high-risk obligations to 2 December 2027 and Annex I systems to 2 August 2028. The sandbox provisions of Section 10 of Act LXXV entered into force on 2 August 2026 without a published operating sandbox.
Policy Lever: Hungary combines binding EU-derived instruments with national designation and procedural rules, using the National Artificial Intelligence Strategy 2025–2030 and the Artificial Intelligence Coalition as the soft-law and consultation layer. Economic support comes from EuroHPC compute projects, while the statutory sandbox under Section 10 of Act LXXV of 2025 is unimplemented and the market surveillance function sits inside a ministry rather than a standalone agency.
Governance Type: Governance is centralised in the executive: the AI market surveillance authority, transferred to the Minister of Science and Technology by Government Decree 139/2026 (VIII.31.) and split across named ministry departments in September 2026, acts as general authority and single point of contact, with the National Accreditation Authority notifying and the Magyar Nemzeti Bank covering AI in financial services. Coordination is statutory through the Hungarian Artificial Intelligence Council and the Government Commissioner for AI, with judicial review available but no AI case law and no subnational tier.
Actor Involvement: Industry and academic bodies hold standing advisory seats on the Hungarian Artificial Intelligence Council and contributed through the Artificial Intelligence Coalition to the 2025–2030 strategy, while domestic civil society organisations have no institutionalised role. International engagement runs through EU channels, principally the EU AI Board and EuroHPC projects.
Enforcement Level: Penalties up to HUF 13.3 billion and inspection powers exist on paper, with no AI-specific decision, audit or monitoring report published since the framework entered into force.
Specific Laws: EU AI Act / Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (2024), Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 (Digital Omnibus on AI) (2026), Act LXXV of 2025 on the Implementation in Hungary of the European Union Regulation on Artificial Intelligence (2025), Government Decree 344/2025 (X.31.) on the Implementation of Act LXXV of 2025 (2025), Government Decree 139/2026 (VIII.31.) amending Government Decree 90/2026 (V.13.) on the Duties and Powers of the Members of the Government (2026), National Artificial Intelligence Strategy 2025–2030 adopted by Government Resolution 1324/2025 (IX.3.) (2025)

Regulation Status: Iceland has no AI-specific binding law: the EU AI Act is still under scrutiny for EEA incorporation with no Joint Committee Decision adopted as of October 2026, leaving the Act on Data Protection and Processing of Personal Data No. 90/2018 as the operative binding law. The legislative programme of the 158th session of Althingi lists a Bill on Deepfakes banning certain uses of AI in line with European rules for November 2026, and the Minister of Culture, Innovation and Higher Education announced in September 2026 both an own-initiative AI bill and a later implementation bill. A justice-ministry draft bill authorising police use of AI facial recognition was in public discussion in September 2026.
Policy Lever: Iceland governs AI through soft law and funding: the AI Policy 2021, the AI Action Plan 2025-2027, central guidance on public-sector AI use, Persónuvernd guidance, and AI infrastructure, language-technology and skills funding in the Industrial Policy action plan 2026-2027. The task force report 'Gervigreind til góðs', delivered on 9 October 2026 with 69 proposals, adds advice rather than powers.
Governance Type: AI oversight is centralised in the Ministry of Culture, Innovation and Higher Education and Persónuvernd, with cross-ministry coordination handled case by case through the AI Action Plan 2025-2027 and the 2026 task force on the government's approach to AI. Municipalities have no regulatory role and independent review has so far touched data protection rather than AI.
Actor Involvement: Industry, academia and civil society feed in through open Samráðsgátt consultations and ministry working groups rather than standing bodies, with the July 2026 task force a temporary cross-sector forum. Internationally Iceland signed the Council of Europe Framework Convention on Artificial Intelligence in 2024 and acts through the EEA EFTA incorporation process, Nordic cooperation and the OECD.
Enforcement Level: Enforcement touching AI rests entirely on Persónuvernd's data protection powers, with no AI-specific sanctions, designated AI authority or AI audit programme.
Specific Laws: Act on Data Protection and Processing of Personal Data No. 90/2018, AI Policy 2021, AI Action Plan 2024-2026 (2025), AI Action Plan 2025-2027 (2025), Bill on Deepfakes announced in the legislative programme of the 158th session of Althingi (2026), Industrial Policy of Iceland action plan 2026-2027 (2026), Gervigreind til góðs report of the task force on the government's approach to artificial intelligence (2026), Council of Europe Framework Convention on Artificial Intelligence and Human Rights, Democracy and the Rule of Law (signed 2024)

Regulation Status: India's only horizontal AI obligations are the synthetic-media duties introduced by the Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Amendment Rules, 2026, in force since 20 February 2026, which require labelling, provenance metadata, user declarations and three-hour takedown of court- or government-flagged deepfakes. Beyond that content layer, AI is governed by the non-binding India AI Governance Guidelines (November 2025), sectoral instruments such as the SEBI (Intermediaries) (Amendment) Regulations, 2025, and general law including the Information Technology Act, 2000 and the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023. Minister Ashwini Vaishnaw announced on 8 October 2026 that MeitY would publish a regulation-focused consultation paper on AI safety; no dedicated AI statute has been introduced in Parliament.
Policy Lever: Policy runs through soft law and money: the seven-Sutra India AI Governance Guidelines, the RBI FREE-AI Framework with its June 2026 draft model risk management guidance, SEBI and IRDAI sectoral guidance, and the IndiaAI Mission's compute, dataset and startup funding. Binding leverage rests on the 2026 IT Amendment Rules administered by MeitY and the SEBI AI responsibility provisions, while the IndiaAI Safety Institute, the AI Governance and Economic Group and its Technology and Policy Expert Committee hold coordination and advisory roles without enforcement mandates.
Governance Type: MeitY is the lead body, supported by the inter-ministerial AI Governance and Economic Group created in April 2026, its Technology and Policy Expert Committee and the IndiaAI Safety Institute, with financial and telecom regulators acting within their statutory remits. Courts shape the agenda through deepfake and personality-rights rulings, while state governments confine themselves to AI promotion rather than regulation.
Actor Involvement: Consultation is real but episodic: industry, academic and civil-society comments shaped the 2025 Guidelines and the synthetic-media rules, with academics holding the most durable roles through the drafting committee, the Technology and Policy Expert Committee and the IndiaAI Safety Institute research network. Internationally India is at the frontier, having hosted the February 2026 AI Impact Summit and secured the New Delhi Declaration on AI Impact, while remaining outside binding AI treaties.
Enforcement Level: Enforcement consists of ministry notices, summonses and advisories to platforms, with the February 2026 synthetic-media duties backed by loss of safe harbour rather than by published AI-specific sanctions decisions.
Specific Laws: Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Amendment Rules (2026), Information Technology Act (2000), Digital Personal Data Protection Act (2023), Digital Personal Data Protection Rules (2025), India AI Governance Guidelines – Seven Sutras (2025), SEBI (Intermediaries) (Amendment) Regulations (2025), RBI Framework for Responsible and Ethical Enablement of Artificial Intelligence – FREE-AI (2025), RBI Draft Guidance on Regulatory Principles for Model Risk Management (2026), IndiaAI Mission (2024), New Delhi Declaration on AI Impact (2026), AI Governance and Economic Group (2026), Technology and Policy Expert Committee (2026)

Regulation Status: Indonesia has no enacted binding cross-sector AI instrument: the Presidential Regulations on AI Ethics and on the National AI Roadmap 2026-2029, which would introduce a risk-based classification with high-risk requirements set by each ministry, were finalised and initialled by all ministers but still awaited President Prabowo's signature on 30 October 2026. Binding rules that address AI exist only in narrow fields, through Minister of Health Decree No. HK.01.07/MENKES/951/2026 on marketing authorisation for software-based medical devices and Press Council Regulation No. 1/2025 on the use of artificial intelligence in journalistic works. The rest of governance rests on the non-binding Stranas KA 2020-2045, Komdigi ethics guidance, OJK banking AI governance guidance, and general law on electronic systems and personal data.
Policy Lever: Policy runs through soft instruments — the national strategy, Komdigi ethics guidance, OJK banking AI governance guidance and the Press Council AI guideline — plus capability programs such as the AI Center of Excellence and university AI hubs. Komdigi coordinates AI policy as a ministry directorate without a legal AI mandate, and sectoral ministries are told to write their own AI rules once the Perpres is signed.
Governance Type: Governance is centralised in Komdigi as orchestrator, with OJK, the Ministry of Health and the Press Council acting in their own sectors and BRIN providing technical input, coordinated case by case during Perpres drafting. Sub-national governments have no regulatory role and courts have not reviewed AI rules.
Actor Involvement: Industry and academia feed into AI policy through consultations, working groups and research partnerships, while civil society input is occasional and unstructured. Internationally Indonesia co-founded the World Artificial Intelligence Cooperation Organization, signed the Paris AI declaration, joined the India AI Impact Summit 2026 panel and works through ASEAN and UNESCO AI governance instruments.
Enforcement Level: Enforcement touching AI runs through general electronic information and data protection law, exemplified by the January 2026 blocking of Grok, with no AI-specific penalties, designated authority or audit regime.
Specific Laws: Indonesian Artificial Intelligence National Strategy 2020-2045 (Stranas KA, 2020), Circular Letter of the Minister of Communication and Informatics No. 9/2023 on Artificial Intelligence Ethics, Press Council Regulation No. 1/Peraturan-DP/I/2025 on Guidelines for the Use of Artificial Intelligence in Journalistic Works, Komdigi Artificial Intelligence Guidelines (2025), Indonesian Banking Artificial Intelligence Governance guidance (OJK, 2025), Financial Services Authority Regulation No. 30/2025 on Governance and Risk Management for Financial Sector Technology Innovation Operators, Minister of Health Decree No. HK.01.07/MENKES/951/2026 on Guidelines for Marketing Authorisation of Software-Based Medical Devices, Government Regulation No. 71/2019 on Electronic Systems and Transactions, Law No. 27/2022 on Personal Data Protection, Law No. 1/2024 on the Second Amendment to the Electronic Information and Transactions Law, Draft Presidential Regulation on Artificial Intelligence Ethics (pending 2026), Draft Presidential Regulation on the National Artificial Intelligence Roadmap 2026-2029 (pending 2026), Copyright Bill amending Law No. 28/2014 with provisions on AI training and AI-generated works (in deliberation 2026)

Regulation Status: The National AI Development Law, approved by the Majlis on 19 August 2026, confirmed by the Guardian Council on 26 August 2026, promulgated by Speaker Ghalibaf on 13 September 2026 and communicated for execution by President Pezeshkian on 19 October 2026, is Iran's first binding AI-specific statute, establishing the National AI Organization under the President, a four-tier risk classification and an AI Security Evaluation and Certification Centre. Its twelve articles bind executive bodies across sectors, yet operative obligations depend on secondary rules that do not exist: the organization's statute is still to be submitted to the Council of Ministers, risk-level criteria and cybersecurity directives are unissued, and Article 12 carves out security and defence bodies. The National Artificial Intelligence Document of the Islamic Republic of Iran (2024) and the National AI Roadmap (2025) remain policy documents.
Policy Lever: Iran's dominant levers are state financing and institution-building: the statutory National AI Development Fund of 10,000 billion tomans, sovereign compute and data-centre programmes, a mandated National AI Market, and the National AI Organization acting as secretariat of the National AI Steering Council. Regulatory sandboxes and national AI standards are mandated by Article 7 of the National AI Development Law but are not operating, and no AI procurement rules or published technical guidance exist.
Governance Type: Governance is centralized in the presidency through the National AI Organization and the National AI Steering Council, with the Supreme Council of Cyberspace and security institutions shaping digital policy and the Ministry of ICT and the Vice Presidency for Science and Technology executing parts of the roadmap. Provinces hold no role, and independent judicial or civil oversight of AI is absent, while the Majlis Industries and Mines Commission added a mandatory role for the Seminaries Management Centre in setting sharia requirements.
Actor Involvement: AI policy is formulated by the state, with technical input channelled through the Majlis Research Center, government research institutes and the Supreme Council of the Cultural Revolution rather than structured consultation of industry or independent civil society. International activity is confined to bilateral cooperation with China and Russia and BRICS fora.
Enforcement Level: No AI-specific penalty or enforcement decision exists, and the statutory evaluation and certification machinery is not operating, leaving action against AI services to the general filtering and computer-crimes regime.
Specific Laws: National AI Development Law (2026), National Artificial Intelligence Document of the Islamic Republic of Iran (2024), National AI Roadmap (2025), Computer Crimes Law (2009)

Regulation Status: Iraq has no enacted AI statute; the binding treatment of AI rests on the Communications and Media Commission's Framework Regulations for Digital Platforms and Services of 17 February 2025, which name Artificial-Intelligence Platforms as a licensed category and require compliance with Iraqi AI rules as they are made. The draft Regulatory Framework for Artificial Intelligence Services in the Republic of Iraq, issued under Legislative Order No. 65 of 2004 and opened for a 30-day public consultation on 23 September 2026 with risk-tiered licensing and fines up to IQD 200 million, has not been adopted. The Iraqi National Strategy for Artificial Intelligence (INSAIN) 2024-2030 remains a policy document without legal force.
Policy Lever: Iraq governs AI mainly through executive strategy, the INSAIN 2024-2030 framework and the Communications and Media Commission's general telecommunications and IT powers, with education and training programmes as the principal economic levers. A draft AI services regulation is the first attempt at a binding AI-specific lever, and no regulatory sandbox or AI procurement rule exists.
Governance Type: AI policy is directed top-down from the Prime Minister's Office through the Higher Committee for Artificial Intelligence, with the Communications and Media Commission drafting and applying rules on AI services and individual ministries such as Interior issuing internal AI controls. Kurdistan Region bodies pursue separate AI projects, and independent or judicial review of AI governance is absent.
Actor Involvement: Structured domestic participation is limited to the Communications and Media Commission's open comment periods, most recently the 30-day consultation on the draft AI services regulation that closed in October 2026, which creates no standing seats for industry, civil society or universities. Externally Iraq engages UNESCO AI ethics training and Arab regional digital frameworks, and its Minister of Communications has proposed an international AI and social media framework at the United Nations.
Enforcement Level: Enforcement touching AI occurs solely through the Communications and Media Commission's general licensing and digital content powers, and the supervision and fines of up to IQD 200 million proposed in the draft AI services regulation are not yet in force.
Specific Laws: Draft Regulatory Framework for Artificial Intelligence Services in the Republic of Iraq (2026, public consultation opened 23 September 2026), Framework Regulations for Digital Platforms and Services (2025), Regulation for Organizing Digital Content in Iraq (2023), Iraqi National Strategy for Artificial Intelligence (INSAIN) 2024-2030, Controls and Ethics of AI Use in the Ministry of Interior (2026), Legislative Order No. 65 of 2004 establishing the Communications and Media Commission, Electronic Signature and Electronic Transactions Law No. 78 of 2012

Regulation Status: Ireland's regime combines the directly applicable EU AI Act with the Regulation of Artificial Intelligence Act 2026 (No. 31 of 2026), commenced 31 July 2026, which creates national supervision, investigation and fining machinery and the AI Office of Ireland. Prohibitions, AI literacy, general-purpose AI duties and, from 2 August 2026, transparency and penalty provisions apply, while Annex III high-risk obligations were moved to 2 December 2027 and Annex I products to 2 August 2028 by Regulation (EU) 2026/1744. Coverage is horizontal and purpose-built for AI, and the framework remains inside a transition period with the sandbox and a further Digital Omnibus implementing bill outstanding.
Policy Lever: Ireland uses binding EU and national AI instruments enforced through designated sectoral authorities, supplemented by public-service and regulator guidance and funded adoption programmes such as Intelligence: Applied and the AI Future Skills programme. The statutory AI regulatory sandbox and national AI register are provided for in the Regulation of Artificial Intelligence Act 2026, with the sandbox programme still in preparation by the AI Office of Ireland.
Governance Type: Ireland runs a distributed, sector-based model in which fifteen designated regulators act as market surveillance authorities in their own domains while Oifig IS na hÉireann coordinates, maintains the national AI register and is the single point of contact with the European Commission. Courts enter mainly through High Court confirmation of fines and judicial review, and no sub-national tier regulates AI.
Actor Involvement: Industry, academic and civil society experts hold standing advisory roles through the AI Advisory Council, the AI Literacy Taskforce and NESC, with wider input via public consultation and the Oireachtas Joint Committee on Artificial Intelligence. Ireland is embedded in EU and Council of Europe AI governance and used its 2026 Presidency of the Council of the European Union to host the International AI Summit and deliver the Dublin Declaration.
Enforcement Level: A full investigation and penalty regime is in force and applicable from August 2026, but the only AI-related enforcement so far has been data-protection inquiries rather than decisions under AI-specific rules.
Specific Laws: EU Artificial Intelligence Act / Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (2024), Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 amending the AI Act (Digital Omnibus on AI) (2026), Artificial Intelligence Act (Governance and Enforcement) Regulations 2025 / S.I. No. 366/2025 (2025), Regulation of Artificial Intelligence Act 2026 (No. 31 of 2026), Digital Ireland - Connecting our People, Securing our Future: National Digital and AI Strategy (2026), Intelligence: Applied national AI adoption programme (2026), Dublin Declaration on Trustworthy, Safe and Sovereign Artificial Intelligence (2026), Guidelines for the Responsible Use of Artificial Intelligence in the Public Service (2025), AI - Here for Good: National Artificial Intelligence Strategy Refresh (2024)

Regulation Status: Israel has no horizontal AI statute and governs AI through the December 2023 Policy on Artificial Intelligence Regulation and Ethics, sector guidance and the Protection of Privacy Law 5741-1981 as amended by Amendment 13 (in force 14 August 2025). The single AI-specific binding instrument is the Central Elections Committee's labelling regime for AI-created or AI-altered campaign material, applying to material first published on or after 26 July 2026 and operative through the 27 October 2026 election. Government Resolution 4255 of 16 June 2026 and the National AI Program launched on 10 August 2026 address compute, talent and adoption rather than obligations on developers or deployers.
Policy Lever: Policy runs on funding and soft law: the National AI Directorate's compute, talent and adoption programmes under Government Resolution 4255, Israel Innovation Authority grants, an operating healthcare AI regulatory sandbox, and guidance from the Privacy Protection Authority, the National Digital Agency and the financial regulators' interagency taskforce. The only AI-specific binding lever is the election-advertising labelling requirement.
Governance Type: Governance follows a lead-body-plus-sectoral model, with the National AI Directorate in the Prime Minister's Office coordinating ministries and sectoral regulators acting under their own statutes, joined by a formal interagency taskforce in finance. Judges shape practice directly through the judge-chaired Central Elections Committee and court rulings on AI-generated pleadings, and no subnational tier has any role.
Actor Involvement: Industry and academia engage through published consultations, Israel Innovation Authority programmes and advisory work on the National AI Program, while domestic civil society is confined to occasional public comment. Internationally Israel signed the Council of Europe Framework Convention on Artificial Intelligence in 2024, participates in OECD AI work and pursues bilateral compute and AI partnerships.
Enforcement Level: Enforcement is concentrated in election-period removal orders against unlabelled or misleading AI campaign content from July 2026 and in privacy sanctions under the Protection of Privacy Law, including the fines on EY Israel and PwC Israel in March 2025.
Specific Laws: Protection of Privacy Law 5741-1981 (Amendment 13, in force 2025), Election (Modes of Propaganda) AI labelling regulations for the 26th Knesset election (2026), Israel's Policy on Artificial Intelligence Regulation and Ethics (2023), Government Resolution 4255 'Accelerating Artificial Intelligence in Israel and Establishing Global Leadership' (2026), National AI Program (2026), National AI Directorate establishment decision (2025), Guide for Responsible AI Use in the Public Sector (2025), Interagency Taskforce on AI in the Financial Sector Final Report (2026), Ministry of Justice Regulatory Sandbox Legislative Guidelines (2025), Council of Europe Framework Convention on Artificial Intelligence and Human Rights, Democracy and the Rule of Law (signed 2024)

Regulation Status: Italy applies Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 directly and has completed its national layer: Law No. 132/2025, Legislative Decree No. 160 of 9 September 2026 (in force 30 September 2026) on police use of AI, biometric recognition, civil liability and new criminal provisions including Article 437-bis of the Criminal Code, and Legislative Decree No. 179 of 7 October 2026 (in force 23 October 2026) on supervisory authorities, penalties, sandboxes, employment, training and healthcare. Prohibitions, AI literacy, general-purpose model duties and Article 50 transparency apply today, while Annex III high-risk obligations were postponed to 2 December 2027 by Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 and existing police systems have a one-year adaptation period. The framework is horizontal and sector-specific at once, reaching healthcare, employment, education, justice, public administration, copyright and deepfakes.
Policy Lever: Italy combines four binding AI instruments with ministerial and AgID guidance, an AgID-ACN regulatory sandbox established by Legislative Decree No. 179/2026, AI procurement and literacy duties for public bodies, and a €1 billion state-backed venture fund. AgID and ACN carry legal AI mandates whose inspection and sanctioning powers entered into force on 23 October 2026 and have not yet been used.
Governance Type: Governance is centralised at national level but distributed among AgID as notifying authority, ACN as market surveillance authority and single point of contact, the financial supervisors and the Garante, coordinated through statutory mechanisms and a committee at the Presidency of the Council of Ministers. Regions act only through the Unified Conference and service delivery, while courts and the independent data protection authority have altered outcomes.
Actor Involvement: Industry, unions and academia feed in through AgID consultations, parliamentary hearings on the implementing decrees, ministerial working groups and the expert committee behind the national AI strategy, none of which confers a standing governance role. Internationally Italy is active through its 2024 G7 presidency, EU AI Act negotiation and the Council of Europe Framework Convention on AI.
Enforcement Level: Penalties for AI-specific obligations are comprehensive and took effect on 23 October 2026, while the enforcement record so far consists of data protection decisions against AI providers rather than decisions under AI-specific law.
Specific Laws: Law No. 132 of 23 September 2025 on Artificial Intelligence (2025), Legislative Decree No. 160 of 9 September 2026 adapting national law to Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (2026), Legislative Decree No. 179 of 7 October 2026 on national AI authorities, penalties, sandboxes and training (2026), EU AI Act / Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (2024), Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 (Digital Omnibus on AI) (2026), Italian Strategy for Artificial Intelligence 2024-2026 (2024), Ministry of Labour AI Guidelines No. 180/2025 (2025), Council of Europe Framework Convention on AI CETS No. 225 (2024)

Regulation Status: Jamaica has no AI statute: AI is reached by the Data Protection Act (2020), the Cybercrimes Act (2015) and the Cybercrimes (Amendment) Act (2026), whose passage in February 2026 rejected Opposition calls for express AI and deepfake provisions. The one AI-specific binding instrument is Practice Direction No. 1 of 2025, issued by Chief Justice Bryan Sykes, governing disclosure and permitted use of generative AI in court proceedings. A first National AI Policy is being drafted following the National AI Task Force recommendations (2024) and the UNESCO Readiness Assessment launched in April 2026.
Policy Lever: Policy runs through advisory and preparatory levers: the reconstituted National AI Task Force with policy and legislative deliverables, its 2024 recommendations, the UNESCO Readiness Assessment, a public consultation on the draft national policy, and funded AI skills and public-service AI literacy programmes. The only binding lever written for AI is the judiciary's 2025 practice direction, and the recommended National AI Policy Oversight and Implementation Committee has not been created.
Governance Type: AI policy is centralised in the Office of the Prime Minister through the Minister without Portfolio for Science, Technology and Special Projects, supported by the National AI Task Force, with sectoral regulators engaging within existing mandates. The judiciary acts independently of the executive track through its own practice direction, and there is no sub-national regulatory layer.
Actor Involvement: Participation is channelled through the reconstituted National AI Task Force drawing on industry, academia, public institutions and civil society, reinforced by the UNESCO readiness consultation and the public consultation on the first National AI Policy. Internationally Jamaica works through UNESCO's AI ethics framework, the Caribbean Telecommunications Union's Caribbean AI Task Force and CARICOM processes.
Enforcement Level: Enforcement relating to AI rests on general data protection and cybercrime powers plus court-internal sanctions under the 2025 practice direction, with no AI regulator, AI audit regime or published AI enforcement decision.
Specific Laws: Data Protection Act (2020), Cybercrimes Act (2015), Cybercrimes (Amendment) Act (2026), Practice Direction No. 1 of 2025 (Use of Generative Artificial Intelligence in Court Proceedings), National Artificial Intelligence Policy Recommendations (2024), UNESCO Artificial Intelligence Readiness Assessment Report for Jamaica (2026)

Regulation Status: Japan governs AI through a horizontal promotion statute, the Act on Promotion of Research, Development and Utilization of AI-Related Technologies (Act No. 53 of 2025), in force since 1 September 2025, which establishes the AI Strategy Headquarters, effort duties and a duty to cooperate with state measures rather than enforceable compliance obligations. Implementation on the policy side is advanced, with AI Basic Plan Phase I (23 December 2025) and Phase II (14 July 2026) and the AI Utilization Guidelines of 19 December 2025, while the Act Partially Amending the Act on the Protection of Personal Information (Act No. 56 of 2026, promulgated 17 July 2026) adds biometric and children's data rules inside general data protection law with phased commencement. Liberal Democratic Party proposals of 23 April 2026 to attach penalties for sexual deepfakes and AI copyright infringement have not been enacted.
Policy Lever: Policy runs on soft law and money: a maintained guidance suite from the AI Strategy Headquarters, the Japan AI Safety Institute and ministries, compute and R&D subsidies, a regulatory sandbox, and procurement rules that bind ministries and require Chief AI Officers. The only AI-specific statute confers advisory and information-gathering powers, so institutional capacity is substantial but non-coercive.
Governance Type: Governance is centrally coordinated by the statutory AI Strategy Headquarters under the Prime Minister, with the Cabinet Office secretariat and sectoral ministries plus the Japan AI Safety Institute working within existing remits. Sub-national bodies have no role beyond their own usage rules, and independent scrutiny comes through ordinary litigation.
Actor Involvement: Industry and academic experts sit on the advisory structures around the AI Strategy Headquarters and ministry study groups, while domestic civil society participates mostly through written public consultations. Japan is a convenor internationally through the Hiroshima AI Process, the AI safety institute network and OECD and standards work.
Enforcement Level: Enforcement is advisory, resting on information gathering, administrative guidance and naming, with monetary penalties available only under general statutes.
Specific Laws: Act on Promotion of Research, Development and Utilization of AI-Related Technologies (AI Promotion Act, Act No. 53 of 2025), AI Basic Plan Phase I (2025) and Phase II (2026), Guidelines for Ensuring the Appropriateness of Research and Development and Utilization of AI-Related Technology (AI Utilization Guidelines, 2025), AI Business Operator Guidelines v1.1 (2025), Act Partially Amending the Act on the Protection of Personal Information (Act No. 56 of 2026), Act on the Protection of Personal Information (2003), Copyright Act Article 30-4 (2018), Guideline for Japanese Government's Procurements and Utilizations of Generative AI v2.0 (2026), Intellectual Property Strategic Program 2026, Hiroshima AI Process International Guiding Principles (2023)

Regulation Status: Jordan has no cross-sector AI law; the binding layer is sectoral, consisting of the Central Bank of Jordan's Artificial Intelligence Framework for the Banking Sector issued in August 2025 and a Prime Ministry circular of July 2026 barring AI generation or alteration of national emblems, flags and official seals across government institutions. The economy-wide instruments—the Jordanian Artificial Intelligence Policy (2020), the National Charter of Ethics for Artificial Intelligence (2022) and the Jordanian Artificial Intelligence Strategy and Implementation Plan 2023-2027—remain voluntary, and Personal Data Protection Law No. 24 of 2023 contains no AI-specific provision.
Policy Lever: Policy runs mainly through soft law—the Jordanian Artificial Intelligence Policy 2020, the National Charter of Ethics for Artificial Intelligence 2022, the AI Strategy and Implementation Plan 2023-2027 and the Jordanian Digital Transformation Strategy and Implementation Plan 2026-2028—supported by public-sector training and entrepreneurship incentives. The single binding lever on private actors is the Central Bank's banking AI framework, supervised by an existing regulator rather than a purpose-built AI authority.
Governance Type: Governance is centralised in MoDEE's AI division, with the Central Bank of Jordan as the one sectoral regulator issuing AI rules and the Prime Ministry directing government-wide AI use through circulars. Oversight is executive, with no subnational tier and no judicial or independent review of AI rules.
Actor Involvement: Industry, civil society and academia were consulted in drafting the AI Policy, the Ethics Charter and the AI Strategy and appear in strategy governance structures, but hold no standing formal decision roles. Internationally Jordan works with the EU, UN ESCWA, UNIDO and ITU and joins declarations rather than binding AI instruments.
Enforcement Level: Enforcement is nascent: AI obligations carry no dedicated penalties, oversight rests on existing supervisory and administrative powers, and no AI-specific enforcement decision has been published.
Specific Laws: Jordanian Artificial Intelligence Policy (2020), National Charter of Ethics for Artificial Intelligence (2022), Jordanian Artificial Intelligence Strategy and Implementation Plan 2023-2027, Personal Data Protection Law No. 24 of 2023, Central Bank of Jordan Artificial Intelligence Framework for the Banking Sector (2025), Prime Ministry Circular on the Use of Artificial Intelligence with National Emblems, Flags and Official Seals (2026), Jordanian Digital Transformation Strategy and Implementation Plan 2026-2028

Regulation Status: Kazakhstan regulates AI through a dedicated horizontal statute, Law No. 230-VIII 'On Artificial Intelligence', in force since 18 January 2026, with a risk-based classification, prohibited practices, mandatory labelling of AI-generated content, high-risk system duties and liability insurance. The Digital Code No. 255-VIII adds rights to explanation and human review of fully automated decisions from 11 July 2026, and Law No. 326-VIII of 24 June 2026 refined definitions and data-protection interfaces. Implementing orders on classification criteria, documentation and the trusted digital objects register have been adopted, while further secondary acts remain in preparation.
Policy Lever: Policy combines binding law—the AI Law, administrative-offence penalties, the Digital Code and ministerial orders establishing classification criteria and the trusted digital objects register—with heavy state investment in compute and startup ecosystems through the National AI Platform, Alem.AI, Astana Hub and Data Center Valley. Guidance and standards remain thin relative to the binding layer, and the authorised ministry has not published use of its compliance powers.
Governance Type: AI governance is concentrated in the Ministry of Artificial Intelligence and Digital Development as the authorised body, with its AI and Data Management Committee and the State Technical Service performing technical verification, coordinated through a Prime Minister's implementation order and the Presidential Council on AI Development. Regions implement projects without regulatory powers, and independent review rests on newly created statutory rights rather than established case law.
Actor Involvement: Industry and academic experts channelled input through parliamentary working groups and state-linked institutions such as Alem.AI, Astana Hub and Astana IT University, while organised labour entered the process through the tripartite declaration on human oversight of AI at work of 7 October 2026. Internationally, Kazakhstan positions itself as the Central Asian hub, hosting AI & Digital Bridge-2026 and convening an international presidential AI advisory council, but is party to no binding AI instrument.
Enforcement Level: Penalties for AI-specific breaches are defined and registration and classification machinery is running, but no enforcement decision under the AI Law has been published.
Specific Laws: Law No. 230-VIII 'On Artificial Intelligence' (2025, in force 18 January 2026), Law No. 231-VIII amending legislation on artificial intelligence and digitalisation (2025), Law No. 232-VIII amending the Code of Administrative Offences (2025), Digital Code of the Republic of Kazakhstan No. 255-VIII (2026, in force 11 July 2026), Law No. 326-VIII amending legislation on digitalisation, personal data protection, road traffic and advanced transport technologies (2026, effective 25 August 2026), Prime Minister's Order No. 2-r on measures to implement the laws on artificial intelligence and digitalisation (2026), Order No. 171/NҚ on criteria for classifying informatisation objects as artificial intelligence systems (2026), Order No. 279/NҚ approving the Rules for forming and maintaining the register of trusted digital objects (2026), Presidential Decree declaring 2026 the Year of Digitalization and Artificial Intelligence (2026), Nationwide Strategy 'Digital Qazaqstan' to 2029 (2026)

Regulation Status: Kenya has no binding AI-specific instrument in force. The Artificial Intelligence Bill, 2026 (Senate Bills No. 4 of 2026), sponsored by Senator Karen Nyamu and published on 19 February 2026, was read a First Time on 2 April 2026 and referred to the Senate Standing Committee on Information, Communication and Technology, which reported in October 2026 recommending that the Senate not proceed with it on grounds that it regulates too broadly and too punitively. Regulation of AI therefore runs through the Data Protection Act, 2019, the Computer Misuse and Cybercrimes Act, 2018 and the ODPC Guidance Note on Artificial Intelligence (July 2026), which explains existing duties rather than creating AI-specific obligations.
Policy Lever: Kenya governs AI through soft instruments, standards and spending: the National Artificial Intelligence Strategy 2025-2030, the draft Kenya Artificial Intelligence and Other Emerging Technologies Policy, 2026 (consultation closed 4 August 2026), the ODPC Guidance Note on Artificial Intelligence (July 2026) and Kenya Standard KS 3007:2025. Regulatory sandboxes at the Communications Authority and Capital Markets Authority take AI applications, while a statutory AI authority and AI procurement rules remain proposals.
Governance Type: Policy leadership sits with the Ministry of Information, Communications and the Digital Economy, coordinated since 30 June 2026 by a Standing Cabinet Committee on Artificial Intelligence, while the Office of the Data Protection Commissioner, Communications Authority, Capital Markets Authority and Kenya Bureau of Standards act inside existing mandates. Counties hold no AI role and courts have engaged AI only through isolated litigation.
Actor Involvement: Participation runs through published public-participation processes on the Artificial Intelligence Bill, 2026, the draft Kenya Artificial Intelligence and Other Emerging Technologies Policy, 2026 and the ODPC draft guidance notes, drawing industry, KICTANet, CIPESA, Amnesty International Kenya and university researchers rather than standing seats. Internationally Kenya acts through its Special Envoy for Technology, the International Network of AI Safety Institutes, the UN Global Dialogue on AI Governance, Smart Africa and the African Union.
