Enforcement Level: Enforcement touching AI runs entirely through Data Protection Act, 2019 determinations and penalty notices by the Office of the Data Protection Commissioner, with no AI-specific penalties, authority or audit programme in operation.
Specific Laws: Artificial Intelligence Bill, 2026 (Senate Bills No. 4 of 2026), Data Protection Act (2019), Data Protection (General) Regulations (2021), Data Protection (Complaints Handling and Enforcement) Regulations (2021), Computer Misuse and Cybercrimes Act (2018), National Artificial Intelligence Strategy 2025-2030, Draft Kenya Artificial Intelligence and Other Emerging Technologies Policy (2026), ODPC Guidance Note on Artificial Intelligence (July 2026), Kenya Standard KS 3007:2025 Code of Practice for AI Applications

Regulation Status: Kiribati governs the digital sphere through general instruments - the Data Protection Act 2025, Digital Government Act 2023, Electronic Transactions Act 2021 and Cybercrime Act 2021 - none of which imposes obligations on AI systems, models or outputs. The closest provision is the Data Protection Act 2025 right against decisions based solely on automated processing, binding data controllers generally rather than AI developers or deployers. Parliament has no AI bill before it and the government has published no AI strategy.
Policy Lever: Policy effort concentrates on connectivity, cybersecurity and digital government through the National ICT Policy 2019, Kiribati National Cybersecurity Strategy 2020, Digital Government Master Plan and MICT Ministry Strategic Plan 2025-2028. The only AI-specific commitment is the regionally endorsed Pacific Digital and Artificial Intelligence Technology Principles, unaccompanied by national guidance, funding or a dedicated AI body.
Governance Type: Governance is centralised in MICT, whose Digital Transformation Office drives digital reform, alongside the Communications Commission of Kiribati for telecoms licensing. Nothing in the structure is directed at AI, and no independent body, court or sub-national authority has engaged with AI questions.
Actor Involvement: Engagement on AI occurs almost entirely at regional level through the Pacific Islands Forum, where leaders endorsed the Pacific Digital and Artificial Intelligence Technology Principles in September 2026 as the basis for a Pacific AI Governance Framework in 2027. Domestic industry, civil society and academic participation in AI policy is absent.
Enforcement Level: Enforcement capacity is directed at data protection and cybercrime, with no AI-related investigation, sanction or monitoring activity.
Specific Laws: Data Protection Act 2025, Digital Government Act 2023, Electronic Transactions Act 2021, Cybercrime Act 2021, Communications Act 2013, National ICT Policy 2019, Kiribati National Cybersecurity Strategy 2020, Digital Government Master Plan, MICT Ministry Strategic Plan 2025-2028, Pacific Digital and Artificial Intelligence Technology Principles (2026)

Regulation Status: Kosovo has no AI-specific legislation, and the only instrument reaching AI is Law No. 06/L-082 on Personal Data Protection (2019), which the Information and Privacy Agency applies without any AI-specific provision. AI features only in the e-Government Strategy Kosovo 2023-2027 and the Digital Agenda of Kosovo 2030 as a technology for public-service pilots. Alignment with Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 remains analytical: the Information and Privacy Agency launched its impact assessment of the EU AI Act for data protection on 16 June 2026 with the Office of the Prime Minister's Strategic Planning Office and the Ministry of Digitalization, and a readiness assessment began in 2026, with no bill before the Assembly.
Policy Lever: Policy action is limited to preparatory analysis: the Information and Privacy Agency's impact assessment of Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 on personal data protection, launched 16 June 2026 with the Office of the Prime Minister and the Ministry of Digitalization and Public Administration, and a 2026 readiness assessment for harmonisation. No AI-specific binding instrument, guidance, funding programme, sandbox or dedicated institution exists.
Governance Type: Governance is undeveloped rather than plural: the Information and Privacy Agency acts as focal point through its data protection mandate, the Ministry of Digitalization and Public Administration owns digital strategy, and the Office of the Prime Minister's Strategic Planning Office joined the 2026 EU AI Act impact assessment. Municipalities have no AI role and no judicial or independent review of AI has taken place.
Actor Involvement: Engagement runs through donor- and university-hosted events, notably the Artificial Intelligence Policy Validation Workshop at RIT Kosovo in July 2026 with government, security institutions, industry and academia, rather than institutionalised consultation. International activity is confined to EU accession alignment work and regional digital governance, including the Western Balkans artificial intelligence council agreed in October 2026, with no AI treaty or standards commitment.
Enforcement Level: Enforcement touches AI only indirectly through Law No. 06/L-082 on Personal Data Protection, with no AI-specific sanction, decision or audit practice.
Specific Laws: Law No. 06/L-082 on Personal Data Protection (2019), Law No. 06/L-081 on Access to Public Documents (2019), e-Government Strategy Kosovo 2023-2027 (2023), Digital Agenda of Kosovo 2030

Regulation Status: Kuwait has no AI-specific legislation imposing obligations; AI is governed through general data-protection, electronic-transactions and cybercrime instruments plus the draft Kuwait National AI Strategy 2025-2028 and CITRA's Guide for Adopting Artificial Intelligence in the State of Kuwait v1.0. Ministerial Decision No. 159 of 2026 added "artificial intelligence services and solutions" as a licensable commercial activity, a classification step without compliance duties. The parliamentary bill to establish a Public Authority for Artificial Intelligence lapsed when the National Assembly was dissolved in May 2024 and has not been revived by decree.
Policy Lever: Policy works through soft instruments and promotion: the draft Kuwait National AI Strategy 2025-2028, CITRA's AI adoption guide, the Central Bank of Kuwait Wolooj sandbox and Microsoft skilling and data-centre partnerships. The only binding AI-named measure, Ministerial Decision No. 159 of 2026, is a business-licensing classification rather than a compliance regime.
Governance Type: AI responsibilities sit with executive bodies - the Central Agency for Information Technology, CITRA, the National Cybersecurity Center, the Central Bank of Kuwait and the Ministry of Commerce and Industry - linked only by ad hoc project cooperation, with the strategy's steering committee unestablished. Governance is centralised in the executive with no sub-national tier and no judicial or independent oversight of AI.
Actor Involvement: Engagement is government-led with business input through CITRA's consultation and vendor partnerships, plus an International Labour Organization-Kuwait Chamber of Commerce and Industry study of private-sector AI adoption. Domestic civil society is absent, academic input stays inside universities, and international activity runs through the Digital Cooperation Organization, GCC ministerial channels and the UN Global Dialogue on AI Governance.
Enforcement Level: Nothing AI-specific is enforced; supervision of AI users rests on general data-protection, cybercrime and banking powers that have produced no recorded AI case.
Specific Laws: Kuwait National AI Strategy 2025-2028 (draft, 2025), Guide for Adopting Artificial Intelligence in the State of Kuwait v1.0 (CITRA, 2026), Ministerial Decision No. 159 of 2026 adding artificial intelligence services and solutions as a licensed commercial activity, CITRA Data Privacy Protection Regulation (Decision No. 26 of 2024), Cybercrime Law No. 63 of 2015, Electronic Transactions Law No. 20 of 2014, National Cybersecurity Center (Decision No. 37 of 2022), Kuwait Vision 2035 (2017), lapsed bill establishing the Public Authority for Artificial Intelligence (2023)

Regulation Status: AI regulation runs through Chapter 23 (Articles 191-197) of the Digital Code of the Kyrgyz Republic, in force since February 2026, which defines AI systems and AI systems of heightened danger, sets design and use principles, assigns liability and grants a right to human review of automated decisions. Two binding Cabinet acts operationalise the high-danger tier: the Resolution of 2 December 2025 on danger-assessment methodology and risk-management requirements, and Order No. 1181-t of 31 December 2025 on the content of the conformity declaration. Much of the standard-setting is delegated to self-regulatory organisations, the Regulation on the Ethics of Artificial Intelligence remains a consultation draft from 28 September 2026, and no supervisory authority has been designated.
Policy Lever: Levers combine the binding AI chapter of the Digital Code with its two implementing Cabinet acts on danger assessment and conformity declarations, and executive instruments such as the Concept of Digital Transformation for 2024-2028 and the National Council on Artificial Intelligence Development. Ethics rules, sandbox use and funding remain at draft or announcement stage, and industry standard-setting is handed to self-regulatory organisations.
Governance Type: AI governance is concentrated in the executive, with the Presidential Affairs Directorate absorbing the digital ministry's AI functions in April 2026 and the National Council on Artificial Intelligence Development providing formal interministerial coordination. Sub-national bodies have no regulatory role, oversight of AI decisions rests on the Digital Code's paper right to human review, and professional self-regulatory organisations rather than courts shape day-to-day standards.
Actor Involvement: Participation is executive-led but channels industry through the National Council on Artificial Intelligence Development and through self-regulatory organisations, while civil society groups such as the Media Policy Institute intervene mainly via public consultation on Cabinet drafts. International engagement runs through Commonwealth of Independent States model law work, Shanghai Cooperation Organisation and Eurasian Economic Union digital cooperation, and UNESCO ethics commitments.
Enforcement Level: AI duties under the Digital Code and its implementing Cabinet acts operate through self-declaration, with no AI-specific penalties, no designated supervisor and no recorded enforcement action.
Specific Laws: Digital Code of the Kyrgyz Republic (Law No. 178 of 31 July 2025, in force February 2026), Law on Enactment of the Digital Code of the Kyrgyz Republic (No. 179 of 31 July 2025), Cabinet of Ministers Resolution of 2 December 2025 approving requirements for the methodology of assessing the danger of artificial intelligence systems and requirements for artificial intelligence systems of heightened danger, Cabinet of Ministers Order No. 1181-t of 31 December 2025 on requirements for the declaration of conformity of artificial intelligence systems of heightened danger, Cabinet of Ministers Resolution No. 29 of 22 January 2025 on the National Council on Artificial Intelligence Development (as amended by Resolution No. 844 of 29 December 2025), Presidential Decree of 30 April 2026 on urgent measures for the effective implementation of digital transformation, Concept of Digital Transformation of the Kyrgyz Republic for 2024-2028, draft Regulation on the Ethics of Artificial Intelligence (2026)

Regulation Status: Laos has no binding AI rule in force or formally proposed; the only AI-specific document is the draft National Strategy on Artificial Intelligence 2026-2035, approved in principle in September 2026 and sent back to the Ministry of Technology and Communications for revision on infrastructure, databases, personnel and priority applications. General digital instruments, namely the Law on Cybersecurity (No. 87/NA, 2025, published on the Lao Official Gazette 20 March 2026), Law on Cyber Crime (2015), Law on Electronic Data Protection (2017), Law on Electronic Transactions (2012, amended 2022) and Law on Telecommunications (2011), contain no provision written for AI. The amended Law on Anti-Cybercrime presented to the 2nd Ordinary Session of the 10th National Assembly on 20 October 2026 was justified by AI-generated scams and deepfakes, but its twelve defined offences address digital content and fraud generally.
Policy Lever: Policy action consists of strategy drafting, the UNESCO-supported AI Ethics Readiness Assessment report, government AI service pilots such as LaoAI and G-Chat, and investment promotion for AI and data centres under the 2026-2030 agenda. No AI-specific binding instrument, national AI guidance, regulatory sandbox, AI procurement rule or body with a legal AI mandate exists.
Governance Type: AI policy is centralised in the Ministry of Technology and Communications, with other ministries involved only when the Prime Minister's monthly government meeting reviews draft documents. No subnational, judicial or independent body exercises AI oversight.
Actor Involvement: Domestic industry, civil society and academia were consulted through the UNESCO-led readiness assessment and the January 2026 national AI workshop, with no standing role afterwards. International engagement is channelled through UNESCO, the UN Country Team, ESCAP's APCICT and non-binding ASEAN digital instruments.
Enforcement Level: Nothing AI-specific is enforced in Laos, and AI-related conduct is addressed only through general cybercrime, cybersecurity and electronic data law.
Specific Laws: Draft National Strategy on Artificial Intelligence 2026-2035 (approved in principle September 2026), AI Ethics Readiness Assessment Methodology Country Report (2026), Law on Cybersecurity (No. 87/NA, 2025, published on the Lao Official Gazette 20 March 2026), Law on Anti-Cybercrime (Amended) (draft presented to the National Assembly October 2026), National Digital Economy Strategy (2024), Law on Electronic Data Protection (2017), Law on Cyber Crime (2015), Law on Electronic Transactions (2012, amended 2022), Law on Telecommunications (2011)

Regulation Status: Latvia relies on the directly applicable EU AI Act, whose prohibitions, general-purpose AI rules and Article 50 transparency marking apply while Annex III high-risk duties run only from 2 December 2027 under Regulation (EU) 2026/1744. National AI-specific law comprises the Law on the Latvian Artificial Intelligence Centre with its 14 May 2026 amendments, Cabinet Regulation No. 12 of 13 January 2026 on the special regulatory environment, the Financial Market Digital Operational Resilience and Artificial Intelligence Use Law in force since 1 October 2025, and Criminal Law deepfake provisions. Market surveillance responsibilities were allocated through a Cabinet informative report rather than a general implementing statute, and a horizontal penalties law is still absent.
Policy Lever: Policy runs through binding instruments — the AI Act, the AI Centre Law, Cabinet Regulation No. 12 of 13 January 2026 and the financial market AI law — with the AI Centre's special regulatory environment as the operating innovation tool, now hosting two selected projects. Guidance is limited to VARAM's AI Act information pages and sandbox documentation, and the Centre itself is under-resourced and facing structural reorganisation.
Governance Type: AI governance is led by the Ministry of Smart Administration and Regional Development (VARAM) as coordinator and single contact point, with supervision spread across more than ten sectoral market surveillance authorities, Latvijas Banka for financial-sector AI and the Data State Inspectorate for prohibited practices. The Ombudsman provides independent fundamental rights oversight; no subnational tier participates.
Actor Involvement: The Artificial Intelligence Centre institutionalises industry and university participation through LIKTA and the Latvian Universities Association as co-founders alongside VARAM, while civil society participates only via public consultation on draft legislation. External engagement runs through EU structures, the Council of Europe Framework Convention and Baltic digital cooperation.
Enforcement Level: Penalty ceilings exist in EU law and in the financial market AI law and supervisors are named, but no AI-specific enforcement decision or routine AI monitoring has been published in Latvia.
Specific Laws: EU AI Act (Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, 2024), Digital Omnibus on Artificial Intelligence (Regulation (EU) 2026/1744, 2026), Law on the Latvian Artificial Intelligence Centre (Mākslīgā intelekta centra likums, 2025) with amendments of 14 May 2026, Cabinet Regulation No. 12 'Procedure by which the Artificial Intelligence Centre organises the special regulatory environment and data processing' (Ministru kabineta noteikumi Nr. 12, 2026), Financial Market Digital Operational Resilience and Artificial Intelligence Use Law (Finanšu tirgus digitālās darbības noturības un mākslīgā intelekta izmantošanas likums, 2025), Criminal Law Section 90.1 on influencing the election process using deepfake technology (2024), Digital Transformation Guidelines 2021-2027 (2020), National AI Strategy 'Par mākslīgā intelekta risinājumu attīstību' (2020)

Regulation Status: Lebanon has no binding AI legislation. Governance rests on the National Digital Transformation and Artificial Intelligence Strategy launched on 7 November 2025, a draft National Artificial Intelligence Strategy 2032 opened for public consultation in 2026, the draft Law establishing the Ministry of Technology and Artificial Intelligence approved by the parliamentary Information Technology Committee on 13 January 2026 and by a subcommittee on 27 October 2026, and a draft Digital Authority law. AI-related conduct is reached only by general instruments, principally Law No. 81/2018 on Electronic Transactions and Personal Data, which has no AI-specific provision and no supervisory authority.
Policy Lever: Policy runs through a non-binding strategy, ministerial memoranda of understanding with firms including Oracle, Roland Berger and Sofrecom, and funded capacity programmes such as NUMŪ, the UAE-supported AI training initiative and the World Bank-backed digital transformation programme administered by OMSAR. No AI-specific binding instrument, regulatory sandbox or AI procurement rule exists, and the lead office has no legal AI mandate.
Governance Type: AI policy is concentrated in a single ministerial office that drafts both the strategy and the enabling legislation, with sectoral regulators holding no AI mandate and coordination limited to interministerial contacts and parliamentary committee review of the MITAI bill. Civil society has criticised the concentration of vaguely defined powers in one ministry, and no independent or judicial body shapes AI rules.
Actor Involvement: Engagement is government-led: industry, donors and academia are convened at MITAI summits, through advisory memoranda and via the open consultation on the draft National Artificial Intelligence Strategy 2032, while digital-rights organisations such as SMEX submit comments without a formal seat. International work runs through the Digital Cooperation Organisation, UNESCO, UN ESCWA, the World Bank and bilateral cooperation with the United Arab Emirates rather than treaty or standards bodies.
Enforcement Level: Nothing AI-specific is enforced, the only penalties that could reach AI use come from general law, and no authority, audit or monitoring practice is in place.
Specific Laws: National Digital Transformation and Artificial Intelligence Strategy (2025), Draft National Artificial Intelligence Strategy 2032 (2026, in public consultation), Draft Law establishing the Ministry of Technology and Artificial Intelligence (MITAI) (2025, pending before Parliament), Draft Digital Authority Law (2025, pending before Parliament), Law No. 81/2018 on Electronic Transactions and Personal Data

Regulation Status: Lesotho has no AI-specific legislation. The Artificial Intelligence Policy and Implementation Plan dated 2025 is publicly available only as a second draft, was validated with stakeholders in August 2026 alongside a Data Management Policy and a Broadband and Shared Infrastructure Policy, and proposes institutions that have not been created. AI falls under general law, principally the Data Protection Act 2011 (Act No. 5 of 2012) and the sector mandate of the Lesotho Communications Authority, while the Cybercrime Bill 2026 and Cybersecurity Bill 2026 remain in stakeholder consultation.
Policy Lever: Policy runs through a ministry-led draft AI policy, a United Nations-supported National AI Strategy and Data Centre Blueprint process begun in August 2026, and capacity-building workshops. Economic activity centres on the Convalt Energy hydropower and AI data centre project and a government agricultural AI chatbot rather than funded AI programmes, a regulatory sandbox or AI procurement rules.
Governance Type: AI governance is centralised in the Ministry of Information, Communications, Science, Technology and Innovation, which authored the draft Artificial Intelligence Policy and Implementation Plan, with the Lesotho Communications Authority holding only a general ICT mandate. Coordination occurs through United Nations-supported workshops, and no subnational, judicial or independent-review body participates.
Actor Involvement: Domestic engagement is event-based: a multi-stakeholder validation workshop in August 2026 and United Nations-supported capacity sessions, without standing consultative bodies or published consultation records. Internationally Lesotho is prominent, piloting the United Nations Blueprint for National AI and Data Strategies, addressing the United Nations Global Dialogue on AI Governance, and aligning with the African Union Continental Artificial Intelligence Strategy.
Enforcement Level: Enforcement is absent: no AI-specific obligation is in force, the Data Protection Commission that would apply general data-protection penalties remains unestablished, and no AI audit or monitoring has been carried out.
Specific Laws: Artificial Intelligence Policy and Implementation Plan (2025, second draft), National AI Strategy and Data Centre Blueprint (under development, 2026), Data Protection Act 2011 (Act No. 5 of 2012), Lesotho Communications Authority Act (2012), ICT Policy (2005), Cybercrime Bill 2026 (pending), Cybersecurity Bill 2026 (pending), Africa Declaration on Artificial Intelligence (2025)

Regulation Status: Liberia has no dedicated AI legislation, no national AI strategy and no binding AI-specific instrument. The legal base built in 2026 is general: President Joseph Boakai signed the Cybercrime Act and the Data Protection Act of Liberia, and the Ministry of Posts and Telecommunications issued the "Whole of Government" National Digital Strategy (2025-2029) and a Draft National Data Governance Policy (2026), none of which regulates AI systems, models or outputs.
Policy Lever: Policy activity on AI consists of UNDP-supported capacity building: the AI Training Programme for ministries and public institutions, the UNDP AI Sprint, a UNDP-Intel AI capacity partnership, and work with the University of Liberia towards a first Master of Science in Artificial Intelligence. No binding AI instrument, published AI guidance, sandbox, procurement rule or designated AI body exists.
Governance Type: AI-adjacent oversight defaults to the Ministry of Posts and Telecommunications and the Liberia Telecommunications Authority under general ICT law, a centralized channel with no AI remit. Coordination is limited to whole-of-government digital planning and donor-convened consultations, with no subnational function and no independent or judicial review touching AI.
Actor Involvement: Involvement in AI is driven by UNDP and partners such as Intel rather than by domestic stakeholders, with the University of Liberia as the main national counterpart and the National Elections Commission engaging regionally on AI in elections. Industry and civil society have no structured role because no domestic AI policy process has been opened.
Enforcement Level: Liberia has no AI-specific enforcement framework, sanctions, designated authority or monitoring practice, leaving only untested general cybercrime and data protection penalties.
Specific Laws: Data Protection Act of Liberia (2026), Cybercrime Act (2026), "Whole of Government" National Digital Strategy (2025-2029), Draft National Data Governance Policy (2026), National Cybersecurity Strategy (2025-2029)

Regulation Status: Libya has no binding AI legislation. Governance rests on three non-binding instruments, the National Artificial Intelligence Policy issued by the General Authority for Communications and Informatics on 17 May 2024, the National Artificial Intelligence Strategy 2026-2030 and the National Charter for Artificial Intelligence Ethics adopted in Tripoli on 1 June 2026, whose legislation pillar defers a legal framework to the future. The only binding AI-specific act, Cabinet Decision No. 40 of 2025, establishes the National Programme for Artificial Intelligence and Digital Transformation rather than regulating AI systems.
Policy Lever: Policy runs through soft instruments, the National Artificial Intelligence Policy (2024), the National Artificial Intelligence Strategy 2026-2030 and the National Charter for Artificial Intelligence Ethics, plus one institutional decree, Cabinet Decision No. 40 of 2025. Institutional capacity amounts to a thinly resourced programme attached to the Government Communication Centre and a ministerial portfolio for digital economy and artificial intelligence, with the Strategy's initiatives unfunded.
Governance Type: AI policy is centralised in the Prime Minister's Office through the Minister of State for Digital Economy and Artificial Intelligence, with the General Authority for Communications and Informatics, the General Information Authority and the Government Communication Centre as the other state actors. Coordination is ad hoc through ministerial consultation, no sub-national tier participates, and no independent review mechanism exists.
Actor Involvement: Preparation of the National Artificial Intelligence Strategy 2026-2030 took place inside the state apparatus, with all thirteen consulted bodies being ministries, state regulators or state-linked companies, and only the Libyan Technology Foundation joining a strategy meeting from outside government. Externally, Libya participates in United Nations, International Telecommunication Union and UNESCO artificial intelligence dialogues and is an African Union member.
Enforcement Level: Enforcement is absent because no AI-specific obligation binds anyone, no authority owns AI oversight, and only general cybercrime and electronic transactions penalties could touch AI conduct.
Specific Laws: National Artificial Intelligence Strategy 2026-2030 (2026), National Charter for Artificial Intelligence Ethics (2026), Cabinet Decision No. 40 of 2025 Approving the National Programme for Artificial Intelligence and Digital Transformation (2025), National Artificial Intelligence Policy of the State of Libya (2024), Law No. 5 of 2022 Regarding Combating Cybercrimes, Law No. 6 of 2022 Concerning Electronic Transactions

Regulation Status: Liechtenstein has no AI-specific binding legislation in force: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 and its amending Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 (Digital Omnibus on AI) are marked EEA-relevant but remain under scrutiny by the EEA EFTA states, and the government confirms in BuA Nr. 34/2026 that the AI Act will apply directly only after EEA incorporation. The sole domestic AI-specific instrument is the non-binding KI-Strategie der Liechtensteinischen Landesverwaltung adopted on 14 April 2026, which governs the administration's own use and makes staff training mandatory. Private-sector AI is addressed only through general instruments, notably the Datenschutzgesetz, financial-market supervision and the criminal, media and personality law provisions described in the deepfake Postulat response.
Policy Lever: Policy runs through soft instruments: the Datenschutzstelle's guidance on AI chatbots under data protection law, the Stabsstelle für Digitale Innovation's AI Act information material, and the April 2026 public-administration AI strategy prepared by the Task Force Künstliche Intelligenz. The Datenschutzstelle and the Finanzmarktaufsicht address AI inside their existing mandates, without a dedicated AI remit, an AI sandbox or AI procurement rules.
Governance Type: Competence is spread thinly across the Stabsstelle für Digitale Innovation, which represented Liechtenstein at EU AI Board meetings through the Office for Financial Market Innovation and Digitalisation, the Datenschutzstelle and the Finanzmarktaufsicht, with the Task Force Künstliche Intelligenz as the only standing coordination body. Governance is purely national, and judicial or ombudsman review of AI has not been exercised.
Actor Involvement: International engagement dominates: participation in drafting and signature of the Council of Europe Framework Convention on Artificial Intelligence, observer presence at EU AI Board meetings, and EEA EFTA scrutiny of the AI Act and the Digital Omnibus on AI. Domestic industry, civil society and academic input stays informal and case-by-case, without a standing AI consultation body.
Enforcement Level: Enforcement rests on general data protection, criminal and civil law, with no AI-specific sanctions, no designated AI authority and no AI enforcement decision on record.
Specific Laws: EU AI Act / Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (2024, pending EEA incorporation), Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 Digital Omnibus on AI (2026, under EEA EFTA scrutiny), KI-Strategie der Liechtensteinischen Landesverwaltung (2026, non-binding), Postulatsbeantwortung betreffend Massnahmen gegen Missbrauch durch Deepfakes BuA Nr. 34/2026 (2026), Interpellationsbeantwortung betreffend Künstliche Intelligenz, Cloud-Computing und technologische Infrastruktur BuA Nr. 59/2026 (2026), Datenschutzgesetz (2019), Cyber-Sicherheitsgesetz LGBl. 2025/111 (2025), Council of Europe Framework Convention on Artificial Intelligence CETS 225 (signed 2025)

Regulation Status: Lithuania governs AI through the directly applicable EU AI Act, whose prohibitions, AI literacy, GPAI and Article 50 transparency and marking obligations bind today, while Annex III high-risk duties were pushed to 2 December 2027 by the Digital Omnibus on AI (Regulation (EU) 2026/1744). National implementation rests on the January 2025 amendments to the Law on Technology and Innovation (XV-105) and the Law on Information Society Services (XV-106), effective 1 April 2025, which named the Communications Regulatory Authority (RRT) as market surveillance authority and single point of contact and the Innovation Agency as notifying authority. The dedicated Law on Implementation of the European Union Artificial Intelligence Act, which assigns high-risk supervision to eleven bodies and sets complaint, investigation and liability procedures, passed the Seimas deliberation stage on 15 October 2026 with the adoption vote scheduled for 5 November 2026.
Policy Lever: Binding force comes from the EU AI Act and the two January 2025 implementing laws, supplemented by RRT guidance and FAQs, the Seimas resolution on public-sector AI use and the 2026–2035 National AI Strategic Guidelines. Economic levers are substantial: an operating €3 million AI regulatory sandbox at the Innovation Agency, Lithuanian-language AI resources exceeding €42 million, an SME adoption programme, the LitAI innovation hub and a GovAI competence centre for the public sector.
Governance Type: Governance is centralised around RRT as single coordinating authority and contact point, with the Innovation Agency as notifying authority and sandbox operator; the bill before the Seimas would extend sectoral supervision to eleven bodies including the Bank of Lithuania, the Lithuanian Transport Safety Administration and the National Agency for Education. Sub-national bodies have no role and non-governmental scrutiny is limited to general administrative courts.
Actor Involvement: Industry and academia feed in through the National AI Governance Forum, ministry consultations on the draft implementation law and the Innovation Agency sandbox, while domestic civil society participates only episodically and holds no standing role. International engagement runs through the EU AI Board, EU standardisation work and Council of Europe and OECD processes.
Enforcement Level: EU AI Act penalty ceilings apply and RRT publishes guidance and answers queries on the transparency and marking rules in force, but no AI-specific investigation, decision or audit programme is documented while the national implementation law awaits its final vote.
Specific Laws: EU AI Act / Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (2024), Digital Omnibus on AI / Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 (2026), Law on Technology and Innovation amendments No. XV-105 (2025), Law on Information Society Services amendments No. XV-106 (2025), Draft Law on Implementation of the European Union Artificial Intelligence Act No. XVP-1564 (2026), National Artificial Intelligence Strategic Guidelines 2026-2035 approved by Order No. 4-156 (2026), Lithuanian Artificial Intelligence Strategy (2019), AI Strategy Action Plan 2023-2026

Regulation Status: Luxembourg's binding AI framework is the directly applicable EU AI Act, whose prohibitions, AI literacy duty, general-purpose AI rules and Article 50 transparency obligations apply, while Annex III high-risk requirements run only from 2 December 2027 under the Digital Omnibus on AI (Regulation (EU) 2026/1744). The national implementing instrument, Bill of Law 8476 filed on 23 December 2024, is still in committee, so no authority, penalty regime or statutory sandbox is legally in place and the CNPD acts as de facto coordinator and contact point.
Policy Lever: The binding lever is the EU AI Act, supplemented by CNPD soft law (AI literacy guidance, transparency marking practice, sandbox charter, DaProLab and training sessions) and ILNAS standardisation work. Economic levers dominate: the MeluXina-AI AI Factory, the Mistral AI partnership, the Accelerating Digital Sovereignty 2030 national AI strategy and the CNPD–AI Factory ReMI initiative with its Sandkëscht sandbox.
Governance Type: Governance follows a lead-plus-sectoral design in which the CNPD is proposed as national coordinator and default market surveillance authority alongside roughly eight sectoral regulators, with ALIA named as a fundamental rights authority. Coordination remains informal because the statutory arbitration provisions are still being revised in committee, and there is no subnational layer.
Actor Involvement: Industry speaks through Luxembourg's statutory professional chambers, which formally opined on Bill 8476, and through the ReMI working groups, while academic input comes from the University of Luxembourg, LIST and the AI Factory. Domestic civil society participation is marginal; internationally Luxembourg is active in the EU AI Board, the AI Office network, OECD work and European standardisation.
Enforcement Level: Enforcement is preparatory: no competent authority is legally designated, no national penalties are in force and no AI-specific decision or audit programme exists.
Specific Laws: EU AI Act / Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (2024), Digital Omnibus on AI / Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 (2026), Bill of Law No. 8476 implementing the AI Act (2024, pending), Accelerating Digital Sovereignty 2030 – National AI Strategy (2025), Law of 4 April 2025 implementing the Digital Services Act, Law of 28 February 2025 implementing the General Product Safety Regulation, Bill of Law No. 8364 transposing NIS2 (2024)

Regulation Status: No dedicated AI statute or binding AI rule is in force; AI falls under the general Law on Personal Data Protection (2020) and is framed by the non-binding ICT Development Strategy SMART/MK 2030. The first draft National Artificial Intelligence Strategy, prepared by a Ministry of Digital Transformation working group, was released for consultation in October 2026 with adoption targeted for end-2026, and a separate law on the use of AI is announced for 2027. The Council of Europe Framework Convention on Artificial Intelligence (CETS No. 225), signed 8 May 2026, is neither ratified nor transposed.
Policy Lever: Policy runs through non-binding strategy and funded infrastructure: SMART/MK 2030, the draft National AI Strategy, and the Vezilka National Centre for Artificial Intelligence hosted by FINKI within the European AI Factory network. No regulatory sandbox, AI procurement rules, or body with a statutory AI mandate exists.
Governance Type: Governance is centralised in the Ministry of Digital Transformation, with the Agency for Personal Data Protection supervising data protection and no sectoral or municipal AI role. Scrutiny outside the executive has come from a single State Audit Office performance audit on AI use in the public sector.
Actor Involvement: Domestic input flows through an ad hoc ministerial working group of experts and the academic sector, with FINKI running the national AI centre, while industry and civil society contribute only through announced consultation on the draft strategy. International engagement is the strongest channel through the CETS No. 225 signature, EuroHPC participation, and EU accession alignment.
Enforcement Level: Enforcement reaching AI is confined to general data-protection supervision by the Agency for Personal Data Protection, with no AI-specific sanctions, decisions, authority, or recurring monitoring.
Specific Laws: Law on Personal Data Protection / ZZLP (2020), ICT Development Strategy SMART/MK 2030 (2025), Council of Europe Framework Convention on Artificial Intelligence and Human Rights, Democracy and the Rule of Law CETS No. 225 (signed 8 May 2026), draft National Strategy for Artificial Intelligence (2026), State Audit Office performance audit report on the possibility of using artificial intelligence in the public sector (2025)

Regulation Status: Madagascar has no AI-specific legislation in force. Governance falls back on Loi n° 2014-038 du 9 janvier 2015 sur la protection des données à caractère personnel with Décret n° 2023-1541, and Loi n° 2014-006 sur la lutte contre la cybercriminalité, neither of which regulates AI systems. The pending projet de loi n° 042/2026 reforming cybercrime law, filed on 28 August 2026, covers misuse of digital technologies including coordinated automated manipulation networks, but its vote was postponed and no AI-specific obligation applies.
Policy Lever: Policy action remains confined to the Plan Stratégique Numérique 2023-2028, sectoral AI deployments in customs and civil-registry digitisation, and convening events such as the Indian Ocean Artificial Intelligence Summit held in Antananarivo in May 2026. No AI strategy, guidance document, sandbox or AI-mandated institution has been created.
Governance Type: AI matters sit with the Ministère du Développement Numérique, de la Transformation Digitale, des Postes et des Télécommunications, with the newly operational CMIL covering personal data and digital regulation generally. Coordination is event-driven, sub-national bodies have no role, and independent review of AI is untested.
Actor Involvement: Engagement is largely ministerial and outward-facing, through UNESCO, the World AI Conference, African Union digital frameworks and UN cybercrime treaty ratification. Domestic industry and academia appear at summits and donor projects rather than in policy processes, and civil society influence has been exercised through public protest against the cybercrime bill rather than consultation.
Enforcement Level: Nothing AI-specific is enforced, and the general data protection and cybercrime penalties that could reach AI have produced no published decision even though the CMIL became operational in 2026.
Specific Laws: Loi n° 2014-038 du 9 janvier 2015 sur la protection des données à caractère personnel (2014), Décret n° 2023-1541 d'application de la loi n° 2014-038 (2023), Loi n° 2014-006 sur la lutte contre la cybercriminalité (2014), Plan Stratégique Numérique 2023-2028, Projet de loi n° 042/2026 portant lutte contre la cybercriminalité (2026, pending), Projet de loi n° 043/2026 autorisant la ratification de la Convention des Nations Unies contre la cybercriminalité dite Convention de Hanoï (2026, pending)

Regulation Status: Malawi has no AI-specific binding instrument; the Electronic Transactions and Cyber Security Act (2016) and the Data Protection Act (2024), enforced by MACRA as data protection authority, are the only laws reaching AI and contain no AI provisions. A National Artificial Intelligence Strategy and an accompanying Artificial Intelligence Bill covering government and private-sector AI use are being drafted under the Ministry of Information and Communications Technology, and the Bill has not reached Parliament, whose sitting scheduled for 9 November to 11 December 2026 was postponed.
Policy Lever: Policy action is preparatory: a draft National Artificial Intelligence Strategy, the UNESCO-supported Artificial Intelligence Readiness Assessment Methodology Report validated in July 2026, MACRA's regulatory sandbox and the donor-funded Chichewa language data trust. No funded national AI programme, AI procurement rule or body with a legal AI mandate exists.
Governance Type: AI governance is centralised in the Ministry of Information and Communications Technology, with MACRA the only regulator applying law to AI and the Ministry of Education, Science and Technology and the National Commission for Science and Technology joining readiness work through ad hoc workshops. Oversight comes from parliamentary committees and investigative journalism rather than from courts or an independent AI review body.
Actor Involvement: Consultation runs through national strategy workshops, the UNESCO readiness assessment led by the Ministry of Education, Science and Technology, and the COMESA regional process, drawing in government, industry, academia and development partners. Domestic civil society engages mainly by challenging MACRA's surveillance and monitoring activity rather than through standing consultative roles.
Enforcement Level: Enforcement touching AI rests entirely on general communications, cybercrime and data protection powers exercised by MACRA, producing public warnings and registration enforcement rather than decisions under AI-specific rules.
Specific Laws: Electronic Transactions and Cyber Security Act (2016), Data Protection Act (2024), Draft National Artificial Intelligence Strategy (2026), draft Artificial Intelligence Bill (2026), Malawi Artificial Intelligence Readiness Assessment Methodology Report (2026)

Regulation Status: Malaysia has no binding AI-specific legislation in force. The AI Governance Bill, drafted by the Ministry of Digital and AI Malaysia Berhad on a risk-based design covering accountability, risk management and incident reporting, completed public consultation in July 2026, went to Cabinet in September 2026 and is expected in the Dewan Rakyat in early 2027; the Cybercrimes Act 2026, passed by the Dewan Rakyat on 1 July 2026 and the Dewan Negara on 20 July 2026, creates deepfake and manipulated intimate image offences but comes into operation on a date yet to be appointed. AI is otherwise governed by general law and by the non-binding National Guidelines on AI Governance and Ethics (2024) and the MY-AI Standards platform.
Policy Lever: Policy runs on soft law and economic levers: the AIGE guidelines, MY-AI Standards platform, National AI Action Plan 2026-2030, the MRANTI AI sandbox pilot, startup and talent funding, and Bank Negara Malaysia's discussion paper on AI in the financial sector. Institutional capacity sits with AI Malaysia Berhad, the Malaysia AI Safety Institute, MDEC, CyberSecurity Malaysia and the Department of Personal Data Protection, none holding an AI-specific legal mandate pending the AI Governance Bill.
Governance Type: Policy is centralised in the Ministry of Digital through AI Malaysia Berhad, which institutionalised the National AI Office in July 2026 and houses the Malaysia AI Safety Institute, with sectoral regulators applying their own remits to AI. Subnational activity is limited to Selangor's planned guidelines and white paper, and independent or judicial review of AI matters is undeveloped.
Actor Involvement: Industry, academia, civil society and the public fed into the AI Governance Bill through engagement sessions and the Unified Public Consultation portal in July 2026, but no group holds a standing formal role. Internationally Malaysia is active in ASEAN AI governance, bilateral AI partnerships and international standards alignment.
Enforcement Level: Enforcement touching AI occurs only under general communications, online safety and data protection law, with no AI-specific sanctions, authority or audit regime pending the AI Governance Bill and the commencement of the Cybercrimes Act 2026.
Specific Laws: National AI Roadmap (AI-Rmap 2021-2025), National Guidelines on AI Governance and Ethics (AIGE 2024), Cyber Security Act 2024, Personal Data Protection (Amendment) Act 2024, Online Safety Act 2025 (Act 866, in force 1 January 2026), MY-AI Standards Platform (2026), National AI Action Plan 2026-2030 (AI Nation 2030), Malaysia AI Safety Institute (MY-AISafe, 2026), Cybercrimes Act 2026 (passed by both Houses July 2026, commencement date not appointed), proposed AI Governance Bill (public consultation July 2026)

Regulation Status: Maldives has no binding AI-specific legislation; the National AI Masterplan 2025-2035, announced in October 2024 and recommended for finalisation by the UNESCO AI Readiness Assessment Report of 31 July 2025, is still in draft. President Muizzu announced in April 2026 that a bill establishing a legal framework for AI would be submitted to the People's Majlis, but the 2026 legislative programme that reached parliament covers data protection, digital identity and digital transformation rather than AI systems. AI is addressed only incidentally through the Cyber Security Act (Law No. 17/2023), the Electronic Transactions Act (2022) and general media law.
Policy Lever: Policy runs through strategy drafting, alignment with UNESCO's ethics framework and capacity-building ventures, chiefly the Maldives AI Lab created with Bank of Maldives in May 2026. No binding AI instrument, regulatory sandbox, AI procurement rule or body with a statutory AI mandate exists.
Governance Type: AI governance is centralised in the Ministry of Homeland Security and Technology and executed by the Maldives Digital Service, NCIT and the state-owned Maldives Innovation and Digital Company (MINDCo). Coordination with other agencies has been project-based through the UNESCO readiness assessment, and subnational and independent-review layers are absent.
Actor Involvement: Engagement has been driven by UNESCO's readiness assessment, which drew in government agencies, academics and some stakeholders, and by the public-private AI Lab with Bank of Maldives. Domestic industry and civil society hold no standing formal role in AI policymaking.
Enforcement Level: Maldivian law creates no AI obligations to enforce, and no authority has opened an AI case or conducted AI audits.
Specific Laws: National AI Masterplan 2025-2035 (draft, announced 2024), UNESCO AI Readiness Assessment Report for Maldives (2025), announced bill on regulation of Artificial Intelligence (2026), Cyber Security Act (Law No. 17/2023), Electronic Transactions Act (2022), Maldives Communications Authority / ICT Act (2017), Privacy and Personal Data Protection Bill (2026), Maldives 2.0 Digital Transformation Bill (2026), Digital Identity Bill (2026), Maldives Media and Broadcasting Regulation Act (Act No. 16/2025)

Regulation Status: Mali's only AI-specific legal text, Ordonnance n°2023-022/PT-RM of 4 August 2023 creating the Centre d'Intelligence Artificielle et de Robotique du Mali, establishes a research and training institution and places no obligation on anyone who builds or uses AI. No AI bill, decree or regulation governing AI systems has been tabled, and Loi n°2013-015 of 21 May 2013 on personal data protection contains no provision written for AI.
Policy Lever: Policy runs through institution-building and public investment rather than rules: CIAR-Mali operates a newly funded campus and training programmes, and the Conseil des ministres instituted an annual national AI forum in April 2026. The Politique Nationale de Développement de l'Économie Numérique validated in October 2024 frames digital policy without AI-specific guidance, standards, sandbox or procurement rules.
Governance Type: AI sits with transition-government ministries, the Ministry of Higher Education and Scientific Research for CIAR-Mali and the Ministry of Communication and Digital Economy for digital policy, with the APDP linked only through an ethics partnership. Governance is centralised, with no sub-national competence and no judicial or independent review of AI measures.
Actor Involvement: AI activity is state-led and academic, concentrated in CIAR-Mali and public research institutions, with industry and diaspora experts convened only through the annual national AI forum created in April 2026. Domestic civil society has no formal role, and international engagement is generic rather than AI-specific.
Enforcement Level: AI is unenforced: no AI-specific obligation, penalty, enforcement authority or audit programme exists, and only the data protection regime administered by the APDP reaches AI incidentally.
Specific Laws: Ordonnance n°2023-022/PT-RM du 04 août 2023 portant création du Centre d'Intelligence Artificielle et de Robotique du Mali (2023), Décret n°2023-0420/PT-RM fixant l'organisation et les modalités de fonctionnement du CIAR-Mali (2023), Loi n°2013-015 du 21 mai 2013 portant protection des données à caractère personnel (2013, amended 2017), Politique Nationale de Développement de l'Économie Numérique (2024), Forum national de l'Intelligence Artificielle instituted by the Conseil des ministres (2026)

Regulation Status: Malta's binding framework is the EU AI Act as amended by the Digital Omnibus on AI (Regulation (EU) 2026/1744), operationalised nationally by Legal Notice 226 of 2025 (Artificial Intelligence Regulations) and Legal Notice 227 of 2025 designating the Information and Data Protection Commissioner. Prohibitions, general-purpose AI duties, AI literacy and Article 50 transparency obligations apply today, while stand-alone Annex III high-risk obligations were moved to 2 December 2027 and Annex I embedded systems to 2 August 2028. Coverage is horizontal and cross-sectoral; the national sandbox has a legal basis but has not opened.
Policy Lever: Malta combines the directly applicable EU AI Act with two 2025 legal notices allocating supervisory roles, MDIA voluntary certification and guidance, and the regulator-issued AI Gaming Charter. Economic levers run through the Technology Assurance Sandbox, Digital Europe-funded pilots and budgeted digitalisation money, while the AI Act sandbox and AI-specific procurement rules remain absent.
Governance Type: Governance rests on a dual-authority model: MDIA as default market surveillance authority, notifying authority and single point of contact, and the IDPC for data-sensitive and fundamental-rights-related high-risk systems, with statutory coordination toward the MFSA and MGA. No sub-national tier regulates AI, and the complaint and appeal channels created in 2025 have not yet produced independent review of an AI decision.
Actor Involvement: Industry and academia engage through MDIA and MGA consultations, certification schemes and strategy workstreams, while domestic civil society has no standing formal role. Internationally Malta is a Council of Europe AI convention signatory, an EU AI Board member and a GPAI member since 13 February 2026.
Enforcement Level: Penalties are legislated and authorities designated and resourced, but no AI-specific enforcement decision or market-surveillance report has been published.
Specific Laws: EU AI Act / Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (2024), Digital Omnibus on AI / Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 (2026), Artificial Intelligence Regulations – Legal Notice 226 of 2025 (S.L. 591.05), Artificial Intelligence (Designation of the Information and Data Protection Commissioner for the purposes of Regulation (EU) 2024/1689) Regulations – Legal Notice 227 of 2025, Malta Digital Innovation Authority (Amendment) Act XIX (2024), Malta Digital Innovation Authority Act (Cap. 592, 2018), The Ultimate AI Launchpad: A Strategy and Vision for Artificial Intelligence in Malta 2030 (2019), MGA–MDIA AI Gaming Charter (2026)

Regulation Status: The Republic of the Marshall Islands has no AI-specific legislation in force or in the legislative process. Its 2025 digital package — the Digital Transformation and Identity Verification Act 2025, Electronic Transactions Act 2025, Cybersecurity Act 2025, Cybercrimes Act 2025 (31 MIRC Ch. 5) and Personal Data Protection Act 2025 (6 MIRC Ch. 4, which binds only core Government ministries and agencies and designates the Economic Policy, Planning and Statistics Office as competent authority) — contains no provision written for AI systems or their outputs. Forum Leaders' endorsement of the Pacific Digital and Artificial Intelligence Technology Principles in September 2026 has produced no binding domestic follow-up.
Policy Lever: Policy effort is concentrated on connectivity, electronic identity, cybersecurity and public-sector data protection under the 2025 legislative package and the Digital Republic of the Marshall Islands Project. The only AI-facing instrument is the regional Pacific Digital and Artificial Intelligence Technology Principles, a high-level statement with no domestic funding, procurement rule, sandbox or institutional owner.
Governance Type: Governance is centralized in a small-state executive, with the Ministry of Transportation, Communications and Information Technology leading digital matters and the Economic Policy, Planning and Statistics Office acting as data protection authority for core Government. No AI remit is assigned to any body, and neither local councils nor courts nor independent review bodies have engaged with AI.
Actor Involvement: Domestic AI governance involves no structured participation by industry, civil society or academia because no national process has been established. Engagement is at declaration level: co-sponsorship of the 2024 UN General Assembly resolution on safe, secure and trustworthy artificial intelligence, accession to the Lagatoi Declaration on Digital Transformation of the Pacific in 2023, and endorsement of the Pacific Digital and Artificial Intelligence Technology Principles in 2026.
Enforcement Level: AI is not enforced against in any form, with only generic Cybercrimes Act 2025 penalties theoretically reaching AI-assisted offences and no designated authority, action or monitoring.
Specific Laws: Pacific Digital and Artificial Intelligence Technology Principles (2026, regional instrument endorsed by the Republic of the Marshall Islands at the Fifty-Fifth Pacific Islands Forum), Cybercrimes Act 2025 (31 MIRC Ch. 5, general cybercrime law with no AI provision), Personal Data Protection Act 2025 (6 MIRC Ch. 4, public-sector data protection with no AI provision), Digital Transformation and Identity Verification Act 2025, Cybersecurity Act 2025, Electronic Transactions Act 2025

Regulation Status: Mauritania's AI governance rests entirely on the National Artificial Intelligence Strategy 2024-2029 adopted by the Ministry of Digital Transformation, Innovation and Modernization of Administration, which sets five priorities including data governance and ethical AI but imposes no obligations. No AI-specific statute, decree or bill exists, and Law No. 2017-020 on the Protection of Personal Data still lacks the implementing decrees needed to operate. The Africa AI Governance Index 2026 country profile confirms the absence of AI-specific rules and of any monitoring report.
Policy Lever: Policy action consists of the National Artificial Intelligence Strategy 2024-2029 and donor-funded capacity building through the West Africa Regional Digital Integration Program, whose Mauritanian component was extended to AI data infrastructure, skills and sectoral deployment in June 2026. No AI procurement rule, regulatory sandbox or published AI guidance exists, and no body holds a legal AI mandate.
Governance Type: AI governance is concentrated in a single ministry, with implementation support from the World Bank and no sectoral regulator, interministerial body or independent review mechanism. Subnational authorities play no part, and judicial or ombudsman oversight of AI has not materialised.
Actor Involvement: Engagement is government-led and episodic: ministry events on the National Artificial Intelligence Strategy 2024-2029 drew universities and firms, while domestic advocacy operates outside any formal channel. International involvement is limited to summit attendance and African Union frameworks rather than AI treaty or standards work.
Enforcement Level: Nothing AI-specific is enforced, as the only binding exposure is the penalty regime of a personal data protection law that still awaits implementing decrees.
Specific Laws: National Artificial Intelligence Strategy of Mauritania 2024-2029 (2024), Law No. 2017-020 on the Protection of Personal Data (2017)

Regulation Status: Mauritius has no horizontal binding AI legislation; the National AI Strategy 2025-2029 ("AI for Mauritius", adopted by Cabinet on 13 February 2026) and the FAIR Guidelines launched on 10 April 2026 are non-binding. The single binding AI-specific instrument remains the Financial Services (Robotic and Artificial Intelligence Enabled Advisory Services) Rules 2021, supported by the Financial Services Commission's non-binding Fintech Series Guidance Notes No. 4 of September 2025. The Data Protection Act 2017 touches AI only incidentally, and the Economic and Financial Measures (Miscellaneous Provisions) Act 2026 addresses AI through the AI City Scheme inserted as section 14AA of the Economic Development Board Act rather than through conduct rules.
Policy Lever: Policy runs mainly through soft law and fiscal incentives: the National AI Strategy 2025-2029 and FAIR Guidelines developed with UNDP support, FSC guidance for non-bank financial services, and budget measures including the Public Sector AI Programme, start-up support, AI investment tax credits under the Finance Act 2026 and the AI City Scheme enacted in the Economic and Financial Measures (Miscellaneous Provisions) Act 2026. Institutional capacity rests on the MITCI AI Unit without statutory powers alongside the Financial Services Commission, the Data Protection Office and the National Computer Board; the Mauritius Artificial Intelligence Council proposed in the 2018 strategy was never constituted.
Governance Type: Governance pairs a central ministerial AI Unit at MITCI with sectoral regulators, the Financial Services Commission for AI in non-bank finance and the Data Protection Office for data aspects, coordinated informally rather than through a statutory body. There is no sub-national tier and independent review of AI has not been exercised by courts or the ombudsman.
Actor Involvement: The National AI Strategy 2025-2029 and FAIR Guidelines emerged from one-off multi-stakeholder consultations involving industry, start-ups, academia and civil society rather than standing advisory bodies. International engagement is channelled through UNDP technical cooperation and African Union and Smart Africa membership.
Enforcement Level: Enforcement capacity exists only in non-bank financial services through the Financial Services Commission's licensing and sanctioning powers, and no AI-specific action or audit has been published.
Specific Laws: National AI Strategy (2018), Data Protection Act (2017), Financial Services (Robotic and Artificial Intelligence Enabled Advisory Services) Rules (2021), Digital Transformation Blueprint 2025-2029, FSC Fintech Series Guidance Notes No. 4 on the Responsible Use of Artificial Intelligence in Financial Services (2025), National AI Strategy 2025-2029 "AI for Mauritius" (2026), FAIR Guidelines (2026), Economic and Financial Measures (Miscellaneous Provisions) Act 2026 (AI City Scheme), Finance Act 2026 (investment tax credit on artificial intelligence expenditure)

Regulation Status: No general AI law is in force: the Ley General para Regular y Fomentar la Inteligencia Artificial drafted by the Senate commission chaired by Rolando Zapata Bello (223 articles) and the Ley General para el Desarrollo de la Inteligencia Artificial y el Impulso del Futuro Digital filed on 29 September 2026 remain without a committee vote, as do several initiatives to amend article 73 of the Constitution to give Congress AI competence. Binding AI provisions exist only inside adapted general law—the decree reforming the Ley Federal del Trabajo and the Ley Federal del Derecho de Autor published on 14 May 2026 against unauthorised AI cloning of voice, image and performances, and the 2025 data protection rules on automated decision-making—supplemented by Instituto Nacional Electoral guidelines that ban deepfakes in electoral propaganda and were tightened on 3 September 2026 to protect minors.
Policy Lever: Mexico governs AI mainly through programmatic and soft-law levers—the Plan Nacional de Inteligencia Artificial, the Principios de Chapultepec, the ATDT Fábrica de IA, the Coatlicue supercomputer project and public-sector AI training—alongside a single AI-specific binding reform in labour and copyright law. No body holds statutory AI compliance powers, and neither AI procurement rules nor a regulatory sandbox exists.
Governance Type: Oversight is dispersed across the ATDT, SECIHTI, the Secretaría Anticorrupción y Buen Gobierno, sectoral regulators and the autonomous Instituto Nacional Electoral, coordinated informally through the Plan Nacional de Inteligencia Artificial rather than a statutory mechanism. States legislate on AI independently of any federal framework, with dozens of local laws and penal reforms already approved.
Actor Involvement: Industry and academia feed into AI policy through Senate commission roundtables, university forums and the Propuesta de Agenda Nacional de Inteligencia Artificial 2024-2030, while domestic civil society has no standing channel. International engagement runs through UNESCO readiness work, OECD forums and regional declarations rather than binding treaties.
Enforcement Level: Penalties reach AI conduct through copyright, labour, data protection and electoral rules, but no AI enforcement authority, published AI sanction decision or auditing regime exists.
Specific Laws: Decreto por el que se reforman la Ley Federal del Trabajo y la Ley Federal del Derecho de Autor en materia de inteligencia artificial (2026), Ley Federal de Protección de Datos Personales en Posesión de los Particulares (2025), Ley Federal de Telecomunicaciones y Radiodifusión (2025), Plan Nacional de Inteligencia Artificial (2026), Principios de Chapultepec (2026), Propuesta de Agenda Nacional de Inteligencia Artificial 2024-2030, Lineamientos y principios para el desarrollo estratégico y uso regulado de la inteligencia artificial en el Instituto Nacional Electoral (INE/JGE175/2025), Ley General para Regular y Fomentar la Inteligencia Artificial (draft, 2026), Ley General para el Desarrollo de la Inteligencia Artificial y el Impulso del Futuro Digital (iniciativa, 2026)

Regulation Status: The Federated States of Micronesia has no AI-specific legislation and no binding AI rules in force or before the Twenty-Fourth Congress. Technology policy is limited to the National ICT and Telecommunications Policy (2012), the Cybersecurity Roadmap (2021), and a pending Personal Data Protection Act of 2025 covering national government departments, none of which contain provisions written for AI systems.
Policy Lever: Policy levers for AI are absent: no binding instrument, guidance document, funding or sandbox program, or dedicated institution. Government digital effort concentrates on connectivity, cybersecurity capacity-building and a pending data protection bill.
Governance Type: No AI governance structure of any kind exists at national or state level, so there is nothing to coordinate and no independent review of AI decisions. Sectoral bodies such as the Telecommunications Regulation Authority operate without any AI remit.
Actor Involvement: Domestic engagement on AI policy is absent across industry, civil society and academia because no AI policy process has been opened. International involvement is confined to general UN membership and Pacific regional digital and ICT dialogues, including Pacific Islands Forum digital transformation commitments.
Enforcement Level: There is no AI enforcement framework, designated authority, penalty or monitoring activity in the Federated States of Micronesia.

Regulation Status: Moldova has no cross-sector AI law; the binding rules written for AI are the Framework Regulation on Academic Integrity in Higher Education Institutions approved on 24 June 2026 and the accompanying Ministry of Education and Research anti-plagiarism methodological standards. The Ministry of Economic Development and Digitalization opened drafting of a law on artificial intelligence on 21 May 2026, and the Central Electoral Commission's Electoral Code amendments on electoral influencers and AI in campaigns remain drafts. Law No. 195/2024 on Personal Data Protection, applicable since 23 August 2026, contains no AI-specific provision, and the Council of Europe Framework Convention on Artificial Intelligence stays signed and unratified.
Policy Lever: Policy is delivered through soft instruments and funding: the White Paper on Data Management and Artificial Intelligence (2024), the draft National Programme on Artificial Intelligence and Data Management 2026-2030 consulted to 12 May 2026, the Moldova AI Hub launched in October 2026, and the FAIMA AI antenna. Institutional machinery is the Ministry of Economic Development and Digitalization plus the consultative Sub-Council for Artificial Intelligence and Applied Research, neither with compliance powers.
Governance Type: Governance is centralised in the Ministry of Economic Development and Digitalization, with sectoral ownership split between the Ministry of Education and Research for academic AI rules, the National Centre for Personal Data Protection for data, and the Central Electoral Commission for campaign content. The Sub-Council for Artificial Intelligence and Applied Research provides the formal coordination venue; there is no subnational tier and no judicial or ombudsman practice on AI.
Actor Involvement: Industry, universities, United Nations agencies and development partners hold standing consultative roles through the Sub-Council for Artificial Intelligence and Applied Research and the Moldova AI Hub consortium, while civil society participates mainly via government public consultations. Internationally Moldova is a Framework Convention signatory without ratification, hosted the Council of Europe Committee of Ministers session of 15 May 2026 in Chisinau, and aligns its drafting with the EU AI Act under accession negotiations.
Enforcement Level: Enforcement is nominal: sanctions reach only unauthorised AI use in universities, no authority holds an AI mandate, and no AI-specific decision has been published.
Specific Laws: White Paper on Data Management and Artificial Intelligence (2024), Framework Regulation on Academic Integrity in Higher Education Institutions (2026), Methodological Anti-Plagiarism Standards for Higher Education Institutions (2026), Law No. 195/2024 on Personal Data Protection (applicable 23 August 2026), Council of Europe Framework Convention on Artificial Intelligence and Human Rights, Democracy and the Rule of Law (CETS No. 225) - signature 2024, draft law on artificial intelligence (drafting initiated 21 May 2026), draft National Programme on Artificial Intelligence and Data Management 2026-2030, draft Electoral Code amendments on online electoral advertising and artificial intelligence (2026), National Smart Specialisation Programme "Smart Moldova" 2024-2027 (Government Decision No. 588/2024)

Regulation Status: Monaco has no AI statute; artificial intelligence is governed through Law No. 1.565 of 3 December 2024 on the protection of personal data, enforced by the Autorité de Protection des Données Personnelles. Two narrow AI-relevant texts remain unenacted: Projet de loi n° 1.087 on video protection and remote biometric identification, still awaiting a vote before the Conseil National after the APDP's December 2025 opinion and criticism during the October 2026 budget debates, and Proposition de loi n° 281 on online hate content, which defines deepfakes and was adopted by the Conseil National on 29 June 2026 without being taken up as a government bill.
Policy Lever: Policy is delivered through non-binding strategy and state-funded digital programmes — Extended Monaco, Extended Monaco Enterprises with Digital FlashUp, and sovereign cloud — now steered by the Délégation Interministérielle au Numérique created on 2 October 2026 with a direction covering AI in the administration. The only binding levers reaching AI are the general personal-data rules enforced by the APDP.
Governance Type: Governance is highly centralised: the Prince's Government sets digital and AI policy through the Délégation Interministérielle au Numérique, with the APDP the sole independent authority whose statutory powers touch AI. External checks are limited to the APDP's published opinions on bills such as Projet de loi n° 1.087 and judicial review before the Tribunal Suprême.
Actor Involvement: Participation is government-led, with industry reached through state digital programmes and no standing seats for civil society or universities. International engagement rests on Council of Europe data protection instruments rather than AI-specific treaties, the Framework Convention on Artificial Intelligence remaining unsigned.
Enforcement Level: Enforcement touching AI occurs only under personal data law through the APDP, with no AI-specific sanction, audit or published decision.
Specific Laws: Law No. 1.565 on the Protection of Personal Data (2024), Act No. 1.566 approving ratification of the Protocol amending Convention 108 (2024), Law No. 1.383 for a Digital Principality (2011, as amended), Projet de loi n° 1.087 on video protection and remote biometric identification (pending before the Conseil National), APDP Délibération n° 2025-022 giving an opinion on Projet de loi n° 1.087 (2025), Proposition de loi n° 281 on strengthening measures against online hate content (adopted by the Conseil National, 2026), Sovereign Ordinance creating the Délégation Interministérielle au Numérique (2026), Extended Monaco digital transformation programme (2019)

Regulation Status: Mongolia governs AI through policy rather than law: the National Strategy on Big Data and Artificial Intelligence adopted by Government Resolution No. 108 in September 2025, the Digital First policy and the designation of 2026 as the Year of Big Data and Artificial Intelligence. A Law on Artificial Intelligence remains in drafting between the Ministry of Digital Development, Innovation and Communications and the Ministry of Justice and Home Affairs and has not reached the State Great Khural, so AI use is covered by general law, principally the Law of Mongolia on Personal Data Protection (2021), together with the public-procurement and customs provisions on AI in the Law on Economic Freedom adopted on 2 July 2026.
Policy Lever: Policy runs on non-binding levers: the adopted national AI strategy, the Digital First policy, skills and infrastructure programs including the Oracle training partnership, the planned GPU-cluster AI Centre and the National Data Repository, plus tax and customs incentives for AI infrastructure. Institutional work sits with the ministry's Big Data and Artificial Intelligence Department and the National Council on Artificial Intelligence, neither of which can impose obligations, and no regulatory sandbox operates.
Governance Type: AI governance is centralized in the Ministry of Digital Development, Innovation and Communications, with a cross-ministry National Council on Artificial Intelligence and a parliamentary group on AI and big data providing coordination. Sectoral regulators engage only through studies such as the Financial Regulatory Commission's review of AI in financial services, and sub-national authorities and independent review bodies play no part in shaping AI rules.
Actor Involvement: Strategy development drew structured but ad hoc input from industry, academia and civil society through UNDP-facilitated workshops, the February 2025 national conference and the May 2025 academic discussion, with no standing statutory consultative bodies. International engagement runs through UNDP, the Oxford Global Cyber Security Capacity Centre, the United Kingdom and a corporate partnership with Oracle rather than binding AI agreements.
Enforcement Level: No AI enforcement exists, with oversight confined to one-off readiness assessments and sectoral studies and penalties available only under general data protection law.
Specific Laws: National Strategy on Big Data and Artificial Intelligence (2025, Government Resolution No. 108), Digital First policy (2025), Digital Nation Strategy, Law of Mongolia on Personal Data Protection (2021), Law of Mongolia on Economic Freedom (2026), Five-Year Development Guidelines of Mongolia for 2026-2030 (2025), draft Law on Artificial Intelligence (in preparation, 2025-2026)

Regulation Status: Montenegro has no AI-specific binding instrument: AI systems are reached only by general law, principally the Law on Personal Data Protection in force since 19 September 2026 with its automated decision-making and profiling provisions, the Criminal Code and the Copyright and Related Rights Act. The first National Artificial Intelligence Strategy 2026-2030 with Action Plan for 2026 is still being drafted by the Working Group coordinated by the Ministry of Public Administration, and the Ministry of Justice's announced law on misuse of artificial intelligence has not reached Parliament. The Law on the Implementation of Regulation (EU) 2022/2065 on Digital Services, adopted on 8 October 2026, aligns platform regulation but contains no AI-specific duties.
Policy Lever: Policy is delivered through soft and economic instruments: the UNDP Artificial Intelligence Landscape Assessment, the strategy drafting process, MontEDIH, EuroCC/NCC high-performance computing support, the Next Gen Gov AI training for civil servants and donor-funded AI infrastructure for the judiciary. Binding effect comes only from general statutes, and no body holds a legal AI mandate, compliance guidance or regulatory sandbox.
Governance Type: AI policy is centralised in the Ministry of Public Administration, with the Ministry of Justice handling criminal-law aspects of AI misuse and the Agency for Personal Data Protection covering data issues under general law. Coordination is through an ad hoc strategy working group, municipalities have no role, and independent or judicial scrutiny of AI arises only through general-law disputes.
Actor Involvement: Industry, academia and civil society engage through consultative sessions and workshops of the AI Strategy Working Group coordinated by the Ministry of Public Administration rather than through standing statutory roles. Internationally Montenegro signed CETS No. 225, participates in Council of Europe expert work, EU Digital Europe and EuroCC programmes and UNDP cooperation, and held the 2026 Berlin Process presidency and Western Balkans Digital Summit.
Enforcement Level: Nothing AI-specific is enforced: sanctions and investigations reach AI only through data protection and criminal law, and monitoring is limited to a single donor-funded readiness study.
Specific Laws: Law on Personal Data Protection ("Službeni list CG" 133/2026, in force 19 September 2026), Law on the Implementation of Regulation (EU) 2022/2065 on Digital Services (2026), Law on Electronic Identification and Trust Services ("Službeni list CG" 92/2026), Criminal Code of Montenegro, Copyright and Related Rights Act, Digital Transformation Strategy 2022-2026, Education Reform Strategy 2025-2035, Council of Europe Framework Convention on Artificial Intelligence and Human Rights, Democracy and the Rule of Law (CETS No. 225, signed 5 November 2024), draft National Artificial Intelligence Strategy 2026-2030 with Action Plan for 2026

Regulation Status: Morocco's binding AI rules are confined to elections: article 51-bis introduced by Organic Law 53.25 criminalises dissemination of falsified or AI-generated electoral content with two to five years' imprisonment and fines up to 100,000 dirhams, and HACA Superior Council Decision 50-26 of 16 June 2026 bars deceptive AI-generated electoral content and requires labelling of AI-produced broadcast material. Outside elections AI is handled through general law — Law No. 09-08 on personal data, applied to AI processing by the CNDP, and Law No. 05-20 on cybersecurity applied by the DGSSI. The Digital X.0 framework law covering data, AI and digital identity is still under examination at the General Secretariat of the Government, and the parliamentary bill creating a National Agency for Artificial Intelligence has not been adopted.
Policy Lever: Policy runs mainly on soft and economic levers: the Maroc IA 2030 roadmap, now in its operational phase with JAZARI regional institutes, data centres and sovereign language models, the Maroc Digital 2030 strategy, CNDP and HACA guidance, and AI and digital sovereignty allocations in the 2027 finance bill. The only binding levers are the electoral AI provisions, and no institution holds a statutory AI compliance mandate.
Governance Type: Governance is centralised in the Ministry of Digital Transition and Administrative Reform, with the CNDP, HACA and DGSSI acting on AI only inside their existing mandates and coordination organised case by case around the Assises nationales and the Digital X.0 draft. Regions have no regulatory role, and independent or judicial scrutiny of AI appears only through election-period prosecutions.
Actor Involvement: Industry and universities feed in through the Assises nationales de l'intelligence artificielle, roadmap workshops and the JAZARI institute agreements, while domestic civil society participation is occasional. International engagement is the broadest channel, covering the UNESCO ethics recommendation, African Union continental AI initiatives and digital partnerships with the European Union, France and Gulf states.
Enforcement Level: Enforcement touches AI only through the electoral criminal provisions and HACA's time-bound broadcast monitoring, supplemented by CNDP action under Law No. 09-08, with no dedicated AI authority or published AI-specific sanctions.
