Specific Laws: Organic Law No. 53.25 amending Organic Law No. 27.11 on the Election of Members of the House of Representatives (2026), HACA Superior Council of Audiovisual Communication Decision No. 50-26 (2026), Law No. 09-08 on the Protection of Individuals with Regard to the Processing of Personal Data (2009), Law No. 05-20 on Cybersecurity (2020), Digital X.0 Framework Law (draft, 2025), Maroc IA 2030 National AI Roadmap (2026), Maroc Digital 2030 Strategy (2024), Bill for the Establishment of the National Agency for Artificial Intelligence (2024, retabled 2026), CNDP Communiqué on Artificial Intelligence Processing of Personal Data (2025)

Regulation Status: The only binding AI-specific instrument is Decreto n.º 14/2026 of 17 April 2026, which establishes the National Commission for Artificial Intelligence (CNIA) as a consultative and technical advisory body to the Council of Ministers and creates no obligations for those who build or use AI. The National AI Strategy (ENIA) remained a draft after the public consultation of 4 May to 4 June 2026 and continued stakeholder engagement through October 2026, and Ministry of Education and Culture rules on AI in education were still being prepared for the Council of Ministers. Lei n.º 13/2026 on cybersecurity, Lei n.º 14/2026 on cybercrime and the personal data protection bill approved by the Council of Ministers on 3 March 2026 contain no AI-specific provisions.
Policy Lever: Policy runs through one institutional decree, a draft national strategy and donor-backed experimentation, with INTIC leading delivery alongside UNESCO, the ITU, the European Union, the African Union and the World Bank. Preparation of a national AI regulatory sandbox and a health-sector sandbox with the Instituto Nacional de Saúde continued without either becoming operational, and CNIA advises rather than enforces.
Governance Type: Authority is concentrated in INTIC, with CNIA supplying decree-based interministerial coordination directly under the Council of Ministers. Provincial structures participate through consultation only, and judicial or independent review of AI governance is absent.
Actor Involvement: Domestic participation is consultative and episodic, channelled through the ENIA public consultation, provincial workshops and meetings with operators, universities and the newly launched AMIA. International engagement is the most structured element, spanning WAICO founding membership and programmes with the ITU, UNESCO, the European Union, the African Union and the World Bank.
Enforcement Level: No AI-specific obligation, penalty or enforcement action exists, and oversight rests on INTIC's general ICT powers and CNIA's advisory opinions.
Specific Laws: Decreto n.º 14/2026, de 17 de Abril – Cria a Comissão Nacional de Inteligência Artificial (CNIA) (2026), Estratégia Nacional de Inteligência Artificial / National AI Strategy – ENIA (draft, 2026), Lei n.º 13/2026, de 1 de Julho – Lei de Segurança Cibernética (2026), Lei n.º 14/2026, de 1 de Julho – Lei dos Crimes Cibernéticos (2026), Proposta de Lei do Regime Jurídico de Protecção de Dados Pessoais (bill before the Assembleia da República, 2026), Lei das Transacções Electrónicas n.º 3/2017, Decreto n.º 71/2025 – Regulamento dos Centros de Dados, Decreto n.º 70/2025 – Regulamento de Computação em Nuvem

Regulation Status: Myanmar has no AI-specific legislation in force and none in the legislative process; the National AI Strategy (2025-2030) and National AI Policy drafted under the Ministry of Science and Technology since 2025 remain unpublished and unadopted. Cybersecurity Law No. 1/2025 defines artificial intelligence and licenses digital platform and cybersecurity service providers, but places no duty on AI developers or deployers. Regional assessments group Myanmar with Cambodia and Lao PDR among ASEAN members lacking a dedicated national AI strategy or agency.
Policy Lever: Policy action is confined to a ministry-led drafting process, announced university AI innovation centres and alignment with the ASEAN Guide on AI Governance and Ethics. No AI-specific binding instrument, national guidance, regulatory sandbox or AI procurement rule exists, and no body holds statutory powers over AI.
Governance Type: AI policy is centralized in the Ministry of Science and Technology under an executive dominated by the military leadership, with coordination limited to occasional inter-ministerial drafting meetings. Regions and states play no part, and no independent or judicial check on AI-related policy operates.
Actor Involvement: Engagement is government-internal, with limited industry presence through a Myanmar Computer Federation AI taskforce, universities involved mainly as implementers of announced innovation centres, and civil society excluded. International involvement runs through ASEAN soft-law alignment, bilateral cooperation with China and founding membership of the World Artificial Intelligence Cooperation Organization signed in July 2026.
Enforcement Level: Enforcement touching AI rests on general cybersecurity and platform licensing powers, with no AI-specific obligation, authority, case or monitoring.
Specific Laws: Cybersecurity Law No. 1/2025, draft National AI Strategy (2025-2030), draft National AI Policy (2025), Digital Economy Development Master Plan (2021-2025), Myanmar e-Governance Master Plan 2030, Agreement on the Establishment of the World Artificial Intelligence Cooperation Organization (2026)

Regulation Status: No binding AI-specific instrument exists: the Artificial Intelligence Readiness Assessment Report (2025) records the absence of AI legislation, an Artificial Intelligence Act is under development without being tabled, and the draft National Artificial Intelligence Strategy was at national validation in September 2026. Cabinet in October 2026 directed the Ministry of Information and Communication Technology and the Office of the Prime Minister to develop an internal policy on AI use by civil servants, an instrument that is not yet written and would bind only the public service. AI-related harms are handled under the Communications Act (2009), general criminal law and public advisories.
Policy Lever: Policy runs through diagnostics and institution-building: the Artificial Intelligence Readiness Assessment Report (2025), the draft National Artificial Intelligence Strategy, and the National Artificial Intelligence Institute launched on 23 September 2026 with software development, datasets, innovation and research and development centres. A Communications Regulatory Authority of Namibia sandbox framework and responsible-AI guidelines are in preparation, and no AI-specific binding instrument, AI procurement rule or compliance power exists.
Governance Type: AI governance sits with national executive bodies: the Ministry of Information and Communication Technology on policy and legislation, the National Commission on Research, Science and Technology hosting the National Artificial Intelligence Institute, the Office of the Prime Minister on public-service AI use, and the Communications Regulatory Authority of Namibia on communications matters. Regional and local government have no AI function, and courts and independent oversight bodies have not entered the field.
Actor Involvement: Participation is workshop-based and episodic, through the UNESCO ethics consultation, the Readiness Assessment launch, the 215-expert strategy process and ministry meetings with firms including Deloitte & Touche Namibia. International channels, notably UNESCO, the International Telecommunication Union, the African Union, SADC and the Smart Africa Alliance, carry the strongest and most continuous engagement.
Enforcement Level: With no AI-specific obligations in force, activity is confined to awareness work on deepfakes and AI-enabled scams and to general communications and cybersecurity powers held by the Communications Regulatory Authority of Namibia and Nam-CSIRT.
Specific Laws: Artificial Intelligence Readiness Assessment Report (2025), draft National Artificial Intelligence Strategy (2026), Cabinet directive on an internal public-service artificial intelligence policy (2026), Cybercrime Bill (2026, draft), Data Protection Bill (draft), Communications Act (2009), National Digital Strategy, National Digital Economy Roadmap (2022)

Regulation Status: Nauru has no AI-specific legislation, bill or national AI strategy, and the Nauru National Digital Transformation Strategy 2025-2030 covers connectivity, digital services and planned data-protection, cybersecurity and electronic-transactions laws without AI provisions. The Cybercrime Act 2015 and Communications and Broadcasting Act 2018 reach computer and communications conduct generally and contain no rule written for AI systems or their outputs.
Policy Lever: Policy effort is confined to connectivity, e-government delivery and the legislative pipeline for data protection, cybersecurity and electronic transactions set out in the Nauru National Digital Transformation Strategy 2025-2030. The only AI-relevant reference point is the regional Pacific Digital and Artificial Intelligence Technology Principles endorsed in September 2026, with no domestic guidance, funding, sandbox or mandated institution.
Governance Type: Authority over digital matters is concentrated in the Department of Information and Communications Technology within a unitary micro-state administration. No sectoral regulator, district authority or independent review body plays any part in AI governance.
Actor Involvement: Nauru's AI engagement is entirely external, through Pacific Islands Forum endorsement of the Pacific Digital and Artificial Intelligence Technology Principles, which are to feed a regional AI governance framework for consideration in 2027, and through UNESCO membership. Domestic industry, civil society and academia have no involvement because no domestic AI policy process exists.
Enforcement Level: Nauru has no AI obligations, penalties, enforcement authority or monitoring arrangements.
Specific Laws: Nauru National Digital Transformation Strategy 2025-2030 (2025), Cybercrime Act 2015, Communications and Broadcasting Act 2018, Pacific Digital and Artificial Intelligence Technology Principles (2026, regional, endorsed by Pacific Islands Forum Leaders)

Regulation Status: Nepal governs AI chiefly through the cabinet-approved National Artificial Intelligence (AI) Policy 2082 of August 2025, a non-binding strategy promising AI legislation and an AI Regulation Council. The only binding AI-written rules remain the Election Code of Conduct 2082 prohibitions on AI-generated misinformation and deepfakes in campaigning, in force since 18 January 2026, supplemented by the Supreme Court's Judiciary Information and Communication Technology Policy 2083 of July 2026, which permits AI for legal research and administration and bars it from writing judgments. The Science, Technology and Innovation Ordinance 2083 and the Nepal Academy of Science, Technology and Innovation Ordinance 2083, issued on 16 October 2026, carry the umbrella science and technology framework forward, while a dedicated AI bill has not reached parliament.
Policy Lever: Policy runs through a non-binding national strategy, the National AI Centre under the Ministry of Information and Communication, and the Ministry of Science, Technology and Innovation created on 13 May 2026, which issued draft Science, Technology and Innovation Regulations 2083 for public comment. Promised levers such as the AI Regulation Council, regulatory sandboxes and provincial AI Excellence Centres have no legal basis or operations.
Governance Type: AI governance is concentrated in the Ministry of Information and Communication, which drafted the policy and hosts the National AI Centre, while the Election Commission, the Ministry of Science, Technology and Innovation and the judiciary act within their own spheres. Formal inter-agency machinery and any provincial role remain unrealised, and independent scrutiny is limited to election monitors and digital rights groups reporting on AI-generated content.
Actor Involvement: Industry bodies, digital rights organisations and academics engage through seminars, public comment on draft technology rules and donor projects rather than institutionalised AI consultation, and participation stays concentrated in Kathmandu. International engagement is declaratory and development-partner based, covering the New Delhi Declaration on AI Impact and UN forums.
Enforcement Level: Enforcement touching AI exists only in the electoral sphere, where the Election Commission monitored and warned about AI-generated deepfakes during the March 2026 election, while no authority enforces AI obligations elsewhere.
Specific Laws: National Artificial Intelligence (AI) Policy 2082 (2025), Election Code of Conduct 2082 (2026), Judiciary Information and Communication Technology Policy 2083 (2026), Science, Technology and Innovation Ordinance 2083 (2026), National Advertising Policy 2026, Individual Privacy Act 2075 (2018)

Regulation Status: The directly applicable EU AI Act governs AI in the Netherlands, with prohibited practices and AI literacy applying since 2 February 2025, general-purpose AI obligations since 2 August 2025 and Article 50 transparency duties since 2 August 2026, while Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 (Digital Omnibus on AI, in force 27 July 2026) moved Annex III high-risk obligations to 2 December 2027 and Annex I to 2 August 2028. National implementation remains unfinished: the draft Uitvoeringswet AI-verordening that designates supervisors, penalties and the joint regulatory sandbox was consulted from 20 April to 1 June 2026 and sent to advisory bodies, but has not been enacted. Alongside the AI Act, the Autoriteit Persoonsgegevens exercises algorithm-specific oversight through the General Data Protection Regulation and the Uitvoeringswet AVG.
Policy Lever: The Netherlands pairs the directly applicable AI Act with a dense, maintained soft-law layer—biannual AI and algorithm risk reporting, AP guidance on human intervention and generative AI, the mandatory central-government Algorithm Register and impact assessments—and funded AI investment programmes under the Nationaal AI Deltaplan and AiNed. Supervisory institutions are staffed and preparing, but statutory AI Act powers, national penalties and the single multi-sectoral sandbox await adoption of the Uitvoeringswet AI-verordening.
Governance Type: Supervision is decentralised and hybrid: the Autoriteit Persoonsgegevens and the Rijksinspectie Digitale Infrastructuur coordinate and jointly prepare an AI Coordination Centre and sandbox, while eight to ten sectoral authorities retain their own remits and the RDI serves as single point of contact. Sub-national bodies apply national transparency rules rather than make AI rules, and courts, the Raad van State, the Algemene Rekenkamer and the National Ombudsman exert independent control over public-sector AI.
Actor Involvement: Policy input runs through open internet consultations, AP stakeholder seminars, statutory advisory bodies and the Nederlandse AI Coalitie, which seats industry and knowledge institutions as standing partners while civil society is consulted rather than seated. The country is a highly active participant in EU, OECD, UNESCO, Council of Europe and European standardisation processes.
Enforcement Level: Monitoring and published cross-sector reporting are well developed, yet concluded sanctions rest on data protection law because the national AI Act enforcement architecture and penalties remain in the legislative pipeline.
Specific Laws: EU AI Act (Regulation (EU) 2024/1689) (2024), Digital Omnibus on AI (Regulation (EU) 2026/1744) amending the AI Act (2026), General Data Protection Regulation (2018), Dutch GDPR Implementation Act / UAVG (2018), Uitvoeringswet AI-verordening draft bill (2026, consultation closed 1 June 2026), Nationaal AI Deltaplan (2025), Government Algorithm Register policy (2022)

Regulation Status: New Zealand regulates AI through existing law plus voluntary frameworks: the Strategy for Artificial Intelligence: Investing with Confidence (2025), the Algorithm Charter for Aotearoa New Zealand, the Public Service AI Framework and the Ministry for Regulation's Responsible AI in Action guidance (May 2026) carry no legal force. Binding rules touching AI are the Privacy Act 2020, the Privacy Amendment Act 2025 (IPP3A applying since 1 May 2026) and the Biometric Processing Privacy Code 2025, which became fully applicable to pre-existing biometric processing on 3 August 2026. The only AI-specific legislative proposal, the Deepfake Digital Harm and Exploitation Bill, took submissions to 19 June 2026 and lapsed on the dissolution of Parliament on 1 October 2026 ahead of the 7 November election.
Policy Lever: Policy runs on soft law plus money: voluntary guidance for business, the public service and regulators sits alongside New Zealand Institute for Advanced Technology funding, AI research investment and a small-business AI adoption pilot. Institutional responsibility is distributed across the Government Chief Digital Officer, MBIE and the Ministry for Regulation without any statutory AI mandate, and binding levers remain general privacy, data and consumer law.
Governance Type: Responsibility for AI is dispersed among general and sectoral regulators coordinated informally through Cabinet, the AI Strategy and the Public Service AI Work Programme, with no single AI authority and no subnational layer. Independent review comes from the courts, the Human Rights Review Tribunal, the Human Rights Commission, the Law Commission's review of government automated decision-making commenced on 21 April 2026, and the Government Chief Digital Officer's AI Expert Advisory Panel.
Actor Involvement: Engagement is consultative: industry bodies including the AI Forum New Zealand shape strategy and guidance, civil society and researchers participate through consultations and select committee submissions, and academics sit on the Government Chief Digital Officer's AI Expert Advisory Panel. Internationally New Zealand aligns with OECD principles, the Global Partnership on AI and summit declarations rather than binding instruments.
Enforcement Level: Enforcement touching AI rests on Privacy Act 2020 complaints and the Biometric Processing Privacy Code 2025 handled by the Privacy Commissioner, with no AI-specific penalties, dedicated AI enforcement body or routine AI auditing.
Specific Laws: Privacy Act 2020, Algorithm Charter for Aotearoa New Zealand (2020), Public Service AI Framework (2025), New Zealand's Strategy for Artificial Intelligence: Investing with Confidence (2025), Responsible AI Guidance for Businesses (2025), Responsible AI Guidance for the Public Service: GenAI (2025, updated September 2026), Privacy Amendment Act 2025, Biometric Processing Privacy Code 2025, Customer and Product Data Act 2025, Responsible AI in Action: Practical Steps for Regulators (2026), Deepfake Digital Harm and Exploitation Bill (2025, lapsed on dissolution of Parliament in October 2026)

Regulation Status: Nicaragua regulates AI through no dedicated instrument: the Special Law on Cybercrimes No. 1042 (2020) and Law No. 787 on Personal Data Protection are the texts invoked for AI, and neither was drafted for AI systems. The 2026 developments are the ratification of the Agreement on the Establishment of the World Organization for Cooperation in Artificial Intelligence and three Ministry of Education booklets on ethical AI use, neither of which creates enforceable duties on AI developers or deployers.
Policy Lever: Policy runs through soft instruments and capacity-building: Ministry of Education booklets on ethical AI use (March 2026), TELCOR staff and public-sector training including a September 2026 seminar in China, and a Ministry of Health–PAHO digital transformation roadmap. No AI-specific binding instrument, sandbox, procurement rule or funded AI program is in place.
Governance Type: AI governance is centralized in the executive, with TELCOR as the external interlocutor and the Ministries of Education and Health running sector initiatives under direction from the Copresidency. No formal inter-agency AI coordination mechanism, subnational competence or independent review of AI measures exists.
Actor Involvement: International engagement is the main channel: accession to the China-led World Organization for Cooperation in Artificial Intelligence, participation in the UN Global Dialogue on AI Governance in Geneva, PAHO cooperation on AI in health, and capacity-building with China. Domestic industry and independent civil society have no structured role, and state universities participate only as implementers of government education initiatives.
Enforcement Level: No AI-specific obligation, sanction or enforcement body exists, and oversight is limited to a single health-sector readiness exercise.
Specific Laws: Special Law on Cybercrimes No. 1042 (2020), National Cybersecurity Strategy 2020-2025 (Presidential Decree No. 24-2020), Law No. 787 on Personal Data Protection (2012), Decree approving the Agreement on the Establishment of the World Organization for Cooperation in Artificial Intelligence (2026), Cartillas for the Responsible and Ethical Use and Management of Artificial Intelligence (2026)

Regulation Status: Niger has no AI-specific legislation, no draft AI bill and no adopted national AI strategy; the Ministry of Communication and New Information Technologies announced in July 2025 that a national AI and geospatial strategy would be drafted through an inclusive process, and no such document has been published. AI activity falls under general instruments, chiefly Loi n° 2022-59 of 16 December 2022 on personal data protection (amended by Loi n° 2023-31 and Ordonnance n° 2024-29) and Ordonnance n° 2026-48 of 10 September 2026 on electronic press, neither written for AI. The country remains under military rule, with the Charter of Refoundation in place of the suspended constitutional order and legislation issued by ordinance.
Policy Lever: Policy action is convening and capacity-building rather than instruments: ANSI and partners held the third Semaine de l'Intelligence Artificielle et des Technologies Géospatiales in Niamey on 23-24 July 2026, and the UN Resident Coordinator's Illimi Niger programme trained 140 officials in AI for human security in June 2026. The draft Politique nationale de développement du numérique 2026-2035, validated in March 2026 and still in review in July 2026, is the only strategic document in progress, and no AI strategy, guidance, procurement rule or sandbox exists.
Governance Type: AI sits entirely with the executive, the Ministry of Communication and New Information Technologies setting direction and ANSI implementing digital programmes. The dissolution of the Haute Autorité de Protection des Données à caractère Personnel in June 2026 and the transfer of its functions to ministerial level removed the last independent supervisory layer touching data and automated processing, and there is no designated AI regulator, coordination body, sub-national competence or exercised judicial review.
Actor Involvement: Engagement is event-based: SIATeG 2026 in Niamey gathered government, academia and private-sector participants, and UN agencies deliver AI training to officials, while domestic civil society is absent from the process. Suspension from the African Union and withdrawal from ECOWAS confine external involvement to United Nations and Alliance des États du Sahel channels; the ratified African Union Malabo Convention on Cyber Security and Personal Data Protection is not an AI instrument.
Enforcement Level: No AI-specific obligation, sanction, enforcement action or monitoring programme exists, and supervision of personal data, now exercised by the ministry following the abolition of the HAPDP, reaches AI only through general rules.
Specific Laws: Loi n° 2022-59 du 16 décembre 2022 relative à la protection des données à caractère personnel (2022), amended by Loi n° 2023-31 (2023) and Ordonnance n° 2024-29 (2024); Ordonnance n° 2026-48 du 10 septembre 2026 relative à la presse électronique (2026); Décret n° 2026-310/PRN/PM du 8 juin 2026 supprimant la Haute Autorité de Protection des Données à caractère Personnel (2026); Politique nationale de développement du numérique 2026-2035 (draft, 2026); Niger 2.0 digital strategy (2017). No AI-specific law, regulation or national AI strategy has been adopted.

Regulation Status: Nigeria has no standalone AI statute: the National Digital Economy and E-Governance Bill, whose Chapter Five, Parts XI and XII would create risk classification, transparency duties, sandboxes and enforcement under NITDA, was still passing through the National Assembly in late 2026, and the National Artificial Intelligence Commission (Establishment) Bill and Nigerian Artificial Intelligence Bill remain at committee and second-reading stage. Binding AI-specific obligations are confined to Chapter Five of the Internet Code of Practice 2026 for internet access service providers and the NITDA Guidelines for Clearance of Information Technology Projects 2025 covering federal procurement of AI-enabled systems valued at NGN 10 million or more. The Nigeria Data Protection Act 2023 and its General Application and Implementation Directive 2025 carry most practical oversight of automated processing as general law.
Policy Lever: Policy runs on soft law and money: the National Artificial Intelligence Strategy 2025, NITDA guidance, research grants through the National Centre for Artificial Intelligence and Robotics and skills programmes, with a single binding AI chapter in the Internet Code of Practice 2026 and binding AI procurement clearance for federal institutions. The multi-agency National Regulatory Sandbox is not yet admitting participants, and the bodies holding AI responsibility have no statutory AI remit.
Governance Type: Governance is a lead-body-plus-sectoral-regulator model, with NITDA and the communications ministry setting direction and the data protection, communications and consumer protection regulators applying their own statutes to AI. Coordination is organised through working groups and the National AI Trust, states hold no regulatory role, and judicial review of AI rules has not materialised.
Actor Involvement: Policy-making draws on industry through public hearings, the National AI Trust and the sandbox working group, with civil society and academic input consultative and occasional. Internationally Nigeria is active, having adopted the African Union Continental AI Strategy, completed a UNESCO readiness assessment and aligned with multilateral AI declarations.
Enforcement Level: No enforcement action has been taken under AI-specific rules; sanctions touching AI flow from data protection and cybercrime law, and dedicated AI penalties depend on the pending Digital Economy Bill.
Specific Laws: Nigeria Data Protection Act (2023), Nigeria Data Protection Act General Application and Implementation Directive (2025), Cybercrimes (Amendment) Act (2024), National Artificial Intelligence Strategy — NAIS (2025), NITDA Guidelines for Clearance of Information Technology Projects for Federal Public Institutions (2025), Internet Code of Practice (2026, Chapter Five on artificial intelligence and emerging technologies), NITDA Code of Practice for Artificial Intelligence (draft, 2025), National Digital Economy and E-Governance Bill (2025, pending), National Artificial Intelligence Commission (Establishment) Bill (2025, pending), Nigerian Artificial Intelligence Bill (2025, pending)

Regulation Status: North Korea has no AI-specific legislation, regulation or formal governance instrument, and technology is governed through general sectoral statutes — the Science and Technology Law, the Law on the Introduction of New Technology (revised 2026), the Information Security Law, the Telecommunications Law and the Electronic Authentication Law — none of which contains provisions written for AI systems. The 2026-2030 Five-Year Plan adopted at the Ninth Workers' Party Congress in February 2026 lists information technology and artificial intelligence among development priorities, a planning objective rather than a rule.
Policy Lever: State direction of AI runs through party economic planning, state research institutions and leadership directives — Kim Jong Un's October 2026 call to embed AI in unmanned systems — rather than through policy instruments. No strategy document, guidance, standard, sandbox or AI-mandated institution has been published.
Governance Type: Authority over technology is concentrated in the Korean Workers' Party, the Cabinet and the security apparatus. Governance is centralized and opaque, with no independent regulators, no subnational competence and no judicial or independent review.
Actor Involvement: Domestic industry, civil society and academia are state-controlled, with academic institutes serving as research executors rather than policy advisers. International engagement is confined to UN General Assembly voting against autonomous weapons measures and informal AI research contacts with Russia; the country is not party to the Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons and joins no multilateral AI initiatives.
Enforcement Level: No AI enforcement framework, authority, sanction or monitoring practice exists, and control over technology use is exercised through opaque party and security channels.
Specific Laws: Five-Year Plan for National Economic Development 2026-2030 (2026, names information technology and artificial intelligence as priority areas), Law on the Introduction of New Technology (revised 2026), Science and Technology Law, Information Security Law

Regulation Status: Norway has no AI-specific binding instrument in force. The draft Act on Artificial Intelligence (KI-loven), which would make Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 applicable through a reference provision, drew close to 150 consultation responses in 2025; the Digitalisation and Public Governance Ministry opened a further consultation on the EU AI omnibus (Regulation (EU) 2026/1744) on 30 October 2026 and plans a bill in spring 2027, while the EEA Joint Committee has not incorporated the Regulation. The Public Administration Act adopted 20 June 2025 contains binding rules on automated decisions and explanation of decision logic for public bodies but is not in force.
Policy Lever: Policy runs through soft instruments, funding and sandboxes rather than binding rules: Datatilsynet's regulatory sandbox, Digdir's and Nkom's published AI guidance, and KI-Norge as the national arena for responsible AI and host of the forthcoming AI Act sandbox built with Nkom and Datatilsynet. The government announced a renewed national AI strategy on 5 October 2026 and opened a public call for input on 29 October 2026, building on the National Strategy for Artificial Intelligence (2020) and the National Digitalisation Strategy (2024).
Governance Type: Governance follows a lead-body-plus-sectoral model, with Nkom as coordinating market surveillance authority and national contact point, Datatilsynet covering data protection, and Digdir/KI-Norge coordinating the national arena and the planned sandbox under a formal tripartite arrangement. Oversight is exclusively national, with independent review supplied by courts and the Parliamentary Ombud.
Actor Involvement: Domestic involvement follows the Norwegian consultation and corporatist tradition: the KI-lov and AI omnibus consultations are open to all actors, KI-Norge partners with business, academia and the public sector, and a letter of intent with employer and union confederations covers AI in working life. Internationally Norway acts through the EEA/EFTA track, the Council of Europe Framework Convention on Artificial Intelligence and the OECD.
Enforcement Level: Enforcement against AI rests entirely on general data protection law pending entry into force of the KI-lov, with Nkom designated but not yet empowered.
Specific Laws: Draft Act on Artificial Intelligence (KI-loven) (2025 consultation draft, bill announced for spring 2027), Consultation on the EU AI omnibus Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 (2026), Public Administration Act (forvaltningsloven, LOV-2025-06-20-81, adopted 2025, not in force), Personal Data Act (2018), National Strategy for Artificial Intelligence (2020), National Digitalisation Strategy (2024), renewed national AI strategy under preparation (announced October 2026), EU AI Act Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (EEA incorporation pending), Council of Europe Framework Convention on Artificial Intelligence (signed 2024)

Regulation Status: Oman governs AI mainly through the General Policy for the Safe and Ethical Use of Artificial Intelligence Systems, issued by the Ministry of Transport, Communications and Information Technology on 1 April 2025 and effective 9 April 2025, a risk-based policy without legal binding force. Binding obligations touching AI sit in general law: Royal Decree No. 68/2026, in force 7 September 2026, adds automated-processing and automated-decision-making duties to the Personal Data Protection Law, and the Law on Combating Cybercrime (Royal Decree No. 61/2026) defines artificial intelligence and brings AI systems within 'information system'. Royal Decree No. 50/2026 of 30 April 2026 is AI-titled and binding but creates an Artificial Intelligence Special Zone in Muscat Governorate rather than imposing duties on AI systems.
Policy Lever: Oman relies on a non-binding ethics-and-governance policy, the National Programme for Artificial Intelligence and Advanced Digital Technologies, and investment incentives in the Artificial Intelligence Special Zone created by Royal Decree No. 50/2026. No regulatory sandbox has been published, public-sector AI procurement is governed only by the policy's pre-deployment assessment and approval requirements, and institutional capacity rests with MTCIT without AI-specific legal powers.
Governance Type: Governance is centralized in MTCIT, which issued the General Policy, runs the National Programme and supervises the Personal Data Protection Law, while the Public Authority for Special Economic Zones and Free Zones manages the AI Special Zone in coordination with the ministry. Sector regulators are expected to apply the General Policy in their domains, governorates have no AI role, and oversight of AI decisions runs through the ministry rather than independent or judicial review.
Actor Involvement: Industry and academia feed into AI policy through MTCIT consultations, the National Programme for Artificial Intelligence and Advanced Digital Technologies and partnerships such as Oman GPT and the Green AI Alliance, while domestic civil society has no structured role. International engagement is extensive, covering founding membership of the World Artificial Intelligence Cooperation Organization, the UN Global Dialogue on AI Governance, a World Economic Forum Centre for the Fourth Industrial Revolution partnership and UNESCO ethics assessment.
Enforcement Level: Compliance rests on self-assessment and reporting to MTCIT under a policy carrying no sanctions, with penalties available only through the amended Personal Data Protection Law and the 2026 Cybercrime Law and no published AI-specific enforcement decision.
Specific Laws: National Programme for Artificial Intelligence and Advanced Digital Technologies (2024), General Policy for the Safe and Ethical Use of Artificial Intelligence Systems (2025), Royal Decree No. 50/2026 Establishing the Artificial Intelligence Special Zone in the Governorate of Muscat (2026), Law on Combating Cybercrime (Royal Decree No. 61/2026), Personal Data Protection Law (Royal Decree No. 6/2022) as amended by Royal Decree No. 68/2026

Regulation Status: Pakistan governs AI through executive policy rather than law: the National AI Policy 2025, the Islamabad AI Declaration 2026 and the National Data Governance Policy 2026 set AI-specific expectations, with binding duties on transparency, human review of automated decisions and generative-AI use applying only to federal public bodies. The Regulation of Artificial Intelligence Bill 2024 was introduced in the Senate in September 2024 and stands withdrawn from committee, and private-sector AI is reached only incidentally by the Prevention of Electronic Crimes Act 2016 as amended in 2025. No personal data protection statute has been enacted.
Policy Lever: Policy runs through soft law and money: the National AI Policy 2025, the Islamabad AI Declaration 2026, the draft National Data Governance Policy 2026, the National AI Fund and Ignite programmes. The Pakistan Digital Authority holds the statutory digital and AI governance mandate but has issued no binding AI instrument and used no compliance power.
Governance Type: Authority is concentrated in the Pakistan Digital Authority under the Ministry of Information Technology and Telecommunication, with the National Digital Commission and the AI Council coordinating and sectoral regulators such as the Election Commission of Pakistan acting within existing mandates. Provincial activity is limited to a draft Punjab statute on performers' digital identity, and independent review of AI decisions is not institutionalised.
Actor Involvement: Policy development drew on industry, academic and public-sector input, with the Indus AI Summit 2026 and Indus AI Week drawing startups, students and foreign delegations. Domestic civil society involvement is occasional and criticised as thin, and international engagement is declaratory and bilateral rather than treaty-based.
Enforcement Level: No AI-specific sanction, enforcement decision or audit regime exists, and action against AI-related harm rests on general cybercrime powers.
Specific Laws: National AI Policy (2025), Islamabad AI Declaration on Sovereign, Responsible, and Capability-Driven Artificial Intelligence (2026), National Data Governance Policy (2026, draft), Digital Nation Pakistan Act (2025), Regulation of Artificial Intelligence Bill (2024, Senate, withdrawn from committee), Prevention of Electronic Crimes Act (2016), Prevention of Electronic Crimes (Amendment) Act (2025), Punjab Performers' Digital Identity and Artificial Intelligence Protection Act (2026, provincial draft), Election Commission of Pakistan draft amendments to the Codes of Conduct on AI use in elections (2026)

Regulation Status: Palau has no statute, regulation, executive order or national strategy whose subject is artificial intelligence. AI-related conduct falls only under general instruments such as the Privacy Act provisions of the Palau National Code and the Cybersecurity Act signed in 2026, neither of which mentions AI systems, and no competent authority for AI has been designated.
Policy Lever: Policy effort is directed at cybersecurity and government IT consolidation rather than AI: Executive Order No. 500 (2026) created the Office of Applied Technology and Strategy inside the Office of the President, and the National Cybersecurity Strategy and Policy 2026-2030 was signed with International Telecommunication Union support. Guidance, funding, sandboxes and procurement rules for AI are all absent.
Governance Type: AI governance structures are absent; technology functions are concentrated in the Office of Applied Technology and Strategy under the President and, once the Cybersecurity Act is implemented, in a Bureau of Cybersecurity under the Ministry of Public Infrastructure and Industries. Neither carries an AI mandate, and state governments and independent review bodies play no part.
Actor Involvement: Domestic industry, civil society and academic actors have no structured role in AI policy-making, and technical engagement comes from external partners such as the International Telecommunication Union and MITRE on cybersecurity. International participation rests on general United Nations and UNESCO membership rather than any AI-specific instrument.
Enforcement Level: Nothing specific to AI is enforced in Palau, and only general cybersecurity and privacy penalties could reach AI-related conduct.
Specific Laws: Executive Order No. 500 (2026) establishing the Office of Applied Technology and Strategy, Cybersecurity Act / Senate Bill No. 12-9, SD1, HD2 (2026), National Cybersecurity Strategy and Policy 2026-2030, Privacy Act provisions of the Palau National Code (Title 6) - none of which are AI-specific

Regulation Status: Panama has no AI statute in force: Bill 588 establishing adaptive, risk-based AI governance with regulatory experimentation cleared first debate on 15 April 2026, second on 18 August and third on 19 August 2026, and sits with the Executive for sanction and publication in the Gaceta Oficial, creating no obligations until then. The binding instrument that names AI is institutional — Executive Decree 36 of 7 May 2026, which declares critical and emerging technologies a national priority and creates the National Commission for Critical and Emerging Technologies with an AI Subcommission. Law 81 of 2019 on personal data protection, Law 144 of 2020 on government digital transformation and Law 478 of 2025 on cybercrime remain the operative rules reaching AI, and a criminal-law anteproyecto on malicious AI-generated content was adopted for discussion by the Government Committee in August 2026.
Policy Lever: Panama governs AI through strategy and coordination rather than regulation: the National AI Strategy 2026-2036 (Cabinet Resolution No. 89-26), the National Advanced Technologies Agenda with its USD 105 million semiconductor strand, SENACYT talent funding, and the AI Subcommission created by Executive Decree 36 of 2026, which met for a second session on 21 September 2026 to design the strategy's implementation plan. No AI budget line accompanies the strategy, and the sandbox and AI procurement provisions remain confined to Bill 588.
Governance Type: Coordination runs through the National Commission for Critical and Emerging Technologies chaired from the Ministry of the Presidency, with SENACYT, the National Authority for Government Innovation and ANTAI contributing from existing mandates and the AI Subcommission steering implementation of the national strategy. There is no subnational layer and no AI-specific judicial or independent oversight.
Actor Involvement: Government, industry and academia engage through the National Commission for Critical and Emerging Technologies and the consultative process behind the National AI Strategy, while civil society participates episodically through SENACYT and UNESCO workshops rather than a standing seat. International engagement is active through the UNESCO readiness assessment, the Santiago Declaration, Pax Silica and IDB-supported regional work.
Enforcement Level: No AI-specific penalty, supervisory authority or audit regime exists, leaving ANTAI's data-protection powers under Law 81 of 2019 and criminal law as the only routes touching AI.
Specific Laws: Bill 588 on Adaptive Governance of Artificial Intelligence (2026, approved in third debate 19 August 2026, awaiting executive sanction), Executive Decree 36 of 7 May 2026 creating the National Commission for Critical and Emerging Technologies and its AI Subcommission, National AI Strategy of the Republic of Panama approved by Cabinet Resolution No. 89-26 (2026), National Advanced Technologies Agenda including the National Semiconductor and Microelectronics Strategy (2026), National AI Strategy / ENIA (2021), Law 81 on Personal Data Protection (2019), Executive Decree 285 (2021), Law 144 on Government Digital Transformation (2020), Law 478 on Cybercrime Amendments (2025), Anteproyecto 51 on Penal Code reform for malicious AI use (2026, pending)

Regulation Status: Papua New Guinea has no AI-specific statute in force. The Department of Information and Communications Technology released the Draft PNG Government Artificial Intelligence Adoption Framework: DG × DPI ^ AI on 27 February 2026 and the Draft National Sovereign Digital Transformation and Artificial Intelligence Strategy on 23 March 2026 for consultation, and the fifth draft Data Governance and Data Protection Bill 2026 proposes an interim risk-based regime for prohibited practices, high-risk systems, impact assessment and bias testing. Drafting of amendments criminalising deepfakes, voice cloning and digital impersonation is also under way, leaving the Digital Government Act 2022 as the only enacted digital governance instrument.
Policy Lever: Policy action runs through draft strategy and framework documents and a legislative reform package, not through binding levers. DICT coordinates AI work administratively, and the proposed AI Taskforce, Digital Transformation and Artificial Intelligence Board and restructured department exist only in draft.
Governance Type: AI policy is centralised in the Department of Information and Communications Technology under ministerial and Prime Minister's directives, with NICTA as the sector regulator and the National Executive Council endorsing policy. Provinces play no part and no independent or judicial body has shaped AI rules.
Actor Involvement: Industry, civil society, academia and development partners were invited into DICT's open consultations on the draft AI framework, the sovereign AI strategy and the 2026 digital bills. International engagement is through Pacific regional digital cooperation, bilateral ICT arrangements with Australia and cybercrime treaty accession rather than AI-specific fora.
Enforcement Level: Nothing is enforced because no AI obligation is yet law and no authority has an AI remit.
Specific Laws: Digital Government Act (2022), Draft PNG Government Artificial Intelligence Adoption Framework: DG × DPI ^ AI (2026), Draft National Sovereign Digital Transformation and Artificial Intelligence Strategy (2026), Data Governance and Data Protection Bill (2026), Cyber Security Bill (2026)

Regulation Status: Paraguay has no cross-sector AI statute; the Senate bill that would create an AI regulatory authority was socialised in public hearing in June 2025 and has not been voted. Binding AI-specific texts in force are institutional: Corte Suprema de Justicia Resolución N° 12.677/2026 on AI use in the judiciary, Resolución DINAVISA N° 047/2026 creating an AI unit in health regulation, and Decreto N° 5306/2026 on AI, cloud and data-centre industries. Ley N° 7593/2025 on personal data protection grants rights against automated individual decisions and profiling but applies only from 27 November 2027.
Policy Lever: Policy effort concentrates on promotion and internal state use: Decreto N° 5306/2026 sets special electricity tariffs for AI, cloud and data-centre investment, and the Paraguay-Taiwan sovereign AI compute project advances in a pilot phase, while the Hoja de Ruta Nacional de Inteligencia Artificial, the UNESCO Readiness Assessment Methodology report and the UNDP AI Landscape Assessment provide non-binding direction. No regulatory sandbox, AI procurement rules or body with a statutory AI compliance mandate exists.
Governance Type: Governance centres on MITIC as policy lead, with individual state institutions such as the Corte Suprema de Justicia and DINAVISA issuing rules for their own AI use, and CONACYT co-leading assessment exercises. No designated AI regulator, standing inter-agency mechanism, sub-national competence or independent review body with an AI mandate exists.
Actor Involvement: The UNESCO Readiness Assessment Methodology exercise coordinated by MITIC and CONACYT and the UNDP AI Landscape Assessment brought public bodies, companies, universities and civil society organisations into one-off multisectoral processes, echoed in the Senate public hearing on the AI bill. International engagement runs through UNESCO ethics summits for Latin America and the Caribbean, the Pax Silica Joint Declaration signed in Washington, and bilateral AI compute cooperation with Taiwan.
Enforcement Level: AI rules are not enforced against third parties, as there is no AI sanctions regime, competent authority or audit practice, only internal compliance duties in the judiciary and the health regulator.
Specific Laws: Ley N° 7593/2025 de Protección de Datos Personales (2025), Ley N° 6534/2020 de Protección de Datos Personales Crediticios (2020), Corte Suprema de Justicia Resolución N° 12.677 sobre directrices para el uso de sistemas de inteligencia artificial en el Poder Judicial (2026), Resolución DINAVISA N° 047/2026 (2026), Decreto N° 5306/2026 sobre industrias convergentes de inteligencia artificial, computación en la nube y data centers (2026), Hoja de Ruta Nacional de Inteligencia Artificial (2025), Informe de Metodología de Evaluación del Estado de Preparación en Inteligencia Artificial - UNESCO RAM Paraguay (2025), Panorama de la Inteligencia Artificial en Paraguay - PNUD AI Landscape Assessment (2026)

Regulation Status: Peru regulates AI through Law No. 31814 (2023) and its Reglamento, Supreme Decree No. 115-2025-PCM, whose first adequacy deadline expired on 10 September 2026 for the public powers, autonomous bodies and private operators in health, education, justice, security, economy and finance. Coverage is horizontal by design, but transport, commerce, labour, production, agriculture, energy, mining, the remaining sectors and smaller firms have until 2027-2029, and parts of the institutional machinery foreseen in the Reglamento remain unbuilt.
Policy Lever: Peru combines binding instruments (Law No. 31814, Supreme Decree No. 115-2025-PCM, Law No. 32314, Directiva N° 002-2026-PCM/SGTD on the AI Officer) with the promotional ENIA 2026-2030, which is obligatory for public entities and state enterprises. Economic levers are limited to the operating Catálogo IA Perú, while the sandbox, CNIDIA and the national AI platform remain pending and the SGTD leads with supervisory but no sanctioning powers.
Governance Type: The Presidencia del Consejo de Ministros, through the SGTD, is the national AI authority issuing lineamientos, technical standards, directives and binding opinions, with the data protection authority, Indecopi, the Jurado Nacional de Elecciones and sectoral ministries acting within their own remits. Coordination is formalised inside the executive through the Sistema Nacional de Transformación Digital and the AI Officer network, while subnational governments only implement national rules and independent review of the AI framework has not occurred.
Actor Involvement: Industry, civil society and academia contributed to the 2024 consultations on the draft Reglamento and to the preparation of ENIA 2026-2030, but none holds a standing formal role in AI policy-making. Internationally Peru anchors its framework in OECD and UNESCO instruments and the EU risk-based model and signs regional Latin American AI declarations.
Enforcement Level: Enforcement is indirect: the SGTD monitors and refers cases while the data protection authority, Indecopi and the criminal courts apply pre-existing penalties, and no decision under the AI framework has been published.
Specific Laws: Law No. 31814 - Ley que promueve el uso de la inteligencia artificial en favor del desarrollo económico y social del país (2023), Supreme Decree No. 115-2025-PCM - Reglamento de la Ley N° 31814 (2025), Law No. 32314 - modifies the Penal Code and the Computer Crimes Law to treat the use of artificial intelligence as an aggravating factor (2025), Resolución Ministerial N° 152-2026-PCM - Estrategia Nacional de Inteligencia Artificial 2026-2030 (2026), Resolución de Secretaría de Gobierno y Transformación Digital N° 004-2026-PCM/SGTD - Directiva N° 002-2026-PCM/SGTD que establece el perfil y responsabilidades del Oficial de Inteligencia Artificial (2026), Resolución N° 0844-2025-JNE - Reglamento sobre propaganda electoral, publicidad estatal y neutralidad en periodo electoral (2026), Emergency Decree No. 007-2020 (2020)

Regulation Status: The Philippines has no enacted horizontal AI statute; a House technical working group has consolidated more than 26 bills, including House Bill 9582 (Philippine Artificial Intelligence Development and Governance Act) and Senate Bill 25 (Artificial Intelligence Regulation Act), into a risk-based substitute Artificial Intelligence Development and Regulation Act. Binding AI-specific rules reach only election campaign content under COMELEC Resolution No. 11064 and public-sector AI use under DICT-CSC Joint Memorandum Circular No. 003, Series of 2026, while NPC Advisory No. 2024-04 applies the Data Privacy Act of 2012 to AI systems processing personal data.
Policy Lever: Policy runs mainly through soft instruments - national strategies and roadmaps, NPC and BSP guidance and sector memoranda - backed by two narrow binding issuances for elections and government use. Money and capacity sit in CAIR, NAICRI, the National AI Center and the AI+ Infrastructure Masterplan 2026-2033, with no AI sandbox or AI-specific procurement rules in operation.
Governance Type: AI governance is dispersed across DICT and the Civil Service Commission for public-sector use, DOST and NAICRI for research, NPC for data protection, BSP for finance, CHED for higher education and COMELEC for elections, with DEPDev preparing a national AI governance framework. Coordination works through joint circulars and inter-agency processes, while sub-national and judicial roles remain marginal.
Actor Involvement: Industry, civil society and academia participate through congressional technical working groups, agency consultations and strategy validation sessions rather than standing statutory bodies. Internationally the country is highly active, leading an ASEAN AI legal framework initiative during its 2026 chairmanship and engaging UNESCO AI ethics processes.
Enforcement Level: Enforcement is episodic and remit-bound, resting on COMELEC's election monitoring, NPC action under the Data Privacy Act of 2012 and administrative discipline for government AI use, with no published AI-specific sanction decisions.
Specific Laws: National AI Strategy Roadmap 2.0 / NAISR 2.0 (2024), National AI Strategy for the Philippines – NAIS-PH (2025), COMELEC Resolution No. 11064 on Social Media and AI in Election Campaigns (2024), NPC Advisory No. 2024-04 on Application of the Data Privacy Act to AI Systems Processing Personal Data (2024), DICT-CSC Joint Memorandum Circular No. 003, Series of 2026 on Principles for the Ethical and Responsible Development, Deployment and Use of Artificial Intelligence in Government (2026), Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas Memorandum No. M-2026-031 on Governance Principles for Artificial Intelligence (2026), Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas Memorandum No. M-2026-034 on Frontier AI Cybersecurity Risks (2026), CHED Memorandum Order No. 21, Series of 2026 on Responsible AI Use in Higher Education (2026), Philippines AI+ Infrastructure Masterplan 2026–2033 (2026), Data Privacy Act (Republic Act No. 10173, 2012), House Bill 9582 – Philippine Artificial Intelligence Development and Governance Act (pending, 2026), House Bill 7396 – Artificial Intelligence Development and Regulation Act of the Philippines (pending, 2023), Senate Bill 25 – Artificial Intelligence Regulation Act (pending, 2025)

Regulation Status: Poland applies the directly effective EU AI Act, as amended by the Digital Omnibus on AI (Regulation (EU) 2026/1744), alongside the national Act of 3 July 2026 on Artificial Intelligence Systems (Dz.U. 2026 poz. 1003), in force since 11 August 2026 with its supervision, inspection and penalty chapters applicable from 28 October 2026. Coverage is horizontal and written for AI, but the high-risk obligations are postponed to December 2027 and August 2028, and the national supervisor is still being constituted.
Policy Lever: Policy runs through directly applicable EU rules plus the national implementing statute, backed by UODO data-protection guidance for AI and the Ministry of Digital Affairs guide for public administration. Economic levers include the PLN 1 billion AI Fund, publicly funded Polish language models and a statutory KRiBSI sandbox funded at PLN 35 million that has not begun operating.
Governance Type: Supervision is concentrated in one new authority, KRiBSI, an outlier design in the EU, though its statutory collegiate composition drawn from UOKiK, UKE, KNF and KRRiT embeds inter-regulator coordination inside the body. Judicial review lies with the Warsaw competition and consumer protection court, UODO keeps independent GDPR oversight, and sub-national government has no role.
Actor Involvement: Industry, academia and civil society were consulted on the AI Systems Act and the Policy for AI Development in Poland until 2030 and are represented in the PL/AI advisory group, but the statutory Social Council for Artificial Intelligence attached to KRiBSI has not been appointed and stakeholders hold no seat on the Commission. Internationally Poland is a signatory of the Council of Europe Framework Convention on Artificial Intelligence and an active participant in the EU AI Board and OECD AI work.
Enforcement Level: Penalties and a complaint channel open to any person exist in both EU and national law and KRiBSI's inspection and sanctioning powers took effect on 28 October 2026, but no AI-specific decision has been issued.
Specific Laws: Act of 3 July 2026 on Artificial Intelligence Systems (Dz.U. 2026 poz. 1003); EU AI Act (Regulation 2024/1689, 2024); Digital Omnibus on AI (Regulation (EU) 2026/1744, 2026); Policy for the Development of Artificial Intelligence in Poland from 2020 (Council of Ministers Resolution No. 196, 2020); Policy for AI Development in Poland until 2030 (draft Council of Ministers resolution, 2026); Council of Europe Framework Convention on Artificial Intelligence (2024, signed)

Regulation Status: Portugal has enacted no dedicated national AI statute and relies on the directly applicable EU AI Act, supplemented by Lei n.º 58/2019 (GDPR implementation), Lei n.º 24/96 (consumer protection), Decreto-Lei n.º 57/2008 and Lei n.º 125/2025 (NIS2). Prohibited-practice, AI-literacy, general-purpose AI and transparency obligations bind today, while high-risk duties run from December 2027 and August 2028 under the Digital Omnibus on AI. National implementation is partial: ANACOM supervises and consults on guidance, but the law setting competent authorities, penalties and a regulatory sandbox is outstanding.
Policy Lever: Portugal governs AI through the directly applicable EU AI Act, the designation of ANACOM as supervisor and single point of contact, and funding instruments: the Agenda Nacional de Inteligência Artificial and its Action Plan 2026-2030, the AMALIA national large language model and AI Portugal 2030. Soft law is limited to ANACOM's consulted draft recommendations on prohibited practices and government AI Act guidance, and the Technological Free Zones regime (Decreto-Lei n.º 67/2021) has not been converted into an AI Act regulatory sandbox.
Governance Type: Governance follows a lead-plus-sectoral model in which ANACOM supervises the AI Act and serves as national contact point alongside sectoral and fundamental-rights authorities, with Agenda implementation monitored under the governance model of Resolução do Conselho de Ministros n.º 2/2026. No subnational tier regulates AI, and independent scrutiny comes mainly from the CNPD and the courts.
Actor Involvement: Stakeholder involvement runs through consultations and project consortia rather than standing statutory roles, with industry, academic and civil-society representatives on the accompanying committee of the Agenda Nacional de Inteligência Artificial and universities delivering AMALIA. Internationally Portugal acts through the EU AI Board, the EU Coordinated Plan on AI and Portuguese-language digital cooperation.
Enforcement Level: Enforcement is preparatory: ANACOM informs the market and consults on guidance while national penalty rules are unenacted and no AI Act enforcement decision or audit programme has been published.
Specific Laws: EU AI Act / Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (2024), Digital Omnibus on AI / Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 (2026), Resolução do Conselho de Ministros n.º 2/2026 - Agenda Nacional de Inteligência Artificial e Plano de Ação 2026-2030 (2026), Resolução do Conselho de Ministros n.º 178/2026 - AMALIA (2026), Resolução do Conselho de Ministros n.º 201/2024 - AMALIA (2024), Lei n.º 12-A/2026 - execution of the Digital Services Act (2026), Lei n.º 125/2025 - NIS2 cybersecurity (2025), Lei n.º 58/2019 - GDPR Implementation (2019), Lei n.º 24/96 - Consumer Protection Law (1996, applicable to AI), Decreto-Lei n.º 57/2008 - Unfair Commercial Practices (2008, applicable to AI), Decreto-Lei n.º 67/2021 - Technological Free Zones (2021), Estratégia Digital Nacional (2024), AI Portugal 2030 National Strategy (2019)

Regulation Status: Qatar has no horizontal AI statute; the only binding AI-specific rules are the Qatar Central Bank Artificial Intelligence Guideline (2024) for licensed financial institutions and QICDRC Practice Direction No. 1 of 2026 on the use of AI before the QFC Court and Regulatory Tribunal. The Qatar Financial Markets Authority's draft AI regulations consulted in May 2025 remain unenacted, and the Shura Council's sitting of 27 April 2026 produced a call for a national AI framework rather than a bill. The National Artificial Intelligence Strategy (2019), MCIT ethical AI principles and NCSA secure-AI guidelines stay non-binding.
Policy Lever: Qatar pairs two binding sectoral AI instruments with a soft-law layer of MCIT ethics principles and NCSA secure-AI guidelines, and with funding and capability programmes including AIQAT, ALIF and Fanar. Institutional capacity was consolidated by Cabinet Decision No. 34 of 2026, ratified in October 2026, which created a National Center for Artificial Intelligence reporting to the Minister of Communications and Information Technology, while compliance powers over AI remain inside the Qatar Central Bank's existing supervisory machinery.
Governance Type: Governance follows a lead-plus-sectoral pattern: MCIT, its Artificial Intelligence Committee and the new National Center for Artificial Intelligence hold national direction, while the Qatar Central Bank, Qatar Financial Markets Authority, National Cyber Security Agency and Qatar Financial Centre regulate AI inside their perimeters. There is no subnational tier, and independent checks come from the QFC courts and the National Data Privacy Office rather than from broad review of AI policy.
Actor Involvement: Industry participates through regulator consultations, QFC sandboxes and summit partnerships, and academia holds a formal standing role via QCRI's vice-chairmanship of the Artificial Intelligence Committee and the AIQAT programme. Domestic civil society is absent from the process, while international engagement is channelled through GCC and UNESCO fora and Doha's hosting of World Summit AI.
Enforcement Level: Enforcement is confined to the financial sector, where the Qatar Central Bank can act against licensed firms under its AI guideline, and no AI-specific enforcement decision or cross-sector monitoring has been published.
Specific Laws: Qatar National Artificial Intelligence Strategy (2019), Cabinet Decision No. 10 of 2021 establishing the Artificial Intelligence Committee, Personal Data Privacy Protection Law (Law No. 13 of 2016), Qatar Central Bank Artificial Intelligence Guideline (2024), NCSA Guidelines for Secure Adoption and Usage of Artificial Intelligence (2024), MCIT Principles and Guidelines for Ethical Development and Deployment of Artificial Intelligence (2024), QICDRC Practice Direction No. 1 of 2026 on the Use of Artificial Intelligence, Cabinet Decision No. 34 of 2026 establishing the National Center for Artificial Intelligence

Regulation Status: Binding AI rules in Romania come entirely from the directly applicable EU AI Act, whose prohibitions, AI literacy, general-purpose AI and transparency duties bind operators in all sectors, while the high-risk block was postponed to 2 December 2027 and 2 August 2028 by the Digital Omnibus on AI, Regulation (EU) 2026/1744. No standalone domestic AI statute exists: competent authorities were only proposed by a Government memorandum of 12 March 2026 and the implementing law conferring control procedures and the penalty regime remains in preparation. A parliamentary bill filed in October 2026 to prohibit AI-provided legal advice is the only domestic AI-specific legislative initiative.
Policy Lever: Romania governs AI through the directly applicable EU AI Act alongside the non-binding National Artificial Intelligence Strategy 2024-2027 approved by Government Decision No. 832/2024, with economic support channelled via EU instruments rather than dedicated national AI funds. The AI regulatory sandbox required by Article 57 of Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 is not operational and the designated authorities still await the statutory mandate contained in the pending implementing law.
Governance Type: Governance centres on ANCOM as national market surveillance authority and single point of contact, with the Financial Supervisory Authority and the National Bank of Romania for financial-sector high-risk systems, ANSPDCP for biometrics, migration and justice uses, and ADR as notifying authority. Allocation of these roles derives from a Government memorandum rather than statute, sub-national bodies play no part, and independent oversight comes only from general-mandate institutions such as the Ombudsman and the courts.
Actor Involvement: Domestic participation is channelled through the consultative Romanian Committee for Artificial Intelligence established by MCID Order No. 20484/2023, which combines ministry, industry and academic members, while non-governmental organisations contribute only through general public consultation on draft acts. Internationally Romania acts within the European AI Board and the EU legislative process and adheres to the OECD AI Principles.
Enforcement Level: Obligations under Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 bind Romanian operators, yet no national authority can inspect or fine because the law establishing control procedures and the sanctions regime has not been adopted, leaving the record free of any AI enforcement decision.
Specific Laws: EU AI Act / Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (2024), Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 Digital Omnibus on AI amending the AI Act (2026), National Artificial Intelligence Strategy 2024-2027 approved by Government Decision No. 832/2024, MCID Order No. 20484/2023 establishing the Romanian Committee for Artificial Intelligence, Government memorandum of 12 March 2026 designating national competent authorities and the single point of contact for the AI Act, Law No. 190/2018 implementing the GDPR

Regulation Status: Russia's framework statute, Federal Law No. 243-FZ On Supporting the Development of Artificial Intelligence Technologies in the Russian Federation, has been in force since 1 September 2026 but regulates only large foundation models, introducing sovereign and national model statuses, data-localisation requirements and a copyright exception for training. Developer obligations, labelling tools on platforms with more than 500,000 daily users and related government powers take effect on 1 March 2027, with a transition to 2032 for foreign systems already deployed in sensitive areas; mandatory universal labelling of AI-generated content was removed before adoption. Presidential Decree No. 490 (National AI Strategy to 2030) and the experimental legal regime laws FZ-123 and FZ-258 complete the framework.
Policy Lever: Policy mixes a framework statute with industrial-policy levers: support measures and financing for sovereign and national model developers, state-funded compute, access to state data for training, and regulatory sandboxes under FZ-258 and the Moscow regime under FZ-123. Soft law runs through the National Code of Ethics in the Field of Artificial Intelligence and Rosstandart standards, while the substance of binding duties is delegated to secondary acts still to be issued.
Governance Type: Authority is concentrated in the federal executive, with the Presidential Commission created by Decree No. 116 coordinating the Government, the Ministry of Digital Development, the Ministry of Economic Development, the FSB, sectoral regulators and the Bank of Russia. Sub-national bodies, principally Moscow, implement nationally created experimental regimes, and independent judicial or civil-society oversight of AI is absent.
Actor Involvement: AI policy-making is a state-industry affair in which the largest technology companies and the AI Alliance Russia shaped both the 2026 statute and the ethics code, academia contributes through research centres and standards committees, and domestic civil society is excluded. International engagement runs through BRICS and CIS formats and promotion of a sovereign-AI model rather than multilateral treaty frameworks.
Enforcement Level: Enforcement is nominal because the obligations capable of sanction under FZ-243 only become applicable on 1 March 2027, no AI-specific penalties exist in the Code of Administrative Offences, and no authority has exercised compliance powers over AI.
Specific Laws: Federal Law No. 243-FZ On Supporting the Development of Artificial Intelligence Technologies in the Russian Federation (2026), National Strategy for the Development of Artificial Intelligence until 2030 approved by Presidential Decree No. 490 (2019, updated 2024), Presidential Decree No. 116 on the Commission under the President of the Russian Federation on the Development of Artificial Intelligence Technologies (2026), Federal Law No. 123-FZ on the experimental legal regime in the sphere of digital innovation in Moscow (2020, updated 2024), Federal Law No. 258-FZ on experimental legal regimes in the sphere of digital innovation (2020), National Code of Ethics in the Field of Artificial Intelligence (2021)

Regulation Status: Rwanda governs AI through dedicated but non-binding instruments: the Cabinet-approved National AI Policy of April 2023, the AI Readiness and Maturity Framework, and RURA's Guidelines on the Ethical Development and Implementation of Artificial Intelligence. Legal effect comes only from general instruments, chiefly Law No. 058/2021 Relating to the Protection of Personal Data and Privacy and Law No. 24/2016 Governing Information and Communication Technologies. The National Artificial Intelligence Agency, approved by Cabinet on 8 June 2026 and given its senior leadership on 27 October 2026, coordinates development and adoption without imposing enforceable AI obligations.
Policy Lever: Rwanda relies on soft law and investment: the National AI Policy, the AI Readiness and Maturity Framework, RURA ethical guidelines, the National Data Sharing Policy (2025), and funded vehicles such as the Rwanda AI Scaling Hub and C4IR Rwanda, alongside the National Bank of Rwanda regulatory sandbox that is open to fintech rather than AI specifically. Institutional capacity is consolidating in the National Artificial Intelligence Agency, now staffed at leadership level but mandated to coordinate adoption, investment and an AI Factory technical unit rather than to enforce rules.
Governance Type: AI governance is centralised in the executive, with MINICT and the National Artificial Intelligence Agency leading and sectoral regulators applying their existing powers. There is no subnational tier and no judicial or independent-review involvement in AI rule-making.
Actor Involvement: Industry and academia feed in through drafting workshops, C4IR Rwanda and UNESCO- and UNDP-supported processes rather than standing formal bodies, and domestic civil society input has not recurred since the 2023 policy drafting. Internationally Rwanda acts as convenor and norm entrepreneur through the Global AI Summit on Africa, the Africa Declaration on Artificial Intelligence, the Smart Africa Alliance and the UN Global Dialogue on AI Governance.
Enforcement Level: Enforcement touching AI runs solely through the data-protection powers of the National Cyber Security Authority, with no AI-specific obligations, sanctions or published enforcement decisions.
Specific Laws: National AI Policy (2023), AI Readiness and Maturity Framework for Rwanda (2023), Guidelines on the Ethical Development and Implementation of Artificial Intelligence (RURA), Cabinet decision establishing the National Artificial Intelligence Agency (2026), National Data Sharing Policy (2025), Law No. 058/2021 Relating to the Protection of Personal Data and Privacy, Law No. 24/2016 Governing Information and Communication Technologies

Regulation Status: South Sudan has no AI-specific legislation, draft bill or national AI strategy. The Cybercrime and Computer Misuse Act 2026, signed on 18 February 2026 and enforced since 17 July 2026 under Presidential Directive No. 03/2026, regulates hacking, critical infrastructure, online content and investigative powers without any AI provision, and the Data Protection Bill announced for 2026 remains unintroduced.
Policy Lever: Policy activity is confined to general digital law and connectivity work, including the Cybercrime and Computer Misuse Act 2026, the SUDESA Strategic Framework for the Digital Transformation of South Sudan's Government and Public Sector, and the National Spectrum Management and 5G Strategy begun in 2026. AI features only in capacity-building such as the National Communication Authority's AI app development bootcamp and UNESCO-supported training, not in any rule, guidance or funding instrument.
Governance Type: AI governance is absent rather than centralized: digital policy is led by the Ministry of Information, Communication Technology and Postal Services and the National Communication Authority without any AI mandate, and the only new coordination structure, the National Cyber-Security Steering Committee created on enforcement of the Cybercrime and Computer Misuse Act 2026, covers cyber offences. Judicial and independent engagement is limited to challenges to that Act.
Actor Involvement: Domestic engagement on AI is unstructured, with activity limited to community events such as IndabaX South Sudan and donor-run training including the National Communication Authority's all-female AI app development bootcamp. International involvement consists of signing the Africa Declaration on Artificial Intelligence (Kigali, 4 April 2025) alongside African Union and UNESCO membership, without a national alignment process under the African Union Continental Artificial Intelligence Strategy.
Enforcement Level: Enforcement is confined to the general Cybercrime and Computer Misuse Act 2026, operated by a specialised unit under the Internal Security Bureau with criminal penalties, while no AI-specific obligation, authority or monitoring exists.
Specific Laws: Cybercrime and Computer Misuse Act 2026 (signed 18 February 2026; enforced from 17 July 2026 under Presidential Directive No. 03/2026), Cybercrimes and Computer Misuse Provisional Order 2021, SUDESA Strategic Framework for the Digital Transformation of South Sudan's Government and Public Sector, National Spectrum Management and 5G Strategy (under development, 2026), Data Protection Bill (announced for 2026, not introduced), Africa Declaration on Artificial Intelligence (Kigali, 2025, signed) — no domestic instrument is AI-specific

Regulation Status: Saint Kitts and Nevis regulates AI only through general technology and consumer law: the Electronic Transactions Act (Cap. 18.44), the Consumer Protection Act, 2023 adopted from the CARICOM model, and the Data Protection Act, 2018, which was passed on 4 May 2018 and gazetted on 7 June 2018 but has never been brought into force. No AI-specific legislation exists, no AI bill is before the National Assembly, and no national AI strategy has been published. The only connection between binding law and AI is the government's positioning of consumer protection law as the route to fair and responsible AI.
Policy Lever: The policy toolkit contains no AI-specific binding or soft-law instrument of national origin, no AI funding programme, sandbox or procurement rule, and no body with an AI mandate. Activity consists of the state's own adoption of AI tools, notably the Ministry of Justice and Legal Affairs' AI assistant for public legal information and planned AI-based traffic management, alongside endorsement of the regional UNESCO Caribbean Artificial Intelligence Policy Roadmap through CARICOM.
Governance Type: Governance of AI-related technology is concentrated in central government ministries, with no lead AI body, no sectoral allocation and no coordination mechanism. The Nevis Island Administration holds no AI competence, and courts and independent oversight bodies have not addressed AI, although the judiciary has itself begun using AI-assisted legal information services.
Actor Involvement: Domestic AI policy-making involves no structured input from industry, civil society or academia, since no national AI policy process has been opened. Engagement is international and regional: statements at the United Nations General Assembly, participation in the UN Youth and AI dialogue, and endorsement of the UNESCO Caribbean Artificial Intelligence Policy Roadmap through CARICOM.
Enforcement Level: Nothing AI-specific is enforced or monitored, and only generic consumer and electronic transactions penalties could reach AI-related conduct.
Specific Laws: Data Protection Act, 2018 (passed 4 May 2018, not in force), Electronic Transactions Act (Cap. 18.44, 2011), Consumer Protection Act (2023), UNESCO Caribbean Artificial Intelligence Policy Roadmap (endorsed by CARICOM COTED, 2026)

Regulation Status: Saint Lucia has no AI-specific legislation, no draft AI bill and no AI provisions inside general statutes. The partially proclaimed Data Protection Act, Cap 8.18 is the only instrument touching automated processing, and its logic-disclosure limb in Part V has not been commenced. The Minister for Education and Digital Transformation called in January 2026 for rules on AI use in school-based assessments, and no text has been introduced.
Policy Lever: Policy action is confined to broader digital transformation work: the DigiGov e-services platform, the National Authentication Framework digital ID launched in 2026, and a planned UNECLAC-supported regulatory sandbox for digital innovation. Beyond the general Data Protection Act, Cap 8.18, no AI funding, procurement rule, guidance document or mandated institution exists.
Governance Type: Governance of AI is centralised and informal, resting on one ministerial portfolio with no dedicated regulator, no statutory coordination body and no judicial or independent-oversight input. Regional structures, in particular CARICOM and the Caribbean Telecommunications Union Caribbean AI Task Force, provide the only organised forums in which Saint Lucia participates.
Actor Involvement: Structured participation in AI policy is international rather than domestic, through UNESCO ethics processes, CARICOM digital work and the Caribbean Telecommunications Union Caribbean AI Task Force. Domestically, engagement is event-based, with business interest surfacing at the AI Summit Saint Lucia and through the Saint Lucia Chamber of Commerce rather than through any government consultation.
Enforcement Level: Enforcement capacity for AI is absent, with no AI-specific duties, designated authority or recorded action, and monitoring limited to regional readiness studies.
Specific Laws: Data Protection Act, Cap 8.18 (2011, partially in force 2023)
