Regulation Status: Saint Vincent and the Grenadines has no AI-specific legislation, bill or subsidiary regulation. AI is reached only incidentally by the Electronic Transactions Act (2007), the Cybercrime Act (2016) and the Telecommunications Act (2001), none of which contains a provision written for AI systems, and the Privacy Act (2003) has never been brought into force, leaving no data-protection baseline for automated decision-making.
Policy Lever: Policy activity is confined to general digital transformation through the five-year digital transformation strategy process and the Caribbean Digital Transformation Project, neither of which creates AI guidance, funding windows, procurement rules or a sandbox. Regionally endorsed material such as the Caribbean Telecommunications Union's Caribbean AI Task Force Final Report (2026) and the UNESCO Caribbean Artificial Intelligence Policy Roadmap endorsed by CARICOM in July 2026 remains advisory and untranslated into national instruments.
Governance Type: Governance is highly centralized: the National Telecommunications Regulatory Commission is the sole standing authority touching AI-adjacent matters, operating within the regional ECTEL treaty structure, while the ministry responsible for digital transformation sets direction alone. There is no subnational tier and no judicial or independent-review practice shaping AI rules.
Actor Involvement: Engagement on AI is almost entirely external, through Caribbean Telecommunications Union ministerial dialogues, the CARICOM-level Caribbean AI Task Force process and the 4th UNESCO Global Forum on the Ethics of AI. Domestically there is no structured consultation channel on AI policy for industry, civil society or academia.
Enforcement Level: Enforcement capability extends only to general criminal and electronic-transactions penalties, with no AI-specific obligation, designated enforcer or monitoring and audit practice.
Specific Laws: Electronic Transactions Act (2007), Cybercrime Act (2016), Telecommunications Act (2001), Privacy Act (2003, not in force)

Regulation Status: Samoa has no dedicated AI legislation, no binding AI rules and no AI bill before the Legislative Assembly. The National Communications & Information Technology Policy Samoa 2025/26-2030/31 and the Samoa National Cybersecurity Strategy 2025/26-2030/31, launched by the Deputy Prime Minister on 17 April 2026, define artificial intelligence and set trust, safety and responsible data use as principles without creating legal duties. AI activity falls under general telecommunications, crimes and digital identity law.
Policy Lever: Policy action is confined to soft framing in the National ICT Policy 2025/26-2030/31 and National Cybersecurity Strategy 2025/26-2030/31, which treat artificial intelligence as an emerging risk and opportunity, plus the MCIT-UNDP AI trust and safety workshop. No funded AI programme, sandbox, procurement rule or body with a legal AI mandate exists.
Governance Type: Governance is centralised in the Ministry of Communications and Information Technology, whose Digital Transformation and Innovation Division owns digital and cybersecurity policy. Sectoral regulators, subnational authorities and independent review bodies play no AI role, and coordination occurs only through one-off ministry-led events with international partners.
Actor Involvement: Engagement runs through ministry-led consultation events rather than standing structures, with industry, community and expert participants in the National ICT Policy validation, Samoa Digital Week 2026 and the MCIT-UNDP AI workshop. International partners, chiefly UNDP and Pacific regional forums, supply most AI governance input.
Enforcement Level: No AI enforcement framework, penalty, authority or monitoring practice exists, leaving only incidentally applicable telecommunications, digital identity and cybercrime penalties.
Specific Laws: National Communications & Information Technology Policy Samoa 2025/26-2030/31 (2026), Samoa National Cybersecurity Strategy 2025/26-2030/31 (2026), Pathway for the Development of Samoa 2025/26-2030/31, National Digital Identification Act 2024

Regulation Status: San Marino has no AI-specific legislation in force or in the legislative pipeline; artificial intelligence is reached only incidentally through Law No. 171/2018 on personal data protection, enforced by the Autorità Garante per la protezione dei dati personali. The Republic signed the Council of Europe Framework Convention on Artificial Intelligence and Human Rights, Democracy and the Rule of Law on 5 September 2024 but has not ratified it, and the treaty is not in force internationally. The EU–Andorra–San Marino Association Agreement, authorised by the Council of the European Union on 16 July 2026 and signed in Brussels on 19 October 2026, is the channel through which internal-market rules including EU AI legislation would later reach San Marino, with incorporation still pending.
Policy Lever: Policy levers consist of a general data-protection law and a generic high-technology enterprise incentive regime administered by San Marino Innovation S.p.A., recast by Decreto Delegato 16 ottobre 2026 n.159 after the repeal of Decreto Delegato 20 luglio 2026 n.91. No AI strategy, guidance document, AI funding line or body with a statutory AI mandate exists.
Governance Type: Governance is fully centralised in the executive, with the data-protection Garante as the only independent authority whose remit touches AI and San Marino Innovation S.p.A. acting as the state's innovation arm. There is no coordination mechanism, no sub-national layer and no judicial or independent-review practice shaping AI rules.
Actor Involvement: Engagement on AI is predominantly external, through the Council of Europe treaty process, International Monetary Fund and World Bank constituency meetings and European Union accession fora. Domestic involvement is limited to innovation-sector agreements brokered by San Marino Innovation, university-hosted debate and a 2024 citizens' petition, with organised civil society absent.
Enforcement Level: Enforcement reaches AI only indirectly through the data-protection powers of the Garante per la protezione dei dati personali, with no AI-specific penalties, decisions or monitoring.
Specific Laws: Law No. 171 of 21 December 2018 (Protection of Natural Persons with Regard to the Processing of Personal Data), Council of Europe Framework Convention on Artificial Intelligence and Human Rights, Democracy and the Rule of Law (signed 5 September 2024, not ratified), Decreto Delegato n.101/2019 on high-technology enterprises as recast by Decreto Delegato 16 ottobre 2026 n.159, EU–Andorra–San Marino Association Agreement (signed 19 October 2026)

Regulation Status: São Tomé and Príncipe has no AI-specific legislation, draft bill or sectoral AI rule. The applicable framework remains general: Law No. 3/2016 on the Protection of Personal Data, Law No. 7/2017 establishing the National Personal Data Protection Agency (ANPDP), and the Cybercrime Law of 2017, none written for AI systems. The UNESCO Readiness Assessment Methodology country profile places the country at a predominantly consumption stage of AI and identifies regulation and institutional set-up as foundational steps still to be taken.
Policy Lever: Policy activity on AI is limited to the UNESCO-supported readiness diagnostic and its roadmap of recommendations covering regulation, capacity-building and institutional reform. Digital policy runs through the National Digital Governance Strategy (Resolution No. 35/2020/CM), the National Cybersecurity Strategy 2024-2028 and the World Bank Digital São Tomé and Príncipe project, none of which creates AI obligations, AI funding or an AI mandate.
Governance Type: Governance is centralised in a single national government, with INIC leading digital policy and the ANPDP operating as the sole independent digital regulator under Law No. 7/2017, whose powers do not extend to AI as such. No AI-specific authority, coordination mechanism, subnational competence or independent review role exists.
Actor Involvement: International organisations drive what AI engagement exists: UNESCO conducted and published the Readiness Assessment Methodology country report, UNU-EGOV supports the digital governance strategy with INIC, and African Union membership brings the Continental AI Strategy alongside ratification of the Malabo Convention. Domestic industry, civil society and universities have no structured role in AI policy-making.
Enforcement Level: No AI rules exist to enforce, and the ANPDP's general data protection mandate, which UNESCO identifies as needing strengthened enforcement, has produced no recorded AI-related action.
Specific Laws: Law No. 3/2016 on the Protection of Personal Data (2016), Law No. 7/2017 on the Organisation and Functioning of the National Personal Data Protection Agency (2017), Cybercrime Law (2017), National Digital Governance Strategy approved by Resolution No. 35/2020/CM (2020), National Cybersecurity Strategy 2024-2028 (2023), African Union Convention on Cyber Security and Personal Data Protection ratified 25 September 2023, UNESCO AI Readiness Assessment Methodology country report for São Tomé and Príncipe (2025)

Regulation Status: Binding AI obligations are confined to AI-written provisions inside general law: the Copyright Law (Royal Decree M/169) and its Implementing Regulations, in force since 12 August 2026, permit reproduction of lawfully published works to develop AI products and algorithms under stated conditions, and the Personal Data Protection Law reaches automated processing and profiling without AI-specific duties. The dedicated AI instruments—AI Ethics Principles, Generative AI Guidelines, Deepfakes Guidelines, AI Adoption Framework and the National AI Risk Management Framework (SDAIA-P145)—are non-binding. The draft Global AI Hub Law (CST, consultation 2025) and the draft Responsible AI Policy (SDAIA, consultation closed 3 May 2026) have not been enacted.
Policy Lever: Policy runs mainly through SDAIA's maintained soft-law suite, funded Vision 2030 programmes, operating regulatory sandboxes and public-sector adoption leverage, with the 2026 designation of the Year of Artificial Intelligence framing the agenda. Binding levers reach AI only through the Personal Data Protection Law and the AI-training provisions of the 2026 Copyright Law.
Governance Type: Governance is centralized in SDAIA, which sets strategy, issues the AI frameworks and enforces the Personal Data Protection Law, with CST, SAIP and the Digital Government Authority acting inside their own mandates. There is no subnational tier and no independent body shaping AI rules.
Actor Involvement: Participation is consultation-based through the Istitlaa platform, with no standing seats for industry, civil society or academia. Internationally the Kingdom is active in UN, UNESCO and G20 AI governance work and hosts major AI events and the UNESCO-affiliated ICAIRE, without acceding to a binding AI treaty.
Enforcement Level: Enforcement reaches AI only through general law, chiefly the Personal Data Protection Law administered by SDAIA's violation-review committees, with no sanction or published decision attached to an AI-specific obligation.
Specific Laws: National Strategy for Data and AI – NSDAI (2020), Personal Data Protection Law – Royal Decree M/19 (2021, in force 2023) and its Implementing Regulations (amendment consultation 2026), AI Ethics Principles – SDAIA (2023), Generative AI Guidelines – SDAIA (2024), Deepfakes Guidelines – SDAIA (2024), AI Adoption Framework – SDAIA (2025), National Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework – SDAIA-P145 (2026), Copyright Law – Royal Decree M/169 (2026, in force 12 August 2026) and its Implementing Regulations issued by SAIP (31 July 2026), Cabinet decision designating 2026 the Year of Artificial Intelligence (2026), Draft Responsible AI Policy – SDAIA (consultation closed May 2026), Draft Global AI Hub Law – CST (2025)

Regulation Status: Senegal has no binding AI-specific legislation; AI is governed through the non-binding Stratégie Nationale pour le Développement de l'Intelligence Artificielle (2023) and the New Deal Technologique Horizon 2034 launched in February 2025. Binding digital legislating remains general: Law No. 25/2026 on the protection of critical information infrastructures and digital security was adopted on 20 August 2026, and Law No. 2008-12 on personal data is the instrument the regulator applies to AI processing. A regional parliamentary workshop in Dakar from 16 to 18 September 2026 and an October 2026 presidential-adviser call for a transdisciplinary AI commission discussed future rules without producing a national bill.
Policy Lever: Policy runs on non-binding strategy, training and investment rather than regulation: the SNDIA, the New Deal Technologique Horizon 2034, a joint ministerial plan to train more than 35,000 civil servants, and the Senegal AI Scaling Up programme targeting 500,000 people. Binding levers reach AI only through data-protection and digital-security law administered by the Commission de Protection des Données Personnelles and the Autorité de Régulation des Télécommunications et des Postes.
Governance Type: AI policy is centralised in the Ministry of Telecommunications and Digital Affairs, with the Commission de Protection des Données Personnelles and the Autorité de Régulation des Télécommunications et des Postes acting within their existing data and telecoms remits. Sub-national authorities have no role, and independent scrutiny of AI decisions comes only from data-protection supervision.
Actor Involvement: Industry, civil society and academia are consulted through the SNDIA process, the UNESCO Readiness Assessment Methodology exercise and events such as Afrik'IA, but none holds a standing formal role. International engagement is the strongest channel, through the African Union, Smart Africa, UNESCO, the Hiroshima AI Process Friends Group and United Nations discussions on autonomous weapons.
Enforcement Level: Enforcement touching AI occurs only under data-protection and digital-security law, with no AI-specific obligation, penalty or dedicated supervisor.
Specific Laws: National Strategy for the Development of Artificial Intelligence in Senegal (SNDIA) (2023), New Deal Technologique Horizon 2034 (2025), Law No. 2008-12 on the Protection of Personal Data (2008), Law No. 25/2026 on the Protection of Critical Information Infrastructures and Digital Security (2026), African Union Convention on Cyber Security and Personal Data Protection (Malabo Convention) (ratified 2016)

Regulation Status: Serbia has no binding AI law in force: artificial intelligence is addressed through the Strategy for the Development of Artificial Intelligence 2025-2030, the 2023 Ethical Guidelines and general legislation on data protection, electronic commerce and information security. The Ministry of Science, Technological Development and Innovation working group has produced only a working version of a Law on Artificial Intelligence modelled on the EU AI Act, with risk classification, prohibited practices, labelling of AI-generated content, an Artificial Intelligence Agency and conformity-assessment bodies, and with the defence and security sectors excluded; adoption is targeted for December 2026 and no official draft has reached the National Assembly. The draft Law on Personal Data Protection published for consultation on 30 July 2026 would add AI risk tiering, mandatory impact assessments and prior Commissioner opinions for high-risk AI processing, and remains a draft after the consultation closed on 10 September 2026.
Policy Lever: Policy is delivered through strategy, ethics guidance and spending: the Strategy for the Development of Artificial Intelligence 2025-2030 with its action plan, the 2023 Ethical Guidelines, the state-funded Institute for Artificial Intelligence of Serbia, the National AI Platform and Science Fund and Innovation Fund programmes. Coordination sits with the advisory Council for Artificial Intelligence, which holds no compliance powers, and the regulatory sandbox, conformity-assessment bodies and high-risk register remain tied to the pending draft law.
Governance Type: Governance is centralised in the Ministry of Science, Technological Development and Innovation, supported by the cross-ministerial Council for Artificial Intelligence and a drafting working group, with the Office for IT and eGovernment running the National AI Platform. No independent AI regulator exists, subnational authorities play no part, and independent scrutiny has not produced any AI decision.
Actor Involvement: Participation in domestic rule-making is invitation-based: industry bodies, NALED and academic experts sit in the ministry working group, while digital-rights groups comment from outside and the AI law working version has not gone to public consultation, unlike the draft Law on Personal Data Protection. Internationally Serbia is highly active, having chaired the Global Partnership on Artificial Intelligence, hosted the Belgrade Ministerial Declaration, joined the AI Opportunity Partnership and aligned its draft law with the EU AI Act as an accession candidate.
Enforcement Level: No AI-specific obligations, penalties, supervisory authority or audit regime are in force, and the single AI-related data protection complaint ended without action.
Specific Laws: Strategy for the Development of Artificial Intelligence in the Republic of Serbia 2025-2030 (Official Gazette RS No. 5/2025), Strategy for the Development of Artificial Intelligence in the Republic of Serbia 2020-2025 (Official Gazette RS No. 73/2019), Ethical Guidelines for the Development, Application and Use of Reliable and Responsible Artificial Intelligence (2023), Law on Personal Data Protection (2018), Draft Law on Artificial Intelligence (2026, working version in preparation), Draft Law on Personal Data Protection (2026, public consultation 30 July-10 September 2026), Belgrade Ministerial Declaration on Artificial Intelligence (2024)

Regulation Status: Seychelles has no dedicated AI legislation and no AI bill in the National Assembly; the Data Protection Act, 2023 (Act 24 of 2023), in force since 22 December 2023 and enforced by the Information Commission, reaches AI only as general data law. The AI-specific instruments are both non-binding policy: the National Artificial Intelligence in Education Framework 2026-2030, published in March 2026 and approved by Cabinet on 22 July 2026 for state schools, and the Seychelles Digital & AI Strategy 2026-2031, approved by Cabinet on 28 October 2026 as the national framework for digital and AI transformation. The National Institute of Science, Technology and Innovation Act, 2025 (Act 24 of 2025) names artificial intelligence among the institute's promotional functions without creating obligations on AI developers or users.
Policy Lever: Policy runs through Cabinet-approved strategy and sectoral frameworks, ministry-led capacity building with the Commonwealth of Learning and World Bank technical support, and an approved sovereign Government Cloud and Datacentre Project intended to supply local AI computing. No AI-specific binding instrument, disbursed AI funding line, regulatory sandbox or AI procurement rule is in place.
Governance Type: AI governance sits with central executive bodies: the Department of Information Communications Technology under the Vice-President for digital and AI policy, the Ministry of Education and Human Resource Development for the education framework, and the Information Commission and Information and Communications Technologies Authority applying general data and communications law. A formal Inter-Ministerial Digital and AI Coordination Committee has been approved but not yet constituted, and districts, courts and independent review bodies play no part.
Actor Involvement: Domestic engagement is event-based: a National Assembly seminar on artificial intelligence in March 2024, the 2026 National Innovation Fair, the July 2026 validation workshop on the National Digital & AI Strategy covering public institutions, private sector, academia and civil society, and the Digital Economic Transformation Forum approved in September 2026. External linkage comes from World Bank support for the digital economy and education work, the Commonwealth of Learning teacher-competency programme, and membership of UNESCO and the African Union.
Enforcement Level: Enforcement touching AI rests entirely on general data protection and communications law, with no AI-specific penalties, no recorded actions and only framework-level monitoring commitments in schools.
Specific Laws: Seychelles Digital & AI Strategy 2026-2031 (2026), National Artificial Intelligence in Education Framework 2026-2030 (2026), Data Protection Act, 2023 (Act 24 of 2023), National Institute of Science, Technology and Innovation Act, 2025 (Act 24 of 2025)

Regulation Status: Sierra Leone has no enacted AI-specific legislation and none before Parliament. The Ministry of Communication, Technology and Innovation, working with the World Bank Group, produced a Draft Sierra Leone AI Readiness Diagnostic Report and consulted on it over three days in May 2026 as the basis for a first National AI Strategy, which remains unadopted. AI-related conduct falls under general law, chiefly the Cyber Security and Crime Act 2021, while the Cabinet-approved National Data Protection Policy of April 2026 awaits a merged data protection and access-to-information law.
Policy Lever: Policy runs through donor-funded programmes rather than law, with the Sierra Leone Digital Transformation Project financing the AI readiness diagnostic, a civil-service digital and AI literacy programme and the National AI and Deepfake Awareness Campaign launched in Freetown in September 2026. The Bank of Sierra Leone fintech regulatory sandbox is not AI-specific, and no AI procurement rules or AI-specific binding instruments exist.
Governance Type: AI governance is concentrated in central government, with the Ministry of Communication, Technology and Innovation as lead and the Directorate of Science, Technology and Innovation and Ministry of Information and Civic Education as implementing partners. Coordination happens inside individual World Bank-financed projects, with no statutory mechanism, subnational competence or independent oversight.
Actor Involvement: Domestic participation is limited to the one-off May 2026 engagement on the Draft AI Readiness Diagnostic Report, in which government, media, civil society and private-sector actors took part, and no body holds a standing advisory seat. International engagement is more active, combining World Bank partnership, African Union Continental AI Strategy membership, endorsement of the Call for Control of Frontier AI Models and presidential advocacy at the 81st UN General Assembly.
Enforcement Level: With no AI rules in force, there is nothing to enforce and no penalties, designated authority or monitoring of AI systems.
Specific Laws: Cyber Security and Crime Act (2021), National Communications Authority Act (2022), National Innovation and Digital Strategy (2019-2029), National Data Protection Policy (2026) [Cabinet-approved], Data Protection and Right to Access Information Bill (2025) [draft, not enacted], Sierra Leone AI Readiness Diagnostic Report (2026) [draft, non-binding], National AI Strategy [under development], National AI and Deepfake Awareness Campaign (2026)

Regulation Status: Singapore governs AI chiefly through AI-explicit voluntary instruments: the Model AI Governance Framework family including the Model AI Governance Framework for Agentic AI (2026), AI Verify, the IMDA Transparency Guidelines for Generative AI Chatbots of 20 July 2026, the PDPC Advisory Guidelines on Use of Personal Data in Generative AI of 20 July 2026, and the MAS Guidelines on Artificial Intelligence Risk Management issued 7 October 2026 with phased compliance by 2027 and 2028. Binding duties are confined to AI-generated content under the Elections (Integrity of Online Advertising) (Amendment) Act 2024, the Online Safety (Relief and Accountability) Act 2025 in force from 29 June 2026, and Penal Code amendments criminalising AI-generated intimate images and child abuse material from 17 August 2026. The Personal Data Protection Act 2012 supplies the general legal base, read through PDPC guidance that makes generative-AI notification expected of organisations relying on legitimate interests.
Policy Lever: Policy runs on voluntary frameworks, testing infrastructure and money: the Model AI Governance Frameworks, AI Verify and its testing-firm accreditation scheme, the PDPC generative AI guidelines, IMDA chatbot transparency guidelines and the MAS AI Risk Management Guidelines and Toolkit, backed by the National AI Missions, research funding and testbeds. Binding levers remain the election deepfake ban, the Penal Code AI-image offences and the online safety regime applied by existing regulators.
Governance Type: AI governance is centralised in IMDA and MDDI with the AI Verify Foundation as delivery vehicle, while MAS, PDPC, the Online Safety Commission and the Elections Department handle their own domains under National AI Council coordination. There is no subnational tier, and judicial involvement is limited to ordinary remedies and the new online-safety statutory torts.
Actor Involvement: Industry and academia have continuing structured roles through the AI Verify Foundation, the Singapore AI Safety Institute at NTU and sectoral work with MAS, while domestic civil society is engaged only through periodic consultations. International engagement is intensive, spanning the AI Safety Institute network, OECD processes, ASEAN leadership and joint testing with Japan.
Enforcement Level: Enforcement reaches AI only through narrow content offences and general statutes such as the Personal Data Protection Act 2012, with penalties defined but no published sanction yet imposed under an AI-specific provision.
Specific Laws: National AI Strategy (2019), National AI Strategy 2.0 (2023), National AI Strategy Update (2026), Model AI Governance Framework (2019, updated 2024 for Generative AI), Model AI Governance Framework for Agentic AI (2026), Personal Data Protection Act (2012, amended 2020), PDPC Advisory Guidelines on Use of Personal Data in Generative AI (2026), IMDA Transparency Guidelines for Generative AI Chatbots (2026), Elections (Integrity of Online Advertising) (Amendment) Act (2024), Online Safety (Relief and Accountability) Act (2025), Criminal Law (Miscellaneous Amendments) Act (2025), Online Criminal Harms Act (2023), Online Safety (Miscellaneous Amendments) Act (2022), MAS Guidelines on Artificial Intelligence Risk Management (2026), MAS AI Risk Management Toolkit (2026), Scams (Countermeasures) and Other Matters Act (2026)

Regulation Status: Slovakia is governed by the directly applicable EU AI Act, whose prohibitions, AI-literacy, general-purpose AI and Article 50 transparency obligations apply today, while Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 postponed high-risk duties to December 2027 and the machine-readable marking of pre-existing generative systems to 2 December 2026. Nationally, Act No. 56/2018 Coll. on conformity assessment of products was amended by Act No. 318/2025 Coll. with effect from 1 January 2026, and the Act on State Administration in the Field of Artificial Intelligence and European Data Regulation (parliamentary print 1447) is awaiting second reading with proposed effect from 1 January 2027. No standalone Slovak AI statute is in force.
Policy Lever: Policy rests on the directly applicable EU AI Act plus the conformity-assessment amendment in Act No. 318/2025 Coll., supplemented by MIRRI guidance, CERAI advisory opinions and EU codes of practice. Economic levers are European Digital Innovation Hubs, supercomputing and AI-skills funding; the regulatory sandbox and dedicated supervisory staffing are provided for only in the pending state-administration bill.
Governance Type: Governance is concentrated in MIRRI as coordinator, single contact point and prospective general AI market surveillance authority, with sectoral supervision split among the Office for Personal Data Protection, National Security Authority, Slovak Trade Inspection, Office for Inspection Service and Ministry of Justice under the pending act. A separate digital integrity body was dropped on budgetary grounds, no subnational layer exists, and independent scrutiny is limited to CERAI's advisory role.
Actor Involvement: Industry, academia and trade unions feed into AI policy through the AIslovakIA platform, CERAI, the interdepartmental comment procedure and a 2026 memorandum with the Technology Trade Union, while NGOs have no standing statutory seat. Internationally Slovakia acts through the EU AI Board, OECD and GPAI and has signed the Council of Europe Framework Convention on Artificial Intelligence.
Enforcement Level: Penalties exist on paper through the directly applicable AI Act and Act No. 318/2025 Coll., but no Slovak authority is yet legally empowered or resourced and no AI enforcement decision has been issued.
Specific Laws: EU AI Act – Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (2024), Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 amending the AI Act (2026), Act No. 56/2018 Coll. on Conformity Assessment of Products as amended by Act No. 318/2025 Coll. (2025), Government Bill on State Administration in the Field of Artificial Intelligence and European Data Regulation, parliamentary print 1447 (2026), Act No. 18/2018 Coll. on Personal Data Protection (2018), Act No. 69/2018 Coll. on Cybersecurity (2018), Government Plenipotentiary for Artificial Intelligence (2025), Action Plan for Digital Transformation of Slovakia 2023–2026 (2023), CERAI Standing Commission on Ethics and Regulation of Artificial Intelligence (2020)

Regulation Status: Slovenia applies Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 directly, operationalised by the Act on the Implementation of the EU Regulation on Harmonised Rules on Artificial Intelligence (ZIUDHPUI, Uradni list RS 85/25, in force 21 November 2025), which names competent authorities, offences and fines and creates the National Council for Ethics in Artificial Intelligence. Prohibited practices, AI literacy, general-purpose AI and Article 50 transparency duties apply, while Annex III high-risk obligations were postponed to 2 December 2027 and Annex I obligations to 2 August 2028 by Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 (Digital Omnibus on AI, in force 27 July 2026). Sector-specific duties appear in the Media Act (ZMed-1), which requires labelling of generative-AI content and places AI-assisted content under editorial responsibility.
Policy Lever: The binding layer is Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 as amended by the Digital Omnibus Regulation (EU) 2026/1744, implemented by ZIUDHPUI and complemented by AI-content labelling in ZMed-1, with soft law in the National Strategy for Artificial Intelligence until 2030 (adopted 5 March 2026), AKOS guidance and Information Commissioner opinions. Economic levers include the Slovenian AI Factory, the AI Competence Centre, European Digital Innovation Hubs and NpUI financing, while the AKOS regulatory sandbox is in preparation after a public call closing 30 September 2026.
Governance Type: The Ministry for Digital Transformation steers AI policy while supervision is divided among AKOS, the Information Commissioner, the Bank of Slovenia, the Insurance Supervision Agency, the Market Inspectorate and the Information Society Inspectorate, linked by the coordination council of supervisory authorities created by ZIUDHPUI. Oversight is wholly national, and independent input comes from the Information Commissioner and the National Council for Ethics in Artificial Intelligence rather than from courts or sub-national bodies.
Actor Involvement: Preparation of the National Strategy for Artificial Intelligence until 2030 drew on ministries, research institutions, business, the public sector and civil society through public consultations and endorsement by the Economic and Social Council, and AKOS opened the sandbox thematic area to public proposals. Academic experts hold statutory seats on the National Council for Ethics in Artificial Intelligence, while international engagement runs through the EU AI Board, OECD work and the Council of Europe Framework Convention.
Enforcement Level: Tiered fines are legislated in ZIUDHPUI and supervisory powers have applied since 2 August 2026, but enforcement to date consists of guidance and opinions rather than decisions or sanctions.
Specific Laws: EU AI Act / Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (2024), Digital Omnibus on Artificial Intelligence – Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 (2026), Act on the Implementation of the EU Regulation on Harmonised Rules on Artificial Intelligence – ZIUDHPUI (2025), Media Act – ZMed-1 (2025), National Strategy for Artificial Intelligence until 2030 – NsUI 2030 (2026), National Programme to Promote the Development and Use of AI in the Republic of Slovenia by 2025 – NpUI (2021), Digital Slovenia 2030 Strategy (2023)

Regulation Status: Solomon Islands has no AI-specific legislation, regulation or bill. AI is addressed only in planning and administrative documents: the SIG ICT Services Digital - Data, People, Technology and Cyber Strategy 2026-2030 lists an AI for Government project and an intention to develop ethical AI guidelines, the ICT for Education Master Plan 2026-2030 covers AI literacy, and the Ministry of Education and Human Resources Development has issued a policy on student use of AI in examinations. General data law is also absent, as the Data Protection and Privacy Bill drafted with UNCTAD support remains unenacted.
Policy Lever: Policy runs through strategy documents and donor-supported projects rather than instruments, with the Ministry of Communication and Aviation and the Ministry of Education and Human Resources Development each pursuing AI items in their own plans. No funded AI program, regulatory sandbox, procurement rule or dedicated AI institution exists.
Governance Type: Governance is centralized in national ministries, with AI responsibilities appearing in separate ministerial strategies rather than in any designated regulator or coordination mechanism. Provincial administrations and independent review bodies play no part in AI policy.
Actor Involvement: Engagement on AI is predominantly external, through the Pacific Islands Forum and donor partners including UNCTAD, UNDP and the World Bank. Domestic industry and civil society have no structured role, and academic input is confined to one-off education dialogues.
Enforcement Level: Enforcement is absent because no AI-specific obligation, penalty or supervisory authority exists.
Specific Laws: SIG ICT Services Digital - Data, People, Technology and Cyber Strategy 2026-2030, Solomon Islands ICT for Education Master Plan 2026-2030, Pacific Digital and Artificial Intelligence Technology Principles (2026), National Cyber Security Policy (2024), National ICT Policy (2017), draft Data Protection and Privacy Bill (2024)

Regulation Status: Somalia has no AI-specific legislation, draft bill or national AI strategy; AI reaches the statute book only through the Data Protection Act (Law No. 005 of 2023), whose Article 23 gives a right not to be subject to decisions based solely on automated processing and whose transparency duties cover automated decision-making and profiling. Governmental engagement with AI remains convening activity, principally the National Communications Authority's Second AI Summit Somalia 2026 in Mogadishu in June 2026, which addressed AI governance without producing a binding instrument.
Policy Lever: Policy action on AI is limited to convening and research: the National Communications Authority hosts the annual AI Summit Somalia with World Bank SCALE-UP support, and Somali National University opened the Somali National Artificial Intelligence Centre in July 2026 for AI research, capacity building and policy input. No AI guidance, standard, sandbox, procurement rule or statutory AI mandate has been created.
Governance Type: Governance is centralised and informal: the National Communications Authority acts as de facto AI convenor and the Data Protection Authority administers automated-decision rights under the Data Protection Act (Law No. 005 of 2023). Coordination happens around summits rather than through standing mechanisms, federal member states play no part, and no judicial or independent oversight of AI exists.
Actor Involvement: Engagement is strongest from academia, with Somali National University and Zamzam University co-organising the national AI summit and Somali National University hosting the Somali National Artificial Intelligence Centre; industry and civil society take part as summit attendees rather than through formal consultation. International involvement runs through African Union membership, cooperation with Saudi Arabia's Communications, Space and Technology Commission on AI regulation, and UNESCO ethics-of-AI implementation work.
Enforcement Level: Enforcement touching AI is confined to general data protection measures, such as the Data Protection Authority's 2026 mandatory registration directive under Article 32 of the Data Protection Act, with no AI-specific penalties, authority or monitoring.
Specific Laws: Data Protection Act (Law No. 005 of 2023), Communications Act (2017)

Regulation Status: No cross-sector AI statute exists: the Draft South Africa National Artificial Intelligence Policy gazetted on 10 April 2026 was withdrawn after fictitious AI-generated citations were found and formally retracted by Government Gazette on 12 June 2026, with a redraft due before Cabinet by March 2027. The one binding AI obligation is the Electoral Code of Conduct Countering Disinformation in the Local Government Elections, promulgated on 4 September 2026, which requires AI-generated audio, images, video and text to be identified as synthetic content before distribution. Everything else rests on general law, principally the Protection of Personal Information Act and its section 71 on automated decision-making.
Policy Lever: Policy runs through soft instruments and capacity programmes: the National AI Policy Framework (2024), the FSCA and Prudential Authority AI report, SABS draft adoptions of ISO/IEC AI standards, and DCDT-funded AIISA hubs. The expert panel rebuilding the withdrawn draft policy is advisory, and the FSCA has deferred new AI rules pending Financial Stability Board guidance.
Governance Type: Governance centres on the Department of Communications and Digital Technologies, with sectoral regulators applying their own statutes to AI and the Electoral Commission owning the single binding AI rule. Coordination is occasional and bilateral, provinces have no regulatory role, and legislative and public-complaint scrutiny is episodic.
Actor Involvement: Participation is consultative and task-bound: a gazetted comment window cut short by the withdrawal, SABS standards comment, summit and survey-based industry engagement, and academic experts given a formal but temporary review role. Internationally the government is active through the G20 AI Task Force, the African Union AI agenda and UNESCO, without being party to an AI treaty.
Enforcement Level: Enforcement reaching AI is confined to election-period complaint handling by the Electoral Commission and to general POPIA enforcement notices and administrative fines, none of which have turned on AI.
Specific Laws: Protection of Personal Information Act (POPIA) No. 4 of 2013 (fully effective 2021), Local Government: Municipal Electoral Act No. 27 of 2000, Electoral Code of Conduct Countering Disinformation in the Local Government Elections (gazetted 4 September 2026), National AI Policy Framework (2024), National AI Government Summit Discussion Document (2024), Draft South Africa National Artificial Intelligence Policy (gazetted 10 April 2026, withdrawn and retracted by Government Gazette 12 June 2026), Artificial Intelligence in the South African Financial Sector report of the Financial Sector Conduct Authority and Prudential Authority (2025), South African Bureau of Standards draft AI standards (2026)

Regulation Status: South Korea has a horizontal, dedicated AI statute: the Framework Act on the Development of Artificial Intelligence and the Establishment of a Foundation for Trustworthiness (AI Basic Act) and its Enforcement Decree took effect on 22 January 2026, imposing transparency, safety, high-impact AI and domestic representative duties with extraterritorial reach. Implementation is well advanced — five MSIT guidelines issued on 22 January 2026 and revised 29 January 2026, two notices, decree amendments effective 21 July and 20 August 2026 — but MSIT operates a grace period of at least one year in which fact-finding investigations, corrective orders and administrative fines are generally withheld except in cases of serious harm. Further amendments on AI Hub training-data delivery cleared the Cabinet on 13 October 2026 for April 2027 application.
Policy Lever: Korea pairs a binding core — the AI Basic Act and Decree, election and sexual-crime deepfake provisions, and the Personal Information Protection Act amended with effect from 11 September 2026 raising surcharges to 10% of total revenue — with a maintained body of MSIT and PIPC guidance. Economic levers are large and operating, including the 2026 AI budget, the National AI Computing Center, the ICT regulatory sandbox and reformed AI public procurement rules, while MSIT's compliance powers stay unused during the grace period.
Governance Type: MSIT administers the AI Basic Act with the Korea AI Safety Institute, while the PIPC, KCC, NEC and sectoral regulators apply their own remits to AI, coordinated through the statutory presidential National AI Strategy Committee that met in plenary on 25 February 2026 and conducted policy field visits through October 2026. Sub-national bodies execute national plans rather than regulate, and independent checks run through the PIPC and the courts.
Actor Involvement: Industry and academic experts hold standing appointments on the presidential National AI Strategy Committee and on the AI Basic Act institutional improvement task force, while civil society input runs through public comment rounds and task force places rather than reserved statutory roles. Internationally Korea is a frontrunner through the Seoul AI Safety Summit, the International Network of AI Safety Institutes and OECD, GPAI and APEC work.
Enforcement Level: Penalties exist across the AI Basic Act but are held in abeyance during the grace period, so active enforcement touching AI comes from election deepfake takedowns, criminal deepfake prosecutions and PIPC action under the amended Personal Information Protection Act, with MSIT limited to chasing unfiled domestic representative designations after only Anthropic completed its filing by August 2026.
Specific Laws: Framework Act on the Development of Artificial Intelligence and the Establishment of a Foundation for Trustworthiness / AI Basic Act (Act No. 20676, 2025, effective 2026), AI Basic Act partial amendment (Act No. 21311, 2026), AI Basic Act Enforcement Decree (Presidential Decree No. 36053, 2026, as amended by Presidential Decrees No. 36506 and No. 36580, 2026), AI Basic Act and Framework Act on the Promotion of the Data Industry amendments on AI Hub training data (2026, effective April 2027), Personal Information Protection Act as amended (Act No. 21445, in force 11 September 2026), Public Official Election Act deepfake provisions (2023), Act on Special Cases Concerning the Punishment of Sexual Crimes as amended (2024), Presidential Decree on the Establishment and Operation of the National AI Strategy Committee (2025), Korea AI Action Plan 2026-2028 (2026), National AI Strategy (2019)

Regulation Status: Spain is governed by the directly applicable EU AI Act, as amended by the Digital Omnibus on AI (Regulation (EU) 2026/1744, in force 27 July 2026), whose prohibitions and AI-literacy duties have applied since 2 February 2025, general-purpose AI model duties since 2 August 2025 and Article 50 transparency duties since 2 August 2026, with Annex III high-risk obligations postponed to 2 December 2027 and Annex I product-embedded obligations to 2 August 2028. The national Proyecto de Ley Orgánica para el buen uso y la gobernanza de la inteligencia artificial, approved by the Council of Ministers on 26 May 2026, lapsed on 6 October 2026 when the Cortes were dissolved for the 29 November 2026 general election, so the only domestic AI-specific binding instruments are Royal Decree 729/2023 and Royal Decree 817/2023.
Policy Lever: The binding layer combines the EU AI Act with two royal decrees creating AESIA and the pre-AI Act regulatory sandbox, supported by a maintained AESIA guidance pack updated in August 2026 and the technical guides produced through the sandbox pilot whose results report was published in September 2026. Economic levers include ENIA, the Digital Spain 2026 Agenda, Cátedras ENIA chairs and the Plan IA360 EUR 600 million adoption voucher, while AESIA has the mandate and staff but no operative sanctioning regime.
Governance Type: AESIA is the designated lead supervisor and market surveillance authority, with the AEPD, CNMC and financial regulators acting on AI within their own remits and coordination resting on interministerial and advisory structures rather than a statutory framework, since the bill that would have fixed the architecture lapsed. Regions deliver and fund AI programmes without regulatory autonomy, and independent review comes from occasional judicial decisions and consultative bodies.
Actor Involvement: Industry, academia and civil society feed into AI policy through public consultations, the regulatory sandbox and advisory bodies, with academia the most institutionalised via the International AI Advisory Council and the Cátedras ENIA chairs. Spain is highly active internationally in the EU AI Board, OECD, UNESCO and Council of Europe processes.
Enforcement Level: Penalties for AI Act breaches remain unavailable in Spain because the law needed to define infringements and confer sanctioning powers lapsed, so data-protection decisions by the AEPD are the only AI-related sanctions.
Specific Laws: EU AI Act – Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (2024), Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 Digital Omnibus on AI amending Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (2026, in force 27 July 2026), Royal Decree 729/2023 on the AESIA Statute (2023), Royal Decree 817/2023 establishing the controlled testing environment for artificial intelligence (2023), Proyecto de Ley Orgánica para el buen uso y la gobernanza de la Inteligencia Artificial (2026, lapsed 6 October 2026), Estrategia Nacional de Inteligencia Artificial – ENIA (2020), Digital Spain 2026 Agenda (2021), Plan IA360 (2026), Order ETD/1180/2022 on Cátedras ENIA (2022), Order TDF/304/2025 (2025)

Regulation Status: AI governance rests on the non-binding National AI Strategy 2024-2028 (AI Sri Lanka 2028) and the University Grants Commission's National Policy Framework for the Use of Artificial Intelligence in the State University System, launched on 8 May 2026 and issued in October 2026; no AI-specific legislation is enacted or before Parliament. The Personal Data Protection Act No. 9 of 2022, as amended by Act No. 22 of 2025, binds data processing and covers solely automated decisions, but Gazette 2498/16 of 22 July 2026 brings Sections 2 and 3 and Parts I and III into operation only on 1 January 2027. The Online Safety Act No. 9 of 2024 regulates online content generally with no provision written for AI.
Policy Lever: Sri Lanka uses strategy documents, sectoral frameworks, funding and capacity-building rather than binding AI instruments, with AI literacy training for civil servants delivered with UNESCO and GovTech Sri Lanka. The Central Bank FinTech sandbox and the Personal Data Protection Act operate under general mandates, and no AI procurement rules or AI regulatory body are in force.
Governance Type: AI policy is concentrated in the Ministry of Digital Economy and the Presidential Secretariat's digital economy advisory structure, with sectoral regulators confined to existing mandates and no dedicated AI regulator. Coordination is informal, running through the Presidential Secretariat committee, the UNESCO readiness assessment steering committee and national events.
Actor Involvement: Industry, academia and civil society participate through consultations, drafting committees and national events such as Sri Lanka AI Week 2026, but none hold standing statutory roles. International engagement is bilateral and declaratory, covering the UNESCO ethics recommendation, the UNESCO readiness assessment launched in October 2026, and cooperation discussions with the United States, Singapore and China.
Enforcement Level: No AI-specific sanctions, authority or monitoring exist, and the Data Protection Authority's general powers begin only with the commencement of Parts I and III on 1 January 2027, for which it has issued Personal Data Protection Circular No. 01/2026 as preparatory guidance.
Specific Laws: National AI Strategy 2024-2028 (AI Sri Lanka 2028) (2024), National Policy Framework for the Use of Artificial Intelligence in the State University System of Sri Lanka (2026), Personal Data Protection Act No. 9 of 2022, Personal Data Protection (Amendment) Act No. 22 of 2025, Online Safety Act No. 9 of 2024

Regulation Status: The binding record consists of the prime-ministerial decree of 5 November 2025 creating the Sudanese Data and Artificial Intelligence Authority, the Digital Transformation Authority and the Sudanese Cybersecurity Authority, an institutional measure imposing no duties on developers or deployers. On 1 November 2026 the Council of Ministers approved three bills submitted by the Minister of Communications and Digital Transformation, including the Data and Artificial Intelligence Regulation Bill 2026, which awaits promulgation. Sudan still has no data protection statute, and armed conflict since April 2023 limits state reach over parts of the territory.
Policy Lever: Policy action is institutional and legislative rather than regulatory: three authorities created by decree in November 2025 under the Ministry of Communications and Digital Transformation, and three bills on cybersecurity, data and AI, and digital transformation approved by the Council of Ministers on 1 November 2026. No AI guidance, standard, funding instrument, sandbox or procurement rule accompanies them, and the main external input remains a UNESCO-supported project on AI and information technology in the education system.
Governance Type: Authority is concentrated in the Ministry of Communications and Digital Transformation, which supervises the Sudanese Data and Artificial Intelligence Authority, the Digital Transformation Authority and the Sudanese Cybersecurity Authority, and which drafted the three 2026 digital bills with the Ministry of Justice. Legislative power is exercised by the Council of Ministers in the absence of a parliament, conflict leaves parts of the country outside government administration, and no judicial or independent check on AI governance operates.
Actor Involvement: AI policy is made inside government, with bills drafted by the Ministry of Justice and the Ministry of Communications and Digital Transformation and approved by the Council of Ministers without published input from industry, universities or civil society. External engagement runs through the founding signature of the World Artificial Intelligence Cooperation Organization convention in July 2026, African Union membership and UNESCO project support.
Enforcement Level: Enforcement does not exist: no AI obligation is in force, no penalty, case or audit is recorded, and the Sudanese Data and Artificial Intelligence Authority has exercised no power since its creation.
Specific Laws: Prime Ministerial Decree establishing the Sudanese Data and Artificial Intelligence Authority, the Digital Transformation Authority and the Sudanese Cybersecurity Authority (2025), Data and Artificial Intelligence Regulation Bill (2026, approved by the Council of Ministers, not in force), Cybersecurity Regulation Bill (2026, approved by the Council of Ministers, not in force), Digital Transformation Regulation Bill (2026, approved by the Council of Ministers, not in force)

Regulation Status: Suriname has no AI-specific legislation and no AI bill before De Nationale Assemblée; AI is touched only by general instruments such as the Wet Elektronisch Rechtsverkeer (2017) and the still-pending Ontwerpwet Bescherming Privacy en Persoonsgegevens, which remains on the Assembly's "in behandeling" list. The Suriname National Digital Strategy 2023-2030 treats artificial intelligence as an emerging driver in education, public services and finance without creating obligations. Governmental activity centres on the UNESCO Readiness Assessment Methodology 2.0 exercise launched on 27 August 2026, intended to inform a future integrated national AI strategy.
Policy Lever: Policy action consists of ministry-led diagnostic and capacity work: the Ministry of Economic Affairs, Entrepreneurship and Technological Innovation runs the UNESCO RAM 2.0 assessment with the Ministry of Education, Science and Culture, supported by surveys, interviews and sectoral consultations. No binding instrument, published AI guidance, funded AI programme, sandbox or body with a statutory AI mandate exists.
Governance Type: Governance is concentrated in the Ministry of Economic Affairs, Entrepreneurship and Technological Innovation, which works with the Ministry of Education, Science and Culture and the e-Government directorate on the UNESCO readiness assessment. No independent regulator, district authority or judicial body has an AI remit.
Actor Involvement: International engagement drives Suriname's AI agenda through the Santiago Declaration, the India AI Impact Summit Declaration of February 2026 and UNESCO's Readiness Assessment Methodology 2.0. Domestic participation runs through the broad but time-limited RAM consultation, in which industry, civil society and academic institutions take part without any standing role.
Enforcement Level: Nothing is enforced because no AI obligation, sanction or supervisory authority exists.
Specific Laws: Suriname National Digital Strategy 2023-2030, Wet Elektronisch Rechtsverkeer (2017), Ontwerpwet Bescherming Privacy en Persoonsgegevens (draft, pending before De Nationale Assemblée)

Regulation Status: Eswatini has no AI-specific legislation, bill or subsidiary rule. The Data Protection Act 5 of 2022, Computer Crime and Cybercrime Act 6 of 2022 and Electronic Communications and Transactions Act 2022 govern data and digital conduct generally, with the Data Protection Act's automated decision-taking right the closest provision to AI. A National AI Strategy is in drafting under the Ministry of Information, Communications and Technology, and a National Data Governance Policy announced in 2026 will determine whether dedicated law is needed.
Policy Lever: Policy action consists of strategy drafting, training events and partnership-based capacity building: the Ministry of Information, Communications and Technology ran an AI in Governance Training Programme for Members of Parliament in June 2025, and the Eswatini Standards Authority launched an AI Safety and Standards Centre of Excellence with AICE Africa in Mbabane on 27 October 2026. Funding programs, AI procurement rules and sandboxes are absent, and the Eswatini Communications Commission exercises data-protection powers without an AI remit.
Governance Type: AI governance is centralised in the executive, with the Ministry of Information, Communications and Technology driving strategy, the Eswatini Communications Commission acting as Data Protection Authority, and the Eswatini Standards Authority newly engaged on AI standards. Coordination is event-driven, and no subnational or independent review layer exists.
Actor Involvement: Engagement runs mainly through international and technical channels: UN Eswatini, the United Nations Global Dialogue on AI Governance, the African Union Continental AI Strategy framing, and the ESWASA-AICE Africa centre. Domestic industry and civil society take part in conferences and dialogues rather than structured consultation on AI policy.
Enforcement Level: Enforcement touching AI exists only through data-protection and cybercrime powers exercised by the Eswatini Communications Commission as Data Protection Authority, with no AI-specific obligations, sanctions or audits.
Specific Laws: Data Protection Act 5 of 2022, Computer Crime and Cybercrime Act 6 of 2022, Electronic Communications and Transactions Act (2022), Eswatini Digitalisation Strategy (2024–2028), Eswatini National Cybersecurity Strategy (2022–2027), National FinTech Strategy for the Kingdom of Eswatini (2025–2030), Office of the Auditor-General Strategic Plan (2026–2030), National Data Governance Policy (in preparation, 2026)

Regulation Status: Sweden is governed by the directly applicable EU AI Act, whose prohibitions, GPAI rules and Article 50 transparency duties apply while Annex III high-risk obligations were postponed to 2 December 2027 by the Digital Omnibus on AI, Regulation (EU) 2026/1744. Nationally, lagen (2026:806) om användning av AI-system för ansiktsigenkänning i realtid för brottsbekämpande ändamål entered into force on 1 July 2026, but the complementary AI Act statute and ordinance proposed in SOU 2025:101 remain unenacted and the national competent authorities are designated only through 31 December 2026.
Policy Lever: The principal lever is the directly applicable EU AI Act, supplemented by the national facial-recognition act, GDPR supervision by IMY and sectoral regimes, with soft law in the February 2026 AI strategy action plan, PTS AI Act guidance and IMY's published supervision plan. Economic levers include Vinnova and AI Sweden funding, participation in European AI gigafactories, and a PTS assignment to establish the statutory AI regulatory sandbox required by 2 August 2027.
Governance Type: Governance is plural within a coordinated structure: PTS leads coordination and is the EU contact point, IMY covers prohibited practices, biometrics and law enforcement, Finansinspektionen covers finance, and Läkemedelsverket and Swedac cover medical devices and conformity assessment, with further sectoral authorities proposed in SOU 2025:101. Independent scrutiny comes from the Council on Legislation, administrative courts, the Institute for Human Rights and the ombudsman institutions, while municipalities and regions implement rather than legislate.
Actor Involvement: Policy-making runs through the Swedish inquiry and remiss system, which gave industry, unions, disability and human-rights organisations, the bar association and research funders published roles on SOU 2025:101 and SOU 2025:12. Internationally Sweden acts through the EU AI Board, Council negotiations, OECD work, European AI standardisation and EuroHPC.
Enforcement Level: EU-level obligations apply and authorities are designated with budget for AI tasks, but Sweden has issued no AI Act enforcement decision and its national sanction provisions remain unenacted.
Specific Laws: EU AI Act / Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (2024), Digital Omnibus on AI / Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 (2026), Lag (2026:806) om användning av AI-system för ansiktsigenkänning i realtid för brottsbekämpande ändamål (2026), Proposition 2025/26:150 Polisens användning av AI för ansiktsigenkänning i realtid (2026), SOU 2025:101 Anpassningar till AI-förordningen (2025, proposed), SOU 2025:12 AI-kommissionens färdplan för Sverige (2025), Sveriges AI-strategi med handlingsplan (2026), Swedish Data Protection Act (2018:218), National Approach to Artificial Intelligence (2018)

Regulation Status: Switzerland has no horizontal AI statute. The Federal Council's 12 February 2025 decision commits it to ratify the Council of Europe Framework Convention on Artificial Intelligence, signed 27 March 2025, through mainly sector-specific amendments; on 28 October 2026 the Federal Council took note of interim results and the consultation on the implementing federal act covering transparency, data protection, non-discrimination, supervision and risk assessment is set for spring 2027. Operative rules come from the revised Federal Act on Data Protection, the Ordinance on Automated Driving in force since 1 March 2025, and supervisory guidance from FINMA and the Federal Data Protection and Information Commissioner.
Policy Lever: Policy runs on general law plus a growing soft-law stack: FINMA Guidance 08/2024, FDPIC guidance on the Federal Act on Data Protection, the 2020 Federal Council AI Guidelines, the Strategy for the Use of AI Systems in the Federal Administration, and OFCOM's October 2026 report on sector-specific measures and Guide on an AI Code of Conduct, with OFCOM mandated to build an administration-wide knowledge exchange on sector self-regulation by end-March 2028. Research funding through the Swiss AI Initiative and CSCS is substantial, while institutional capacity sits with coordination bodies and sectoral regulators that have no AI-specific legal mandate.
Governance Type: Governance is deliberately sectoral: FINMA, Swissmedic, OFCOM, the Federal Roads Office and the FDPIC act within existing remits, the Competence Network for Artificial Intelligence at the Federal Chancellery serves as the administration's contact point, and the Federal Office of Justice leads the implementing bill with OFCOM and the Directorate of International Law. Cantons implement data-protection rules and run initiatives such as the Zurich Innovation Sandbox for AI, while review of AI-related decisions proceeds through the independent FDPIC and ordinary courts.
Actor Involvement: Industry is engaged beyond consultations through sector dialogues and the voluntary AI code of conduct track coordinated by OFCOM, while civil society and academia contribute via the ordinary consultation procedure, expert reports and cantonal sandbox projects rather than standing AI bodies. Internationally Switzerland is highly active as a signatory of the Council of Europe AI Convention and through OECD and Geneva-based processes.
Enforcement Level: Enforcement relies on pre-existing data-protection and prudential powers, with FINMA's supervisory reviews of AI governance in finance and FDPIC data-protection investigations the only concrete activity and no decision under AI-specific law.
Specific Laws: Federal Act on Data Protection / FADP (2023), Ordinance on Automated Driving / VAF (2025), FINMA Guidance 08/2024 on Governance and Risk Management when using Artificial Intelligence (2024), Federal Council Guidelines on Artificial Intelligence for the Confederation (2020), Strategy for the Use of Artificial Intelligence Systems in the Federal Administration (2025), Digital Switzerland Strategy (2025), Council of Europe Framework Convention on Artificial Intelligence – signed by Switzerland (2025), OFCOM Report on Sector-Specific Measures for the Regulation of Artificial Intelligence and Guide on an AI Code of Conduct (2026), draft Federal Act on Communication Platforms and Search Engines (2025)

Regulation Status: Syria has no AI-specific binding instrument. Artificial intelligence is named in Law No. 25 of 2024 establishing the Ministry of Communications and Information Technology and in Decree No. 183 of 7 October 2026 creating the National Advanced Technology Track for AI, cybersecurity, robotics and data-science education, while the only binding rules reaching AI systems are those of Personal Data Protection Law No. 12 of 2024 and its Executive Instructions. The transitional government has announced an intention to regulate AI and has concentrated on fibre, data-centre and data-transit projects such as the Ebla agreement of September 2026.
Policy Lever: Policy levers are promotional: ministry-sponsored events (AI-SYRIA 2025, SYNC 2026, Syria HiTech 2026), the 'Mujtama Thakaa' digital-community project with the Ministry of Social Affairs and Labour, the 2026-2045 technology foresight roadmap, and infrastructure partnerships with Elm, Dell Technologies and aiXplain. Decree No. 183 of 2026 adds an AI education pathway, while binding obligations come only from general data protection law.
Governance Type: AI governance is centralised in one ministry, with the only cross-body arrangement being the joint ministerial supervision of the education track created by Decree No. 183 of 2026. Sub-national authorities and independent review institutions play no role in AI.
Actor Involvement: Domestic engagement comes from associations and universities—the Syrian Computer Society, the Syria AI Foundation launched in Damascus on 11 July 2026, the Syrian Association for Artificial Intelligence and Entrepreneurship, and new AI centres at Damascus and Aleppo universities—rather than from any government consultation on AI policy. International involvement consists of the Digital Cooperation Organization Charter signature, the 2024 Global AI Governance Initiative endorsement and ministerial participation in the Seoul digital and AI summit of October 2026.
Enforcement Level: Enforcement is absent: only general data protection penalties could reach AI uses, and no authority, case or monitoring programme exists.
Specific Laws: Law No. 25 of 2024 establishing the Ministry of Communications and Information Technology (defines emerging technologies including artificial intelligence), Personal Data Protection Law No. 12 of 2024 and its Executive Instructions (2024), Constitutional Declaration of the Syrian Arab Republic (2025), Decree No. 183 of 2026 establishing the National Advanced Technology Track, Digital Cooperation Organization Charter signature (2026), Global AI Governance Initiative endorsement (2024)

Regulation Status: The Artificial Intelligence Basic Act, in force since 14 January 2026, is a horizontal, principles-based statute of 20 clauses that sets seven governance principles, names the National Science and Technology Council as central competent authority, required government bodies to complete AI risk assessments within six months and obliges them to adopt internal AI control rules by January 2027. Operational private-sector duties depend on sectoral risk-based regulations built on the Ministry of Digital Affairs AI Risk Taxonomy and Assessment Framework published 7 July 2026, which is advisory and does not itself bind firms. Penalties reaching AI outputs today come only from the 2023 deepfake amendments to the Public Officials Election and Recall Act and the Criminal Code.
Policy Lever: Taiwan pairs one horizontal statute and narrow criminal and election provisions on synthetic media with a growing body of sectoral soft law from MODA, the Financial Supervisory Commission and the Ministry of Health and Welfare, plus large state funding for AI infrastructure, compute and talent. Institutional mandates are legally grounded in the Artificial Intelligence Basic Act but carry no compliance or sanctioning powers.
Governance Type: Governance is centrally organised: NSTC is the statutory lead, MODA owns the risk taxonomy architecture, and sectoral ministries translate it into their own guidance, coordinated through the Premier-chaired National AI Strategy Special Committee. There is no subnational regulatory tier, and independent review of AI rules is incidental to criminal cases on synthetic media.
Actor Involvement: Industry and academia hold places in the National AI Strategy Special Committee, while civil society participates through episodic consultation rather than a standing role. International engagement is constrained to declarations, standards alignment and multistakeholder fora because Taiwan is excluded from treaty-based AI instruments.
Enforcement Level: Enforcement is confined to criminal and election deepfake provisions and to public-sector self-assessment, since the Artificial Intelligence Basic Act sets no penalties and no authority holds AI compliance powers.
Specific Laws: Artificial Intelligence Basic Act (2026), AI Risk Taxonomy and Assessment Framework (2026), Public-Sector AI Application Reference Handbook (2026), Executive Yuan Implementation Plan for the Artificial Intelligence Basic Act (2026), Guidelines for Medical Institutions Applying Generative Artificial Intelligence (2026), Guidelines for the Use of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in the Financial Industry (2024), Core Principles and Related Promotion Policies for the Use of Artificial Intelligence (AI) by the Financial Industry (2023), Public Officials Election and Recall Act deepfake amendments (2023), Presidential and Vice Presidential Election and Recall Act deepfake amendments (2023), Criminal Code deepfake amendments (2023), Taiwan AI Action Plan 2.0 (2023-2026), AI Technology R&D Guidelines (2019)

Regulation Status: Tajikistan regulates AI through non-binding planning instruments: the Strategy for AI Development of the Republic of Tajikistan until 2040 (Government Resolution No. 483 of 30 September 2022, amended by Resolution No. 83 of 31 January 2025) and the AI components of the Medium-Term Programme for the Development of the Digital Economy for 2026-2030. The Strategy requires preparation of a draft Law "On Artificial Intelligence" defining the basis of state regulation, which has not reached the Majlisi Namoyandagon, and the Strategy is being revised to raise the AI contribution target from 5% to 8% of GDP across 17 sectors. Government acts adopted in 2026 create institutions rather than obligations, such as Resolution No. 120 of 10 March 2026 establishing the State Institution "Institute of Digital Technologies and Artificial Intelligence".
Policy Lever: Policy runs through planning and promotion: the Strategy until 2040, the Medium-Term Programme for the Development of the Digital Economy for 2026-2030, the designation of 2025-2030 as Years of Development of the Digital Economy and Innovation, IT Park and IT Hub Dushanbe incentives, and the new Institute of Digital Technologies and Artificial Intelligence. Delivery is coordinated by the Agency for Innovation and Digital Technologies under the President, which has no compliance mandate over AI.
Governance Type: AI governance is centralized in the Agency for Innovation and Digital Technologies under the President, which drafts strategy, monitors programme delivery and convenes an Interdepartmental Commission on Artificial Intelligence Regulation alongside the AI Council under the Ministry of Industry and New Technologies. Subnational authorities and independent review bodies play no part.
Actor Involvement: Domestic AI policy is made within government, with industry represented only through the AI Council and academia only as a delivery partner. Internationally Tajikistan is highly active, authoring two UN General Assembly AI resolutions, proposing a coordinated AI legal framework in the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation and the CIS Interparliamentary Assembly, and proposing a Central Asian regional AI centre.
Enforcement Level: With no binding AI rules in force, nothing is enforced and oversight consists of programme-delivery monitoring by the Agency for Innovation and Digital Technologies.
Specific Laws: Strategy for AI Development of the Republic of Tajikistan until 2040 (Government Resolution No. 483 of 30 September 2022, amended by Resolution No. 83 of 31 January 2025), Medium-Term Programme for the Development of the Digital Economy for 2026-2030 (2025), Government Resolution No. 120 of 10 March 2026 on the State Institution "Institute of Digital Technologies and Artificial Intelligence"

Regulation Status: Tanzania has no AI-specific legislation in force and no AI bill before Parliament; AI deployment is governed by general law, principally the Personal Data Protection Act Chapter 44 (2022) with Regulations GN No. 449C of 2023, the Cybercrimes Act 2015, the Electronic Transactions Act 2015 and the Electronic and Postal Communications Act 2010. AI-specific activity remains non-binding: the National Guidelines for Artificial Intelligence in Education launched in January 2025, the Policy Framework for Artificial Intelligence in the Tanzania Health Sector (2022), the Ministry of Communication and Information Technology Guidelines for the Secure and Ethical Use of Artificial Intelligence (2025) and the Tanzania National Artificial Intelligence Strategy Framework released in draft in July 2025 and still unadopted. The government stated in May 2026 that it is accelerating a national AI policy and in June 2026 that it plans a dedicated AI institution.
Policy Lever: Policy runs through soft-law levers: sectoral AI guidelines for education and health, ministry guidelines on secure and ethical AI use, the draft Tanzania National Artificial Intelligence Strategy Framework informed by the UNESCO-supported Artificial Intelligence Readiness Assessment Report of 2025, and the National Digital Economy Strategic Framework 2024-2034. Economic levers are limited to the Bank of Tanzania fintech regulatory sandbox and AI scholarship and innovation-hub funding, with no body holding a statutory AI mandate.
Governance Type: AI policy is centralised in the Ministry of Communication and Information Technology and the Tanzania ICT Commission, with the Personal Data Protection Commission, TCRA, Bank of Tanzania and sector ministries acting separately under their own statutes. Coordination is ad hoc, sub-national bodies have no role, and independent or judicial review of AI governance is absent.
Actor Involvement: Industry, civil society and academia are consulted through the UNESCO-supported readiness assessment, the July 2025 National AI Forum and the 2026 National AI Conference, but hold no standing formal role in AI policy-making. International engagement runs through UNESCO, the African Union Continental Artificial Intelligence Strategy, Smart Africa and WIPO discussions rather than binding instruments.
Enforcement Level: Enforcement touching AI occurs only under general data protection, cybercrime and communications powers, with no AI-specific sanction, designated AI authority or recurring AI audit.
Specific Laws: Personal Data Protection Act, Chapter 44 (2022), Personal Data Protection (Personal Data Collection and Processing) Regulations GN No. 449C (2023), Cybercrimes Act (2015), Electronic Transactions Act (2015), Electronic and Postal Communications Act (2010), Bank of Tanzania (Fintech Regulatory Sandbox) Regulations GN No. 540 (2024), National Guidelines for Artificial Intelligence in Education (2025), Guidelines for the Secure and Ethical Use of Artificial Intelligence (2025), Policy Framework for Artificial Intelligence in Tanzania Health Sector (2022), Tanzania National Artificial Intelligence Strategy Framework (draft, July 2025), Artificial Intelligence Readiness Assessment Report: Tanzania (2025), National Digital Economy Strategic Framework 2024-2034

Regulation Status: Thailand has no enacted comprehensive AI statute: ETDA published the Draft Act on Artificial Intelligence for public consultation on 2/9 July 2026, comments closed 14 August 2026, and the text still awaits Office of the Council of State review and Cabinet submission, with no bill before the National Assembly. Binding AI-specific obligations in force remain confined to the Office of the Consumer Protection Board notification requiring disclosure labels on AI-generated or AI-edited advertising images and video and the Civil Court regulation of 17 November 2025 on disclosure and verification of AI-generated content in pleadings. Bank of Thailand and Securities and Exchange Commission instruments set supervisory expectations rather than enforceable AI duties.
Policy Lever: Thailand governs AI mainly through soft law and capacity-building - ETDA generative AI and executive governance guidelines, Bank of Thailand and SEC sector frameworks, PDPC and NCSA guidance - alongside two narrow binding instruments on AI advertising and AI-prepared court filings. Economic levers include the 25-billion-baht national AI development framework and national compute and data investments, while the AI Governance Sandbox announced by ETDA in October 2026 and ETDA's statutory supervisory powers remain preparatory.
Governance Type: Governance runs through ETDA as lead body under MDES, with sectoral regulators and the courts issuing their own AI rules, coordinated by the Prime Minister-chaired National AI Committee and the National Digital Economy and Society Committee. No subnational tier regulates AI, and independent oversight is limited to the judiciary's rules on AI use in proceedings.
Actor Involvement: Participation is consultative rather than institutionalised: industry, law firms and foreign technology associations submitted comments on the 2026 draft AI Act, academia contributes through NECTEC, NSTDA and strategy working groups, and civil society input is episodic. Internationally Thailand is prominent, hosting the UNESCO Global Forum on the Ethics of AI and positioning the AI Governance Practice Centre as a regional hub.
Enforcement Level: Enforcement rests on general consumer-protection and court procedural sanctions attached to two narrow AI rules, with no AI-specific enforcement decisions reported and ETDA's statutory supervisory powers still in draft.
Specific Laws: Draft Act on Artificial Intelligence (2026, public consultation 2 July - 14 August 2026), Office of the Consumer Protection Board Notification on AI-Generated Advertising Content (2025), Civil Court Regulation on the Use of Artificial Intelligence in Preparing Pleadings and Documents (2025), Guidance of the President of the Supreme Court on the Use of Artificial Intelligence in the Performance of Judicial Case Work B.E. 2568 (2025), Bank of Thailand Guiding Principles for Artificial Intelligence Risk Management (2025), SEC Governance Framework for Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning (2025), ETDA Guidelines for Application of Generative AI with Good Governance for Organizations (2024), AI Governance Guideline for Executives (2026), National AI Strategy and Action Plan (2022-2027), National AI Development Framework FY2026-2027 (2025), Digital Thailand - AI Ethics Guideline (2022), Draft Royal Decree on Business Operations Using AI Systems (2022), Draft Act on the Promotion and Support for National AI Innovations (2023)

Regulation Status: Togo has no binding AI legislation, no AI bill before the Assemblée nationale and no AI provision in its digital statutes; Loi n°2019-014 of 29 October 2019 on personal data protection and Loi n°2018-026 on cybercrime reach AI only incidentally. Work stays at preparatory stage: the national AI strategy launched in 2024-2025 is still unadopted, and a projet de Code du numérique intended to cover artificial intelligence, cloud and data protection is being drafted under the Projet d'Accélération Numérique du Togo.
Policy Lever: Togo governs AI through programmes rather than rules: Togo AI Lab applies data science to public policy with CEGA Berkeley, the Togo AI Summer School 2026 trains 100 young people, and the Challenge national des langues locales and Voix du Togo collect voice and text data for national-language models. No AI-specific binding instrument, published guidance, regulatory sandbox or AI procurement rule exists.
