Governance Type: AI policy is concentrated in the ministry responsible for public service efficiency and digital transformation, operating through Togo AI Lab, with the Ministry of Justice and Human Rights involved in the strategy process and sectoral regulators ARCEP, ANCy and IPDCP holding no AI remit. Coordination is event-driven, there is no subnational tier, and no judicial or independent review has touched AI.
Actor Involvement: Domestic participation is occasional and event-driven: the December 2025 strategy forum, the ISOC-Togo national Internet Governance Forum of 19 June 2026 devoted to AI and digital sovereignty, and research or data partnerships with CEGA, Zindi, Umbaji and UNDP. Internationally Togo acts through African Union and ECOWAS digital frameworks and multilateral events, including the AI for Good Global Summit in July 2026 and the Seoul global summit in October 2026.
Enforcement Level: Nothing AI-specific is enforced in Togo, and the general powers of IPDCP, ARCEP and ANCy have not been exercised against AI systems.
Specific Laws: Loi n°2019-014 relative à la protection des données à caractère personnel (2019), Loi n°2018-026 relative à la lutte contre la cybercriminalité (2018, amended 2022), Stratégie nationale d'intelligence artificielle du Togo (in preparation since 2024), projet de Code du numérique (in drafting since 2025), Politique nationale d'utilisation de l'intelligence artificielle dans l'Enseignement technique et la Formation professionnelle (in preparation since 2025)

Regulation Status: Tonga has no AI-specific legislation in force or before the Legislative Assembly. The digital statute book enacted in 2025 — the Privacy Act 2025, the Cybersecurity Act 2025, the Computer Crimes Act 2025 and the Electronic Transactions Act 2025 — regulates personal data, critical infrastructure and electronic dealings generally; the only provision touching automated systems is the Privacy Act's section 44 right concerning decisions based solely on automated processing, and that Act commences only on Cabinet proclamation. Government technology activity centres on connectivity, the TongaPass digital identity, and government data-centre modernisation under the U.S. Trade and Development Agency feasibility agreement signed 2 September 2026.
Policy Lever: Tonga operates no AI-specific lever: its single relevant commitment is the regionally endorsed Pacific Digital and Artificial Intelligence Technology Principles, and the National Reserve Bank of Tonga's FinTech Regulatory Sandbox Framework is confined to financial services. Funding flows to connectivity and data-centre infrastructure rather than to AI programmes.
Governance Type: Authority over digital matters is concentrated in national ministries, chiefly MEIDECC and the Digital Transformation Department, with the National Reserve Bank of Tonga supervising financial technology. No AI regulator, coordinating body, subnational competence or independent review role exists.
Actor Involvement: AI engagement is external and declaratory, conducted through the Pacific Islands Forum, where Leaders endorsed regional AI principles in September 2026 and directed work toward a Pacific AI Governance Framework for consideration in 2027. Domestic industry, civil society and academia have no structured role.
Enforcement Level: Enforcement touching AI is limited to the general penalties of the Cybersecurity Act 2025 and Computer Crimes Act 2025, with no AI-specific sanction, competent authority, decision or monitoring practice.
Specific Laws: Privacy Act 2025 (Act 34 of 2025, awaiting commencement by Cabinet proclamation), Cybersecurity Act 2025, Computer Crimes Act 2025, Electronic Transactions Act 2025, Tonga National Cybersecurity Framework (2022), Digital Government Strategic Framework 2019-2024, Tongan Data Exchange Policy and Framework (2021), Pacific Digital and Artificial Intelligence Technology Principles (2026, regional endorsement)

Regulation Status: Trinidad and Tobago has no AI-specific legislation in force, no AI bill before Parliament and no adopted national AI strategy; policy work sits at the diagnostic stage through the UNESCO Readiness Assessment Methodology and the UNDP AI Landscape Assessment, validated at a national workshop on 27 February 2026. The Data Protection Act 2011 remains only partially proclaimed and contains nothing written for AI, so AI systems are governed by incidental general law alone.
Policy Lever: Policy runs entirely on non-binding levers: the UNESCO and UNDP readiness assessments, the AI Academy capacity-building pilot with UNDP, CAF and UNICC, the Anansi national AI assistant, the FutureReadyTT education initiative, an OpenAI partnership and memoranda with United Arab Emirates technology entities. The Ministry of Public Administration and Artificial Intelligence hosts this work without statutory AI powers, and no sandbox, AI funding scheme or AI procurement rule is in place.
Governance Type: Governance is centralised in the Ministry of Public Administration and Artificial Intelligence, which also has portfolio responsibility for the Telecommunications Authority of Trinidad and Tobago, while sectoral regulators carry no AI remit and no formal coordination mechanism links them. Courts, the Ombudsman and independent review bodies have played no part in shaping AI policy.
Actor Involvement: Industry, civil society and academia entered the process through one-off diagnostic channels: the UNESCO RAM survey, January 2026 sector consultations and the UWI-hosted validation workshop, none of which created standing advisory roles. International engagement is the most developed strand, through UNESCO, UNDP, CARICOM, the Caribbean Telecommunications Union AI Task Force, bilateral cooperation with India and the United Arab Emirates, and a partnership with OpenAI.
Enforcement Level: Enforcement of AI rules does not exist, since there are no AI obligations, no designated AI authority, and the general data protection regime itself remains largely unproclaimed and unenforced.
Specific Laws: Data Protection Act (2011), Digital Transformation Strategy 2024-2027

Regulation Status: AI governance rests on general instruments: Organic Act No. 2004-63 on Personal Data Protection, Decree-Law No. 2022-54 on Combating Cyber Offences and the Startup Act, none of which contain AI-specific obligations. The Organic Bill on Protection of Personal Data, covering profiling and automated decision-making, remained in committee hearings at the Assembly of the Representatives of the People through 2026, and the National AI Strategy (2026-2030) presented at the August 2026 ministerial council is a non-binding policy document. The ATUGE TunisIA white paper calls for a framework law on AI covering biometrics and generated content, confirming that none exists.
Policy Lever: Tunisia relies on soft-law strategy documents and innovation-economy instruments, notably the Startup Act framework, the Anava fund and donor-supported programmes including GIZ cooperation, rather than binding rules. INPDP and ANSI act only within data protection and cybersecurity mandates and hold no AI compliance powers.
Governance Type: AI-relevant oversight is concentrated in a lead ministry, with INPDP and ANSI confined to adjacent mandates and coordination occurring through periodic restricted ministerial councils. Sub-national bodies play no role and judicial or independent review of AI decisions has not materialised.
Actor Involvement: Industry and academia feed AI policy through consultations, workshops and the ATUGE TunisIA white paper, while domestic civil society participates mainly through advocacy rather than standing roles. International engagement is comparatively strong, resting on Convention 108 ratification, African Union and Arab ICT Organization digital cooperation, and participation in global AI summits.
Enforcement Level: Enforcement reaches AI only indirectly through data protection and cybercrime law, with no AI-specific sanctions, decisions or audit regime on record.
Specific Laws: Organic Act No. 2004-63 on Personal Data Protection (2004), Decree-Law No. 2022-54 on Combating Cyber Offences (2022), Startup Act (Law No. 2018-20, amended), National AI Strategy and Roadmap (2021-2025), National AI Strategy (2026-2030), Organic Bill on Protection of Personal Data (2025, before the Assembly of the Representatives of the People)

Regulation Status: No dedicated AI law is in force; the horizontal Yapay Zeka Kanun Teklifi (Esas No. 2/2234) and the Bill on Amendments to Certain Laws Regarding Artificial Intelligence (Esas No. 2/3358) remain in committee at the Grand National Assembly. The one binding AI-specific rule in force came through the amendments to the Regulation on Commercial Advertisement and Unfair Commercial Practices (Official Gazette, 1 July 2026, applicable 1 August 2026), which require disclosure of AI use in advertising and prohibit misleading AI-generated digital replicas of real persons. Everything else reaching AI is general law, Law No. 6698 on the Protection of Personal Data and Law No. 5651 on internet publications, alongside policy instruments such as the Türkiye Artificial Intelligence Action Plan (2026-2030).
Policy Lever: Turkey works mainly through strategy and guidance: the Türkiye Artificial Intelligence Action Plan (2026-2030) enacted by Presidential Circular No. 2026/9, its predecessor National Artificial Intelligence Strategy (2021-2025), and KVKK's generative and agentic AI guides. Enforceable levers are confined to the advertising regulation's AI transparency rules and to data-protection law applied by KVKK.
Governance Type: AI policy is centralised in the Presidency and the Ministry of Industry and Technology, with the National Technology and Artificial Intelligence General Directorate as lead body and the Cybersecurity Presidency's Public AI General Directorate handling public-sector AI, while sectoral regulators apply their own mandates. A presidentially chaired National Artificial Intelligence Board and a National Artificial Intelligence Ethics Board are the designed coordination layer; there is no subnational role and judicial activity concerns content blocking rather than review of AI rules.
Actor Involvement: Industry, universities and civil society organisations fed into the Türkiye Artificial Intelligence Action Plan (2026-2030) and the TBMM Artificial Intelligence Research Commission, whose 2026 report recommended a framework AI act and accession to the Council of Europe Framework Convention; none of these actors holds a standing formal role, and the multi-stakeholder National Artificial Intelligence Ethics Board remains to be set up. Internationally Turkey stays at declaration level, with standards participation through TÜRKAK accreditation for ISO/IEC 42001.
Enforcement Level: Enforcement touching AI runs through general data-protection, consumer and internet legislation, with the Grok investigation and access-blocking of AI-generated content as the visible actions and no published decision under any AI-specific provision.
Specific Laws: Regulation Amending the Regulation on Commercial Advertisement and Unfair Commercial Practices (2026, AI transparency and digital replica provisions in force 1 August 2026), Türkiye Artificial Intelligence Action Plan (2026-2030) enacted by Presidential Circular No. 2026/9 (2026), National Artificial Intelligence Strategy 2021-2025 (2021), Presidential Decree No. 191 renaming the National Technology and Artificial Intelligence General Directorate (2025), Presidential Decree No. 192 expanding the Cybersecurity Presidency's artificial intelligence data governance duties (2025), Yapay Zeka Kanun Teklifi / Draft Artificial Intelligence Law Bill (Esas No. 2/2234, 2024, in committee), Bill on Amendments to Certain Laws Regarding Artificial Intelligence (Esas No. 2/3358, 2025, in committee), TBMM Artificial Intelligence Research Commission Report (2026), Law No. 6698 on the Protection of Personal Data (2016), Law No. 5651 on Regulation of Publications on the Internet (2007), Law No. 7578 amending Law No. 5651 on digital games and social media (2026), KVKK Guidance on Agentic AI (2026), KVKK Guidance on the Use of Generative Artificial Intelligence Tools in Workplaces (2026), KVKK Guide on Generative Artificial Intelligence and the Protection of Personal Data (2025)

Regulation Status: No AI-specific legislation is in force. The Cabinet of Ministers meeting of 24 January 2026 ordered work on a national AI legal framework covering rules of use, allocation of responsibility, state agency powers and national standards, and the Ministry of Communications is drafting a National Artificial Intelligence Strategy with UNDP support under the State Programme for the Development of the Digital Economy for 2026-2028. Nothing has been submitted to the Mejlis, and the Law On Information about Private Life and its Protection addresses AI nowhere.
Policy Lever: Policy is delivered through presidential resolutions and state programmes rather than law, chiefly the Concept and the State Programme for the Development of the Digital Economy of Turkmenistan for 2026-2028, which fund AI pilots, a national data processing centre and a planned AI Competence Centre at Turkmentelecom. There is no AI-specific binding instrument, published guidance, regulatory sandbox or AI procurement rule.
Governance Type: Decision-making is concentrated in the President and the Cabinet of Ministers, with the Ministry of Communications and Turkmentelecom acting as executing arms and coordination occurring episodically in Cabinet sessions on the digital system. Sub-national administrations have no role and independent review of technology policy is absent.
Actor Involvement: AI policy is shaped by state bodies working with the United Nations Development Programme, which convened the March and May 2026 national AI strategy seminars, while the government promotes an International Code for the peaceful use of AI in international relations. Domestic industry and civil society have no channel into the process, and academic participation is confined to capacity-building events.
Enforcement Level: Nothing is enforced because no AI obligation, penalty or supervisory authority has been created.
Specific Laws: State Programme for the Development of the Digital Economy of Turkmenistan for 2026-2028 and its Action Plan (2026), Concept for the Development of the Digital Economy in Turkmenistan for 2026-2028 (2025), Law of Turkmenistan No. 519-V On Information about Private Life and its Protection (2017); a National Artificial Intelligence Strategy is in draft

Regulation Status: Tuvalu has no AI-specific legislation, draft bill or regulatory proposal, and foundational digital law remains incomplete, with a Cybercrime Bill pending and no dedicated data-protection statute. The Tuvalu National ICT Policy (2023) and Tuvalu National Broadband Plan (2024) name artificial intelligence only as an emerging technology alongside cloud computing and the Internet of Things, setting connectivity, digital-government and cybersecurity priorities. Government attention centres on climate survival, the Digital Nation project and submarine-cable connectivity.
Policy Lever: Policy effort is confined to connectivity and digital-government delivery under the Tuvalu National ICT Policy (2023) and the Tuvalu National Broadband Plan (2024), neither of which creates AI obligations, guidance or funding. The only AI-relevant commitment is the regional, non-binding Pacific Digital and Artificial Intelligence Technology Principles endorsed in September 2026, and public-sector capacity in a state of roughly 11,000 people remains absorbed by climate resilience and basic service delivery.
Governance Type: Digital policy is centralised in the government ICT department and the state-owned Tuvalu Telecommunications Corporation, with no AI remit allocated anywhere and no coordination mechanism, sub-national tier or independent review body touching AI.
Actor Involvement: No domestic stakeholder process on AI exists for industry, civil society or academia. Engagement is external and declaratory: as a Pacific Islands Forum member Tuvalu endorsed the Pacific Digital and Artificial Intelligence Technology Principles in September 2026 and supports work towards a regional AI governance framework to be considered by Leaders in 2027, without participating in AI-specific standards or treaty processes.
Enforcement Level: No AI enforcement framework, penalty, authority or monitoring practice exists in Tuvalu.
Specific Laws: Tuvalu National ICT Policy (2023), Tuvalu National Broadband Plan (2024), Pacific Digital and Artificial Intelligence Technology Principles (2026, regional and non-binding)

Regulation Status: Uganda regulates AI entirely through horizontal law, principally the Data Protection and Privacy Act No. 9 of 2019 (Cap. 97) with its 2021 Regulations and the Computer Misuse Act (Cap. 96), neither of which addresses algorithmic transparency or automated decision-making. The Artificial Intelligence Bill 2025 is a draft that has not been introduced, and the National AI and Emerging Technologies Strategy, originating in a Cabinet directive for an AI policy, was still in preparation when the Ministry of ICT and National Guidance launched the National Data Strategy 2026/27-2030/31 on 20 October 2026 as its stated foundation.
Policy Lever: Policy levers are preparatory: a strategy in drafting, the ITU National AI Landscape Assessment, the UNESCO Readiness Assessment, an AI Task Force, and general-law guidance from the Personal Data Protection Office. The National Data Strategy 2026/27-2030/31 launched on 20 October 2026 with UNDP and UN Global Pulse support addresses responsible use of emerging technologies but creates no binding AI obligations, and economic tools are limited to donor-funded innovation work in health, agriculture and public services.
Governance Type: AI governance is centred on the Ministry of ICT and National Guidance and NITA-U, with the Personal Data Protection Office, Uganda Communications Commission and Bank of Uganda touching AI within existing mandates and the UCC pursuing AI-based online content filtering. Coordination is through the National AI Focal Point and an AI Task Force rather than a statutory body, local government has no role, and external checks are confined to data-protection complaints.
Actor Involvement: Government, industry, academia and civil society met in structured but non-standing consultations during the UNESCO AI Readiness Assessment process in February and May 2026 and the strategy engagements that closed in March 2026. International cooperation is the densest axis, spanning UNESCO, ITU, UNDP, the African Union, a 30 September 2026 parliamentary exchange with Kenya and a 29 October 2026 ministerial meeting with Egypt, alongside Uganda's October 2026 call for developing-country inclusion in global AI governance.
Enforcement Level: Enforcement touching AI flows exclusively through general regulators applying data protection, communications and cybercrime law, illustrated by the Personal Data Protection Office rulings against Google LLC and against Meta Platforms and WhatsApp LLC in February 2026, with no AI-specific sanction, authority or audit regime.
Specific Laws: Data Protection and Privacy Act No. 9 of 2019 (Cap. 97), Data Protection and Privacy Regulations 2021, Computer Misuse Act (Cap. 96), Artificial Intelligence Bill 2025 (draft, not tabled), National Artificial Intelligence and Emerging Technologies Strategy (in development, 2026), Uganda National Data Strategy 2026/27-2030/31 (launched 20 October 2026), Uganda National AI Landscape Assessment (ITU, 2024), Uganda AI Readiness Assessment Report (UNESCO, validated 26 May 2026), National Information Security Framework 2026

Regulation Status: Ukraine has no cross-sector AI law in force; the Ministry of Digital Transformation working group, convened in June 2026, has drafted the first two sections and 15 articles of a European-integration AI bill aligned with the EU AI Act, with submission planned for the fourth quarter of 2026. Binding AI-specific rules exist only as experimental-project regimes: the 2024 AI and Blockchain Sandbox resolution and Cabinet of Ministers Resolution No. 310 of 12 March 2026 on military-purpose AI goods and their export. The Council of Europe Framework Convention on Artificial Intelligence, signed 15 May 2025, awaits ratification by the Verkhovna Rada.
Policy Lever: Policy runs on soft law and economic tools: the Roadmap, White Paper, voluntary Code of Conduct, sectoral guidance, labelling recommendations and the 2026 AI terms dictionary sit beside an operating AI and Blockchain Sandbox that has taken over 90 applications and reviewed 15 products, plus defence AI grant and platform programmes. Legal authority stays with the Ministry of Digital Transformation as policy lead, which holds no compliance powers pending the drafted AI law.
Governance Type: AI governance is centralized in the Ministry of Digital Transformation, which sets strategy, runs the sandbox and drafts the forthcoming law, while the Ministry of Defence administers the military AI experimental regimes and other agencies execute tasks under the 2025-2026 Action Plan. Independent review rests on the Ombudsman's general mandate, and no subnational tier participates.
Actor Involvement: Consultation is broad but advisory: companies, NGOs and academics join the Expert Committee, the 2026 working group of more than 100 participants and the consultation on the AI Strategy to 2030, none of which confers decision-making power. International engagement is active through treaty signature awaiting ratification, EU AI Act alignment work and the September 2026 proposal to open the national sandbox to European partners.
Enforcement Level: Compliance rests on voluntary and reputational incentives, with no AI-specific penalties, enforcement decisions, supervisory authority or audit regime in place.
Specific Laws: Concept for the Development of Artificial Intelligence in Ukraine (Cabinet of Ministers Order No. 1556-r, 2020), Action Plan for Implementation of the Concept of AI Development in Ukraine for 2025-2026 (Cabinet of Ministers Order No. 457-r, 2025), Roadmap for AI Regulation in Ukraine (2023), White Paper on Artificial Intelligence Regulation (2024), Policy on Development of Artificial Intelligence in Priority Spheres of Economy until 2026 - Cabinet of Ministers Order (2024), Cabinet of Ministers resolution establishing the AI and Blockchain Sandbox experimental project (2024), Voluntary Code of Conduct on Ethical and Responsible Use of Artificial Intelligence (2024), WINWIN 2030 Global Innovation Strategy (2024), draft National Artificial Intelligence Development Strategy until 2030 (2025), Cabinet of Ministers Resolution No. 310 of 12 March 2026 on the Experimental Project for the Development of Military-Purpose Goods in the Field of Artificial Intelligence Technologies and the International Transfer (Export) of Such Goods, Cabinet of Ministers pilot project on access to the Ministry of Defence artificial intelligence platform (2026), Law of Ukraine On Personal Data Protection No. 2297-VI (2010), Law of Ukraine On the Basic Principles of Ensuring Cybersecurity of Ukraine No. 2163-VIII (2017), Council of Europe Framework Convention on Artificial Intelligence and Human Rights, Democracy and the Rule of Law CETS 225 (signed 2025, not ratified)

Regulation Status: No horizontal federal AI statute exists; binding federal AI rules reach election campaigning and the use of AI inside government, while the Personal Data Protection Law (Federal Decree-Law No. 45 of 2021) and the Child Digital Safety Law (Federal Decree-Law No. 26 of 2025) are general instruments applied to AI. Free-zone rules such as DIFC Data Protection Regulation 10, enforceable from January 2026, bind only within those jurisdictions. The Federal Authority for Artificial Intelligence and Data, approved on 14 June 2026, may propose AI legislation that has not been enacted.
Policy Lever: Policy runs mainly through soft law (UAE Charter for AI 2024, National AI Strategy 2031, CBUAE Guidance Note 2026, agentic AI design guidance) and very large state-backed investment and infrastructure programmes, with binding AI rules confined to elections, government use and free zones. Institutional capacity was consolidated in June 2026 into the Federal Authority for Artificial Intelligence and Data, which has not exercised compliance powers over private actors.
Governance Type: Governance combines a consolidated federal centre reporting to the Cabinet with emirates and free zones that write and enforce their own AI and data rules. Courts, ombudsmen and independent review bodies play no visible role in shaping AI policy.
Actor Involvement: Industry is consulted through free-zone, sectoral and sandbox processes while domestic civil society is absent from AI policy-making and academic input is informal. International engagement is intense, spanning UN processes, multilateral declarations and bilateral government-to-government AI frameworks.
Enforcement Level: AI rules are backed mainly by general-law penalties and supervisory expectations, with no published AI-specific enforcement decision and a federal AI authority that has not used compliance powers.
Specific Laws: UAE National AI Strategy 2031 (2017), Federal Decree-Law No. 45 of 2021 on the Protection of Personal Data (PDPL), UAE Charter for the Development and Use of Artificial Intelligence (2024), Abu Dhabi Law No. 3 of 2024 establishing the Abu Dhabi Artificial Intelligence and Advanced Technology Council, DIFC Data Protection Regulations Regulation 10 (2023, enforceable January 2026), National Elections Committee Policy on the Use of Artificial Intelligence (2025), Federal Decree-Law No. 26 of 2025 on Child Digital Safety, National AI System Cabinet integration decision (2026), CBUAE Guidance Note on Consumer Protection and the Responsible Adoption and Use of Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning by Licensed Financial Institutions (2026), Cabinet federal governance framework for the Agentic AI Project (2026), Federal Authority for Artificial Intelligence and Data establishment decision (2026)

Regulation Status: The United Kingdom has no horizontal AI statute: the Artificial Intelligence (Regulation) Bill [HL] fell at the end of the 2024-26 session on 30 April 2026, and the Regulating for Growth Bill announced in the May 2026 King's Speech creates sandbox powers rather than AI duties. Binding provisions written for AI sit inside data protection law—the Data (Use and Access) Act 2025 automated decision-making safeguards in UK GDPR Articles 22A-22D (in force 5 February 2026) and the Data Protection Act 2018 (Code of Practice on Artificial Intelligence and Automated Decision-Making) Regulations 2026, in force 12 May 2026, whose code has not yet been drafted. Sector regulators, including the Information Commission, Financial Conduct Authority, Ofcom and the Medicines and Healthcare products Regulatory Agency, apply existing law to AI under the Department for Science, Innovation and Technology framework.
Policy Lever: Policy runs on soft law and money: five cross-sector principles, the DSIT Blueprint for AI regulation, regulator AI strategies required of 19 regulators in January 2026, and funded programmes including AI Growth Zones, the sovereign AI programme and the advisory AI Growth Lab opened for legal services. The single AI-specific binding instrument, SI 2026/425, obliges the Information Commission to write an AI and automated decision-making code rather than imposing duties on developers.
Governance Type: Oversight is dispersed across statutorily independent sector regulators coordinating through the Digital Regulation Cooperation Forum and the DSIT central function, with no single AI authority. Parliamentary committees and ordinary courts supply episodic external scrutiny, and no AI rules are made by devolved or local bodies.
Actor Involvement: Industry input is structured through consultations, the AI Opportunities Action Plan and the AI Growth Lab, while civil society and academia contribute through consultations, select committee inquiries and research partnerships rather than standing roles. Internationally the UK signs and hosts AI governance processes selectively, with the Council of Europe convention signed but not ratified.
Enforcement Level: Enforcement touching AI runs entirely through general-law powers of sector regulators, with model-level monitoring concentrated in the non-enforcing AI Security Institute.
Specific Laws: Data (Use and Access) Act 2025, Data Protection Act 2018 (Code of Practice on Artificial Intelligence and Automated Decision-Making) Regulations 2026 (SI 2026/425), UK GDPR / Data Protection Act 2018, Online Safety Act 2023, A pro-innovation approach to AI regulation white paper (2023), DSIT Blueprint for AI regulation (2025), AI Opportunities Action Plan (2025), AI Growth Lab (2026), Regulating for Growth Bill (announced 2026)

Regulation Status: The United States has no comprehensive federal AI statute; the TAKE IT DOWN Act (2025) remains the only federal AI-specific law binding private actors, with platform notice-and-removal duties enforceable since 19 May 2026. Other federal AI-specific obligations are executive instruments binding agencies and contractors — Executive Order 14319 with OMB Memorandum M-26-04, OMB M-25-21 and M-25-22, Executive Order 14409 of 2 June 2026, and Executive Order 14434 of 29 September 2026 renaming AI as "Super Intelligence" and directing a legislative proposal. Executive Order 14365 and the March 2026 National Policy Framework push preemption of state AI laws, but Congress has enacted no preemption or comprehensive statute.
Policy Lever: Policy runs through a thin binding layer (TAKE IT DOWN Act, OMB procurement and use memoranda, NDAA defense AI provisions), a dense soft-law layer centred on the NIST AI Risk Management Framework and the Center for AI Standards and Innovation, and large funding programmes including the Genesis Mission and NAIRR. Federal AI procurement rules bind agencies and vendors, but no federal regulatory sandbox is operating.
Governance Type: Governance is highly fragmented: federal agencies act in parallel under their own authorities while more than 45 states legislate independently, and the executive contests the Texas, California, Colorado and Connecticut regimes through the DOJ AI Litigation Task Force. Coordination is executive-led via OSTP and the Chief AI Officer Council, and litigation over state statutes makes courts central.
Actor Involvement: Industry has the deepest structured access through standards work, procurement engagement and the voluntary frontier-model framework under Executive Order 14409; civil society and academia contribute mainly through public comment and research programmes. Internationally the country is active in standards bodies and bilateral agreements but avoids binding multilateral instruments.
Enforcement Level: Enforcement is real but narrow: the FTC polices TAKE IT DOWN Act removal duties and uses general consumer-protection powers against deceptive AI claims, while state attorneys general enforce state AI statutes.
Specific Laws: TAKE IT DOWN Act (2025), Executive Order 14179 Removing Barriers to American Leadership in Artificial Intelligence (2025), America's AI Action Plan (2025), Executive Order 14319 Preventing Woke AI in the Federal Government (2025), Executive Order 14365 Ensuring a National Policy Framework for Artificial Intelligence (2025), Executive Order on the Genesis Mission (2025), Executive Order 14409 Promoting Advanced Artificial Intelligence Innovation and Security (2026), Executive Order 14434 Inaugurating the Era of Super Intelligence (2026), National Policy Framework for Artificial Intelligence (2026), OMB Memorandum M-25-21 (2025), OMB Memorandum M-25-22 (2025), OMB Memorandum M-26-04 Increasing Public Trust in Artificial Intelligence Through Unbiased AI Principles (2025), National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2026 (P.L. 119-60) artificial intelligence provisions (2025), NIST AI Risk Management Framework (2023), Texas Responsible Artificial Intelligence Governance Act (2025), California SB 53 Transparency in Frontier Artificial Intelligence Act (2025), Colorado SB 26-189 (2026), Connecticut Artificial Intelligence Responsibility and Transparency Act (2026)

Regulation Status: Uruguay has no comprehensive AI statute: Articles 74 and 75 of Law 20.212 (2023) oblige Agesic to design a national data and AI strategy, and Decreto 276/025 of December 2025 sets a governance scheme with impact assessments, time limits and supervision for controlled testing environments and data spaces used for data and AI projects. Agesic told the Senate in June 2025 it was preparing an AI bill with a strong rights component, but the Executive confirmed in March 2026 that it would not be sent, and no bill is before Parliament. The Council of Europe Framework Convention on Artificial Intelligence, signed in September 2025, remains unratified, and AI processing of personal data falls under Law 18.331 (2008), which contains no AI-specific provision.
Policy Lever: Policy is delivered through Agesic's statutory strategy mandate, soft-law strategies and recommendations, and funding instruments: the Uruguay Innova controlled testing environments launched with MIEM, Agesic, ANII and URCDP, and the Instituto Vidart national AI centre. Binding levers remain confined to Decreto 276/025 and general data protection law.
Governance Type: Governance is national and centralized on Agesic, which coordinates formally through the Public Sector Strategic Committee for AI and Data and the interinstitutional committee evaluating controlled testing environments. Departmental governments play no part, and external checks run only through data protection complaints and ordinary courts.
Actor Involvement: Participation is strongest internationally, through signature of the Council of Europe Framework Convention, the UNESCO Recommendation on the Ethics of AI, OECD AI work and the Montevideo Declaration. Domestic industry, civil society and academia are consulted and can apply to the sandbox and the Instituto Vidart, but hold no standing formal roles.
Enforcement Level: Enforcement of AI obligations is not operational, with supervision confined to projects admitted to controlled testing environments and sanctions available only through the general data protection regime.
Specific Laws: Law 18.331 Personal Data Protection Law (2008), Law 20.212 Articles 74 and 75 (2023), Decreto 276/025 regulating controlled testing environments and data spaces for data and artificial intelligence (2025), National Artificial Intelligence Strategy 2024-2030, Agesic AI Regulatory Recommendations (2024), Agesic guideline on controlled testing environments (2026), Council of Europe Framework Convention on Artificial Intelligence and Human Rights, Democracy and the Rule of Law (signed September 2025), Artificial Intelligence Strategy for Digital Government (2020)

Regulation Status: Uzbekistan regulates AI through Law No. ZRU-1115 of 21 January 2026, which defines artificial intelligence, bars legally significant decisions taken solely by AI, requires labelling of AI-generated content and adds fines for unlawful AI-based personal data processing, and through the Ethical Rules for the Creation, Implementation and Use of AI-Based Solutions (Order No. 3787, registered 14 March 2026, in force 17 June 2026), binding every developer, implementer and user in any sector. The framework is horizontal and principle-based rather than risk-tiered, with no high-risk classification, conformity assessment or registration regime. National AI standards promised by the Strategy for the Development of Artificial Intelligence Technologies until 2030 remain unissued.
Policy Lever: Policy rests on one horizontal binding law, a binding ministerial ethics order, and development instruments: Cabinet Resolution No. 425 on priority AI projects, Decree PF-189 on AI procurement, GPU purchasing and investment allowances, and PP-320's $100 million allocation. An AI regulatory sandbox remains at the design stage under a UNDP framework guide, and the Enterprise Uzbekistan special legal regime covering AI and regulatory testing, enacted by constitutional law in August 2026, takes effect on 21 January 2027.
Governance Type: AI governance is centralised in the Ministry of Digital Technologies, which drafts legislation and issued the Ethical Rules, with Uzkomnazorat as supervisory inspectorate and the Coordination Commission for the Digital Uzbekistan 2030 Strategy handling inter-agency coordination. The unitary structure leaves no sub-national regulatory role, and judicial or ombudsman scrutiny of AI decisions has not materialised.
Actor Involvement: Participation runs through state-convened structures: the Artificial Intelligence Alliance, ministerial consultations on Law No. ZRU-1115, and expert input from the AI and Digital Economy research centre. Internationally Uzbekistan works with UNESCO, including preparations for an international expert forum on AI ethics, and with UNDP, while independent domestic civil society has no standing role.
Enforcement Level: Penalties reach only unlawful AI-based personal data processing, Uzkomnazorat supervises under its general informatisation remit, and no AI-specific enforcement decision or audit programme has been published since the rules took effect.
Specific Laws: Strategy for the Development of Artificial Intelligence Technologies until 2030 (PP-358, 2024), Law on Amendments and Supplements to Certain Laws in Connection with Artificial Intelligence Regulation No. ZRU-1115 (2026), Ethical Rules for the Creation, Implementation and Use of Artificial Intelligence-Based Solutions No. 3787 (2026), Presidential Decree No. PF-189 on Additional Measures for the Further Development of Artificial Intelligence Technologies (2025), Presidential Resolution No. PP-320 on Additional Measures to Support Artificial Intelligence Projects (2025), Cabinet of Ministers Resolution No. 425 on Priority Projects in the Field of Artificial Intelligence Technologies in 2025-2026 (2025), Constitutional Law on the International Centre for Digital Technologies Enterprise Uzbekistan (2026), Law on Informatisation (as amended), Law on Personal Data (as amended by Law No. ZRU-1125, 2026)

Regulation Status: Vanuatu regulates AI through general digital law rather than a dedicated AI instrument: the Digital Transformation Act No. 42 of 2025 lists artificial intelligence and AI-related data services as a permit category and tasks the Department of Communications and Digital Transformation with developing AI frameworks, while the Data Protection and Privacy Act No. 13 of 2024 grants a right not to be subject to solely automated decision-making. Coverage stops at licensing and data protection, with no transparency, high-risk or conformity obligations. Implementing permit regulations, guidance and an operational enforcement body are absent.
Policy Lever: Levers are general digital-governance instruments plus regional principles: permits and penalties under the Digital Transformation Act No. 42 of 2025, data protection limits on automated decisions, and ethical-AI aspirations in the ICT Policy 2025. There is no AI funding scheme, sandbox, procurement rule or resourced AI unit.
Governance Type: Authority is concentrated in the Department of Communications and Digital Transformation, with the Telecommunications and Radiocommunications Regulator covering telecoms and the Digital Safety Authority established on paper under Act No. 15 of 2024 but not yet operating. The statutory National Digital Transformation Steering Committee provides cross-government coordination, while provinces, courts and the Ombudsman play no part in shaping AI rules.
Actor Involvement: Engagement is government-led, with industry input through ICT and digital legislation consultations and forum sessions, and universities and community groups appearing only as event participants. Vanuatu's most substantive AI activity is regional: it backed the Pacific Digital and Artificial Intelligence Technology Principles and argued for enforceable, consent-based protection of Pacific traditional knowledge used in AI systems.
Enforcement Level: Penalties attach to the AI permit category and to data protection breaches, but no AI enforcement action, audit or monitoring has occurred and no resourced authority exercises the powers.
Specific Laws: Digital Transformation Act No. 42 of 2025, Data Protection and Privacy Act No. 13 of 2024, Digital Safety Authority Act No. 15 of 2024, ICT Policy 2025, National Cyber Security Strategy 2030, Pacific Digital and Artificial Intelligence Technology Principles (2026, endorsed)

Regulation Status: Vatican City State regulates AI through a single dedicated binding instrument, Decree No. DCCII of the Pontifical Commission for Vatican City State, adopted 16 December 2024 and in force since 1 January 2025, which sets principles of human dignity, transparency and data protection, prohibits discriminatory, manipulative and dignity-violating uses, attributes authorship of AI-generated content to the Governorate, and creates an internal AI Commission. Coverage is institutional rather than horizontal: it binds State bodies, not the Roman Curia or private operators, and the announced follow-up laws and implementing regulations remain absent from the Governorate's published legislation. The new Fundamental Law of Vatican City State of 31 July 2026 contains no AI provisions, and the encyclical Magnifica Humanitas (2026) carries doctrinal rather than civil-law force.
Policy Lever: The lever mix is one binding decree combined with a dense body of ethical and doctrinal soft law, namely the Rome Call for AI Ethics, Antiqua et Nova and the encyclical Magnifica Humanitas. No economic instruments exist, and institutional capacity rests on two thinly staffed commissions, one inside the Governorate and one spanning several curial bodies.
Governance Type: Authority is concentrated in the Pontifical Commission for Vatican City State and its Governorate, with an internal AI Commission chaired by the Secretary General drawing on the legal, telecommunications and security offices. Coordination across the Holy See runs through the Interdicasterial Commission on Artificial Intelligence created in May 2026, while no subnational layer and no independent judicial or ombudsman review of AI exists.
Actor Involvement: Participation is internally clerical and externally diplomatic: the Pontifical Academies hold standing advisory roles, companies engage by signing the Rome Call for AI Ethics, and the Holy See speaks on AI at the United Nations, UNESCO and the G7. Domestic civil society has no entry into the closed legislative process, and the Vatican does not sit in treaty-based technical standards bodies.
Enforcement Level: Prohibitions exist on paper under Decree No. DCCII, but no penalties are defined, the Governorate's AI Commission has published no decisions or monitoring reports, and oversight amounts to internal vetting of AI experimentation.
Specific Laws: Guidelines on Artificial Intelligence – Decree No. DCCII of the Pontifical Commission for Vatican City State (2024, in force 2025), Rome Call for AI Ethics (2020), Antiqua et Nova – Doctrinal Note on Artificial Intelligence (2025), Magnifica Humanitas – Encyclical Letter of Pope Leo XIV on Safeguarding the Human Person in the Time of Artificial Intelligence (2026), Interdicasterial Commission on Artificial Intelligence – Rescript of Cardinal Michael Czerny (2026)

Regulation Status: Venezuela's AI framework consists of a pending bill and executive soft instruments: the Proyecto de Ley para el Desarrollo y Uso Ético de la Inteligencia Artificial cleared first discussion on 19 November 2024 and sits in the Plan Básico Legislativo 2026-2027 awaiting second discussion, while the Ministry of Science and Technology issued the Código de Ética para el Desarrollo y Aplicación Responsable de la Inteligencia Artificial on 19 February 2026 with nine non-binding principles. The Plan Nacional de Inteligencia Artificial 2025-2031, presented on 27 October 2026, projects a national AI institute as regulator. Binding obligations on AI systems exist in no sector.
Policy Lever: Policy operates through executive soft instruments: the Código de Ética (2026) and the Plan Nacional de Inteligencia Artificial 2025-2031 built on talent formation, sovereign compute, open data and regional AI cooperation. Delivery rests with a MINCYT directorate without legal powers, and no funded scheme, regulatory sandbox or AI procurement rule has been published.
Governance Type: AI governance is concentrated in the national executive, with MINCYT as sole rector and the National Assembly's Comisión Permanente de Educación, Salud, Ciencia, Tecnología e Innovación handling the pending bill. Sub-national authorities and independent review bodies play no part.
Actor Involvement: Participation is government-led and outward-facing: ministers present the Plan Nacional de Inteligencia Artificial at UNESCO, WSIS and ALBA fora, while domestic input from industry, civil society and universities stays at announced consultation, training and beneficiary status. No standing advisory body gives non-state actors a formal seat.
Enforcement Level: Nothing is enforced because no AI obligation is legally binding and no authority holds an AI supervisory mandate.
Specific Laws: Proyecto de Ley de Inteligencia Artificial / Proyecto de Ley para el Desarrollo y Uso Ético de la Inteligencia Artificial (2024, approved in first discussion 19 November 2024, pending second discussion), Código de Ética para el Desarrollo y Aplicación Responsable de la Inteligencia Artificial (2026), Plan Nacional de Inteligencia Artificial 2025-2031 (2026), Plan Básico Legislativo 2026-2027 (2026), Ley de Infogobierno (2013), Special Law Against Cybercrimes (2001)

Regulation Status: Vietnam governs AI through the standalone Law on Artificial Intelligence No. 134/2025/QH15, in force since 1 March 2026, which sets three risk tiers, prohibited practices, deepfake labelling and transparency duties, and notification of medium- and high-risk systems. Implementing detail came with Decree No. 142/2026/ND-CP (1 May 2026) and the Prime Minister's high-risk list in Decision No. 33/2026/QD-TTg (15 August 2026) covering 46 system types in six sectors, and the national AI portal ai.dda.gov.vn opened on 28 August 2026. Compliance for systems already operating is phased to 1 March 2027 generally and 1 September 2027 in healthcare, education and finance, and the administrative-sanctions decree remains outstanding.
Policy Lever: Vietnam pairs binding instruments (Law No. 134/2025/QH15, Decree No. 142/2026/ND-CP, Decision No. 33/2026/QD-TTg) with soft law in Circular No. 05/2026/TT-BKHCN on the National AI Ethics Framework and Decision No. 1290/QD-BKHCN on responsible AI research. The Ministry of Science and Technology is the lead institution, operating the one-stop AI portal, self-declaration registration, a controlled sandbox announced in October 2026, and a National AI Development Fund for 2026-2027, with the fine schedule still pending.
Governance Type: AI governance is concentrated in the Ministry of Science and Technology, with sectoral ministries applying the Decision 33 high-risk list in health, education, finance and transport and provincial People's Committees executing tasks assigned by Decision No. 367/QD-TTg. Coordination is formalised through that implementation plan and a Prime Minister-chaired national AI committee, and no independent body or court shapes AI rules.
Actor Involvement: Policy-making is state-led, with formal consultation on the draft AI Law and implementing decree attracting domestic and foreign industry submissions and academic input, while independent civil society has no structured role. Internationally Vietnam is active through ASEAN, hosting the ASEAN Law Forum 2026 on AI in Hanoi, UNESCO ethics implementation, and bilateral cooperation with China, Japan and South Korea.
Enforcement Level: The AI Law provides suspension, recall and liability tools and statutory fine ceilings, but the detailed administrative penalty decree is pending and no AI-specific enforcement decision has been published while transition deadlines run into 2027.
Specific Laws: Law on Artificial Intelligence No. 134/2025/QH15 (2025), Decree No. 142/2026/ND-CP (2026), Decision No. 33/2026/QD-TTg on the list of high-risk AI systems (2026), Circular No. 05/2026/TT-BKHCN on the National AI Ethics Framework (2026), Decision No. 367/QD-TTg on the plan for implementation of the Law on Artificial Intelligence (2026), Decision No. 1671/QD-TTg approving the National Strategy on Artificial Intelligence to 2030, vision to 2045 (2026), Decision No. 1290/QD-BKHCN on responsible AI research and development guidelines (2024), Law on Digital Technology Industry No. 71/2025/QH15 (2025), Decree No. 353/2025/ND-CP on digital technology sandbox (2025), Decree No. 330/2026/ND-CP on administrative penalties in cybersecurity and personal data protection (2026)

Regulation Status: Yemen has no AI-specific law, draft bill or regulator, and neither the internationally recognised government in Aden nor the de facto authority in Sana'a has published an AI framework. Digital policy remains confined to the National Cybersecurity Strategy approved in January 2023, the Strategic Orientation towards Digital Transformation Project launched by the Ministry of Communications and Information Technology in March 2025, and a still-unenacted draft law on combating information technology crimes, none of which addresses AI. Armed conflict and parallel ministries keep AI entirely unregulated.
Policy Lever: Yemen operates no AI policy levers: no binding rules, published guidance, funding, procurement conditions or sandbox, and no public body with an AI remit. AI-adjacent public activity is confined to civil-service training courses and donor-supported digital transformation projects.
Governance Type: AI governance structures are absent, with the ministry that would normally lead digital policy duplicated between the Aden government and the Sana'a authority. Governorates, courts and independent review mechanisms play no part in AI oversight.
Actor Involvement: Structured domestic engagement in AI policy is absent; the main multi-stakeholder event was the academically organised Yemen AI Summit in Sana'a in June 2026, which drew around 400 academics, private-sector participants and officials and announced a Yemeni Artificial Intelligence Association. International participation consists of attendance at summits and UN-convened workshops rather than treaty or standards work.
Enforcement Level: AI enforcement does not exist anywhere in the country, with no penalties, authority, actions or monitoring in place.

Regulation Status: Zambia's AI framework rests on the non-binding National Artificial Intelligence Strategy 2024-2026, launched by the Ministry of Technology and Science in November 2024, which calls for a National AI Policy, a National AI Council and technical working groups. Cabinet approved in principle in April 2025 a Bill to repeal and replace the Data Protection Act No. 3 of 2021 and extend it to artificial intelligence, machine learning and data analytics, and the National Assembly passed a motion on 25 June 2025 urging a legal framework for AI, but no AI bill has been tabled. AI-related conduct is reached only through the Data Protection Act No. 3 of 2021, the Cyber Security Act No. 3 of 2025 and the Cyber Crimes Act No. 4 of 2025, which contain no AI-specific provisions.
Policy Lever: Policy action consists of a non-binding national strategy, its planned advisory structures and partner-supported programmes such as the National AI Data Centre initiative and public-sector AI training run with Huawei. No AI-specific binding instrument, published regulatory guidance, AI procurement rule or AI-dedicated sandbox is in operation.
Governance Type: AI governance is centralized in the Ministry of Technology and Science, with the Smart Zambia Institute coordinating government adoption and ZICTA, the Office of the Data Protection Commissioner and the Zambia Cyber Security Agency applying general technology law. The coordination bodies promised by the strategy remain on paper, sub-national authorities have no role, and no judicial or independent review has touched AI.
Actor Involvement: Government-convened consultations draw industry, academia, civil society, youth and development partners into strategy and readiness-assessment work, but none of these actors holds a standing formal role. International engagement runs through UNESCO, the African Union Continental Artificial Intelligence Strategy and the Smart Africa Alliance rather than binding AI instruments.
Enforcement Level: No AI-specific obligation, sanction or enforcement decision exists, and oversight is limited to general data protection and cyber security regulators plus the one-off UNESCO readiness assessment.
Specific Laws: National Artificial Intelligence Strategy 2024-2026 (launched November 2024), Data Protection Act No. 3 of 2021, Cyber Security Act No. 3 of 2025, Cyber Crimes Act No. 4 of 2025, National ICT Policy (2023)

Regulation Status: Zimbabwe governs AI through the non-binding National Artificial Intelligence Strategy 2026-2030, approved by Cabinet in October 2025 and launched by President Mnangagwa at the New Parliament Building on 13 March 2026. The strategy's governance pillar promises a National AI Act with a risk-based framework and national AI technical standards; no AI bill has been drafted or tabled. Binding obligations touching AI come only from the Cyber and Data Protection Act [Chapter 12:07] and Statutory Instrument 155 of 2024, which address personal data generally.
Policy Lever: Policy rests on one soft-law instrument, the National Artificial Intelligence Strategy 2026-2030, supplemented by data-protection law; flagship economic initiatives including Project Pangolin, the Innovation Crucible sandbox and the Mugove/Umqele/Isabelo fund are announced rather than funded and operating, and the AI4I Grand Challenge held in Mutare from 27 July to 1 August 2026 was a one-off innovation competition. Institutional capacity is limited to ministry-led coordination bodies that lack statutory AI mandates.
Governance Type: AI governance is centralised in the Ministry of Information Communication Technology, Postal and Courier Services, with POTRAZ acting as data protection authority and hosting the strategy's Steering Committee, and the National Digital Regulatory Committee named as prospective AI regulator under presidential chairmanship. Subnational and independent-review roles are absent, and the coordination architecture exists on paper rather than in statute.
Actor Involvement: Industry, civil society, academia, diaspora representatives and development partners fed into the 2025 workshops that produced the strategy, but participation is episodic rather than institutionalised. International engagement runs through UNESCO readiness assessment support, United Nations partnership and African Union and SADC processes.
Enforcement Level: Enforcement touching AI operates solely through POTRAZ's data protection mandate, whose mandatory controller inspections started on 1 September 2026, with no AI-specific penalties, decisions or audits.
Specific Laws: National Artificial Intelligence Strategy 2026-2030 (2026), Cyber and Data Protection Act [Chapter 12:07] (2021), Cyber and Data Protection (Licensing of Data Controllers and Appointment of Data Protection Officers) Regulations, Statutory Instrument 155 of 2024 (2024), POTRAZ Regulatory Notice 2 of 2026 (2026), Postal and Telecommunications Act [Chapter 12:05]
